articles.title: AMD’s Venice-X maxes out family at 5.3 GHz, returning 3D V-Cache to data center after four years — chips target HPC workloads with PCIe 6.0 and 1.6 TB/s memory bandwidth
articles.text:
AMD’s Venice-X maxes out family at 5.3 GHz, returning 3D V-Cache to data center after four years — chips target HPC workloads with PCIe 6.0 and 1.6 TB/s memory bandwidth
Venice-X maxes out the family's frequency for the first time.
AMD missed out on deploying Turin-X CPUs in the previous generation, giving its 3D V-Cache tech a four-year hiatus from the data center following the launch of Genoa-X in 2023. In the second half of next year, 3D V-Cache is coming back for HPC with Venice-X, matching the 96 cores and 1,152 MB of L3 cache available on the EPYC 9684X (Genoa-X), but with vastly higher clock speeds, PCIe 6.0, and nearly four times the per-socket memory bandwidth.
After first bringing hybrid bonding to EPYC processors with Milan-X in 2022, AMD followed up a little over a year later with Genoa-X. Turin came and went without a chip sporting stacked SRAM, but now, it’s back with Venice-X. The critical change this time around doesn’t come from big jumps in core count — and consequently cache — as is the case with the standard SP7 lineup. Rather, it’s the 5.3 GHz boost clock speed, another pillar of Venice broadly, that’s particularly beneficial in the HPC workloads Venice-X targets.
| AMD EPYC -X Chips |  |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SKU | Family | Cores / Threads | Base / Boost Clock (GHz) | L3 Cache | TDP | 
| EPYC 7773X | Milan-X | 64 / 128 | 2.2 / 3.5 | 768 MB | 280 W | 
| EPYC 9684X | Genoa-X | 96 / 192 | 2.55 / 3.7 | 1,152 MB | 400 W | 
| EPYC 9006X (SKU unknown) | Venice-X | 96 / 192 | X.X / 5.3 | 1,152 MB | Unknown (likely 400 to 600 W) | 
As you can see from the top EPYC -X chips from previous generations, boost clocks were significantly lower for the X chips, and higher frequencies were available within the standard chips from each family. Milan scaled up to 4.1 GHz, while Genoa could climb to 4.4 GHz, just not on the EPYC -X chips. Venice-X brings up to the maximum 5.3 GHz boost clock available across the range, unifying a high frequency with a large pool of bonded L3 for HPC workloads.
There are still details missing about Venice-X, including the base frequency, how many SKUs are in the lineup and what their specs are, and the TDP (though the 400 to 600 W range available to other Venice CPUs is likely). The chips appear to use the SP7 socket, however, keeping with previous EPYC -X chips.
The platform comes with 96 PCIe 6.0 lanes, while the smaller SP8 platform targeting enterprises trades memory channels for PCIe lanes. Venice-X comes with the full 16-channel memory setup available on SP7, including support for MRDIMMs at 12,800 MT/s that can drive the quoted 1.6 TB/s of per-socket memory bandwidth.
The critical marriage with Venice-X for HPC workloads, according to AMD, is high frequency with a large pool of stacked cache. AMD currently maintains both 3D V-Cache and high-frequency EPYC chips in its HPC fleet to run its internal EDA workloads. AMD Fellow Phil Steinke says the company runs performance analysis on these workloads to characterize performance, optimize EPYC designs, and push partners to optimize their software.
The biggest consumer on the HPC fleet by far are function verification workloads at over half of AMD's used compute, according to Steinke. These are logic simulations that show up in tools like Cadence Xcelium, and Steinke says the EPYC team is running these workloads “24 x 7 x 365.”
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
An example of one such workload is above, measuring IPC with AMD's uProf monitoring utility. With 3D V-Cache, AMD says this workload completes 40% faster at around double the instructions per clock. AMD didn't clarify which chips it was comparing or what application it was using. However, the comparison is between an EPYC fleet with and without 3D V-Cache.
Steinke says AMD is able to now move toward a single chip with Venice-X, maintaining the cache advantages in workloads like functional verification while driving the EDA workloads more sensitive to frequency. "I mentioned we have a mix of high frequency and 3D V-Cache CPUs in our data center, and that's because through Milan and Genoa, the high frequency parts were always a little higher on the frequency side," Steinke said. "You don't have that dichotomy [with Venice-X]. You can get the best of both worlds in a single CPU, and this is what we're really excited to be picking up for our own use."
AMD hasn't shared any benchmarks for Venice-X yet, but it provided some more specific HPC benchmarks comparing its high-frequency EPYC 9686F to Intel's Xeon 6980P in several HPC workloads, such as computational fluid dynamics. In AMD's testing, the 9686F was 1.6x faster in these benchmarks while running 32 fewer cores.
We had a chance to test the EPYC 9686F along with the dense EPYC 9996, which you can read more about in our Zen 6 EPYC Venice deep dive and benchmarking article. And indeed, the EPYC 9686F looks very impressive in some of the HPC workloads we ran.
We were only able to test a 2P configuration, and as evidenced by the sole Xeon 6980P, CloverLeaf is sensitive to latency. Even then, the 2P EPYC 9686F completed the complex hydrodynamics simulation in about a third of the time as a single Xeon 6980P.
AMD says it's currently using MEXT, its AI-driven flash-as-DRAM technology, to bolster the amount of memory available for its EDA workloads. When it deploys Venice-X, Steinke says the company will continue using MEXT, which you can read more about in our recent MEXT breakdown on Tom's Hardware Premium.
Venice-X CPUs are launching in the second half of 2027, while SP7 and SP8 Venice CPUs are rolling out now. Also coming in the second half of next year is AMD's Verano, which it's pitching as an AI host node that leverages SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X memory.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: Test ASUS ROG Gjallar : une petite barre pour un gros son, pas sans compromis
articles.text:
Avec le ROG Gjallar, ASUS ne se contente pas de poser une barre de son sous un moniteur. Dolby Atmos, caisson sans fil, HDMI 2.1, Control Hub et nombreux réglages : l’ensemble veut devenir le véritable centre audio d’une configuration gaming. Une proposition séduisante et particulièrement compacte, mais facturée près de 600 euros.
Sur un bureau, le choix entre une paire d’enceintes, un kit 2.1 et un casque dépend généralement autant de l’espace disponible que des performances recherchées. ASUS tente ici une autre approche avec le ROG Gjallar, une barre de son 2.1.2 pensée avant tout pour accompagner un PC et, éventuellement, plusieurs consoles.
Sur le papier, la proposition est particulièrement complète. La barre associe plusieurs transducteurs frontaux à deux canaux orientés vers le haut, tandis qu’un caisson de 6,5 pouces connecté sans fil prend en charge les basses fréquences. Dolby Atmos, HDMI 2.1 avec eARC, USB-C, Bluetooth 5.3, entrée optique et auxiliaire complètent l’ensemble. ASUS ajoute enfin un Control Hub déporté, équipé d’un écran et de microphones. Autant d’éléments qui permettent au Gjallar de se distinguer assez clairement d’une simple paire d’enceintes de bureau. Cela est-il suffisant pour justifier un tarif avoisinant les 600 euros ?
- Format particulièrement compact
- Caisson sans fil efficace et facile à intégrer
- Son généreux et propre, même à bon volume
- Excellente connectique
- Control Hub réussi et Gear Link qui complète
- Très convaincant pour les jeux solo immersifs
- Finitions perfectibles pour cette gamme tarifaire
- Scène stéréo moins large qu’avec de bonnes enceintes séparées
- Grave un peu trop présent / Voix parfois en retrait
- Atmos plus enveloppant que réellement tridimensionnel
- Micro peu adapté au jeu compétitif ou coopératif
- Prix très élevé
Compact, bien pensé… mais pas irréprochable à ce prix
La première bonne surprise vient du format. Avec un peu plus de 60 cm de largeur, le Gjallar est nettement plus compact que ce que ses ambitions pourraient laisser imaginer. Il trouve facilement sa place sous un moniteur et ne vient pas empiéter exagérément sur l’espace disponible sur le bureau. ASUS a également réussi à conserver une hauteur suffisamment contenue pour qu’il ne masque pas le bas de l’écran dans une installation classique.
Le constat est similaire pour le caisson de basses. Avec seulement 12,5 cm de largeur, il se glisse facilement sous un bureau ou contre un meuble. Sa liaison sans fil limite par ailleurs les contraintes de câblage. Durant notre essai, la connexion s’est montrée parfaitement stable. Seul petit détail : après l’allumage de la barre, le caisson demande parfois trois ou quatre secondes supplémentaires avant de se mettre en marche.
Le design reste identifiable comme un produit ROG, notamment grâce à la bande RGB qui traverse la grille frontale, mais ASUS évite heureusement d’en faire trop. Le Gjallar peut ainsi trouver sa place dans un environnement moins typé gaming, y compris dans un petit salon. L’éclairage apporte surtout une petite touche esthétique supplémentaire ; il ne change évidemment rien à l’expérience une fois concentré sur un jeu.
Les finitions nous laissent en revanche un peu plus circonspects compte tenu du tarif demandé. La grille métallique inspire confiance et fait plutôt bonne impression, mais certains plastiques, notamment aux extrémités et à l’arrière de la barre, apparaissent plus quelconques. Rien de rédhibitoire, et l’assemblage reste sérieux, mais on pouvait attendre un niveau de finition plus homogène sur un produit vendu près de 600 euros.
Le Control Hub fait une vraie différence
Le petit boîtier livré avec le Gjallar pourrait passer pour un accessoire supplémentaire destiné à remplir la fiche technique. À l’usage, c’est pourtant l’un des éléments les plus réussis du produit.
Installé à portée de main sur un bureau, le Control Hub rappelle presque une petite interface de mixage. Son écran est lisible, les différents boutons tombent bien sous la main et surtout, sa grande molette centrale est particulièrement agréable à utiliser. Elle permet de modifier rapidement le volume et une pression suffit notamment à couper le son.
Les commandes donnent accès aux fonctions dont on a réellement besoin au quotidien : changement de source, profils audio, lecture ou encore gestion de l’éclairage RGB. Le Control Hub participe clairement à rendre l’expérience plus premium. Son intérêt est toutefois beaucoup plus évident sur un bureau que dans une installation de salon. À proximité du clavier et de la souris, il devient presque une extension naturelle de la barre. À plusieurs mètres du téléviseur, sa pertinence est forcément plus limitée.
ASUS complète l’ensemble avec Gear Link, accessible sur PC mais également via une application mobile. L’outil ne remplace pas le Control Hub : il vient plutôt combler ce qui aurait difficilement pu être intégré dans une interface matérielle aussi compacte.
On y retrouve notamment un égaliseur complet, la gestion des profils, les réglages détaillés du RGB, la luminosité et les animations de l’écran du Control Hub, le délai avant mise en veille ou encore différents paramètres relatifs au microphone. Il est également possible de réaffecter certaines fonctions du bouton Aura.
Gear Link n’est donc pas indispensable au quotidien, mais il apporte suffisamment de possibilités pour mériter que l’on s’y attarde lors de la première configuration.
Un regret subsiste néanmoins : le niveau du caisson aurait mérité d’être directement réglable depuis le Control Hub. C’est exactement le genre de commande que l’on peut vouloir ajuster rapidement selon que l’on écoute de la musique, que l’on joue ou que l’on regarde un film.
Une connectique taillée pour devenir le centre du bureau
C’est probablement sur ce point que le ROG Gjallar se distingue le plus clairement d’un système d’enceintes traditionnel.
USB-C, HDMI 2.1 avec eARC, optique, entrée auxiliaire et Bluetooth 5.3 permettent de connecter plusieurs sources sans avoir à jongler constamment avec les câbles. ASUS prévoit aussi explicitement l’utilisation avec PC, consoles et appareils mobiles.
Dans notre cas, le Gjallar a principalement été utilisé avec un PC relié en HDMI, mais aussi avec un smartphone en Bluetooth et différents ordinateurs portables connectés à notre moniteur. Le passage d’une source à l’autre s’effectue sans difficulté particulière et nous n’avons pas rencontré de problème de reconnaissance ou de connexion.
Tout le monde n’exploitera évidemment pas cette richesse. Un joueur uniquement équipé d’un PC n’aura probablement jamais besoin de la moitié des entrées disponibles. En revanche, pour quelqu’un qui souhaite connecter ordinateur, console et smartphone au même système audio, la proposition prend tout son sens.
C’est aussi ce qui différencie le Gjallar d’un bon kit stéréo ou 2.1 traditionnel : ASUS ne cherche pas seulement à produire du son, mais à simplifier toute l’installation qui l’entoure.
Un son généreux et un caisson qui fait la différence
À l’écoute, le Gjallar adopte une signature plutôt généreuse. Ce n’est pas un système que nous qualifierions de neutre ou d’analytique, mais ce n’est manifestement pas ce qu’ASUS recherche.
Le caisson participe largement au caractère de l’ensemble. Il descend suffisamment bas pour donner du poids aux impacts et aux ambiances sans systématiquement devenir envahissant. Sa présence constitue surtout une vraie différence face à de petites enceintes de bureau qui doivent composer avec les limites physiques de leurs haut-parleurs.
Comparé aux VULKKANO A5 ARC MKII, que nous avons testées récemment, le Gjallar apporte par exemple davantage d’impact dans le grave. Les enceintes VULKKANO conservent en revanche l’avantage sur la largeur de la scène stéréo, conséquence assez logique de deux enceintes pouvant être écartées de part et d’autre du moniteur. Notre précédent test relevait déjà le caractère généreux mais relativement limité dans l’espace des A5 ARC MKII.
C’est précisément pour cette raison qu’il serait hasardeux d’affirmer que le Gjallar est meilleur ou moins bon qu’un kit 2.1 de manière générale. Il ne joue simplement pas avec les mêmes contraintes.
La scène sonore dépasse légèrement les dimensions physiques de la barre, suffisamment pour éviter une restitution complètement étriquée, mais elle reste malgré tout assez centrée. Des enceintes correctement espacées conservent ici un avantage évident.
La propreté du signal est en revanche excellente. Nous n’avons constaté aucun souffle ou bruit de fond perceptible à courte distance, ce qui est particulièrement appréciable pour un produit destiné à être placé à quelques dizaines de centimètres de l’utilisateur.
La barre conserve également une bonne maîtrise lorsque le volume augmente. Sa réserve de puissance est même largement supérieure à ce dont on a besoin dans une utilisation classique sur bureau. À cette distance, mieux vaut rester raisonnable. Cette puissance devient en revanche intéressante lorsqu’il s’agit de diffuser de la musique dans une pièce ou d’utiliser le Gjallar depuis davantage de recul.
Gaming : le jeu immersif est clairement son terrain de prédilection
C’est finalement manette en main que la signature du Gjallar prend le plus de sens. Sur des jeux tels que Black Myth: Wukong ou Death Stranding, le caisson apporte une dimension plus physique aux environnements, aux impacts et aux effets sonores. La restitution est généreuse, ample et suffisamment dynamique pour renforcer l’immersion d’une façon qu’un casque reproduit difficilement de la même manière.
Ce n’est pas nécessairement mieux qu’un casque : c’est surtout une expérience différente. Là où le casque isole davantage et permet de placer précisément les différents éléments sonores, le Gjallar donne plus facilement l’impression que le jeu occupe réellement la pièce.
Le profil Gaming est d’ailleurs plutôt bien calibré pour cet usage. Le grave reste généreux, mais cette emphase nous dérange beaucoup moins dans un titre spectaculaire que lors d’une écoute musicale. Le Dolby Atmos participe lui aussi à cette sensation, mais il convient de tempérer les promesses associées aux deux canaux orientés vers le haut.
Vous cherchez plutôt un casque ? Découvrez notre test du ROG Kithara, sans doute l'un des casques gaming les plus aboutis de l'année.
Oui, la scène gagne en ampleur et le rendu apparaît plus enveloppant. Non, le Gjallar ne crée pas pour autant une véritable bulle sonore autour du joueur. Nous n’avons jamais réellement eu l’impression que des effets provenaient précisément du plafond ou de l’arrière de la position d’écoute. L’apport existe donc, mais il faut davantage le considérer comme une extension de la scène sonore que comme le substitut d’un véritable système multicanal.
La limite devient encore plus évidente sur les FPS compétitifs. Pour profiter d’un jeu solo immersif, la barre fait parfaitement sens. Pour déterminer précisément d’où provient un tir ou un déplacement adverse, un bon casque reste nettement préférable.
Cette remarque vaut également pour le jeu coopératif. Les microphones intégrés au Control Hub peuvent rendre service et Gear Link propose différents traitements destinés à améliorer la captation, notamment une réduction des bruits parasites et de l’écho. Mais l’expérience n’est pas suffisamment convaincante pour remplacer un casque-micro lors de longues sessions avec communication vocale.
Pour la musique, les limites deviennent plus audibles
Le Gjallar est plus facile à prendre en défaut lorsque l’on quitte le jeu vidéo pour revenir à une écoute musicale attentive.
Le mode Musique propose un équilibre globalement agréable, et les différents profils intégrés sont suffisamment pertinents pour que l’on puisse les utiliser sans immédiatement se jeter sur l’égaliseur manuel. Mais la restitution conserve cette tendance généreuse dans le bas du spectre.
Sur nos morceaux de référence, le grave peut ainsi prendre légèrement trop de place et les voix ne se détachent pas toujours aussi clairement que nous l’aurions souhaité. Elles apparaissent parfois un peu en retrait dans le mix.
Ce comportement n’est pas forcément gênant pour une écoute d’ambiance, mais devient plus perceptible lorsque l’on connaît précisément les enregistrements utilisés et que l’on cherche à juger la séparation des différents registres.
C’est là que le positionnement tarifaire du Gjallar devient plus délicat. À près de 600 euros, on peut trouver des ensembles stéréo ou 2.1 plus ambitieux sur le strict terrain acoustique, notamment en matière de largeur de scène, d’équilibre ou de finesse. Toutefois, aucun de ces critères ne résume à lui seul l’intérêt du produit ASUS.
Test Asus ROG Gjallar : l'avis de Clubic
ASUS n’a pas nécessairement conçu le meilleur système audio que l’on puisse acheter avec 600 euros. En revanche, le constructeur livre une solution particulièrement cohérente pour un bureau gaming : compacte, facile à installer, dotée d’un caisson lui aussi peu encombrant, généreuse dans le grave et suffisamment puissante pour dépasser largement le cadre de l’écoute en champ proche.
La connectique est excellente, le passage entre les sources fonctionne comme attendu et le Control Hub constitue une vraie réussite. Gear Link complète intelligemment l’ensemble avec suffisamment de réglages pour adapter le Gjallar à différents usages sans rendre le logiciel incontournable.
Quelques compromis subsistent néanmoins. La scène stéréo reste moins large que celle de bonnes enceintes séparées, la restitution musicale manque parfois d’équilibre, avec des voix légèrement en retrait et un grave un peu trop présent, et le Dolby Atmos apporte davantage d’ampleur qu’une véritable sensation de hauteur. Surtout, près de 600 euros restent difficiles à justifier. À ce tarif, la concurrence ne vient plus seulement des produits gaming mais également de systèmes audio capables d’aller plus loin en matière de restitution pure.
Le Gjallar devient en revanche beaucoup plus intéressant dès lors que l’on accorde une forte importance à la compacité, à la polyvalence et à la simplicité de l’installation. Et si son tarif venait à baisser sensiblement à l’occasion du Black Friday ou d’autres périodes promotionnelles, le compromis pourrait devenir séduisant.
- Format particulièrement compact
- Caisson sans fil efficace et facile à intégrer
- Son généreux et propre, même à bon volume
- Excellente connectique
- Control Hub réussi et Gear Link qui complète
- Très convaincant pour les jeux solo immersifs
- Finitions perfectibles pour cette gamme tarifaire
- Scène stéréo moins large qu’avec de bonnes enceintes séparées
- Grave un peu trop présent / Voix parfois en retrait
- Atmos plus enveloppant que réellement tridimensionnel
- Micro peu adapté au jeu compétitif ou coopératif
- Prix très élevé

articles.title: Google tests Tabletop, letting groups build planning tools with an AI agent - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Google tests Tabletop, letting groups build planning tools with an AI agent
Google LLC today began testing Tabletop, a Google Labs experiment in which groups share an online space and ask an artificial intelligence agent to build the planning tools they need.
In a blog post, Roman Nurik, design and engineering lead at Google Labs, wrote that coordinating a family trip or a potluck goes more smoothly when the whole group can pitch in from one place. Whoever sets up a space adds the links, files and ideas the group has collected, and from there a request to @tabletop produces the tool.
Tools Google lists include itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters and tournament brackets, and there is a set of starter templates that Tabletop users can access as well. Once the space is shared through an invite link posted in the group’s existing chat, everyone can work on those tools at the same time, “like in a Google Doc,” Nurik wrote.
When a guest at an office party in one of Google’s demos ends up seated next to the boss, a request to @tabletop turns the seating chart into one where name badges can be dragged between tables. Any tool can be reworked the same way, according to the Tabletop site.
Google did not say which of its models run Tabletop. When Labs released its Disco browser experiment last December, Gemini 3 was the model it used to turn a person’s open tabs into small web apps.
Tabletop also follows Google’s move in September to let up to six members of a household share the division’s CC agent. Rival OpenAI Group PBC added group chats to ChatGPT a year ago, and up to 20 people can now talk to the chatbot in one thread.
In ChatGPT the chatbot sits inside the conversation as one more member, and OpenAI said at launch that it had taught the model to judge when to join in. Replies in those chats initially came from GPT-5.1 Auto, which chooses a model based on the prompt and on the subscription of whoever ChatGPT is answering. OpenAI also kept personal memory out of group chats entirely.
Tabletop is limited for now to U.S. users 18 and older who sign up through the waitlist at tabletop.google, with Google saying it will let more people in each week. Google’s announcement does not mention pricing or a release outside the U.S.

articles.title: El MIT desarrolló un sistema que permite a los robots entender la intención detrás de una orden: cómo funciona
articles.text:
Los ingenieros del Instituto Tecnológico de Massachusetts (MIT) desarrollaron FLEX, una plataforma que permite a los robots interpretar la intención detrás de órdenes conversacionales y ajustar sus movimientos sin que las personas detallen cada regla de seguridad. El sistema, pensado para futuros robots domésticos y de asistencia, fue presentado en la conferencia anual Conference on Robot Learning, según MIT News.
En las pruebas virtuales —simulaciones desarrolladas por el equipo para validar el sistema—, un brazo robótico llevó a cabo tres tareas: servir café, trasladar una vela y transportar una bola de bowling. Voluntarios interactuaron con el robot escribiendo órdenes en lenguaje natural, como: “No derrames sobre mi computadora portátil”. En todos los casos, el robot siguió la instrucción literal y extendió su razonamiento a objetos no mencionados: evitó otros dispositivos electrónicos, materiales inflamables y objetos frágiles.
La intención detrás de una orden cotidiana
El sistema permite que una persona escriba instrucciones en lenguaje natural mientras el robot ejecuta una tarea. Si debe mover una taza de café sobre una mesa con objetos y recibe la advertencia de no derramar sobre una computadora portátil, FLEX no solo altera la trayectoria para evitar ese aparato: infiere que también debe mantenerse alejado de un teléfono situado en el mismo espacio.
Esa capacidad surge del uso de un modelo de lenguaje de gran tamaño, un sistema de inteligencia artificial entrenado con enormes colecciones de textos, publicaciones en redes sociales, transcripciones de videos y contenido web. En este caso, FLEX emplea GPT-4o para identificar patrones y establecer generalizaciones a partir de las preferencias expresadas por la persona.
Nathan Dennler, investigador posdoctoral del Laboratorio de Ciencias de la Computación e Inteligencia Artificial del MIT, explicó que esos modelos han encontrado innumerables referencias a accidentes cotidianos entre líquidos y dispositivos. “La gente puede haber escrito: ‘Oh, mi teléfono cayó al agua y ahora no funciona’, o ‘Derramé café sobre mi computadora y ahora no funciona’. Así, los modelos de lenguaje de gran tamaño captan la idea de que los líquidos en los dispositivos hacen que las cosas dejen de funcionar”.
La plataforma parte de la premisa de que las palabras suelen contener una intención de mayor alcance que su significado literal. “Las personas entienden esto de forma natural. Pero hay que explicárselo cuidadosamente a un robot, lo que lleva tiempo y esfuerzo”, afirmó Dennler. “FLEX ofrece una interfaz de comunicación con un robot para decirle: ‘Cuando las personas dicen esto, quieren decir aquello’”.
“Los robots usan matemáticas para planificar sus trayectorias, pero no podemos esperar que un consumidor aprenda esas matemáticas para decirle a un robot qué hacer”, sostuvo Dennler. La meta es que el usuario no tenga que aprender un método específico para manejar una máquina, sino que pueda comunicarse mediante lenguaje natural.
Tres etapas para ampliar las instrucciones humanas
FLEX organiza la interpretación de una orden en tres fases. La primera, denominada “Agregar”, incorpora a una lista los elementos del entorno que importan para la tarea a partir de la corrección de la persona.
Si un robot traslada una bola de bowling y recibe la indicación: “No la dejes caer sobre mi taza”, identifica la taza como un objeto que debe evitar. Los sistemas anteriores ya podían modificar su recorrido de ese modo, aunque cada nueva advertencia ampliaba una lista que podía volverse extensa y perder vigencia cuando cambiaba el entorno.
La segunda fase, “Generalizar”, es la innovación central del método. GPT-4o analiza los objetos que el usuario pidió evitar y busca conexiones entre ellos: si se le ordenó no dejar caer una carga sobre una taza, puede inferir que debe evitar todos los objetos frágiles, aunque no hayan sido mencionados.
Dennler señaló que los modelos absorben parte de ese conocimiento cotidiano a partir de los textos con los que fueron entrenados. “Como se han entrenado tanto con esas cosas, parte de ese sentido común queda incorporado en el modelo de lenguaje de gran tamaño”.
La última etapa, “Enmascarar”, utiliza el sistema de visión por computadora del robot para determinar qué objetos ya no están presentes y eliminarlos de la lista. El proceso completo demanda unos cinco segundos.
En las simulaciones, el robot obedeció de forma literal órdenes como: “Mantente alejado de la pila de papeles” y “No dejes caer [la carga] sobre la taza”. A la vez, extendió esas instrucciones para evitar objetos inflamables y proteger elementos frágiles.
“Todos los hogares son diferentes y a cada persona le importan cosas distintas, por lo que ningún robot sale de fábrica sabiendo qué es importante para usted”, dijo Andreea Bobu, profesora asistente de aeronáutica y astronáutica del MIT y responsable de la investigación. “FLEX puede aprenderlo a partir de una o dos frases, en vez de pedirle que detalle cada regla”.

articles.title: El nuevo cubo de basura doble de Lidl es ideal para reciclar en casa y evitar los malos olores en la cocina
articles.text:
Reciclar y tener un cubo separado para cada tipo de basura es algo que deberíamos tener todos en casa. El problema es que esto implica más espacio y puede llegar a ser poco práctico en el día a día. Una solución a esto es tener un cubo de basura con doble compartimento y este de Lidl es un ejemplo ideal: está disponible por 48,99 euros.
Cubo de basura de acero inoxidable
En el momento de escribir este artículo, indica que no quedan muchas unidades. Si no llegas a tiempo o simplemente prefieres una alternativa, tienes este de la marca Amig en Amazon a un precio realmente similar: cuesta 49,62 euros.
Amig - Cubo de reciclaje con pedales para cocina - Cubo de basura con 2 compartimentos extraíbles de 15 L - Capacidad 30 litros - 48 x 32 x 40 cm - Acero inoxidable - Plateado
Un cubo de basura doble para reciclar fácilmente en casa
Al decir que es un cubo doble, a lo que nos referimos es que son dos cubos independientes y que, además, cada uno tiene una capacidad de 15 litros. Podemos colocarle a cada uno su propia bolsa de basura, pudiendo así separar los desechos a diario sin demasiadas complicaciones. Pese a su capacidad, tiene 47,5 centímetros de alto y 33 de ancho.
Un punto muy a favor de este cubo de Lidl es que cuenta con un diseño rectangular y un acabado muy discreto, por lo que no desentona demasiado si lo queremos colocar en un lugar visible de la cocina. Lo podemos elegir en color negro o en un acabado de acero inoxidable.
Más allá de poder separar la basura en el mismo cubo, tiene la ventaja de que podemos extraer cada compartimento gracias al asa que tienen. Y, además, tiene un pedal que nos permitirá abrir cómodamente la tapa sin tener que tocar el cubo con las manos. Su cierre, por cierto, tiene un mecanismo que hace que baje la tapa sola y sin hacer ruido.

articles.title: XGIMI Horizon 30 Pro and Ultra Max Now Available
articles.text:
Wednesday, November 11th 2026
XGIMI Horizon 30 Pro and Ultra Max Now Available
XGIMI, a global leader in premium smart projection and home entertainment, today announced that the HORIZON 30 Pro and HORIZON 30 Ultra Max are officially available for purchase at XGIMI.com. Following its October debut, the new generation of high-performance home projectors combines premium picture quality with flexible setup, making big-screen entertainment a natural fit for everyday living spaces.
The three models - HORIZON 30 Pro, HORIZON 30 Max and HORIZON 30 Ultra Max - combine XGIMI's RGB Triple Laser technology with up to 6,000 ISO lumens of brightness, native contrast reaching 10,000:1, and 4K 120 Hz performance. These combined capabilities deliver brighter pictures, greater depth in darker scenes, and smoother motion for movies, sports, streaming and gaming.Key Features Include:
- Smoother Motion for Every Moment: 4K 120 Hz performance keeps fast-moving action fluid and easy to follow, from live sports and movies to gaming.
- Bright, Vibrant Viewing: RGB Triple Laser technology delivers up to 6,000 ISO lumens of brightness, bringing vivid, colorful images to daytime entertainment and movie nights.
- Deeper Contrast, Greater Detail: The Dual Intelligent Iris System automatically adjusts light as scenes change, helping reveal more detail in bright highlights and dark shadows, with native contrast reaching up to 10,000:1.
- Cinematic Picture Quality: Support for Dolby Vision, HDR10+ and IMAX Enhanced enhances color, contrast and detail, creating a more immersive movie-watching experience.
- Faster, More Responsive Gaming: Low latency and support for VRR, ALLM and AMD FreeSync help reduce delays and keep gameplay smooth and responsive.

articles.title: Elon Musk's Grok Build coding agent is leaking a serious amount of confidential data
articles.text:
Elon Musk's Grok Build coding agent is leaking a serious amount of confidential data
Default options are wreaking havoc again
- Researchers found Grok Build apps were widely exposed due to insecure default sharing settings and discoverable URLs
- Thousands of accessible apps leaked sensitive business data, healthcare records, passwords, and internal documents
- SpaceXSI remediated the issue after disclosure, highlighting security risks in AI-generated application platforms
Grok Build, an AI-powered coding agent built by Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI, has been found leaking a mind-numbing amount of confidential data, thanks to an apparent misconfiguration in how the products are being published on the platform.
SpaceXSI, established when SpaceX and xAI merged, has a product called Grok Build, which allows users to create web applications by simply describing what they want in a chatlike interface. Without having to write any of the code themselves, the users can have an app ready in minutes and publish it directly from the chat interface. The app gets a unique web address in the format <name>.grok.me, where “name” usually consists of four random words. It is something of a privacy feature, to make sure people can’t just guess an app’s location easily.
But according to security researchers Claroc, these addresses can be found through passive DNS services, which collect and index domain names observed in DNS traffic. In other words, anyone can find a published app even if their creator (or no one else, for that matter) ever shared a link for it. As Claroc explained in its report, the researchers did just that, identifying 43,601 addresses under grok.me.
Unlocked apps
But finding someone’s app shouldn’t be a big deal, right? These apps are all password-protected, right? Well, wrong.
The researchers found that almost all of the apps (35,578, or 94.7%) could be accessed without authentication. That means that whatever data they were holding and generating could be accessed with almost no trouble at all. Further investigation uncovered a major oversight - when users want to publish an app, they are offered three privacy choices: “Anyone with the link”, “Invited Users”, and “Only You”. Similar to how Google Docs does it, when you want to share a document.
The problem here, according to Claroc, is that “Anyone with the link” is set as the default option, suggesting that most people building apps on Grok simply weren’t paying attention to the privacy and sharing options.
But still, simply accessing an app doesn’t necessarily have to be a security disaster, right? It’s just an app, right? Well, wrong again. While most apps were “harmless” in that regard (think games, calculators, landing pages), one in ten contained sensitive or internal business information, and 2% exposed information serious enough to warrant a high, or critical severity rating.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Leaking information
Claroc found a hospital employee directory with more than 3,500 names, an intensive care briefing containing patient information, and a trucking company’s recruitment database listing more than 1,000 individuals. It also found an employee timesheet whose downloadable code contained 18 accounts with plaintext passwords, including administrator credentials.
Even SpaceXSI was leaking its own classified information this way. The researchers found 24 open apps containing onboarding plans, employee names lists, a sales territory map of almost 600 strategic accounts and their pipeline, media plans and advertiser decks (all with budget tiers, including one for a US federal agency marked as confidential), seven campaign reports for advertisers around the world, and much, much more. The researchers found one solitary app, an archive of a streaming service’s ad measurement studies, that asked for a password. Everything else was left wide open.
Claroc also tested to see if they could alter the data found in these apps and built two of their own to test the theory out. One allowed unauthenticated visitor to modify a shared contact database, while another automatically granted access to anyone signing in with a Google account (even if they weren’t part of the team).
The researchers notified SpaceXSI about their findings on November 8, and within two days all SpaceXSI apps were no longer available. They are now working through the list and notifying everyone else.
Via Ars Technica

articles.title: Banco digital Ueno colapsó en Paraguay dejó a casi 3 millones de clientes sin acceso a sus cuentas
articles.text:
El Banco Central de Paraguay intervino el 3 de noviembre el banco digital Ueno y suspendió de inmediato su aplicación, sus tarjetas y todos sus servicios. Unos 2,9 millones de clientes, cerca del 60% de los adultos del país, quedaron sin acceso a su dinero, según la propia entidad y el medio NPR.
La decisión del directorio del Banco Central fue unánime y se tomó después de que el índice de solvencia de Ueno cayera por debajo de la mitad del mínimo exigido, según informó BBC Mundo.
El Banco Central activó un proceso de resolución: todos los activos y pasivos de la entidad quedaron congelados hasta determinar cómo se cubren sus obligaciones. La directiva del organismo Liana Caballero confirmó en una conferencia de prensa que ningún servicio de Ueno seguía activo.
Quién recibió su dinero y quién sigue esperando
El Banco Central informó que Ueno tenía alrededor de 1,8 millones de depositantes. Los ahorros se devuelven con el Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos, que cubre hasta 75 salarios mínimos por persona, unos 228,3 millones de guaraníes (cerca de USD 38.000).
La devolución comenzó con quienes tenían hasta 10 millones de guaraníes (unos USD 1.600), sin deudas con Ueno y con una cuenta en otro banco. Después se amplió a depósitos de hasta 40 salarios mínimos. Hasta el 9 de noviembre, más de 1,7 millones de personas habían recuperado todo o parte de su dinero y se habían devuelto unos USD 341 millones, según el Banco Central.
Quedan cuentas pendientes: unos 262.000 clientes no tenían cuenta en otro banco, y las autoridades atribuyeron las demoras a revisiones en curso y a esa falta de cuentas alternativas. Quienes superan el tope de la garantía deberán esperar la liquidación de los activos de Ueno, que según expertos citados por BBC Mundo podría no alcanzar para cubrir todo.
Favio Marcelo Vargas, dueño de una empresa de transporte, dijo a BBC Mundo que nadie de su entorno había cobrado todavía. La asociación de importadores y comerciantes Asimcopar advirtió de una “semiparalización” del comercio, porque dos de cada tres operaciones electrónicas pasan por cuentas de Ueno.
Dinero público y préstamos a empresas del mismo grupo
Ueno nació en 2021 como una empresa financiera digital y operó como banco desde noviembre de 2023. Creció con promociones y reembolsos en compras, y con una apertura de cuentas desde el teléfono más simple que la de la banca tradicional, según NPR y BBC Mundo.
Entre 2023 y septiembre de 2026, los depósitos de organismos estatales en Ueno pasaron de USD 80,2 millones a USD 834,8 millones, según BBC Mundo. Esa suma incluye unos USD 355 millones del Instituto de Previsión Social, que administra pensiones y representaban cerca del 9% de su cartera de inversiones.
El economista Manuel Ferreira, exministro de Finanzas, dijo a NPR que muchos préstamos del banco fueron a empresas ligadas a sus dueños, el Grupo Vásquez, entre ellos USD 146 millones a solo tres compañías. Según Ferreira, algunos pagarés tenían a las mismas personas en ambos lados de la operación.
Peña destituido y ejecutivos detenidos
El presidente Santiago Peña tuvo acciones en la sociedad matriz de Ueno, que vendió en marzo de 2025, y en 2023 designó como presidente del Banco Central a Carlos Carvallo, que había dirigido Ueno, según NPR. Peña renunció el 5 de noviembre y el Senado lo destituyó al día siguiente.
Los fiscales lo imputaron por abuso de confianza y administración en beneficio propio. Sostienen que usó su cargo para que organismos públicos mantuvieran depósitos en el banco. Un juez ordenó su prisión preventiva en una instalación militar. Peña se declaró inocente.
Carvallo también fue detenido, acusado de los mismos delitos y de producir documentos públicos falsos. Ocho ejecutivos de Ueno, entre ellos el director ejecutivo Miguel Vásquez, quedaron presos. El vicepresidente Pedro Alliana asumió la presidencia y completará el mandato hasta agosto de 2028.

articles.title: Prusa launches new carbon-fiber and carbon-nanotube-filled 3D printing filament for electronics manufacturing — material dissipates electrostatic energy for static-sensitive electronics
articles.text:
Prusa launches new carbon-fiber and carbon-nanotube-filled 3D printing filament for electronics manufacturing — material dissipates electrostatic energy for static-sensitive electronics
A new PETG ESD filament just entered the market, and it's a better value than the competition.
Prusa released its new Prusament PETG ESD on Tuesday: a carbon-fiber and carbon-nanotube (CNT)- filled, electrostatic-dissipative (ESD) PETG filament meant to protect static-sensitive electronics. While it’s great for enclosures for a Raspberry Pi, ESP32, and the like, Prusa is targeting the filament more toward electronics production than hobbyist use; however, it’s cheaper than the non-ESD Prusament PETG Carbon Fiber at only $56.99.
Prusa isn’t the only one selling ESD filament; 3DXTech and Polymaker were first to the scene, but Prusa is the first to include carbon fiber alongside carbon nanotubes to provide the ESD properties, improving dimensional accuracy and minimizing warping. 3DXTech sells its ESD-PETG at $105; Polymaker’s Fiberon PETG-ESD is $65.98, but the Prusament PETG ESD is only $56.99 and is the only one with carbon fiber reinforcement.
Non-ESD filaments are generally safe for electronics enclosures; many hobbyists use regular PLA, PETG, and ABS without any problems. And while the extra protection can be appreciated, Prusa positions this not for hobbyists, but for electronics production — PCB fixtures and holders for soldering, IC trays for handling and transport, holders for testing multiple boards at once, etc., as Prusa shows on the PETG ESD product page. It saves on manufacturing costs, reducing the need for CNC-machined ESD trays and fixtures, and can be quickly printed on-site with very little lead time. It’s not necessarily for big businesses only either, as indie hardware developers and smaller-scale manufacturers could use this filament to improve their production line without buying expensive ESD filament.
Prusa has not yet published the datasheet containing details about the strength of the filament, but Prusa claims that the filament has increased stiffness and reduced toughness, similar to Prusament PETG Carbon Fiber’s properties. However, the amount of carbon fiber in PETG ESD may be different from PETG Carbon Fiber, as the latter’s purpose is more for strength than for electronics manufacturing.
Prusa is known to use its own 3D printers to print its own components and use its own products for the 3D printers it sells, and on the product page, Prusa says it uses PETG ESD in its own production line to prevent overcoating the edges when powder coating its print sheets. While it isn’t the first or only ESD filament on the market, it’s certainly the cheapest, and when its strength profile is released or tested independently, it may potentially be more worth it than Prusa’s own PETG Carbon Fiber in certain cases.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 tem melhor oferta já vista no 11.11 e novo design é destaque
Galaxy Z Fold 8 (256 GB) com tela AMOLED flexível e câmera de 50 MP atinge o menor preço que já vimos, com desconto de 18% no Pix com cupom na Amazon durante o 11.11
O Galaxy Z Fold 8 de 256 GB está saindo por R$ 10.299 no Pix com cupom SAMSUNG500 na Amazon. O novo dobrável da Samsung, com design em formato de passaporte, telas AMOLED e câmera de 50 MP, atinge no 11.11 o menor preço já visto pelo Achados, com desconto de 18% sobre o original de R$ 12.599.
O Z Fold 8 chama a atenção para seu design de passaporte, com uma tela interna de 7,6″ AMOLED Dinâmico 2X com taxa de 120 Hz. A externa de 5,5″ é bem compacta, mas confortável para rodar apps.
O chip Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy e os 12 GB de RAM sustentam apps pesados em multitarefa e soluções de IA locais. O kit de câmeras filma em 4K a 60 fps, com duas lentes principais de 50 MP (wide e ultrawide) e duas selfies de 10 MP, sendo a interna ultrawide.
O corpo de alumínio Advanced Armor com dobradiças de titânio do Z Fold 8 traz a estrutura Flex Titanium sob a tela interna, que deixa o vinco interno quase invisível. O vidro Gorilla Glass 2 protege a tela externa, e a certificação IP48 oferece resistência à água e proteção moderada contra poeira.
A bateria de silício-carbono de 4.800 mAh resiste a até 26 horas de reprodução de vídeo, segundo a Samsung. O suporte ao carregamento rápido com fio de 45 W e sem fio de 20 W (Qi2) garante energia para um dia inteiro.
O Galaxy Z Fold 8 (R$ 10.619 no Pix com cupom AQUITEMTECH) será atualizado até o Android 24 e possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, Ultra Wideband (UWB) e NFC.
O 11.11 é uma campanha do varejo da China, que comemora o “Dia dos Solteiros” com ofertas em gadgets com cupons e condições especiais. Lojas como Shopee e AliExpress trouxeram a data ao Brasil, e hoje ela faz parte da campanha da Black Friday 2026, que ocorre em 27 de novembro.

articles.title: NVIDIA : une université chinoise a pu acheter des GPU H200 malgré les restrictions américaines
articles.text:
Les contrôles américains portant sur les puces NVIDIA ne fonctionnent pas très bien. On peut le voir encore avec ce nouveau cas.
Depuis l'explosion de l'affaire extra-conjugales du patron de NVIDIA, on ne cesse de découvrir à quel point les entreprises chinoises ont tout de même réussi ces dernières années à mettre la main sur les puissantes puces de la firme américaine. Ça passait ainsi très souvent grâce à l'aide de la maîtresse de Jensen Huang, Alice Huang, mais aussi par d'autres canaux.
Une université chinoise ayant des liens avec l'Armée populaire de libération a pu mettre la main sur ces GPU H200
Les contrôles à l'export de puces NVIDIA imposés par Washington sont-ils des passoires ? On peut se le demander avec ces informations qui affluent, comme encore aujourd'hui. Reuters nous apprend en effet qu'une université chinoise a encore pu le mois dernier s'offrir des GPU H200.
L'Université polytechnique du Nord-Ouest, située à Xi'an, a pu ainsi acquérir le mois dernier deux puces H200, pour un montant de 874 700 yuans (environ 118 000 euros). Cette université appartient au groupe dit des « Sept Fils de la Défense nationale », un groupement d'universités connues pour les partenariats et les projets de recherche menés étroitement avec l'armée chinoise, l'Armée populaire de libération.
Des puces achetées par un intermédiaire plutôt que directement auprès de NVIDIA
D'après la même source, l'université n'a pas acquis ces puces directement auprès de NVIDIA, mais a, pour le coup, fait passer la commande pour son école de gestion, via la société Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology.
Et ça n'est pas la seule fois où cette université a réussi à mettre la main sur des services permis par NVIDIA cette année. Cinq contrats de location de capacité de calcul ont en effet été passés avec des entreprises chinoises, qui lui permettaient de bénéficier de la puissance des GPU H200 et d'autres puissants accélérateurs d'IA produit par la firme de Jensen Huang. Une annonce qui va mal passer, quand on sait que l'Université polytechnique du Nord-Ouest est inscrite sur l'Entity List (la liste d'exclusion du département du Commerce) depuis déjà 2001, pour sa participation dans des activités présumées de prolifération de missiles et de recherche militaire.
Source : Reuters

articles.title: British inference chip developer Fractile raises $720M in funding - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
British inference chip developer Fractile raises $720M in funding
Fractile Ltd., a British startup that develops artificial intelligence inference chips, has raised $720 million in funding.
Reuters reported today that the Series C round was led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint. They were joined by about a dozen others including the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund, the British Business Bank and Alphabet Inc.’s CapitalG investment arm. Fractile is now worth $7 billion.
Fractile was founded in 2022 by AI researcher Walter Goodwin (pictured), who serves as its chief executive. The company reportedly expects its chips to provide up to 100 times better performance than current silicon. Furthermore, Fractile is promising a 90% reduction in energy use. The chips deliver those improvements by removing the need for AI models to move data to off-chip HBM memory.
Large language models generate prompt responses through a workflow that involves numerous steps. When an LLM completes a processing step, it sends the results to an off-chip HBM memory chip. It then retrieves those results to lay the groundwork for the next step. Those repeated data round-trips take a significant amount of time, which slows down inference.
Fractile is not the only AI chip supplier tackling that bottleneck. Cerebras Systems Inc., which went public in May, offers wafer-size accelerators that reduce data movement by keeping information in a large onboard cache. That cache is faster than off-chip HBM modules. The company’s newest processor, the WSE-3T, can hold 44 gigabytes of data.
Cerebras’ on-chip cache is based on SRAM, a type of memory that was historically added to processors in only small quantities. SRAM cells, the technology’s basic building blocks, have six transistors apiece. Those transistors read and write data faster than the single transistor found in HBM cells. At the same time, SRAM’s speed comes with certain trade-offs: it’s expensive and has limited capacity.
Fractile is taking a different approach to reducing data movement. Instead of integrating SRAM into its inference chips, the company is stacking standard DRAM memory on top of them. Placing a memory module immediately above a processor’s logic circuits minimizes the distance that data has to cover. That speeds up traffic while lowering the amount of electricity needed to shuffle it back and forth.
Samsung Electronics Co. is developing a similar technology. In August, the company debuted an HBM variant called zHBM that can be stacked atop AI accelerators. It uses tiny copper wires to move data to and from the host chip. Samsung says the technology will be eight times faster than HBM5, a future iteration of HBM more performant than the versions in use today.
Fractile, for its part, estimates that its chips will enable LLM to process several thousand tokens per second. It plans to ship the processors as part of rack-scale systems that will also include custom software. Many AI chipmakers offer custom compilers, software tools that automatically turn customers’ LLMs into a format compatible with their silicon.
Fractile expects to start shipping its chips next year.

articles.title: El Black Friday se adelanta con la TCL C6K Pro: una tele Mini LED de gama alta con Google TV, de 55 a 85 pulgadas (y hasta 98 con la C6K)
articles.text:
Con el Black Friday asomando la patita, estamos ante uno de los mejores momentos del año para renovar televisor. Va a depender mucho de lo que estés buscando, aunque cualquier compra se basa en tres pilares: tecnología del panel, tamaño de la diagonal y, claro está, precio. La buena noticia con respecto a esto último es que ya no hay que irse obligatoriamente a los modelos más caros para conseguir una muy buena experiencia a la hora de pelis, fútbol o jugar videojuegos.
TV QD-Mini LED 55" - TCL 55C6K PRO, UHD 4K, TCL AiPQ Processor, Smart TV con Google TV, Dolby Vision-Atmos, Negro
En esa línea, merece la pena considerar ir a por un televisor MiniLED, aunque no cualquiera. Uno que tiene una gran relación calidad-precio es el TCL C6K Pro, especialmente si tenemos en cuenta los precios que podemos encontrar en MediaMarkt: su versión de 55 pulgadas sale por 479 euros.
TCL C6K Pro: ¿merece la pena apostar por un televisor QD-Mini LED?
Como decimos, este televisor de TCL tiene tecnología QD-MiniLED. Esto se traduce en que nos va a ofrecer una mejor calidad de imagen que los televisores LED de toda la vida y la clave está principalmente en la retroiluminación del panel. Mientras que los televisores LED utilizan unos diodos de mayor tamaño, los MiniLED montan diodos más pequeños, lo que permite colocar muchos más en un mismo espacio.
Gracias a esto, el control de la retroiluminación del panel que hace el televisor es mucho más preciso. Pero, ¿en qué vamos a notar eso? Pues lo cierto es que en cualquier contexto, pero especialmente en escenas oscuras. Al tener ese mejor control de la retroiluminación, el panel del televisor mantendrá las escenas oscuras, pero sin perder detalles de los objetos iluminados. Por eso, un MiniLED tiene negros más profundos y un contraste más marcado.
A esta tecnología hay que sumarle una capa de puntos cuánticos (o quantum dots). Esta va a hacer que el televisor tenga una mejor reproducción de color, haciendo que estos tengan un aspecto similar al del mundo real. Uniendo este color más vivo a un negro más profundo, se logra un muy buen resultado en todo tipo de contenidos, ya sean pelis, series, un partido de fútbol o videojuegos.
Este TCL C6K Pro es, además, un televisor muy fino y delgado, lo que hace que sea perfecto para colgar en la pared sin que este desentone con el resto de la habitación. Viene con sistema operativo Google TV, uno muy fácil e intuitivo de usar, con compatibilidad con las principales plataformas de streaming. Cuenta también con Gemini, que nos ayudará a buscar contenidos o nos hará recomendaciones para todas esas veces que no sepamos qué ver.
¿Vas a renovar tu televisor? La distancia de visionado es la clave para elegir diagonal

articles.title: Firefox's built-in VPN outage in Iran — Mozilla blames suspected abuse by third-party apps
articles.text:
Firefox's built-in VPN outage in Iran — Mozilla blames suspected abuse by third-party apps
- Firefox's free built-in VPN temporarily went dark for users in Iran
- Mozilla cited suspected third-party app abuse for the temporary disruption
- The service has now reportedly been restored
Firefox’s free, built-in VPN went offline for some users in Iran, and Mozilla says the cause was a temporary disruption to investigate suspected abuse of the service by unauthorized third-party apps.
The outage prompted complaints on social media platforms and online forums. Users in Iran said the VPN — free and one of the best VPN options in Iran because it needed no extra software — first stopped connecting and then disappeared from the browser entirely.
"It appears that over the past 24 hours, Mozilla has disabled its internal VPN service for users in Iran," one X user wrote on Tuesday, a sentiment echoed across several other posts in Persian and English.
VPNs are by no means a niche tool in Iran — by some estimates, roughly nine in ten Iranian internet users rely on one to bypass state filtering. So, even a brief outage of a popular, free option was quickly felt.
NEW: Leave No Trace — A weekly newsletter on digital privacy and online surveillance.
Leave No Trace investigates the companies and governments putting our digital freedom at risk — and the people fighting back.
📩 Subscribe now to get every edition delivered to your inbox every Friday, launching this September.
Iran's Firefox VPN outage: what we know
The reports circulated first on X and Reddit, where Iranian users described losing access, before being pulled together in a Hacker News post titled "Tell HN: Firefox’s built-in VPN stopped working for some users in Iran.”
According to the post, Firefox users in Iran had used the free VPN for months, even though Iran was never part of the feature’s official rollout. For many users in Iran, it offers a convenient way to reach blocked sites from a browser they already have.
The free tier, introduced into Firefox in 2026, normally comes with a monthly data allowance in exchange for signing in with a Mozilla account — and is separate from Mozilla’s paid, standalone VPN service. As it happens, Mozilla has just lifted that cap, announcing on November 10 that the built-in VPN would offer unlimited data through January 31, 2027.
At first, nobody could say why the outage happened. Some users suspected the Iranian government had blocked Mozilla’s service at the network level, as it has done with other VPN providers. Others blamed Mozilla itself, suggesting it had quietly disabled access for Iranian IP addresses in order to comply with US sanctions.
The eventual answer was neither.
A Mozilla spokesperson confirmed: "We recently discovered potential abuse of Firefox’s free built-in VPN by unauthorized third-party apps and temporarily disrupted access to investigate", before going on to confirm that service has since been restored.
Discovering the outage was a temporary anti-abuse measure rather than a policy change targeting Iran has eventually come as a relief for affected users.
What it means for people in Iran
For now, the episode is a reminder of how tenuous access to the open internet can be.
Using an "unauthorized" VPN has been illegal in Iran since February 2024, and users have reportedly received text messages threatening prosecution for bypassing restrictions.
Iranian users do have alternatives. Proton VPN Free is a long-standing favorite, with obfuscation features built for hostile networks. Indeed, its signups from Iran have repeatedly surged during previous blackouts. There’s also Windscribe Free, which supports censorship-resistant protocols.
With Iran's internet as unpredictable as ever, the last thing its users need is another trusted tool vanishing overnight.
Mark is a Tech Security Writer for TechRadar and has been published on Comparitech and IGN. He graduated with a degree in English and Journalism from the University of Lincoln and spent several years teaching English as a foreign language in Spain. The Facebook-Cambridge Analytica data scandal sparked Mark’s interest in online privacy, leading him to write hundreds of articles on VPNs, antivirus software, password managers, and other cybersecurity topics. He recently completed the Google Cybersecurity Certificate, and when he's not studying for the CompTIA Security+ exam, Mark can be found agonizing over his fantasy football team selections, watching the Detroit Lions, and battling bugs and bots in Helldivers 2.

articles.title: IBM Announces Quantum Nighthawk r3 Processor, Plans to Scale Beyond 1,000 Qubits in 2027
articles.text:
Wednesday, November 11th 2026
IBM Announces Quantum Nighthawk r3 Processor, Plans to Scale Beyond 1,000 Qubits in 2027
IBM (NYSE: IBM) today announced IBM Quantum Nighthawk r3, its next-generation processor, will be built to accurately execute 10,000 quantum operations across 520 qubits to tackle larger, more complex problems while maintaining the speed and quality demonstrated by the current generation Nighthawk available today. In 2027, IBM plans to link two Nighthawk r3 processors into a single system with more than 1,000 qubits.
To be at the frontier of quantum computing, industry-relevant applications demand both computational quality and speed. Speed matters because a quantum computer delivers its answer in samples: each run of a quantum circuit returns one result. Applications increasingly require circuits executing thousands of quantum operations on approximately 100 qubits or more, generating millions to billions of samples. Scale and quality enable increasingly complex computations, but speed determines whether these demanding workloads can be completed in practical timeframes and at a reasonable cost.
Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow"Useful quantum computing hinges on whether results can be delivered with accuracy and speed, both are fundamental. Nighthawk is already showing us what that looks like today. As we scale this architecture to larger and more powerful quantum computers, the capabilities of quantum computation will reach new levels as we integrate more closely with classical resources and march ahead to fault tolerance."
Nighthawk r2: Delivering Speed for Real-World Workloads
Introduced in September, IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 delivers up to 100,000 samples per second while supporting accurate computations with more than 7,500 quantum operations on 120 qubits. Its high-speed qubit reset technology dramatically reduces the time between circuit executions, enabling applications to collect the millions or billions of samples needed for complex computations far more efficiently.
Clients and partners including E.ON, Algorithmiq, and Q-CTRL have executed 34 billion circuits on Nighthawk r2 to date, reporting performance improvements of up to 19x while maintaining the quality needed for scientific computation.
The results are already demonstrating value across industries. E.ON reported a 15x speedup on Nighthawk r2 in quantum machine learning for energy grid optimization. IBM used Nighthawk r2 for a 12x speedup of an experiment ran earlier this year with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which simulated real magnetic materials and produced results consistent with neutron scattering experiments. Both of these speedups were achieved over previous work on IBM Quantum Heron. Quantum Elements and ParityQC are also among the partners reporting significant performance improvements on their own Nighthawk r2 workloads.
The quantum advantage experiments IBM and its partners published in July were first run on IBM Quantum Heron, with circuits and results openly available for independent testing through the community-led Quantum Advantage Tracker. An experiment with Algorithmiq to simulate a heterogeneous quantum material has now been extended to Nighthawk r2, leveraging its speed and connectivity to execute circuits 8 times faster than the original experiment on Heron. At the same time, the new circuits are significantly more challenging for classical computers to simulate, requiring an estimated 240 times more memory to achieve comparable accuracy when using leading classical tensor-network methods.
Nighthawk r3: Scaling to More Than 1,000 Qubits
Building on the performance demonstrated by Nighthawk r2, Nighthawk r3 will extend the same high-speed architecture to larger quantum computers. The new processor is designed to support 10,000 quantum operations on 520 programmable qubits, with 2,034 total physical qubits. It retains r2's square-lattice connectivity and fast operations while introducing 10 chip-to-chip interconnects, called l-couplers, designed to connect processors into larger systems.
IBM has already demonstrated two critical technologies that enable this modular approach. This year, IBM connected Nighthawk r1 processors using four l-couplers, achieving 99.3 percent quantum state transfer fidelity and progressing toward its 99.9 percent target. IBM also connected two cryogenic modules into a single system for the first time, reaching operating temperature in under five days and cooling below 15 millikelvin.
Together, these advances demonstrate critical progress in modularity and provide confidence in IBM's ability to scale Nighthawk to larger quantum computers. In 2027, IBM plans to connect two Nighthawk r3 processors into a single 1,040-qubit system, extending its high-performance architecture to larger and more complex computations.
Quantum Meets Classical on the IBM Quantum Platform
Advancing quantum computers requires continued progress in how they work alongside classical compute to handle errors. Industry-relevant workloads will demand layers of quantum error correction and error mitigation techniques alongside noise learning and post-processing. As quantum workloads scale, they will call for more classical resources, and the challenge now is how to best scale this integration.
To unite these paradigms, IBM Quantum Platform is bringing high-performance (HPC) classical and quantum computing together into a single managed environment. Users can now integrate quantum workflows directly with a range of classical compute - whether from their laptop or a powerful supercomputer - or with the HPC and classical resources that are newly available on the platform.
Users are seeing promising results from these integrations. For example, using the new environment, IBM and RIKEN scientists executed their original sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) workflow roughly 5 times faster while performing 100 times more computations than in the original study. Cleveland Clinic and RIKEN also leveraged the platform to automatically process 608 million samples for modeling biologically relevant structures, 33 times faster than without workflow automation.
Enhanced capabilities will also fuel breakthroughs in quantum error correction. IBM Quantum Platform offers pulse-level capabilities to give researchers precise control over how they can detect, understand, and better correct errors within quantum and classical architectures. This helps them better time operations, reset qubits faster, and extract more information from quantum measurements - giving researchers the visibility to improve error correction at its most fundamental levels.
IBM recently launched a new co-design platform for quantum error correction with Oak Ridge National Laboratory and AMD that physically co-locates Nighthawk with ORNL's Umbra High-Performance Computing (HPC) system, powered by AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPUs.

articles.title: Android Auto prepara cambios en su interfaz y algunos celulares dejarán de ser compatibles
articles.text:
Google avanza en dos frentes simultáneos para Android Auto: por un lado, endureció los requisitos técnicos para conectarse por cable y dejó fuera a los teléfonos más antiguos; por otro, sigue construyendo en silencio un rediseño de interfaz conocido internamente como “Cielo”. Ambos movimientos llegan en paralelo a través de las versiones recientes de la aplicación.
El primer cambio ya es efectivo y afecta a quienes todavía usan equipos con sistemas operativos antiguos. El segundo, en cambio, sigue oculto en el código y solo se conoce a partir de análisis técnicos, sin fecha de lanzamiento confirmada.
Qué cambió en los requisitos mínimos
Google retiró el soporte de Android Auto por cable para teléfonos con Android 9 y Android 10. El requisito mínimo pasó a ser Android 11 o una versión posterior, según detectó el medio especializado ZDNET en la página de ayuda oficial de Google.
El cambio no es aislado: la compañía ya había retirado el soporte de Android 8 en 2024, una versión lanzada en 2017. Android 11, en cambio, llegó por primera vez en 2020, lo que marca una actualización progresiva del umbral mínimo compatible.
Cumplir con la versión de sistema operativo no alcanza por sí solo. Para que la conexión funcione también se necesita un plan de datos activo y que el coche o el estéreo admita el servicio, además de un cable USB de calidad. Los dispositivos con Android Go, la edición ligera del sistema, tampoco pueden utilizar la plataforma.
Según ZDNET, las versiones compatibles van desde Android 11 hasta Android 17. Quienes tengan un teléfono con Android 9 o 10 deberán revisar si existe una actualización de software disponible por parte del fabricante o, en su defecto, considerar cambiar de equipo para no perder el acceso al servicio por USB.
Google ofrece una página central de ayuda para verificar si un vehículo o estéreo es compatible con Android Auto, aunque para conocer con precisión las funciones disponibles en la pantalla de un coche concreto, la recomendación es consultar directamente al fabricante del automóvil.
El rediseño “Cielo” avanza dentro del código
Mientras los requisitos mínimos ya cambiaron, el rediseño visual de Android Auto todavía permanece oculto. Las versiones 18.0 y 18.1, que Google ya distribuye de forma estable, no traen cambios visibles para el usuario, pero sí contienen pistas sobre la renovación que prepara la compañía, según el análisis publicado por 9to5Google el 3 de noviembre.
La principal novedad detectada es un nuevo recurso llamado cielo_launcher, que sugiere el desarrollo de un launcher rediseñado para facilitar el cambio entre aplicaciones como Google Maps, Spotify o WhatsApp sin depender tanto del menú de aplicaciones.
La versión 18.1 suma además nuevos recursos de animación para paneles del tablero que se deslizan, escalan y se desvanecen, efectos que parecen formar parte del mismo proyecto Cielo que Google adelantó meses atrás.
También aparecieron archivos vinculados a los modos claro y oscuro, con elementos específicos para dispositivos Samsung, lo que indica una mayor atención al contraste y la legibilidad de la pantalla según las condiciones de luz al conducir.
A esto se suman recursos de escalado de mapas, pensados para que Google Maps aproveche mejor el espacio disponible según el tamaño de cada pantalla de infotainment, un punto especialmente relevante en autos con pantallas más pequeñas.
Qué prepara Google para el futuro de la plataforma
El rediseño que asoma en el código fue presentado originalmente por Google durante su evento para desarrolladores Google I/O. Allí la compañía mostró una interfaz más flexible, con la incorporación de widgets para consultar información sin abandonar la navegación.
Entre los ejemplos exhibidos figuraron controles de dispositivos inteligentes, información meteorológica y accesos directos a contactos, pensados para reducir la cantidad de pasos necesarios dentro de la aplicación.
Google Maps ocupa un lugar central en ese plan: se espera una integración más amplia en pantalla, con un diseño basado en el lenguaje visual Material 3 Expressive, caracterizado por animaciones más fluidas y una estética renovada.
Por ahora, ninguna de estas funciones llegó a los usuarios finales ni tiene fecha confirmada de lanzamiento. Lo que existe son indicios dentro del código de las últimas actualizaciones, que anticipan hacia dónde se dirige el sistema una vez que el rediseño esté terminado.

articles.title: OpenAI and Georgia county leaders hit with Mafia-style RICO racketeering lawsuit over $30 billion AI data center — residents allege closed-door conspiracy and NDAs were used to push 3.2-gigawatt ‘Project Camellia’ through
articles.text:
OpenAI and Georgia county leaders hit with Mafia-style RICO racketeering lawsuit over $30 billion AI data center — residents allege closed-door conspiracy and NDAs were used to push 3.2-gigawatt ‘Project Camellia’ through
Data center mafia.
Residents of Effingham County, Georgia, just filed a RICO lawsuit against their county commissioners, county leaders, and OpenAI and its affiliates, alleging that they committed various offenses in a conspiracy to get OpenAI’s “Project Camellia” approved. According to the Effingham Herald, the plaintiffs — Dr. Michelle Finch-Mincey, Lehman Mincey Jr., and Raymond Carver — are seeking civil damages, saying that the project has harmed their property values and even pointing out that purchase offers for nearby residential properties have dropped or been withdrawn since the data center was announced.
The lawsuit names all Effingham County Commissioners — Chairperson Damon Rahn, Forrest Floyd, Roger Burdette, Jamie DeLoach, Elizabeth Helmly, and Phil Kieffer — as defendants, alongside County Manager Tim Callanan, Effingham County Industrial Development Authority (IDA) CEO Brandt Herndon, the IDA itself, OpenAI, Octans GA LLC, the entity operating the data center on behalf of OpenAI, and Savannah Industrial Development LLC, the agency involved in the sale of IDA property to Octans and OpenAI.
It’s alleged that the defendants committed fraud and concealment through non-disclosure agreements and misleading public statements so that residents remain unaware of the nature of the projects for as long as possible, and that there was a civil conspiracy “to advance Project Camellia through confidential negotiations and closed-door decisions.” They also claimed that the parties engaged in improper land transactions, zoning violations, and civil racketeering.w
Project Camellia is one of OpenAI’s biggest data center projects planned for construction in Effingham County. The site is expected to cost somewhere between $20 billion and $30 billion, to be built across five phases, with a planned compute capacity of 3.2 gigawatts. The company also promised that it will not affect the community’s utility costs, as it will pay for the full cost of all its required infrastructure upgrades, and that it will have minimal water use due to its closed-loop water system. Despite those promises, it seems that some people are opposing the project because of how the county had allegedly tried to secure the land, tax incentives, and zoning approvals without informing the residents until key decisions were finalized and contracts had been signed.
The RICO Act — or Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act — was originally conceived as a way to counter organized crime, particularly Mafia leadership, who often used low-level members to commit individual crimes and do the dirty work for them. However, Georgia’s RICO Act is less stringent than the federal version, which is why it’s been used multiple times for cases that seemingly had nothing to do with the Mafia. For example, it was in the 2023 election racketeering case against Donald Trump and 18 others in the attempt to overturn the 2020 U.S. presidential election results in the state, and it was also used in Young Thug’s trial after the rapper was accused of running YSL Records as a criminal street gang.
Critics say that Georgia’s version is way too encompassing, though, and that it was being used to squeeze defendants involved in more mundane or common felonies. “When you have a hammer, everything looks like a nail,” Georgia State University professor of criminal justice and criminology Volkan Topalli said in Atlanta Magazine.
The actions of both state officials, OpenAI, and its affiliates are not new, though. There have already been multiple complaints of data center developers and local governments using non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) while they negotiate terms for possible data center projects. Developers say they use this tool to avoid “running afoul of insider trading rules,” but people have pointed out that West Feliciana Parish in Louisiana was able to close a data center deal without resorting to one. An AWS data center in Gilroy, California, is also facing scrutiny after residents only discovered the nature of the project when construction began after a five-year permitting saga that relied on zoning rules that were set 45 years ago.
