articles.title: Así son las alfombras eléctricas para calentar el hogar y ahorrar energía
articles.text:
Las alfombras eléctricas calefactadas son una alternativa económica al suelo radiante para calentar la casa sin necesidad de obras. Su funcionamiento se basa en resistencias internas que generan calor por radiación, con un consumo que puede bajar la factura de luz si se combinan de forma correcta con la calefacción tradicional.
A diferencia de las mantas eléctricas pensadas para el regazo, estos dispositivos se instalan en el suelo y soportan el peso de quien camina sobre ellas e incluso de muebles livianos como mesas bajas.
Qué son y cómo funcionan las alfombras térmicas
Una alfombra térmica es un emisor de calor eléctrico que mantiene una temperatura de consigna para evitar que el frío se acumule en las zonas bajas de una habitación.
En su interior combinan capas antideslizantes e impermeables con un sistema de cables calefactores ubicados entre dos materiales aislantes. La corriente eléctrica que circula por esos cables calienta el aislante, que a su vez transmite el calor al suelo.
El calor se emite por radiación y se distribuye hacia arriba por convección. Las alfombras trabajan a temperaturas máximas de entre 30 °C y 40 °C, por lo que no queman al tacto, y suelen incorporar varios niveles de regulación para ajustar la intensidad según la necesidad del momento.
La mayoría incluye un mando de control similar al de las mantas eléctricas, con el que se elige la potencia o la temperatura deseada. También pueden conectarse a un enchufe inteligente para manejarlas a distancia o integrarlas en un sistema de domótica.
En cuanto a tamaños, existen modelos que superan el metro y medio de largo por otro tanto de ancho, con un grosor similar al de una alfombra tradicional de salón. Los hay con acabados que imitan alfombras clásicas, otros con apariencia de simple esterilla y algunos de un solo color pensados para pasar inadvertidos.
Cómo logran ahorrar energía
El ahorro que ofrecen estos dispositivos se explica por la sensación térmica más que por una reducción directa del gasto. Es posible tener la calefacción programada a una temperatura elevada y, aun así, sentir frío porque este ingresa al cuerpo a través de los pies.
Según profesionales médicos consultados, la cabeza y los pies son las dos zonas por las que se gana o pierde más calor corporal. En los pies, la transmisión de energía desde el suelo ocurre por contacto directo, incluso cuando hay alfombras o moquetas de por medio.
Al proteger los pies del frío del piso con el calor concentrado de la alfombra térmica aumenta la sensación de bienestar. Esto reduce la necesidad de subir la temperatura del sistema de calefacción principal, lo que se traduce en un menor consumo eléctrico general.
Para potenciar ese ahorro se puede sumar un tercer elemento: un ventilador de techo con tecnología inversa. Mientras la alfombra impide que el frío, que pesa más que el calor, se quede pegado al suelo, el ventilador ayuda a redistribuir el calor que tiende a acumularse en la parte superior de las habitaciones.
Cuánto consumen y qué potencia eligen
El gasto eléctrico de estos dispositivos depende de la potencia y del tiempo que permanecen encendidos. Los modelos más pequeños parten de 50 vatios, mientras que los de mayor tamaño alcanzan los 1.000 vatios, suficientes para dar calor a un salón reducido.
En términos de consumo por hora, la potencia suele ubicarse entre 40 vatios-hora (Wh) en los modelos chicos y 700 Wh en los más grandes. Si una alfombra calefactora se usa 10 horas diarias, el consumo total rondaría entre 400 Wh y 7.000 Wh, según el modelo. El costo final de ese consumo depende de la tarifa eléctrica contratada en cada caso.
Ventajas y limitaciones del sistema
Estas alfombras se instalan sin obras: basta un enchufe cercano, y algunas pueden recortarse a medida. Incluyen protección contra sobrecalentamientos, apagado automático y termostato, sin emitir humos ni consumir oxígeno.
Los materiales varían entre vinilo, más duradero y fácil de limpiar, y lana o poliéster, más cálidos al tacto.
Como limitación, no reemplazan la calefacción de toda la vivienda, solo climatizan zonas puntuales, y calientan más despacio que un radiador. Además, requieren una toma eléctrica cercana, donde queda también el mando de control.

articles.title: T-Mobile illegally imposed 50GB cap on low-income home Internet plan, NY says
articles.text:
T-Mobile violated a New York state law by imposing a 50GB-per-month data cap and reducing speeds to less than a megabit per second on home Internet plans it is required to offer people with low incomes, New York government officials alleged.
T-Mobile agreed to a settlement requiring it to scrap the data and speed limits, to offer the required low-income plans to more parts of the state, and to make it easier for customers to find information about the plans. The settlement requires T-Mobile to eliminate the speed limits and expand availability of the plans within 120 days.
The alleged legal violation and the settlement are related to T-Mobile’s wireless home Internet service, not the company’s mobile plans. Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the settlement on Monday, saying that a state investigation found T-Mobile violated the New York Affordable Broadband Act (ABA).
The state law doesn’t specifically mention data caps, but it requires home Internet providers with at least 20,000 customers to offer plans at specific prices and minimum speeds to people who meet income-eligibility requirements. T-Mobile’s policy of reducing speeds after customers exceed a monthly data cap violates the law, New York officials said.
“An investigation by the Office of the Attorney General (OAG) found T-Mobile’s offerings did not meet the ABA’s requirements, which mandate that home Internet providers offer high-speed broadband to income-eligible households for $15 per month at speeds of at least 25 Mbps, or $20 per month for speeds of at least 200 Mbps,” the press release said.
Speeds reduced from 25 Mbps to 600 Kbps
New York says in the settlement with T-Mobile that “after the data cap is reached, the customer’s maximum download speed is reduced from 25 Mbps to 600 Kbps.” New York’s press release said “a typical customer could hit the data cap after about four days of usage.”
Data caps and speed limits aren’t the only restrictions. T-Mobile also “only offers ABA Internet plans to customers in homes that are eligible for 5G home Internet,” preventing residents in 4G-only areas from accessing the plans, the settlement says. The company also prevented search engines from indexing the webpage that provides detailed information about eligibility for and enrollment in ABA plans, it says.
“T-Mobile did not fully comply with the New York Affordable Broadband Act,” New York said in the settlement.
T-Mobile’s ABA webpage confirms that customers are provided only 50GB per month and that speeds after using the allotment are merely “up to 600 Kbps.”
Although the settlement includes a list of the New York AG’s findings, T-Mobile did not admit to any violation. “Respondent neither admits nor denies the OAG’s Finding in paragraph 1-14 above,” the document says.
New York beat industry attempt to kill law
New York started enforcing the Affordable Broadband Act in January 2025 after winning a nearly four-year court battle against broadband industry lobby groups that tried to kill the law. The groups that sued New York in a failed effort to block the law included CTIA, the wireless industry association that represents T-Mobile and other carriers. The law finally took effect a month after the Supreme Court rejected the broadband industry’s challenge.
When contacted by Ars, T-Mobile did not explain why it imposed the restrictions on low-income plans.
“We have a long history of helping customers in New York stay connected through low-cost broadband, and we’re updating our plan to meet the state’s requirements while maintaining the same low price,” T-Mobile said in a statement. “We’ve reached an agreement with the New York attorney general that builds on that commitment, provides greater clarity around our offering and makes the plan available to more eligible customers.”
The settlement with New York applies to T-Mobile’s fixed wireless Internet plans, which can be used for home Internet service as an alternative to wired broadband. The fixed wireless Internet relies on T-Mobile’s cellular network but provides access at a single location, delivering wireless signals to receivers installed at customer homes.
It took almost 18 months for New York to investigate T-Mobile’s compliance and reach a settlement with the company. “In June 2025, the New York Department of Public Service contacted the OAG and relayed concerns about certain features of the plan that T-Mobile was offering to customers eligible for reduced-price Internet service under the ABA,” the settlement said.
T-Mobile only offered plan in 5G areas
It seems that ISPs have generally offered the required plans, though cable company Optimum failed to comply until Ars made some inquiries on behalf of a customer who could not obtain the plan he was entitled to shortly after the law took effect. ISPs knew about the law long in advance due to the multiyear court case that they initiated, but Optimum wasn’t ready to comply with the requirement and rejected the low-income man’s request twice.
New York officials said the AG’s office “found that T-Mobile was only offering ABA plans in areas where it had deployed 5G wireless service, even though it offered full-price Internet plans that could deliver 25 Mbps download speeds in areas where it had 4G service. In addition, T-Mobile specifically coded its website to hide its ABA plan information from search engines, making it difficult for New Yorkers searching for low-priced Internet to find their plans.”
The settlement requires T-Mobile to stop intentionally limiting download speeds, and says the “temporary reduction of download speeds due solely to network congestion shall not constitute a violation of this Assurance.” There’s also an exception in the state law, which says ISPs shall provide 25Mbps “subject to exceptions adopted by the Public Service Commission where such download speed is not reasonably practicable.”
Extending the low-cost service to 4G areas, T-Mobile agreed to provide the low-income plans “at every address at which Respondent offers residential fixed wireless Internet service.” Speeds lower than 25 Mbps would not violate the settlement if T-Mobile “would be unable to provide a minimum download speed of 25 megabits per second to a residential fixed wireless Internet service customer enrolled in a non-ABA Plan at the same address.”
The document says that “T-Mobile offers 5G home Internet to roughly 40 percent of homes in rural areas of upstate New York and 4G (LTE) home Internet to the remainder of homes in the regions where T-Mobile offers fixed wireless service.”
To make its ABA webpage more accessible, the settlement says T-Mobile “shall not include a noindex tag on the webpage, or otherwise prevent search engines from indexing the webpage or presenting a link to the webpage in response to search engine queries.” T-Mobile must also prominently link to the ABA webpage on the part of its website that lists or describes its standard home Internet deals.
New York could sue T-Mobile if it violates the settlement. The ABA’s enforcement mechanism requires the attorney general to sue a broadband provider on behalf of residents. Such lawsuits can recover restitution and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.
ISPs that want to raise another challenge to New York’s law could get help from the Trump administration, which asserts that states must not enforce price regulations or net neutrality laws against any ISP that obtains grants from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. The grants have not been distributed yet, and California argues that the Trump administration does not have authority to preempt such laws.
T-Mobile’s violation of price-lock promise
In addition to this week’s settlement, New York struck a deal with T-Mobile last month over the carrier violating its promise to never raise prices on certain mobile plans that came with a lifetime price guarantee.
A state investigation “found that from 2017 to 2019, T-Mobile advertised ‘Price Guarantee Plans’ to its 4G customers, promising to ‘never change the price you pay,’” the New York attorney general’s office said on October 20. “However, in 2024, T-Mobile changed course and began raising the price of these plans by approximately $5 per phone line. New Yorkers enrolled in approximately 252,957 of these Price Guarantee Plans saw their phone bills increase.”
T-Mobile agreed to give affected customers several reimbursement options and a price lock until May 2029. The attorney general’s office estimated that the agreement would provide up to $38 million in value to customers affected by the price hikes. T-Mobile also agreed to pay the state a fine of $98,834.75.
T-Mobile provided a statement on the price-hike settlement.
“The $38 million cited in the press release is an estimate of potential benefits that a group of long-standing T-Mobile customers may choose to take advantage of, not the amount in refunds or payments,” T-Mobile said. “The agreement provides for approximately $98,000 paid to the state and a range of optional customer benefits. We’re glad to have this matter resolved and remain focused on delivering value to our customers.”
Jon is a Senior IT Reporter for Ars Technica. He covers the telecom industry, Federal Communications Commission rulemakings, broadband consumer affairs, court cases, and government regulation of the tech industry.

articles.title: Montech King 95 3D Pro case review: The King has returned
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
The King 95 3D is a solid, premium-class mid-tower with three tempered-glass panels for panoramic views inside. The seven included Link fans on the Pro version deliver enough airflow and RGB bling, but can get noisy at full speed. For $119 or $199 for the Pro, it’s an excellent update from the original King 95.
Reasons to buy
- + 3-pane window panel views
- + Pro version includes seven fans
- + Integrated GPU support
- + Adjustable angle on bottom fans
- + Cool RGB lighting strip on the outside
Reasons to avoid
- - RGB lighting from the fans is polarizing
- - Lacks vertical GPU mounting option
- - No E-ATX support
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
PC case, cooling, and PSU maker Montech is celebrating its 10th anniversary this year and has released a new flagship ATX chassis, the King 95 3D and 3D Pro. Like the previous King 95, the 3D version keeps the signature 15-degree curved-glass panoramic front panel and adds a top glass panel, giving you a third window and a unique aesthetic for viewing your build. An integrated, contoured ARGB strip follows the chassis's smooth lines, making it look every bit the king of the castle.
Inside, the large mid-tower chassis supports multiple radiators (though only one 360mm), large graphics cards (plus integrated adjustable GPU support), CPU air coolers, and spots for 2.5- and 3.5-inch drives. However, it doesn't support E-ATX motherboards. The King 95 3D supports rear-connect motherboards and has ample room for cable routing and management. The front aluminum panel IO runs vertically, as with previous King cases, and includes a fast USB 3.2 Gen2x2 (20 Gbps) Type-C port. Overall, it has everything you want in a premium chassis. The uncommon three-panel view into your PC is a great way to show off your rig.
The King 95 3D is available for an inexpensive (at least for curved glass) $119.90 if you want to select your own fans. The 3D Pro includes seven pre-installed LINK Fan INF 120 fans for builders who want a more coordinated look out of the box, plus it includes the Lumi hub (a dedicated fan controller), for $199.90. We have the 3D Pro version in our lab and ran the case through thermal and noise testing in its out-of-the-box configuration to show how it performs compared to others. Will it make our best PC cases list? It has a chance. But before we get into the details, here are the case's specifications from Montech.
Montech King 95 3D Product Specifications
| Type | Mid-Tower | 
| Dimensions (H x L x W) | 21 x 21 x 18.8 x 11.8-inches (534 x 480 x 300mm) | 
| Motherboard Support | Mini-ITX, Micro ATX, ATX | 
| Back-connect Motherboard Support | Yes | 
| Color | Black or White | 
| Storage Support | (1) 3.5-inch (2) 2.5-inch | 
| PCIe Expansion Slots | 7 | 
| Fan Support | Top - 3x120 Front - N/A Bottom - 3x120mm Side: - 2x120mm Rear - 2x120mm | 
| Pre-installed fans | (5) Link Fan INF 120 (Reverse blades, side/bottom) (2) Link Fan INF 120 (rear) | 
| Radiator Support | Front - N/A Top - 120/240/360mm Side - 120/240mm Rear - 120mm | 
| CPU Cooler Clearance | 172mm | 
| GPU Clearance | 450mm (max, depends on config) | 
| Vertical GPU Support | No | 
| PSU Length | 220mm | 
| Dust Filters | Side and Bottom | 
| Other features | Great internal views, 7x pre-installed fans (Pro version), integrated GPU support, adjustable angle bottom fans | 
| MSRP | King 95 3D - $119.90 (w/o fans) King 95 3D Pro - $199.90 (w/7 pre-installed fans) | 
| Warranty | 1 Year | 
Features of the King 95 3D
▶️ External Features
From the outside, the King 95 3D Pro looks the part of its royal name. That signature curve and three panes of glass offer a panoramic view inside your case like few others, letting you show off your PC from even more angles. It also features a frosted, continuous LED strip running along the tiered top, right side, and bottom, adding some tasteful bling to the chassis. If you get the Pro version with the seven fans, it’s an RGB light show inside which could be polarizing. I do wish there were an option for preinstalled non-RGB fans, since the seven included ones and the infinity mirror styling may not be for everyone. Still, the curved front corner and clean lines really cement the King 95 3D as one of the better-looking panoramic cases on the market.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Up front, the removable curved glass corner with a smoked tint sets it apart from most others. On the right, the front IO panel runs vertically, with the power button on top and the LED on/off button below. It has three USB ports: one 3.2 Gen2x2 (20 Gbps) Type-C and two USB 3.2 Gen1 (5 Gbps) Type-A ports. Finally, it has a 3.5mm audio jack. That continuous 118-LED strip is visible from the front, running along the top, down the right edge, and along the bottom edge. I’m not a fan of a lot of RGB, but this implementation is tasteful. You can control this lighting through the motherboard software or Montech's Lumi software, which lets you fully customize the fans and RGB strip.
The main window panel also uses a smoke-colored tint, with Montech branding in the upper-right corner, and it's secured to the frame by two captive thumbscrews on the back. To remove it, loosen the thumbscrews, slide the panel back, pull from the top, then lift it out of the slots. Easy. I have to say, the biggest problem with all this glass is keeping it pristine and fingerprint-free.
The other (metal) side panel, behind the motherboard, slots into the frame and is secured the same way. It has filtered venting along the top and side for the fans/radiator locations, plus another area for airflow near the power supply and drive mounting locations. In the middle is a gold placard with Montech King 95 3D 10th anniversary badging. Note: The dust filters on this panel aren't removable, so you’ll need to remove the whole panel to clean things up.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
At the top, we get a better look at the third windowed panel, letting observers peer into the case from a different angle rather than straight on or from the front. We can also see the tiered top and part of the long RGB strip. Taking this panel off isn’t as simple as the rest. Yes, it’s also secured by two captive thumbscrews on the back, but to remove it, you’ll need to open the main window panel to expose a retaining screw, remove it, then loosen the back thumbscrews and slide it to the rear. After you remove the top glass, you can remove the upper and side retaining screws to take it out. When building, I didn’t find this necessary, but it’s good to know you can take it apart if needed.
Looking at the case from behind, one of the first things I noticed was the vertical PSU mounting location on the left. This space supports up to 220mm power supplies, which is all but the largest on the market. On the right, we see space for two 120mm fans, the motherboard I/O, and seven horizontal expansion slots. Unfortunately, Montech says the King 95 3D does not support vertical GPUs.
Underneath the case, there isn’t a lot going on. We get a better look at the four short rubber-bottom ‘feet’ and the removable dust filter. Montech put on its thinking cap and designed the dust filter to slide out from the front, so chances are you won’t have to move your heavy case to clean it.
▶️ Internal Features
Inside, the case uses a dual-chamber design, with the power supply and all wires hidden behind the motherboard tray. At the bottom, we see three Link Fan INF 120s (reverse blade) along with the mirror finish. The magnetically linked, daisy-chainable fans run up to 2,300 RPM (2,200 RPM on the reverse blade), pushing between 65-67 CFM with a maximum rating of 32dBA (29 dBA on the standard blade). A single Link Fan INF 120 costs $19.90, while a 3-pack (with Lumi Hub) is $64.90. If you do the math for seven fans and the Lumi Hub, it’s cheaper to buy them with the case rather than separately.
When powered on, the mirrored sides become an infinity panel, and with all seven matching, it creates a consistent view across the build. The bottom fan bracket is adjustable, with three positions (8 degrees). We left it down during testing, but with it up, you can focus more air towards the GPU and show off whatever fans you put in the space.
The motherboard tray has plenty of cutouts to access the back of the motherboard for easy installation/removal of air coolers or AIO/custom water-cooling blocks. The case also supports rear-connect ecosystems, including Asus BTF, Gigabyte Stealth, and MSI Project Zero boards. Grommets surround the motherboard tray and are in ideal locations, but like most, they pull out easily when you try to route cables, especially those with larger connectors. I wish all case vendors would secure these better, since they're a pain to reinstall, especially when the case is full of cables.
Up top, we can see the huge gap above the motherboard tray for more fans and radiators. The case cooled just fine with the seven included fans and our air cooler, though GPU temps ran a bit warmer in our noise-normalized testing. That top gap is begging to be filled with fans, even if only for aesthetics. If you plan to use an AIO cooler, this isn’t a problem, since the radiator/fans will fill the space.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
From the front, you can see the two Link INF 120mm fans and, at the bottom, the tool-less, adjustable GPU support strut. The back has space to mount two 120mm fans or one 120mm radiator. You can also see the seven horizontal expansion slots held in by thumbnail screws.
Inside, the top of the case above the motherboard space fits up to three 120mm fans or a 360mm radiator. The space is offset back from the motherboard tray, which is a boon for cable management. Normally, there’s barely any room to route the EPS cables, but here there's plenty. Just note that if your build uses air cooling, you will need to fill that area with fans to make it look good. Otherwise, it’s just a blank open space above the motherboard.
On the rear side of the chassis, we get a good look at the space behind the motherboard tray and the fan baffles. There’s plenty of room to route cables, and Montech has multiple pre-installed Velcro straps for cable routing. Even with the power supply installed, there’s plenty of room underneath it to stash excess cables.
At the bottom, we see a simple ARGB hub that consolidates the three different ARGB cables from the fans into one header to control all of them. Montech also includes a magnetic Lumi fan/RGB hub (which supports up to 13 Link Fans total) with both the Pro and non-Pro variants. Oddly, it comes loose/uninstalled on the Pro, but installed on the non-Pro. The box in the lower-right holds one 3.5-inch HDD and a single 2.5-inch drive. The second 2.5-inch drive mounts in the other location at the bottom left, next to the side fans.
We do like the look of the King 95 3D Pro case in black, and I bet it looks great in white with an all-white build too. The curved glass and 3-panel panoramic interior views are great for anyone who’d like to show off their now-ridiculously expensive parts. The included Link Fan INF 120 fans work well and run relatively quietly. If there’s an aesthetic drawback, it's that I’m not a huge fan of all the RGB and infinity mirrors on the pre-installed fans. It’s a lot, and it makes me yearn for an option with preinstalled fans and no RGB. Of course, you can turn them off in the software, or buy the non-Pro and choose whichever fans fit your build.

articles.title: TP-Link LS1210GP PoE+ switch drops to under £50 for Black Friday
articles.text:
The TP-Link LS1210GP 10-port PoE+ switch drops to £49.99 for Black Friday, saving you £33 on your next network upgrade
A straightforward switch for home and small business networks
The TP-Link LS1210GP is a solid choice for expanding a home or small business network without introducing a tangle of power adapters. With eight PoE+ ports, gigabit connectivity, and a fanless design, it can handle IP cameras, wireless access points, and other network devices.
Best For: Home and small business networks, particularly security camera installations and setups requiring several PoE-powered devices.
The Deal: Amazon.co.uk has reduced the price of the TP-Link LS1210GP from £82.99 to £49.99 for Black Friday. That's a £33 saving, or a solid 40% off.
Best TP-Link switch deal
TP-Link LS1210GP offers nine gigabit RJ45 ports, eight PoE+ connections, one SFP port, 61W total power, 250m Extend Mode, automatic PoE recovery, traffic isolation, 20Gbps switching capacity, and fanless operation.
Why we recommend it
The TP-Link LS1210GP offers nine gigabit RJ45 ports, eight of which support PoE+, alongside a gigabit SFP port for fibre connectivity. Its 20Gbps switching capacity provides enough bandwidth for multiple gigabit connections without making the switch itself an obvious bottleneck.
Each PoE+ port can deliver up to 30W, although the total power budget is limited to 61W. You can connect eight PoE devices, but you can't power all eight simultaneously at their maximum rate.
Extend Mode increases PoE transmission distance to 250 metres for surveillance installations, but this comes with a reduction in connection speed to 10Mbps on extended ports.
PoE Auto Recovery can restart unresponsive powered devices automatically, potentially saving a trip to a remotely installed camera or access point, and Isolation Mode separates traffic between connected devices.
For more of our favorites, see our guide to the best network switches we've tested.
Price context & historical value
At £49.99, the TP-Link LS1210GP currently costs £33 less than its usual £82.99 price. The combination of eight PoE+ ports, a dedicated SFP connection, and automatic device recovery makes the current price an attractive option for smaller surveillance networks.
This is the cheapest price we've seen it go for, so if you're after a network switch, we'd definitely recommend you buy it now before the price goes back up again.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the TP-Link LS1210GP if...
If you're installing several IP cameras, access points, or VoIP phones and want a quiet, straightforward gigabit switch with PoE+ support.
❌ Skip the TP-Link LS1210GP if...
If your devices collectively require more than 61W, you need 2.5Gbps networking, or you want advanced managed-switch features such as VLAN configuration via a web interface.

articles.title: ‘What we have done is not enough’: Lenskart CEO a year after IPO
articles.text:
‘What we have done is not enough’: Lenskart CEO a year after IPO
One year after Lenskart’s public listing, CEO Peyush Bansal scrapped blue-light lens upsells and pledged free glasses to 100,000 children to target India’s widespread vision accessibility crisis.
One year after debuting as a public enterprise, optical retail group Lenskart has chosen to evaluate its corporate milestone through the lens of unresolved societal challenges.
In an open statement marking the anniversary of its initial public offering, Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Peyush Bansal acknowledged that despite expanding access to affordable eyewear across India, the core objective of rendering clear vision a universal reality remains unfinished.
The company announced structural operational changes aimed at reducing financial barriers for essential eye care.
“We built a ten thousand crore company. The one thing we started it for is still unsolved,” Bansal stated.
Lenskart was established with an ambition to enable one billion people to see clearly, beginning with targeted efforts across India. The organisation currently supplies approximately 32 million eyewear units annually in India and aims to increase output to 100 million units in its next phase of expansion.
Over several years, the enterprise invested heavily in localised manufacturing capabilities to lower production costs for sophisticated optical products. These investments included developing domestic facilities for progressive lenses, which are multifocal lenses that allow smooth visual transitions across varying distances without visible dividing lines.
The firm also developed local capacity for break-resistant rimless frames and complete prescription pairs priced at Rs 500. Corporate leadership maintains that manufacturing scale serves as an operational tool to solve systemic health issues.
Addressing the rapid digitalisation of daily life in India, where nearly one billion citizens regularly engage with screens, Lenskart announced the immediate removal of extra fees for blue-light filtering coatings. Blue-light filtering lenses contain specialised protective coatings designed to minimise digital glare and eye fatigue caused by prolonged screen exposure. Under the new policy, these protective coatings will come as standard on all prescription eyewear sold by the company in India without additional charges.
Furthermore, the retailer is directing resources toward childhood vision health to combat undetected myopia, a medical term for short-sightedness that hinders clear distance vision and can impair learning outcomes. To mark National Children’s Day on, Lenskart will provide free prescription glasses featuring blue-light filtering lenses to the first 100,000 child visitors across its Indian stores, requiring families to pay only a Rs 199 fitting fee.
In retail optics, specialised lens treatments typically serve as high-margin add-ons. By making screen-ready lenses standard and funding large-scale paediatric eye health initiatives, Lenskart is likely absorbing short-term margin trade-offs in pursuit of broader consumer trust and long-term brand equity.
“Purpose and profit are not a trade-off. In the short term, the right thing for the customer rarely looks like the obvious decision. In the long term, it has worked out every single time,” Bansal noted.

articles.title: Agent substrate: how Kubernetes became the foundation for AI - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Kubernetes had settled into quiet maturity until AI blew the doors back open
Kubernetes has grown from a maturing container orchestrator into the agent substrate that enterprises are counting on to run artificial intelligence. The shift revives old security ideas such as perimeters while raising the stakes for portability across clouds.
Infrastructure providers are racing to make that foundation simpler to deploy and safer to run. Broadcom Inc. used KubeCon to unveil two open-source initiatives, and the show marks a turning point for a project that had seemed settled, according to Dilpreet Bindra (pictured), senior director of engineering in the VCF Division at Broadcom.
“There were a few that were like, Kubernetes is becoming mature, and so things were stabilizing, and they were less energy, I would say. And this KubeCon just blasts those doors wide open because Kubernetes has become the foundation for AI,” Bindra said.
Bindra spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Kubernetes has become the agent substrate and how Broadcom is adding security in depth and workload conformance to make it portable across clouds. (* Disclosure below.)
Securing the agent substrate across clouds
Agents are bringing back security concepts the cloud era had declared dead. Broadcom’s approach is security in depth, using its vDefend firewall at the network perimeter and deeper inside to cut off network access when rogue agents appear, Bindra explained.
“How do you then isolate them in a compute boundary in our vSphere Pods, which is a micro VM, so you can have a very secure runtime,” Bindra said. “You can employ things like Agent Substrate to be able to run within them.”
Portability is the other half of Broadcom’s agenda. The company is co-chairing a new working group on Kubernetes workload conformance, aiming to end the separate validations software makers run for each distribution, including VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, or VKS. It also contributed its VM API project to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, bringing virtual machines into Kubernetes as first-class citizens.
“We want Kubernetes to be Kubernetes wherever it runs in any environment,” Bindra said. “You don’t have to do individual validations of VKS, and then do individual validations of other Kubernetes distributions. You can do it as one Kubernetes.”

articles.title: Zelda : Ocarina of Time défie GTA 6 et signe un démarrage spectaculaire sur Switch 2
articles.text:
Face à l’arrivée de GTA 6 le 19 novembre, Nintendo n’a pas eu froid aux yeux en commercialisant le remake d’un de ses titres les plus emblématiques. Malgré la force de frappe de Rockstar, The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time vient de réaliser un démarrage record sur Nintendo Switch 2.
Sorti initialement sur Nintendo 64, puis sur Nintendo 3DS en 2011, The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time, considéré par beaucoup comme le meilleur opus de la franchise, a fait son grand retour le 5 novembre dernier sur Nintendo Switch 2. Malgré l’aura du titre de Big N, l’arrivée d’un jeu comme GTA 6 quelques jours plus tard aurait pu détourner l’attention des joueurs. Que nenni. Le remake a signé un démarrage impressionnant, avec plus de 5 millions d’exemplaires écoulés en seulement quatre jours. De quoi rappeler que même face à l’un des jeux les plus attendus de l’année, la légende de Zelda n’a rien perdu de sa force et de sa témérité.
Ocarina of Time déjà parmi les jeux les plus vendus de la Switch 2
Quatre jours. C’est le temps qu’il aura fallu au remake d'Ocarina of Time pour atteindre les 5,2 millions d’exemplaires vendus sur la dernière console de Nintendo. Une performance hors norme qui permet à cette refonte du classique de la Nintendo 64 de signer le meilleur démarrage jamais enregistré par un jeu Nintendo Switch 2. Le titre s’empare également de la deuxième place des jeux les plus vendus sur la console, juste derrière Mario Kart World, qui totalise déjà 16,48 millions d’unités.
Autrement dit, The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time a déjà dépassé les ventes cumulées de Donkey Kong Bananza. Pourtant disponible depuis plus d'un an, ce dernier affiche 5,05 millions d'exemplaires écoulés. Le remake de Zelda a donc réussi à le devancer en seulement quatre jours, un écart qui donne toute la mesure de son lancement.
BenQ iScreenBar : la barre lumineuse qui s’accorde avec l’iMac
Des lignes en harmonie avec celles de l’ordinateur d’Apple, une conception rigoureuse, des matériaux sélectionnés, rien n’a été laissé au hasard, tout comme le service qu’elle rend une fois allumée !
Même face à GTA 6, Zelda n’a pas tremblé
Sur les 5,2 millions d’exemplaires vendus en quatre jours, 810 000 l’ont été au Japon. Selon les estimations du journaliste Oscar Lemaire, le remake aurait déjà écoulé près de 250 000 exemplaires en version physique dans l’Hexagone. C’est presque trois fois plus que le démarrage de Call of Duty : Modern Warfare 4, et surtout le meilleur lancement en magasins français depuis la fin de l’année 2024.
Reste maintenant à voir comment Ocarina of Time résistera à l’arrivée de GTA 6. Sur ce terrain, le jeu de Rockstar part avec une longueur d’avance considérable. Selon les estimations de Sensor Tower publiées hier, il comptabilisait déjà 9,6 millions de précommandes numériques, pour près de 942 millions de dollars de revenus. Un chiffre vertigineux, qui laisse présager un lancement commercial d’une tout autre dimension.
Mais ce futur raz-de-marée ne doit pas faire oublier la performance de Zelda. Le remake a réuni 5,2 millions d’acheteurs en quatre jours, sans attendre le passage de GTA 6 pour trouver son public. Et rien ne dit que ces joueurs tourneront le dos au jeu de Rockstar. Beaucoup d’entre eux pourraient très bien avoir envie de retrouver Hyrule sur Switch 2, puis de partir à Vice City sur PS5 ou Xbox. Les deux titres ne s’adressent d’ailleurs pas nécessairement aux mêmes envies. Une chose est sûre : Ocarina of Time n’a pas tremblé face à l’ombre de GTA 6.
Source : Nintendo

articles.title: Toyota is reviving Scion with a tiny Kei pickup built in Indiana
articles.text:
Looking ahead: A section of automotive enthusiasts in the US has long been pleading with Japanese automakers to bring some of their tiny Kei cars and trucks to North America, but those requests have always been dismissed over safety and emissions concerns. This, however, is set to change next year, with Toyota confirming plans to launch the ultra-compact Scion Kei-01 pickup truck in the second half of 2027.
The Kei-01 will be built at Toyota's factory in Princeton, Indiana, which currently assembles the Highlander, Grand Highlander, Sienna Hybrid, and Lexus TX. Toyota is investing $34 million to establish new assembly operations and upgrade production and logistics infrastructure at the plant, which is expected to add around 50 new jobs.
The truck will be powered by a 660cc three-cylinder engine paired with a CVT and standard selectable four-wheel drive with an auto mode and push-button lock-up. Toyota has yet to reveal power and torque figures, but confirmed that the right-hand-drive model coming to the US will be classified as a low-speed vehicle, with its top speed restricted to just 25 mph.
The Kei-01 is also rather diminutive by American pickup standards, measuring just over 11 feet long and under five feet wide, with a three-way fold-down cargo bed rated for up to 600 pounds of payload.
Its extended cabin design with a raised roofline allows for sliding and reclining seats, plus storage space behind them. Toyota added that the truck is designed to comply with the federal safety requirements that apply to low-speed vehicles.
The Kei-01 will herald the relaunch of the Scion sub-brand that Toyota introduced in 2002 as an experimental product line for niche, quirky, and affordable cars to attract younger buyers. It will initially be sold as a fleet vehicle for commercial customers, including small business owners, farmers, municipalities, universities, and other organizations looking for efficient light trucks.
Toyota is also targeting delivery and service providers operating in urban environments, as well as outdoor enthusiasts and hobbyists wanting a versatile utility vehicle. It will be sold through a small network of authorized Scion by Toyota dealers selected from the existing Toyota dealer network, and the company is not looking at the mainstream retail market at launch.
The automaker, however, says it may consider limited retail sales down the line, depending on "market conditions, customer demand, and operational considerations." Toyota has yet to share pricing, the exact launch date, and other key details about the Kei-01, but says it will share more as plans are finalized.
Toyota's announcement comes less than a year after President Donald Trump praised Japanese Kei cars, calling them "cute" and saying he had authorized the US Secretary of Transportation to approve their production in the US, despite concerns over compliance with crash protection, lighting, and emissions standards mandated by US regulators.
Alongside the Kei-01, Toyota also showcased two concept Scion vehicles at events in Ypsilanti Township, Michigan, and Frisco, Texas.
The Scion SxS Concept is an ATV-style off-roader built as a purpose-made side-by-side and powered by a turbocharged four-cylinder hybrid powertrain making more than 300 hp, while the BKE Concept is a compact two-wheeled personal mobility concept aimed at outdoor adventure and the urban commuter market.

articles.title: Se filtra un prototipo del iPhone Air 2 y revela cómo sería el próximo celular ultradelgado de Apple
articles.text:
Apple prepara una nueva generación del iPhone Air, su celular ultradelgado, que buscaría corregir algunas de las principales críticas que recibió el primer modelo. Una fotografía de un supuesto prototipo del iPhone Air 2 comenzó a circular en internet y muestra cambios en el diseño del dispositivo, entre ellos la posible incorporación de una segunda cámara trasera y un cuerpo todavía más delgado.
La filtración fue difundida por el conocido informante Ice Universe a través de X y coincide con reportes anteriores sobre los planes de la compañía. Aunque Apple no ha confirmado la existencia del equipo ni sus características, los rumores apuntan a que el teléfono podría llegar durante la primavera, junto con otros lanzamientos de la marca, como los esperados iPhone 18 y iPhone 18e.
El nuevo modelo tendría como principal objetivo mejorar la experiencia fotográfica y la autonomía, dos aspectos que generaron cuestionamientos durante el lanzamiento de la primera generación. Sin embargo, conseguirlo representaría un desafío de ingeniería: Apple tendría que incorporar más componentes en un espacio todavía más reducido.
El iPhone Air 2 tendría dos cámaras traseras
Una de las novedades más importantes que anticipa la filtración es la presencia de dos sensores fotográficos en la parte posterior. El primer iPhone Air llegó al mercado con una única cámara trasera, una decisión que limitó las posibilidades de fotografía frente a otros celulares de gama alta.
La segunda generación buscaría cambiar esa característica mediante un sistema de doble cámara. Según las informaciones que circulan, el nuevo sensor sería un gran angular de 48 megapíxeles, que acompañaría a una cámara principal con la misma resolución.
Este componente permitiría capturar fotografías con un campo de visión más amplio, una función útil para paisajes, edificios y fotografías grupales en las que se necesita incluir más elementos sin alejarse del lugar.
Entre las especulaciones también figura la posibilidad de que la cámara principal utilice un sensor Sony IMX905, el mismo que se espera para los modelos iPhone 18 Pro. No obstante, este dato todavía no ha sido confirmado y la fotografía difundida por Ice Universe no ofrece detalles técnicos suficientes para verificarlo.
La incorporación de un segundo sensor representaría un cambio importante en la propuesta del iPhone Air 2, que buscaría combinar un diseño ligero con funciones fotográficas más completas.
Apple buscaría fabricar un celular todavía más delgado
El otro aspecto que destaca en la filtración es el grosor del dispositivo. Ice Universe sostiene que el próximo iPhone Air tendrá un cuerpo incluso más delgado que el de su antecesor, aunque no publicó una medida concreta.
El primer iPhone Air tiene un grosor de 0,56 centímetros, característica que lo convirtió en el teléfono más delgado de Apple cuando fue presentado. Actualmente, ese récord corresponde al iPhone Duo, el modelo plegable de la compañía, que alcanza los 0,52 centímetros cuando está desplegado.
Si Apple consigue reducir todavía más las dimensiones del Air 2, tendrá que resolver un desafío importante: incorporar una cámara adicional y una batería de mayor capacidad sin aumentar el tamaño del dispositivo.
Las filtraciones también señalan que el equipo podría integrar una batería de aproximadamente 3.500 mAh. Esta capacidad supondría una mejora frente a las limitaciones de autonomía que recibió el primer modelo, aunque todavía no existen datos oficiales sobre cuánto tiempo podría funcionar con una carga.
La batería será uno de los principales desafíos del iPhone Air 2
La duración de la batería fue uno de los puntos más cuestionados del primer iPhone Air. Su diseño ultradelgado obligó a distribuir los componentes internos en un espacio reducido, lo que condicionó la capacidad energética del teléfono.
Por eso, la segunda generación tendrá que demostrar que puede ofrecer una experiencia más completa sin sacrificar autonomía. No bastará con incorporar otra cámara o reducir algunos milímetros de grosor: también deberá mantener un rendimiento adecuado durante toda la jornada.
El reto para Apple será combinar una batería más grande con un sistema fotográfico más complejo y un diseño todavía más compacto. Para conseguirlo, la compañía tendría que optimizar la distribución interna de los componentes y recurrir a soluciones de miniaturización.
Por ahora, Apple no ha anunciado oficialmente el iPhone Air 2 ni ha confirmado su fecha de presentación. Las filtraciones permiten anticipar algunos de sus posibles cambios, pero será necesario esperar a un anuncio de la compañía para conocer las especificaciones definitivas, el precio y la disponibilidad del próximo celular ultradelgado.

articles.title: Ecobee to end Switch+ smart light switch features, offers compensation
articles.text:
Ecobee will end support for its Switch+ Light Switch early next year, leaving some users stuck without smart features.
Per a support page spotted by the folks over at Sunsetwatch, a monitoring service that tracks smart home products, the Switch+ will lose smart features on March 2, 2027. The Toronto-based (and now American-owned) smart home company says Switch+ will continue working as a regular light switch, but will be losing the following features:
- Ecobee app setup, control, and configuration
- Alexa voice interaction
- Third-party smart home integrations including Alexa, Google Home, SmartThings, and IFTTT, including any existing automations created through these platforms
The one exception here is Apple’s Home app, which will keep working with Switch+. Ecobee says it will continue to be available “as long as it continues to be supported by Apple.”
Switch+ units will continue to work for manual control, as will features like Smart On, Smart Off, and Nightlight, as long as customers set these features up before March 2. However, Ecobee warns that if the Switch+ gets factory reset, then those features will stop working.
After March 2, Ecobee says it will no longer be able to activate or register new Switch+ devices, and its customer support will “have limited ability to assist with Switch+ issues.”
How to get compensation
Thankfully, Switch+ users won’t be left totally out in the cold. Ecobee is offering compensation for the shutdown — Canadian users can claim a $35 Visa or Mastercard gift card for each Switch+ they have installed by completing a form on Ecobee’s website. (U.S. owners can get a US$25 gift card.) The deadline to complete the form is June 30, 2027.
Notably, those who bought a Switch+ on or after March 2, 2026, can instead file a standard warranty claim.
The Switch+ launched in March 2018, so the 2027 shutdown will mark roughly nine years of support. It retailed for around $118.
Source: Ecobee

articles.title: Who could replace Jensen Huang? A highly unscientific list of possible successors | TechCrunch
articles.text:
It’s almost inconceivable that Nvidia would fire its rock star CEO. Yet here we are, on the precipice of this happening. Over at Kalshi, Jensen Huang’s odds of surviving the week are sitting at a lowly 30%. Even though he built one of the world’s most valuable — and, many would argue, dangerously powerful — companies, the tides have completely turned against him. He has confessed to an extramarital affair, but as of Wednesday afternoon it isn’t even clear whom he meant: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for her country, or Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reports to him and who, five sources told The New York Times in an explosive new report, was also a paramour.
Even if Huang is pushed out as CEO, the board members he has made very rich are unlikely to cut him loose entirely. Barring another shoe dropping, they could keep him on as chairman, a role Nvidia doesn’t currently have. But someone still has to run the company, and there’s no apparent succession plan, which leaves us, like everyone else, to speculate while we wait to see what happens next. While Huang’s 60 direct reports undoubtedly get a closer look, consider this our own parlor game, featuring some obvious and less obvious candidates:
Lisa Su. The AMD CEO runs Nvidia’s most credible rival, as well as a distant cousin of Huang. The Information floated her name this week, but why would she leave her job for his? Her company stands to benefit from every day that Nvidia spends distracted by an investigation, congressional briefings, and all the mini dramas that are sure to follow. Her best move might be to send a nice note and keep her current corner office.
Eric Schmidt. He was the pick of Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, who we talked with earlier this week. Schmidt could “parachute in tomorrow and do a very good job,” Sonnenfeld said, and perhaps he could. He ran Google from 2001 to 2011, chaired the National Security Commission on AI from 2018 to 2021, and now runs the rocket company Relativity Space. Chips, software, government, rockets — it’s an impressive range. Then again, Schmidt would bring a lot of baggage when it comes to his own extramarital dalliances. It’s hard to see him clearing the board for that reason.
Lip-Bu Tan. Intel’s CEO knows chips, and right now he might welcome a very soft landing. Last month, Intel reported third-quarter revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, then warned its fourth-quarter results would fall short of Wall Street’s forecasts. The AI boom has caused a memory-chip shortage, pushing up PC prices and cutting PC sales. That’s hurt Intel (PC chips are a big part of its business), and its stock plunged 20% in after-hours trading on the warning, having already slid more than 30% since September. A move to a company that’s eating everyone’s lunch would be a pretty amazing escape hatch.
Bret Taylor. The former Salesforce co-CEO and OpenAI board chair now runs the AI startup Sierra, and his resume includes a lot of the biggest brands in Silicon Valley. He co-created Google Maps, served as Facebook’s CTO, and chaired Twitter’s board through its sale to Elon Musk. He then took over as OpenAI’s board chair after the “Blip,” Sam Altman’s firing and fast return. When companies need an unflappable, likable adult in the room, they call Taylor. He probably knows nearly every customer Nvidia has, too.
Ian Buck. If the board feels strongly about having a “builder” at the helm, they could do worse than the Nvidia VP who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia’s dominance in AI. Analysts and former employees have floated him as a possible successor, and Kalshi traders give him a middling shot. He’s no household name, but the Stanford PhD seems more viable if Huang can can keep that chairman title and push for a successor he can work with.
Someone else down the hall. Andrew Bell, Nvidia’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, arrived 25 years ago as a fresh Cornell grad and has been on an upward trajectory at the company ever since. Like Buck and dozens of other executives who are presumably being scrutinized, he reports directly to Huang. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is the insider most often named, but analysts say she isn’t necessarily a natural successor as an innovator and visionary, and Bell has the chip pedigree.
The wild card? Lori Huang. Nobody has floated her, but hear us out: Jensen met his wife as lab partners at Oregon State, so she has been working with him since before Nvidia existed. After graduating, she worked at Silicon Graphics as a micro chip engineer (making more money than her husband, he has said), then scaled back to raise the couple’s family, and she now co-leads the family trusts. If the board wants continuity, they could do worse than a humbler Huang who is also a brainiac. There’s a reason they say that behind every great man is a great woman (and vice versa).
Whatever happens next, we’ll know soon.

articles.title: Nintendo unleashes DMCA takedown wave against open-source Switch modchip firmware, 144 tools disabled — Picofly, SX Core, and HWFLY among casualties following criminal trial victory
articles.text:
Nintendo unleashes DMCA takedown wave against open-source Switch modchip firmware, 144 tools disabled — Picofly, SX Core, and HWFLY among casualties following criminal trial victory
Even open-source isn't safe from Nintendo's legal team
Nintendo has set its famously litigious sights on the open-source firmware that powers hardware modchips on Nintendo Switch. Earlier this week, GitHub posted a DCMA request from Nintendo of America confirming that an entire network of 144 total repositories, including the parent repository, was taken down. Mod chip firmware for hardware including SX Core, SX Lite, Picofly, and HWFLY was targeted.
Early original Nintendo Switch consoles shipped with an unpatchable hardware exploit found in the device's recovery mode, which has since been patched in later units such as the Switch Lite and Switch OLED (the modchip hack doesn't work on Switch 2). As such, running custom software on patched Switches requires hardware modification, soldering a microchip like a Picofly, HWFLY, or SX Core to your Switch's motherboard. These chips require firmware, specifically code that can perform the voltage glitching required during boot to hack the Switch.
Rather than playing whack-a-mole with vendors of off-the-shelf microcontrollers, Nintendo has instead issued a DCMA takedown notice to the entire family of GitHub repos hosting this firmware. "The reported repositories offer, link to, or otherwise provide access to mod chip firmware including but not limited to SX Core, SX Lite, Picofly, or HWFLY," the DCMA request from Nintendo reads. "The firmware allows Nintendo Switch modchips to illegally circumvent Nintendo’s TPMs in order to run illegal copies of Nintendo Switch games. Specifically, during operation, the mod chip firmware at the reported repositories circumvents the technological protection measures put in place on the Nintendo Switch console by bypassing the boot sequence.
Nintendo went on to state that because these repositories are designed "primarily" to unlawfully circumvent technological measures controlling access to work protected under the DCMA, distributing mod chip firmware "constitutes unlawful trafficking in technology that is 'primarily designed or produced for the purpose of circumventing a technological measure that effectively controls access' to copyrighted works." In support of this argument, Nintendo cited criminal proceedings brought by the US Department of Justice against Team-Xecuter, a maker and seller of SX Pro, SX Core, and SX Lite modchips.
While these modchips can be (and are) used for game piracy, they unlock a host of features including running homebrew and custom applications, emulation, alternative operating systems, and more. They also enable game modding, custom themes, and even Switch overclocking. Naturally, Nintendo has chosen to focus on their utility in accessing pirated games and bypassing DRM.
Because much of this hardware and firmware is already out in the wild, the move won't have any impact on existing Switch owners who have a modchip installed. However, this will prevent firmware updates to existing modchips, as well as firmware flashing and reflashing. Naturally, it will also prevent future potential hardware modders from hacking their Switch in the same way.
Nintendo is famous for its fervent prosecution of copyright law, but developments in AI are turning this into a drastically more complicated battle. Nintendo's Zelda remake was dumped online on the same day it launched on Switch 2, while earlier this year one developer used AI to bring the original Nintendo 64 version to iOS. In July, Mario Kart Wii was recompiled for PC in 4K with over 200 tracks.

articles.title: Google Wallet: So kannst du künftig deine Haustür mit der App entsperren
articles.text:
Google Wallet: So kannst du künftig deine Haustür mit der App entsperren
Erst vor einigen Wochen hat Google zahlreiche Neuerungen für die Wallet-App angekündigt. Darüber können User:innen etwa seither Quittungen einscannen und abspeichern. Jetzt folgt schon die nächste Neuerung, wie das Unternehmen in einer Ankündigung schreibt. Preview-User:innen können aktuell ein Feature ausprobieren, mit dem sie ihre Haustüren über Google Wallet entsperren können.
Google Wallet: So können Haustüren entsperrt werden
Das ist möglich, indem die Wallet-App mit kompatiblen Smartlocks kommuniziert. Im Grunde können User:innen also einen digitalen Zugang in ihrem Smartphone speichern und den physischen Schlüssel zu Hause lassen. Wenn sie die Tür wieder entsperren wollen, müssen sie lediglich das Smartphone außen an das Smartlock oder ein Keypad halten und schon schließt sich das Schloss selbstständig auf.
Diese beschriebene Variante nutzt NFC am Android-Smartphone, um mit dem Smartlock kommunizieren zu können. Hat das Smartphone auch noch einen Ultrabreitbandsender, kann auch die zweite Entsperrmethode genutzt werden. Dadurch sendet das Smartphone schon aus größerer Entfernung den Befehl, die Tür aufzuschließen. Kommst du also mit Einkäufen in den Händen zurück, wird die Tür automatisch geöffnet und du kannst einfach hineingehen.
So praktisch das Feature auch ist: Um es nutzen zu können, müssen einige Voraussetzungen erfüllt sein. Für die NFC-Entsperrmethode gibt Google ein Smartphone mit Android 9 oder höher vor. Für das Entsperren aus der Ferne muss der UWB-Sender den Aliro-Standard unterstützen. Google nennt hier als kompatible Smartphones die eigenen Pixel-10-Pro-Geräte und aktuellere Modelle sowie ausgewählte Samsung-Galaxy-Smartphones.
Zu guter Letzt musst du aber auch noch ein kompatibles Smartlock besitzen. Zum Launch des Features unterstützt die Google Wallet vorerst nur das Aqara 400, das Schlage Sense Pro und das Nuki Keypad 2 NFC. Das Aqara-Modell kann direkt mit NFC und UWB entsperrt werden. Beim Schlage-Gerät wird UWB nachgereicht, während das Nuki-Smartlock auf NFC beschränkt bleibt. Google betont, dass die Funktion aktuell noch von Preview-User:innen ausgetestet werden soll. In den kommenden Wochen soll das Entsperren dann aber für alle Wallet-Nutzer:innen ausgerollt werden.

articles.title: Anduril says its first satellite can see adversaries maneuver in orbital night
articles.text:
Anduril Industries has announced the successful demonstration of a new satellite-based sensor designed to track other spacecraft that may be hiding their maneuvers in Earth’s shadow.
Funded with Anduril’s internal capital, the company’s oven-sized satellite launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission in July with a package of tech demo payloads: an edge-compute processor, a power-management system adaptable to different mission types, and a long-wave infrared space sensor capable of detecting other objects in orbit.
Anduril reported on the success of the tech demo mission Tuesday. The company’s satellite, named Anduril-216, flies about 590 km (366 mi) above Earth, spending about one-third of each orbit in darkness. Anduril-216’s night passes allow its infrared imager to shine.
“This is a unique sensor that allows us to take imagery in long-wave [infrared],” said Gokul Subramanian, Anduril’s senior vice president of engineering. “What’s unique about that is it’s got a huge dynamic range. It has very low solar exclusion, so we’re blocked by the Sun very rarely, and we can see things in full dark.”
Filling a gap
The US military and a growing number of commercial data providers use a network of radars and optical sensors on the ground and in space to monitor satellite traffic. Anduril acquired one of the commercial satellite-tracking companies, ExoAnalytic Solutions, earlier this year. But there’s a gap in optical tracking as satellites fly in Earth’s shadow, so space traffic monitors could temporarily lose track of a spacecraft if it performs a maneuver in orbital night.
The Space Force is charged with tracking satellites for two primary reasons. First, military commanders want to know if an adversary moves its satellite in a threatening manner. Second, the Space Force issues traffic alerts to global satellite operators if there’s a risk of a collision.
“Right now, we don’t have ground sensors in our adversaries’ sovereign lands, and then in the eclipse period where we are relying heavily on visible sensors, the satellites that are not illuminated by the Sun, we can’t see those,” said Adam Thurn, vice president and general manager of orbital systems at Anduril. “With the long-wave infrared space sensor, we’re looking to close that gap.”

articles.title: Women in tech are reporting higher levels of burnout than ever before — with AI, office attendance and visibility issues all blamed
articles.text:
Women in tech are reporting higher levels of burnout than ever before — with AI, office attendance and visibility issues all blamed
Office attendance, visibility, and pressures around AI productivity among the causes
- Burnout is affecting a concerning 87% of women working in tech, new report finds
- Demand for new AI productivity skills, attendance and visibility, and personal priorities are contributing to the burnout
- 1,500 female-identifying technology professionals surveyed for 2026 Speak Up report
A new survey examining the roles of women working in the tech industry has uncovered a concerning trend: burnout.
Surveying 1,500 female-identifying tech professionals, the 2026 Speak Up report found a worrying 87% said that they were experiencing burnout, with over half considering themselves to be either moderately, very, or extremely burned out.
Various pressures are identifies, but AI has introduced a new dimension to the role of women in tech, contributing to changing expectations and driving that feeling of burnout.
Speak up
The report from Ensono explores how improved AI-driven productivity in the workplace is producing increased pressure on tech-employed women.
AI knowledge and skills among 70% of the subjects is considered to be advanced or expert, with 97% able to identify at least on career benefit from using the technology. But the impact of using AI is one of the elements that have been cited as contributing to burnout. 42% of those surveyed feel that using AI comes with an expectation that more work can be produced in less time.
Furthermore, 34% of the women surveyed felt pressure to be always available for work and 43% were focused on constantly developing new skills for work.
Throw in the drive to be visible and to make a mark – 83% aspire to executive leadership roles – and there is a vast amount of pressure to succeed and to be seen doing so.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Building lasting careers
Burnout is avoidable, of course, with the right workplace policies and clearer expectations for colleagues. AI, visibility, leadership – they’re all challenges, but they do not have to dominate the working day.
Meredith Graham, Ensono’s Chief People Officer, said “Women in technology are developing the AI expertise their organizations need, but continued learning takes time to adjust. With skills confidence continuing to grow, business leaders need to provide clarity on how AI adoption changes work expectations.”
The arrival of AI has disrupted many elements of life and work, evolving expectations in the workplace, and these results suggests employers can do more to protect team members from burnout.
Graham added: “As roles evolve, supporting flexibility and different paths to advancement that help women build lasting careers is fundamental to strengthening business culture.”

He currently heads up the team at smart home website Matter Alpha, and writes about retro gaming at Gaming Retro.
