articles.title: Cognichip reveals how its new AI-assisted program can slash chip design times from months to days — automating labor-intensive tasks cuts design time down, Chief Product Officer explains
articles.text:
Cognichip reveals how its new AI-assisted program can slash chip design times from months to days — automating labor-intensive tasks cuts design time down, Chief Product Officer explains
We speak to Cognichip's Chief Product Officer, Stelios Diamantidis, about its new AI products
Amid the AI gold rush, one particularly fruitful vein of research is the emergence of AI-assisted workflows in electronic design automation (EDA) tools like Cadence Maestro. One such company developing such foundational models is Cognichip, which in September launched Artificial Chip Intelligence (ACI), proprietary AI models developed specifically for semiconductor engineering. ACI deploys the 'industry’s largest training dataset' across semiconductor physics and chip design principles.
ACI Enterprise is Cognichip's deployable platform, which combines these specialized models with agentic workflows, project memory, and computing infrastructure for AI inference. The company describes ACI's approach as a self-learning flywheel, a continuously evolving design environment that brings together specifications, register-transfer level (RTL), and verification results to build a design that meets power, performance, and area (PPA) targets to Pareto limits. We sat down with Cognichip to learn more.
"We have surpassed, I think, over ten million training samples in our datasets that are either things that we designed ourselves directly or things that have been generated through our synthetic technology," says Stelios Diamantidis, Chief Product Officer at Cognichip, in an interview with Tom's Hardware Premium. "We have invented new ways of creating synthetic training samples for semiconductor design. And very importantly, now that we have all these data samples, characterized data samples, we also had to invent new models so that we can capture the data, and we also had to invent new pipelines for training so that we can map the training data to the models themselves."
A self-learning flywheel
Cognichip says ACI can analyze specifications, explore microarchitectural options, generate RTL, verify designs, identify and fix functional problems, and optimize designs to meet PPA targets. The system can also integrate existing IP modules and even produce FPGA implementations. In principle, ACI enables engineers to focus on product requirements and architectural decisions while ACI handles much of the logic implementation and verification work.
"Build the spec, build the RTL, estimate PPA, perform optimizations, run verification, everything," Diamantidis told us while explaining how ACI can develop and evaluate multiple architectural alternatives before engineers select the preferred design. "We do not try to turn the designer into a verification engine; our system is self-verified, so we want the designer to design, and we want our system not only to do the tasks but also verify them."
Because ACI operates as a self-learning flywheel, Cognichip claims engineers can revisit earlier architectural decisions and modify their designs without restarting the entire development process from scratch.
"Architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, all abstractions in the cognitive system are aligned, so the change in microarchitecture is essentially automatically reflected in RTL, and vice versa," Diamantidis explained. "Changes in RTL are automatically reflected in microarchitecture."
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Cognichip says it has participated in more than 40 customer engagements, including projects at Renesas and SiTime. According to the company, these engagements span a wide range of chip designs, from microcontrollers and encryption engines to networking processors, RISC-V CPUs, and AI accelerators.
To illustrate ACI's capabilities, Cognichip points to an evaluation conducted with an unnamed leading fabless semiconductor company. The customer provided an existing 55-page microarchitecture specification, which ACI used to explore architecture options, develop RTL from scratch, and integrate middleware and other components. The system also generated SystemVerilog testbenches, ran simulations, identified and corrected errors, and achieved functional verification closure with over 90% UVM coverage, the company claims. According to Cognichip, the entire process took just 10 days and required only one engineer. By contrast, doing the same job using conventional methods would require a full front-end design team and approximately 20 weeks, Cognichip says.
However, there are several important caveats. First up, the customer had already provided a detailed 55-page microarchitecture specification, so the platform did not begin with a blank sheet. Secondly, Cognichip has not disclosed the complexity of the design, which makes it difficult to assess how much work has been done (or rather, processed). Finally, the reported acceleration applies to front-end engineering rather than the entire chip development process, which also includes physical implementation, tape-out, manufacturing, and silicon validation.
Making very educated guesses/predictions
There is a substantial difference between developing functionally, conducting verified RTL, and prepping a chip design for manufacturing. Although Cognichip's ACI can develop microarchitectures, generate RTL, and optimize designs for PPA, the platform does not perform physical implementation. Tasks such as floorplanning, placement and routing, clock-tree synthesis, physical verification, and signoff still require conventional electronic design automation (EDA) tools from companies like Cadence, Synopsys, and Siemens EDA.
"Today we do not do physical implementation," Diamantidis said. "So, place and route […] is done outside of our system."
This distinction matters because an architecture that meets its estimated PPA targets may fail to achieve them after physical implementation. For example, a design expected to operate at 1 GHz while consuming 15 W could achieve only 800 MHz at 20 W once engineers account for interconnect delays, clock distribution, buffering requirements, congestion, and other physical effects. Such discrepancies can require changes to RTL or even fundamental architectural elements, followed by another round of verification and physical implementation. In some cases, these iterations can consume weeks or months of engineering time.
"That cycle is very expensive in terms of time," Diamantidis said. "Because you are crossing design boundaries, and you are running very long runtimes and all that."
Cognichip claims that ACI can reduce these costly iterations by predicting the physical consequences of architectural decisions before implementation begins. According to Diamantidis, the company has trained its models on internally developed and characterized semiconductor designs, which enables ACI to estimate PPA characteristics and identify potential architectural trade-offs during front-end development.
"We have trained models with full physical stack visibility understanding so that the models can predict the PPA during the front-end design phase." "We can identify those trade-offs before going to physical implementation."
For example, ACI could recommend replacing two independent FIFOs with a single time-multiplexed FIFO to reduce power consumption at the expense of performance. Diamantidis used this hypothetical scenario to illustrate how the platform can evaluate architectural alternatives before engineers commit to a particular implementation.
"If you want to save power here at the cost of 10% of frequency, take these two FIFOs that you have for two different tasks, merge them, make one FIFO, and then time multiplex the two functions over one FIFO," Diamantidis explained.
Cognichip claims that ACI can estimate not only the immediate PPA consequences of such changes but also their potential impact on physical implementation.
"These trade-offs become visible now because we can tell the designer essentially in real time what some of these impacts are going to be to downstream parasitics and downstream congestion and all those kinds of effects."
The general idea behind ACI is to resolve potential architectural problems before RTL reaches physical design engineers rather than wait for implementation results and revise the architecture afterward.
"Our expectation is that there will be no loopbacks to the designer in terms of 'let us do this again because we did not meet this goal or because we ran into congestion issues,'" said Diamantidis.
However, the accuracy of these predictions is critical. Cognichip claims its models can predict certain PPA characteristics with errors of approximately 10% relative to results obtained from conventional EDA tools at the pre-route stage of physical implementation.
Cognichip evaluated its technology using 1,200 open-source designs and compared its predictions with those produced by general-purpose AI models, including Anthropic's Claude Opus and Google's Gemini. According to him, general-purpose models produced errors of approximately 50% – 100%, depending on the metric, whereas Cognichip's models reduced prediction errors to around 10%.
"[General purpose models] do not do well when it comes to predicting delays," Diamantidis said. "So, we take that down to within 10%. Again, 10% because think about it, we are running it at RTL. We do not have much physical information at all, right?"
There is an important distinction, though. Cognichip's reported accuracy refers to pre-route physical implementation results, not final post-route characteristics. Actual routing introduces interconnect and power delivery parasitics as well as other physical effects that can alter timing and power consumption. Consequently, the reported 10% prediction error does not necessarily mean that ACI-generated designs will achieve their estimated PPA targets after physical implementation and signoff.
Another question concerns the range of architectures and manufacturing technologies for which ACI can deliver such accuracy. Although Cognichip says its models incorporate semiconductor physics and account for process-dependent characteristics, it has not disclosed which foundry nodes it supports or how prediction accuracy varies across them.
Diamantidis explained that some architectural decisions are largely independent of manufacturing technology, whereas others become increasingly dependent on the target process node as development progresses.
"[Think about chip development as a tree], at the top of the tree, there are decisions that are not really foundry-specific; they are closer to microarchitecture," he explained. "Then, of course, as you start working your way down the tree, at some point you branch off because the decision may be targeted towards the TSMC node A versus TSMC node B, which will result in different prediction things. But there is a big trunk of decisions that are not really related to the node and are more related to the architecture and the way that the architecture is implemented. What we try to do is we try to think of this whole tree and provide a lot of feedback to designers, especially in a node-agnostic mode, and then, of course, at some point we have to become more node-aware."
This distinction is exceedingly important for complex CPUs, GPUs, and AI accelerators, where physical constraints tend to have substantial impact on architectural decisions. Meanwhile, Cognichip does not claim that ACI must develop such processors as monolithic designs. Instead, the company says its technology can work with individual IP blocks and subsystems, which engineers can subsequently integrate into larger chips. Of course, integration of these individually optimized IP blocks into larger chips is a challenge.
Big chip? Not a problem, but there is a caveat
Although Cognichip says ACI can handle subsystems containing millions of logic gates (i.e., circuits that implement Boolean functions), combining multiple such designs into a complex SoC introduces additional constraints related to interconnect delays, clock distribution, shared memory bandwidth, power delivery, and floorplanning. Consequently, an architecture that achieves Pareto-optimal PPA characteristics as a standalone subsystem may no longer be optimal once integrated into a larger chip. According to Cognichip, ACI can account for these system-level interactions by aligning and optimizing individual blocks against global SoC and subsystem constraints.
“Yes, ACI can align and optimize individual blocks to global SoC and subsystem constraints. It can be applied to both flat and hierarchical optimization problems,” Diamanditis said.
Cognichip is not proposing a fundamentally new SoC development methodology, but rather automating substantial portions of conventional front-end workflows. Its ACI platform supports both flat and hierarchical optimization and can drive the partitioning and propagation of design constraints from the top level to individual blocks. According to Cognichip, ACI can decompose system-level constraints into requirements for individual components and then re-aggregate them as the blocks are integrated.
“ACI does not require a flat design methodology; it can drive hierarchical design from the top or subsystem-top down, ensuring that constraints are decomposed going into components but then re-aggregated when blocks are integrated,” Diamanditis explained.
According to Cognichip, ACI can handle individual IP blocks and subsystems containing millions of logic gates, which can subsequently be combined hierarchically into larger SoCs. The company emphasizes that the complexity of individual partitions, rather than their size, determines how effectively ACI can handle them. However, it remains to be seen how effectively ACI can coordinate architectural decisions and optimize PPA across an entire complex SoC in practice. After all, a Pareto-optimal CPU core, memory controller, and interconnect do not necessarily form a Pareto-optimal SoC, as their interactions introduce additional timing, bandwidth, power, and physical constraints.
Then again, developers of complex SoCs already address these challenges with hierarchical design methodologies, system-level optimization, and integration, so ACI’s focus on individual subsystems does not necessarily represent a significant limitation.
Feedback loops? No need for them!
One of the questions that normally occurs when we talk about a tool that is only aimed at the front end of chip development is how it can handle feedback loops from physical implementation (more on this later). Such feedback loops occur when placement and routing reveal problems with timing, power consumption, die area, or routing congestion that cannot be resolved through physical design optimizations alone. In more serious cases, engineers must revise RTL, pipelines, memory hierarchies, or other architectural elements, which requires another round of functional verification, synthesis, and physical implementation. These iterations can take plenty of time and involve multiple engineering teams, which makes them particularly expensive.
Cognichip says ACI can use physical implementation results to revise RTL and microarchitecture if necessary, although this is not the company's primary focus. Instead, it aims to prevent costly iterations between front-end and back-end design teams by predicting potential problems before physical implementation begins.
"We are still focused very much on what we can do in the front end to prevent these situations rather than fix them."
If physical implementation reveals problems that require changes to RTL or microarchitecture, engineers can return to ACI with the relevant feedback (Cognichip does not specify with which file format that feedback must be submitted) and use the platform to revise their designs. Yet, ACI cannot resolve issues that require changes to the physical implementation itself, such as clock-tree synthesis or placement and routing.
"They can come back to our environments to provide additional guidance, additional prompting, additional information," Diamantidis said. "Then based on that information, we can of course perform an adaptation of the design […] if the issue can be addressed in the design itself, then of course we can do that."
Since feedback loops are expensive, yet necessary parts of semiconductor chip development flow, I had to ask that question explicitly, and the answer was that there would be no need for feedback loops with ACI. As the question and response require a lot of minutiae, we've added them in full below.
Anton Shilov: Can ACI ingest physical implementation reports from Cadence, Synopsys, or Siemens EDA tools, identify architectural bottlenecks, revise the microarchitecture, and RTL, and repeat the process until the design meets its PPA targets?
Stelios Diamantidis: Actually, this is where we depart from conventional approaches. We do not need to wait until physical implementation to identify these issues. We have trained models with full physical-stack visibility, which enables them to predict PPA during the front-end design phase.
For example, suppose you have one design that operates at a certain frequency and consumes a certain amount of power, and another that runs perhaps 20% slower but consumes significantly less power. We can identify these trade-offs before physical implementation.
Ultimately, the changes you want to make involve RTL and design constraints. Traditionally, engineers develop the RTL and constraints and hand them over to the physical implementation team. That team implements the design and reports the results. If the design fails to meet its targets, the front-end team must make changes, and the process starts again.
These iterations are very expensive in terms of time because they cross design boundaries and involve tools with long runtimes.
By training our models on the full physical stack, we can now provide immediate feedback to front-end designers. For example, we might tell an engineer: 'If you want to reduce power consumption at the cost of 10% of your frequency, take two FIFOs that serve different functions, combine them into one, and time-multiplex the two functions over that FIFO.'
That is just one example of a microarchitectural decision. We can make these trade-offs visible to designers in essentially real time because our models can predict their impact on downstream parasitics, routing congestion, and other physical characteristics.
As a result, engineers can make these decisions in a closed loop during front-end development. Once they have resolved the microarchitectural trade-offs and produced well-structured RTL, they can hand the design over to the physical implementation team. Of course, the design still has to go through physical implementation tools.
Our expectation is that there will be no need to return the design to the front-end team because it failed to meet its targets or encountered congestion problems. That is the fundamental change we aim to bring to the transition between front-end and back-end chip development.
Third Party IP? No problem
Modern SoCs typically combine proprietary logic with third-party IP, including processor cores, memory controllers, interface IP, and other reusable components. However, developers do not necessarily have access to the RTL of licensed IP blocks, and licensing agreements may restrict how such information can be used. This raises the question of how ACI can integrate third-party IP without access to its internal implementation.
According to Cognichip, this is not a problem. ACI does not need to examine proprietary RTL to integrate an existing IP block into a larger design. Such IPs provide relevant interface specifications, including pin connections, signals, and their characteristics. ACI can then proceed with necessary integration logic and connect the IP to other subsystems.
"Most people want to take […] third-party licensed IP and optimize the integration of the IP," claims Diamantidis. "We ourselves do not ingest the guts of the IPs, nor do we try to train on any kind of data related to the IPs."
The CPO of Cognichip stressed that ACI Enterprise protects customers' IP within the company's firewalled data centers and prevents it from entering third-party AI training pipelines. The platform provides customer-controlled access to sensitive information, multi-tenant isolation, and security controls validated through a SOC 2 Type II examination. However, these protections do not supersede the licensing restrictions imposed by third-party IP providers.
A new offering
Cognichip's ACI technology could substantially improve chip development productivity by automating labor-intensive tasks such as architectural exploration, RTL development, verification, and PPA optimization.
The company's benchmark with a major chip designer suggests that the potential gains could be considerable, although the complexity of the project remains undisclosed. Such capabilities could be particularly valuable for startups and newcomers to the semiconductor industry, which tend to lack engineering resources and extensive IP portfolios of established chipmakers. By reducing the time, costs, and expertise required to develop custom silicon, ACI could lower the barriers to entry and enable smaller companies to pursue a custom silicon strategy that would otherwise be prohibitively expensive.
However, Cognichip has yet to demonstrate autonomous development of a complete, physically validated chip, let alone a sophisticated CPU or GPU. The company does not perform physical implementation, and its expectations of eliminating costly feedback loops depend on the accuracy of its PPA predictions. It also remains to be seen how effectively ACI can optimize complex SoCs that combine numerous proprietary and third-party IP blocks under common power, performance, and area constraints.
Ultimately, the Cognichip technology's value for leading-edge chip developers will depend not only on how quickly it can produce verified RTL, but also on how closely its predictions match the results of physical implementation and how much engineering work it can eliminate across the entire development cycle.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Google DeepMind releases new advanced robotics AI model and next-generation gene prediction model - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Google DeepMind releases new advanced robotics AI model and next-generation gene prediction model
Alphabet Inc.’s artificial intelligence research lab, Google DeepMind, Tuesday debuted the next generation of Gemini Robotics, the company’s most capable vision-language-action model to date for creating an “AI brain” for robotics.
Separately, DeepMind announced AlphaGenome 2 today, a next-generation AI model that can predict how DNA sequences and their variations affect human cell types, creating a powerful biological tool for fighting disease and drug development.
DeepMind said Gemini Robotics 2.5 enhances dexterity, reliability and safety to help engineers bring robots out of the lab and into dynamic, unstructured, real-world environments where they can coordinate alongside humans.
The company said that with the release of Gemini 4 Argon, the research division has been able to accelerate robot research and reach into physical AI. The new robotics AI model was tested across over 200 distinct tasks and the company said it anticipates scaling even further.
Argon, the company’s frontier artificial intelligence large language model, rolled out in late September, bringing advanced reasoning to the enterprise. Using the capabilities behind this new, flagship model, DeepMind said it allowed Gemini Robotics 2.5 to increase the breadth and speed with which robots can learn new skills and apply them to real-world scenarios.
The 2.5 version makes a significant jump in optimization and performance across three key areas. Boosted dexterity means robots running on 2.5 can perform more tasks with greater accuracy, including using everyday tools to handle delicate, flexible objects. With increased reliability, the new model successfully packed automotive parts with a 96% success rate during real-world proof-of-concept tests at Mercedes-Benz. Finally, DeepMind enhanced safety with improved physical steerability and introduced a new benchmark for testing against jailbreaks.
In evaluations, Robotics 2.5 now achieves a 30% to 100% success rate depending on the task and completes tasks 20% to 30% faster compared with the previous version’s baseline.
The company said that, like previous models, it natively works with many different types of robots, including Apptronik Inc.’s Apollo 2 humanoid robots and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered parallel grippers.
“This is what we built Apollo for: useful work alongside people in real industrial settings,” Apptronik co-founder and Chief Executive Jeff Cardenas said. “Pairing Apollo 2 with Gemini Robotics, we saw the models improve dramatically in just a few weeks of post-training and carry over to Mercedes-Benz production with very little drop-off.”
Gemini Robotics 2.5 is rolling out today via DeepMind’s robotics partners, including Agile Robots SE, Apptronik and Boston Dynamics Inc.
AlphaGenome 2, bridging single-cell biology and human genetics
AI models such as AlphaGenome help drug development and biotechnology companies turn genetic data into testable leads. By predicting how DNA changes affect gene activity and which cells in the body those changes act in, they can guide researchers to promising drug targets and help prioritize experiments.
Announced today, AlphaGenome 2 adds finer detail about specific cell types and states, potentially revealing disease-related effects that broader tissue-level models miss. These predictions guide research rather than replace experimental validation; the model is not approved for clinical or diagnostic use.
The problem researchers face is that every cell in the body carries the same DNA; however, different genes are activated at different times to differentiate cells and adjust their behavior. For example, a heart muscle cell or an immune cell fighting an infection may have the same DNA, but they use the blueprint to produce different proteins, enzymes and other tools to do their job.
DeepMind used global efforts from the Human Cell Atlas, a scientific consortium that mapped gene expression in millions of cells, to give the world an unprecedented view of how different cells use genes. However, predicting the paths and variations that drive activation and expression changes remains a major challenge.
Professor Sarah Teichmann, co-founder of the Human Cell Atlas and professor of Stem Cell Medicine at the University of Cambridge, said what makes Alphagenome 2 so powerful is “how it adapts directly to new single-cell data without retraining, predicting how DNA variants act in newly profiled cell states,” and that it can adapt even from very small samples.
According to DeepMind, the new model can predict core experimental readouts of DNA function as the previous generation, including gene expression, histone modification and chromatin accessibility – but also adds DNA methylation, which is a significant part of epigenetics, which explains how behaviors, environment and life experiences can influence gene activity.

articles.title: La grogne s’intensifie : la Norvège met un immense coup de frein aux data centers
articles.text:
La Norvège vient de mettre en pause les nouveaux raccordements de data centers à son réseau électrique. Une décision qui change la donne pour les géants de la tech dans les pays nordiques, jusqu’alors perçus comme un eldorado.
Car ces pays disposent d’avantages très alléchants. En Norvège, par exemple, l’électricité vient presque entièrement de barrages hydroélectriques : elle est propre et moins chère qu’ailleurs en Europe. Le climat froid attire également puisqu’il aide à refroidir les serveurs, ce qui est essentiel pour leur bon fonctionnement.
D’ailleurs, OpenAI prépare un gigantesque centre de données dans le cadre de son projet Stargate, preuve de l’attrait de cette région. Mais les autorités ont décidé de mettre le holà.
Le réseau électrique norvégien croule sous la demande
En effet, ce 9 novembre Statnett, le gestionnaire du réseau électrique norvégien, a annoncé suspendre les nouvelles réservations de raccordement pour les data centers. Une mesure qui doit durer jusqu’au 1er août 2027 au plus tard et surtout, qui ne touche pas les sites déjà connectés ou ceux dont les exigences techniques sont validées.
Les chiffres sont probants. Aujourd’hui, 800 mégawatts (MW) de data centers sont raccordés, tandis que 4 200 MW sont réservés, 9 100 MW attendent dans la file et 18 000 MW sont demandés. Or, la consommation nationale plafonne à un peu plus de 25 000 MW, et les centres de données représentent trois quarts des nouvelles requêtes reçues cette année. Et pour couronner le tout, leur consommation a déjà quadruplé en trois ans.
Dans ce contexte, Statnett invoque la sécurité du système : le fournisseur doit encore définir comment ces sites réagiront en cas de panne ou de variation brutale de leur consommation. De même, la Norvège produit aujourd’hui plus d’électricité qu’elle n’en consomme et exporte son surplus. Mais l’agence nationale de l’énergie met en garde : si les data centers continuent de se multiplier, le pays pourrait manquer d’électricité et voir les prix grimper.
De plus en plus de restrictions
Le gouvernement prépare, en amont, un système de licences qui favoriserait les sites utiles à la défense, à la police, à la santé ou aux infrastructures critiques, comme les réseaux mobiles et le système financier. En revanche, l’idée sera de freiner les géants mondiaux du cloud et les cryptomonnaies. « Nous voulons des data centers en Norvège, mais nous ne pouvons pas avoir tous les types de data centers », a résumé le ministre du Numérique, Torgeir Micaelsen. Ainsi, les nouveaux venus devraient aussi payer les coûts qu’ils imposent au réseau.
Le climat de défiance face à ces ogres énergétiques, en pleine expansion pour assouvir les besoins de l’intelligence artificielle (IA), semble clairement s’étendre. Alors que les Américains ont fait part de leur mécontentement dans les urnes lors des élections de mi-mandat, des protestations s’organisent aussi sur le Vieux Continent.
D’autant que les voisins de la Norvège serrent eux aussi la vis : le Danemark a gelé de nouveaux accords de raccordement en mars, tandis que la Finlande propose un système à quatre niveaux, et la Suède, qui compte près de 7 000 MW de demandes en attente, étudie des restrictions temporaires. Une tendance malvenue pour les hyperscalers, qui ont engagé des centaines de milliards de dollars dans le développement de ces infrastructures si controversées.

articles.title: Broadcasters call Rogers' Monday Night Hockey removal 'anti-competitive'
articles.text:
Broadcasters Cogeco, Eastlink, and SaskTel have filed a complaint with the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) over Rogers-owned Sportsnet making Monday Night Hockey a Sportsnet+ exclusive.
Within the complaint, the parties specifically call Rogers’ removal of Monday Night Hockey from TV channels “anti-competitive,” noting that consumers who are subscribed to other broadcast providers are being asked to “become direct Rogers subscribers and are being imposed an additional $12.99 monthly surcharge to access this content,” which the parties note is something that the broadcaster doesn’t do for its own subscribers.
In an email to MobileSyrup, Sportsnet offered the following response to the complaint:
“Rogers Cable has paid Sportsnet fair market value to provide Sportsnet+ exclusive content to their TV customers and decided to make it available to them at no extra cost. All TV providers, including Cogeco, Eastlink and SaskTel, have the same opportunity to make the content available as part of their TV offering, but so far have chosen not to. Fans can contact their TV provider about this option. We’ll fully address all issues raised, including Sportsnet’s right to distribute content exclusively on Sportsnet+, as part of the proceeding.”
The complaint says these actions “constitute clear breaches” of the CRTC’s ruling on the Rogers/Shaw merger, under which the company has to “refrain from entering into any agreement for exclusive or preferential distribution of any online programming service or rights necessary for its distribution,” with the parties noting that the Sportsnet+ exclusive games are a “direct departure” from this commitment.
The parties also highlight Rogers’ recent acquisition of Maple Leaf Sports and Entertainment (MLSE), alongside 100 per cent ownership of the Toronto Blue Jays, warning that “if Rogers is permitted to unilaterally siphon core NHL broadcasts such as playoff rounds away from linear TV feeds, no marquee sports content, sports or entertainment, will remain safe from platform fragmentation, and other large, vertically integrated media companies will inevitably follow suit.”
This isn’t the first company to target Rogers with complaints about Monday Night Hockey. Earlier this month, Telus sent out an email to OptikTV customers blaming Rogers for why fans can’t find games. In response, Sportsnet said that all broadcast providers have the ability to make Sportsnet+ content available to their customers, but it’s worth noting that no broadcasters other than Rogers, which owns Sportsnet, have reached an agreement yet.

articles.title: Gemini in action: How voice, agents, and coding tools are changing the way businesses use AI
articles.text:
Gemini in action: How voice, agents, and coding tools are changing the way businesses use AI
At TechSparks 2026, Google Cloud’s Rajesh Shewani walked through how businesses are using Gemini for voice, agents, and coding, and why the systems built around a model now matter as much as the model itself.
Generative AI, in the form most people know it, is only about three years old. In that short time, Rajesh Shewani believes it has already moved through three distinct eras.
First came retrieval: chatbots that answer a question and wait for the next one. Then came agents that take action on a user’s behalf. Now, he said, the industry is entering what he calls the harness era, where orchestration, memory, and guardrails around a model let it carry out work from start to finish.
“An agent is nothing now but a model plus a harness,” said Shewani, Head of AI Customer Engineering for Digital Natives, Startups and ITeS at Google Cloud, at TechSparks 2026.
In a masterclass titled ‘Gemini in action’, Shewani promised a look at what is happening rather than a sales pitch. He covered where businesses are putting AI to work, how voice is becoming an interface, the tools Google uses to build its own software, and the questions organisations need to answer as agents become everyday users of their systems.
Shewani said organizations are no longer just discussing AI but executing in five broad areas.
- Agents, which are changing how companies work and how startups build for other businesses.
- Creative work, from image and video generation to marketing and branding, was one of the earliest areas to take off.
- Multimodal AI, which lets models work with images, video, and voice, not just text.
- Physical AI, including robotics and self-driving cars, which he expects to grow fast as the “brain” of large language models gains a body.
- AI fluency, a priority for traditional organizations in banking, insurance, retail, and telecom.
For those traditional businesses, the worry is less about building models and more about whether employees can use AI in their daily jobs. They don’t need to be experts or developers, he said, but they do need to be fluent.
What every agent needs
The three eras are cumulative, Shewani explained. Agents build on retrieval, and harnesses build on agents. AI is no longer an assistant that appears and disappears, but something closer to an autonomous colleague.
“It’s no longer just about the model,” he said. “It’s the model plus everything that you build around it”, from memory and context management to sandboxing.
He described four things every agent needs:
- A goal: booking a ticket, making an entry in an SAP system, or negotiating a price by voice.
- Instructions: guidance that goes beyond a single prompt and can be stored for reuse, much as new employees learn how an organization works.
- Knowledge: a company’s own data, since models are trained on public information, not internal records.
- Tools: the means to act, such as updating a CRM or placing an outbound call.
Knowledge is where much of the effort is going. Many teams had begun building their own “LLM wikis” for agents, and Google is now trying to standardize the approach with the Open Knowledge Format (OKF). OKF v0.1 represents knowledge as a directory of markdown files with YAML frontmatter, which agents can read directly. Shewani compared its role to what Model Context Protocol (MCP) did for backend integration.
A shared knowledge layer, combining a knowledge graph with plain text, also keeps costs down, he said. Rather than querying everything for every prompt, agents are pointed to structured context, which uses fewer tokens.
Voice becomes the interface
“Voice is becoming the new user interface,” Shewani said, whether for customers, employees, or users who prefer to speak in local languages. He noted that Google DeepMind’s team in Bengaluru is doing extensive work on Indic languages. Gemini Live now supports more than 90 Indian languages and dialects, including Sanskrit, Bhojpuri, and Maithili.
He showed a live translation demo built for Grab, the Southeast Asian ride-hailing platform, in which a passenger and driver who do not share a language coordinate a pickup.
Grab says travellers and driver-partners make more than 10 million voice calls a month, and it has been testing Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, which offers two-way translation in more than 70 languages.
Shewani said Gemini 3.8 Live, launched in September, improves further on noise cancellation and conversations between multiple speakers.
Another demo, built in India, dubbed a news video into Marathi and Malayalam from a single prompt while matching lip movements and facial expressions. Dubbing once required complex pipelines with many steps, he said, but live models have cut those down significantly, making it easier to create training videos and marketing content across languages.
He also showed Citi Sky, Citi’s AI-powered wealth assistant, which uses a virtual avatar to walk clients through options for a maturing certificate of deposit and complete the renewal. For such experiences, latency is critical. “If a flow breaks even for a second or a millisecond, it doesn’t work,” he said.
The stack under the hood
Shewani then walked through the tools that sit beneath these experiences.
Gemini agent is a single agent that can carry out tasks end to end. Google Cloud introduced it on October 8, 2026, and it can keep working in the cloud for hours or days, even when a user’s device is offline.
Shewani gave the example of a procurement team asking it to research options, write a request for proposal, send it to vendors, evaluate responses, and produce a shortlist. According to Google, the agent routes each task to the most suitable model, currently choosing between Gemini and Anthropic’s Claude models.
Gemini Enterprise adds guardrails and quotas for businesses, which Shewani said helps keep costs from running away, a key concern in tokenomics. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian has said nearly 90% of Fortune 100 companies use Gemini Enterprise.
Antigravity is Google’s harness for building software, available as a command-line tool and as extensions for code editors. Shewani said most of Google’s own code is now written using the same harness, known internally as Jetski. Google CEO Sundar Pichai has said 75% of new code at Google is now generated by AI and reviewed by engineers, up from 25% in October 2024.
CodeMender scans code for vulnerabilities, creates patches, tests them in a sandbox, and can integrate with a GitHub repository. When Google DeepMind first announced it in October 2025, it had already contributed 72 security fixes to open-source projects.
Google is also giving every agent its own identity, which Shewani likened to an LDAP directory for agents, so organisations can track which agent took which action.
Choosing the right model for the job
No model can be cheapest, fastest, and most capable at once, Shewani said, so businesses need a range of models and should match each task to the right one. Google’s Flash models are its workhorses for everyday tasks that do not need complex reasoning.
“If I need to get to office every day, I don’t need to have a Ferrari,” he said. For the hardest work, there is Gemini 4 Argon.
Google made Gemini 4 Argon, its latest frontier model, generally available on October 13, 2026, at an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens 95% cheaper. Google says it ranks first on the Vals Index, and Shewani pointed to software engineering, cybersecurity, and knowledge work in finance, legal, HR, and procurement as its main use cases.
He showed two examples. In one, Argon processed more than 80,000 raw files from NASA’s open archive, including CSVs, images, PDFs, logs, and videos, and turned the analysis into a presentation that followed a custom slide template. In another, it wrote more than 5,000 lines of Python to render a photorealistic 3D library interior from scratch, with no graphics libraries or rendering engine.
Argon can also generate up to one million output tokens, not just accept one million as input. Shewani said this helps with tasks such as mathematical proofs and multi-file code generation, where producing one large output instead of many small ones uses fewer tokens and runs faster.
Questions every organization should ask
Shewani closed with the questions businesses need to start answering now that agents are here. Will agents become the primary users of their systems? Are their databases ready for swarms of agents firing queries that no person wrote? How will they manage agents that do things they are not allowed to do?
Roles will change too. “Developers are essentially going to become managers of agents,” he said. Organizations will also need to manage budgets, route tasks across a mix of models, track telemetry and memory, and prepare for agents that generate their own user interfaces.
Asked about education, he said agents are already being used to create content in multiple languages, build AI tutors, generate quizzes, and grade students. Google offers such tools through Google for Education, he noted, and many edtech companies are building their own. In education, he added, avoiding hallucination is critical, which is why grounding agents in a trusted knowledge repository matters.
For Shewani, the shift is clear. The competition between models will continue, but the advantage increasingly lies in what businesses build around them: the knowledge they give agents, the guardrails they set, and the systems ready to work alongside them.

articles.title: Black Friday 2026 en direct : la course aux vraies promos s'accélère ce jeudi 12 novembre
articles.text:
À deux semaines du fameux "vendredi noir", la pression monte d'un cran. Ce jeudi 12 novembre, les e-commerçants multiplient les ventes flash pour anticiper le Black Friday. Pour vous guider dans ce labyrinthe de prix barrés, notre rédaction traque en direct les véritables baisses de tarifs.
L'effervescence du 11 novembre est passée, mais le "Black Month" ne montre aucun signe de ralentissement. À tout juste 15 jours de l'échéance du 27 novembre, Amazon, la Fnac, Darty ou encore Cdiscount accélèrent la cadence. Les ruptures de stock commencent à s'accumuler sur les produits high-tech et l'électroménager les plus plébiscités, exigeant une réactivité de tous les instants.
Toutefois, hors de question de céder à la panique et de tomber dans le piège des fausses réductions qui inondent le web. articles.title: Las cámaras de Ring ahora se mueven: Amazon entra en el mundo de los robots domésticos con un dron que vuela por el salón de casa
articles.text:
Amazon ha ganado fama con sus cámaras y timbres inteligentes Ring, pequeños dispositivos de seguridad que hacen bien su trabajo y que se caracterizaban por una cosa: estaban quietecitos en su sitio. Con Ring Robotics eso cambia a partir de ahora porque sus nuevos dispositivos, un dron y un robot doméstico, podrán campar a sus anchas por casa.
Ambos prometen una vigilancia más completa gracias a que se pueden mover (y a la IA), pero, claro, hay una pregunta que hacerse: ¿queremos realmente que una cámara autónoma recorra los espacios más íntimos de nuestra vida? ¿Y que sea de Amazon?
Índice de Contenidos (6)
La seguridad deja de estar quieta
Las cámaras de seguridad tradicionales tienen una limitación evidente: solo ven lo que ocurre delante de su objetivo. Aunque algunas pueden rotar sobre su eje, Ring quiere resolver los puntos ciegos poniendo la cámara en movimiento. Así, el Ring Drone Cam es un dron doméstico que puede despegar de su base, seguir rutas programadas y acudir a puntos concretos cuando una cámara, un sensor o una alarma detectan algo.
El sistema que lo hace posible se llama AI Pilot. Según Amazon, combina las cámaras del dispositivo, sensores integrados y procesamiento en la nube para construir un plano del espacio, identificar habitaciones y proponer puntos de vigilancia: puertas laterales, ventanas, pasillos o, en una tienda, la caja registradora.
El resultado es fácil de entender, pero tiene implicaciones profundas: la casa deja de tener una cámara fija y pasa a tener un observador móvil que puede situarse casi donde el propietario decida. Amazon lo presenta como una forma de comprobar que las ventanas están cerradas antes de un viaje o de investigar una alerta sin tener que instalar cámaras en cada habitación.
Un dron con límites muy reales
Amazon no presenta el Ring Drone Cam como un dron exterior ni un aparato de vigilancia continua. Es una cámara voladora para interiores, con un campo de visión de 148 grados, rotación de 360 grados, grabación en 2K y dos luces LED para escenas con poca luz.
Su mayor limitación es la batería. Amazon admite que ofrece hasta ocho minutos de vuelo con una batería nueva y completamente cargada, todo ello medido en condiciones controladas, así que en la práctica seguramente será menor. Para una revisión puntual puede ser suficiente, pero para patrullar una vivienda durante un rato, no lo parece.
También hay restricciones de navegación. Amazon advierte de que el rendimiento puede empeorar en presencia de superficies reflectantes, como mármol pulido o suelo mojado, paredes mate y sin rasgos, o cristales sin marco y espejos. En otras palabras: el dron puede funcionar bien en una vivienda moderna, pero no necesariamente en cualquier vivienda moderna.
Ring Rover: un robot patrullero que no descansa
El Ring Rover Cam es la otra mitad de la apuesta. No está pensado para el salón, sino para locales, almacenes, oficinas y pequeños negocios. Amazon lo define como un robot de seguridad autónomo capaz de patrullar rutas, investigar alertas y transmitir vídeo en hasta 4K mientras se desplaza.
Incluye un mástil ajustable que le permite mirar por encima de mostradores, estanterías y otros obstáculos. También incorpora sirena, torre de luces y audio bidireccional, de modo que el responsable del negocio puede hablar con alguien que esté cerca del robot. Amazon asegura que puede cubrir hasta 465 metros cuadrados.
Pero sus limitaciones físicas son notables. El Rover solo opera en interiores de una sola planta, no sube escaleras y no es compatible con bordes curvos, zonas hundidas, cambios de suelo superiores a 3,5 centímetros o suelos negros brillantes. No es un robot doméstico versátil: es un vigilante especializado para un tipo muy concreto de espacio.
Cómo no, la privacidad otra vez en el centro
Amazon habla de “privacidad y seguridad sin concesiones”, y presenta varios mecanismos para respaldarlo: el dron apaga la cámara cuando está en la base, el Rover puede activar un modo de reposo que retrae el mástil y desactiva el micrófono, y ambos dispositivos muestran indicadores luminosos cuando están grabando.
El problema es que la historia reciente de Ring no ayuda a generar confianza. En 2023, la FTC estadounidense acusó a Ring de permitir que empleados y contratistas accedieran a grabaciones de espacios privados de clientes, además de señalar fallos de seguridad que habrían permitido a hackers acceder a unas 55.000 cuentas en Estados Unidos.
Los nuevos vídeos estarán protegidos con el sistema de cifrado Throw Away the Key (TAKE), presentado por Ring en septiembre de 2026. La EFF lo considera una mejora frente a la configuración anterior de Ring, pero insiste en que sigue estando lejos del cifrado de extremo a extremo. Es decir: la empresa mejora la protección, pero no elimina la dependencia del usuario hacia Amazon y su infraestructura.
Un problema de precedentes
No parece que Ring Drone o Ring Rover incorporen reconocimiento facial. Pero Ring ya permite a los propietarios de timbres con cámara activar “Caras Familiares”, una función de reconocimiento facial para visitantes, y esa funcionalidad es objeto de una demanda colectiva. El precedente importa mucho porque una vez que la vigilancia se vuelve móvil, autónoma y conectada a una plataforma más amplia, las fronteras de lo que puede hacer el sistema son más difíciles de controlar.
El Ring Drone es, además, el regreso de una idea que Amazon ya intentó vender en 2021 con el Ring Always Home Cam. Aquel producto se lanzó por invitación como parte del programa “Day 1 Edition”, con un precio inicial de 250 dólares. Cinco años después, la compañía vuelve con una versión más ambiciosa, integrada en Alexa y rodeada de IA.
La diferencia es que ahora el contexto es distinto. La IA generativa y los sistemas de visión artificial han avanzado, pero también lo han hecho las expectativas sobre privacidad, control de datos y límites del vigilancia corporativa. Un dron que patrulla una casa no es solo un gadget llamativo: es una decisión sobre cuánta observación estamos dispuestos a aceptar dentro de nuestro hogar.
Precio y disponibilidad
Tanto el dron como el robot estarán disponibles por el momento solo en Estados Unidos. En concreto, Ring Drone Cam saldrá a la venta el 27 de enero de 2027 en Estados Unidos por 249,99 dólares, unos 224 euros al cambio.
Por su parte, Ring Rover Cam llegará a partir del 16 de diciembre de este 2026 por 999 dólares, unos 900 euros al cambio actual.

articles.title: Death Stranding 2 rejoint le PlayStation Plus Extra et Premium en novembre 2026
articles.text:
Le PlayStation Plus Extra accueillera huit jeux en novembre, dont Death Stranding 2, Dragon Quest III HD-2D Remake et Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii.
Les abonnés Premium pourront aussi découvrir Soul Reaver 2 et Freedom Wars Remastered dès le 17 novembre.
Le 17 novembre, treize jeux quitteront les catalogues, parmi lesquels GTA V et Red Dead Redemption 2.
Le PlayStation Plus Extra accueillera huit jeux en novembre, dont Death Stranding 2, Dragon Quest III HD-2D Remake et Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii.
Les abonnés Premium pourront aussi découvrir Soul Reaver 2 et Freedom Wars Remastered dès le 17 novembre.
Le 17 novembre, treize jeux quitteront les catalogues, parmi lesquels GTA V et Red Dead Redemption 2.
Sony vient de dévoiler les jeux qui arriveront dans les catalogues PlayStation Plus Extra et PlayStation Plus Premium en ce mois de novembre 2026 déjà bien rempli. Death Stranding 2 et Dragon Quest font partie de la liste.
Huit nouveaux jeux vont intégrer les catalogues PlayStation Plus Extra et PlayStation Plus Premium à partir du mardi 17 novembre 2026. Parmi les titres à rejoindre les formules les plus chères du service de Sony, quelques gros titres devraient vous tenir occuper jusqu’à la fin de l’année, siThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time et GTA VI ne suffisent pas.
Sony propose plusieurs formules PlayStation Plus, chacune donnant accès à des avantages et à une sélection de jeux qui lui sont propres. Il existe trois formules : Essential (9,99 € par mois), Extra (15,99 € par mois) et Premium (18,99 € par mois). Vous pouvez vous abonner directement depuis le PlayStation Store ou passer par une carte prépayée PlayStation Plus pour ajouter du crédit à votre compte.
Les nouveaux jeux du PlayStation Plus Extra en novembre 2026
Hell Let Loose (PS5 – 11 novembre)
Ce jeu de tir multijoueur plonge jusqu’à 100 joueurs dans de grandes batailles de la Seconde Guerre mondiale. Ici, pas question de foncer tête baissée : la communication, la coopération et le sens tactique sont essentiels pour espérer l’emporter. Une expérience immersive et exigeante, qui demande de la patience.
Death Stranding 2 : On the Beach (PS5 – 17 novembre)
Sam reprend la route dans un monde postapocalyptique, cette fois pour connecter l’Australie au réseau chiral. Hideo Kojima signe une suite à Death Strading encore plus spectaculaire, avec des paysages magnifiques, une histoire toujours aussi étrange et un gameplay plus riche. Death Stranding 2 est un voyage à part, qui ne plaira pas forcément à celles ceux qui n’accrochent toujours pas au rythme contemplatif de la série.
Dragon Quest III HD-2D Remake est un remake HD-2D du jeu sorti en 1988 au Japon, et revisite un grand classique du jeu de rôle japonais, dans un superbe style graphique. On part à l’aventure pour vaincre le terrible Baramos, avec une équipe à composer et des combats au tour par tour. Une aventure généreuse et nostalgique, mais qui conserve aussi quelques mécaniques à l’ancienne.
Like a Dragon : Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii (PS4/PS5 – 17 novembre)
Goro Majima se réveille amnésique sur une île d’Hawaï et se retrouve embarqué dans une aventure de pirates à la recherche d’un trésor légendaire. Entre combats déjantés, batailles navales et mini-jeux absurdes, Like a Dragon : Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii assume pleinement son côté loufoque. Un épisode généreux et particulièrement fun.
Atomfall (PS4/PS5 – 17 novembre)
Dans une Angleterre alternative des années 1960, une catastrophe nucléaire a transformé une région en zone interdite. Atomfall est un jeu de survie à la première personne mêle exploration, affrontements et enquête dans une ambiance mystérieuse. Une proposition originale qui mise davantage sur l’atmosphère et la découverte que sur l’action pure.
Moto GP26 (PS5 – 24 novembre)
Enfourchez les motos officielles du championnat MotoGP 2026 et affrontez les meilleurs pilotes sur les circuits de la saison. Moto GP26 mise sur une simulation plus poussée et un système de notes des pilotes qui évolue selon leurs performances réelles. Un rendez-vous incontournable pour les amateurs de deux-roues, mais qui demande un peu de maîtrise.
Cricket 26 (PS4/PS5 – 24 novembre)
Autre sport, autres sensations, avec Cricket 26, une simulation officielle de cricket (il en faut). Le jeu propose notamment un mode consacré aux Ashes, la célèbre confrontation entre l’Angleterre et l’Australie, ainsi qu’une carrière de gestion enrichie. Elle s’adresse avant tout aux passionnés de ce sport, avec des mécaniques approfondies et de nombreuses possibilités tactiques.
Trepang 2 (PS5 – 24 novembre)
Dans Trepang 2, vous incarnez un soldat échappé d’un mystérieux laboratoire, doté de capacités surnaturelles et bien décidé à se venger. Ce FPS nerveux mise sur des fusillades ultra-violentes, des ralentis façon Matrix et des affrontements particulièrement musclés. Un défouloir efficace pour celles et ceux qui aiment l’action et que le cricket ennuie.
Les nouveaux jeux du PlayStation Plus Premium en novembre 2026
Raziel poursuit sa quête de vengeance contre Kain dans un univers gothique où les voyages dans le temps et les paradoxes bouleversent le destin de Nosgoth. Suite du jeu culte, Soul Reaver 2 propose un scénario complexe et une ambiance sombre. Un classique qui a très bien vieilli dans ses idées, même si ses combats et ses énigmes peuvent sembler un peu datés.
Freedom Wars Remastered (PS4/PS5 – 17 novembre)
Dans un futur dystopique où chaque être humain est condamné à un million d’années de prison dès sa naissance, vous devez accomplir des missions dangereuses pour espérer réduire votre peine. Freedom Wars Remastered propose des combats contre des créatures géantes, des armes variées et un grappin très pratique pour se déplacer, un peu comme le jeu de Capcom avec des des créatures géantes et des armes variées.
Ils quittent le PS Plus Extra et Premium le 17 novembre 2026

articles.title: Energiesparen: Aufklärung oder Nudging – was wirkt wirklich?
articles.text:
Energiesparen: Was Aufklärung und Nudging wirklich bringen
Energiesparen ist eine Frage der Motivation. Doch wie genau motiviert man Menschen am besten? Eine deutsch-schwedische Studie hat zwei Ansätze empirisch miteinander verglichen: Erstens das sogenannte „Nudging“ – also das mentale „Hinschubsen“ in Richtung energiersparender Verhaltensweisen. Zweitens den „Kompetenz-Boost“ – also die Aufklärung darüber, auf welche Weise sich Energie sparen lässt.
Für einen 24 Wochen langen Versuch rekrutierte das Forschungsteam 140 Studierende in einem Stockholmer Wohnheim und teilte sie in drei Gruppen auf. Die Mitglieder der Nudging-Gruppe bekamen über ein personalisiertes Dashboards wöchentlich mitgeteilt, wieviel Strom sie im Vergleich zum Durchschnitt der Teilnehmenden verbraucht haben – und wieviel im Vergleich zu den sparsamsten 15 Prozent. Das ganze wurde durch fröhliche oder stirnrunzelnde Emojis garniert.
Ein Sechstel eingespart
Die „Booster“ bekamen Aufkleber mit QR-Codes ausgehändigt, die sie auf ihre elektrischen Geräte kleben sollten. Über diese Codes konnten sie regelmäßig neue Spartipps aufrufen – etwa Rezepte zum Kochen mit der Mikrowelle, Hinweise zum Abtauen des Kühlschranks oder zur Reinigung des Radiators. Daneben gab es noch eine unbeeinflusste Kontrollgruppe.
Das zentrale Ergebnis: Beide Versuchsgruppen konnten ihren Stromverbrauch gegenüber der Kontrollgruppe um ungefähr ein Sechstel senken. Der Unterschied zwischen Nudging und Aufklärung war minimal.
Wenig dazugelernt
Allerdings ließen die Einsparungen bei beiden Gruppen gegen Ende des Versuchs wieder nach. Das ist besonders erstaunlich bei der Aufklärungsgruppe. Eigentlich hatten die Forschenden erwartet, dass die regelmäßigen Tipps zu einer höheren Kompetenz in Sachen Energiesparen führen, und damit zu wachsenden Einsparungen. Doch in abschließenden Wissenstests schnitten beide Versuchsgruppen kaum besser ab als die Kontrollgruppe.
Den größten Einfluss auf die erzielte Senkung hatte das Verbrauchsniveau vor dem Versuch. Logisch: Wer viel verbraucht, kann auch viel sparen. Ein weiterer Einflussfaktor war die generelle Kompetenz und Motivation zum Energiesparen. Da die Teilnahme am Versuch freiwillig war, haben sich möglicherweise viele ohnehin schon motivierte Menschen angemeldet. Die Forschenden räumen selbst ein, dass diese Vorselektion die Ergebnisse verfälscht haben könnte. Das bedeutet: In der breiten Bevölkerung sind die Effekte möglicherweise geringer.
Trotzdem gibt es auch eine positive Erkenntnis aus der Studie: Offenbar bringt es schon etwas, überhaupt die Aufmerksamkeit auf das Thema Energiesparen zu lenken – egal, auf welche Weise.

articles.title: Nvidia s'apprêterait à licencier son PDG Jensen Huang suite à une nouvelle révélation
articles.text:
Le patron de Nvidia Jensen Huang est vraiment dans la tourmente. Depuis quelques jours, le scandale a éclaté : il a eu une liaison extra-conjugale avec une femme d’affaires qui pourrait bien être une espionne chinoise. Nvidia avait ouvert une enquête dans la foulée pour faire la lumière sur cette affaire. Mais l’entreprise semble avoir découvert une deuxième liaison, avec une autre salariée de Nvidia : et pour le conseil d’administration, ça ne passe pas.
Une seconde liaison… avec une autre salariée de Nvidia
C’est le New York Times qui a révélé cette deuxième relation ce 11 novembre, selon les informations de sources anonymes. Jensen Huang aurait entretenu une relation amoureuse avec Kimberly Powell, vice-présidente de Nvidia en charge des soins de santé. Il s’agit donc d’une salariée subordonnée à Jensen Huang. Une source de CNBC ajoute même que cette relation ne serait pas nouvelle : les rumeurs circuleraient depuis longtemps chez Nvidia.
Selon deux employés de Nvidia, Huang et Powell auraient été filmés « en train de se montrer affectueux dans un hôtel de San Jose, en Californie, lors d’une conférence de l’entreprise en mars », écrit le journal. Le service de sécurité du dirigeant aurait aperçu le passant filmant la scène et l’aurait interpellé : un accord de confidentialité lui aurait été proposé.
Cependant, le code de conduite de Nvidia stipule que les employés doivent éviter les situations de conflits entre eux. Le conseil d’administration, mis au courant de cette relation, pourrait s’appuyer sur ce code (qui comprend une lettre de Jensen Huang !) pour licencier Jensen Huang. Contacté, le dirigeant de Nvidia s’est refusé à tout commentaire, comme son entreprise.
Des relations extraconjugales qui coûtent cher à Nvidia
Ces deux polémiques autour de relations extra-conjugales pourraient bien coûter sa place à Jensen Huang. D’autres dirigeants de grandes entreprises se sont déjà fait licencier pour des relations avec des salariés subordonnés par le passé aux États-Unis. Une situation qui pourrait paraître ubuesque pour certains : Huang serait remercié pour sa relation avec Powell, mais pas pour celle avec une femme qui pourrait être une espionne chinoise. Jensen Huang pourrait aussi décider lui-même de démissionner de son poste.
Depuis les révélations autour de la relation de Jensen Huang avec une potentielle espionne, Pékin a totalement démenti ces accusations. Quant au président Donald Trump, il continue de soutenir l’homme d’affaires, ce qui est loin d’être étonnant. Il serait même au courant de cette histoire depuis plusieurs mois. Après la clôture de la bourse de Wall Street ce mercredi 11 novembre, l’action de Nvidia avait chuté de plus de 7 %. Une baisse qui n’est pas la première depuis ces dernières semaines : il y avait déjà eu une baisse de 10% en quelques jours. Et avec une valorisation à plusieurs milliards de dollars, chaque baisse coûte des dizaines, voire des centaines de milliards de dollars à Nvidia.

articles.title: Brasil multó a Meta con 1,3 millones de dólares por incumplir órdenes judiciales en la campaña presidencial
articles.text:
El Tribunal Superior Electoral de Brasil multó a Meta con 7,5 millones de reales (unos USD 1,3 millones) por no cumplir órdenes judiciales durante la campaña de la segunda vuelta presidencial. El tribunal aclaró que no hay pruebas de que la empresa actuara a propósito para favorecer a un candidato.
La multa alcanza a Facebook, Instagram y WhatsApp, las plataformas de Meta. Según Reuters, el tribunal concluyó que la empresa entregó parte de la información pedida, pero que otras órdenes no se cumplieron, se cumplieron a medias o se atendieron después de vencidos los plazos.
El caso nació de una denuncia de la coalición del presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Alegó que Meta restringía la distribución de sus publicaciones, que operaban cuentas supuestamente falsas, que fallaba la identificación de contenido generado con inteligencia artificial y que sus herramientas trataban distinto a cada campaña.
Lula enfrentó en la segunda vuelta, el 25 de octubre, al senador Flávio Bolsonaro y ganó la reelección. Según AFP, había acusado a Meta de “manipulación algorítmica” a favor de su rival. Tras la victoria dijo que habrá que regular a las redes sociales.
Cómo se calculó la multa a Meta
El relator, el ministro Marco Aurélio Bellizze, explicó que el monto equivale a tres días de multa de 500.000 reales, del 17 al 19 de octubre, y seis días de 1 millón de reales, del 20 al 25 de octubre. Siete ministros votaron a favor.
Bellizze señaló que la cifra no suma cada orden incumplida, sino que evalúa la conducta global de la empresa: el retraso, el cumplimiento incompleto y la falta de transparencia. Según el diario O Globo, el relator criticó que parte de los datos llegara en otro idioma, agregados o en declaraciones genéricas.
Rechazó además el pedido de la campaña de Lula de subir la multa diaria a 10 millones de reales. Con las elecciones terminadas, dijo, ya no hacía falta aumentar una sanción pensada para forzar el cumplimiento durante la campaña.
Sin pruebas de intención, por ahora
“Los autos registran fallas técnicas reconocidas por la propia empresa”, escribió Bellizze, pero no hay elementos para concluir, de manera preliminar, que hubo una acción deliberada para desequilibrar la elección. Esa conclusión, agregó, exigiría prueba sólida en otro procedimiento judicial. La multa, precisó, no implica que Meta quisiera beneficiar a Lula ni a Bolsonaro.
Bellizze también advirtió que las plataformas digitales condicionan, mediante sistemas algorítmicos poco transparentes, la circulación de información política. Pidió mecanismos de auditoría y fiscalización de esos algoritmos. Explicó que este tipo de acción no permite peritajes técnicos complejos sobre cómo funcionan.
Meta negó las sospechas de favoritismo y reconoció que algunos anuncios de la campaña de Lula se desactivaron por error técnico. Dijo que las cuentas de Lula en Instagram llegaron a 1,5 veces más personas que las de Bolsonaro entre el 16 de agosto y el 25 de octubre. En un comunicado, afirmó que cumple la ley electoral brasileña y que seguirá defendiéndose en los procesos judiciales abiertos.
Meta amplía sistema para detectar a adolescentes que mienten sobre su edad
Meta anunció que extenderá a todo el mundo su tecnología de inteligencia artificial para identificar cuentas de adolescentes, incluso cuando registraron una fecha de nacimiento adulta. La compañía estima que millones de jóvenes adicionales quedarán bajo las Cuentas para Adolescentes, con restricciones de mensajes, contenido y tiempo de uso.
El sistema analiza referencias a cumpleaños, cursos escolares, biografías y fotos o videos para estimar si un usuario tiene entre 13 y 17 años. Meta aclaró que esta estimación no reemplaza la verificación con documento oficial.
La herramienta ya opera en Instagram y Facebook, y llegará antes de fin de año a Threads. En Australia, suma como señal el rango de edad que comparte Apple. La medida se suma a un acuerdo con 52 fiscales generales de Estados Unidos.

articles.title: Airalo lança eSIM único para usar em diferentes viagens • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Airalo lança eSIM único para usar em diferentes viagens
Novo modelo dispensa a instalação de um chip virtual a cada destino e será disponibilizado para todos os clientes.
A Airalo vai permitir que clientes usem o mesmo eSIM em diferentes viagens internacionais. O novo modelo dispensa a instalação de um chip virtual a cada destino, permitindo que o usuário mantenha o perfil no celular e contrate pacotes de dados conforme a viagem.
Segundo a empresa especializada na venda de eSIMs, a mudança é viabilizada por uma infraestrutura de rede central própria. A novidade começou a ser liberada gradualmente na segunda-feira (09/11) e deve levar até 12 meses para alcançar os mais de 30 milhões de clientes da plataforma.
Com o novo modelo, o viajante mantém o mesmo eSIM instalado no celular e contrata pacotes de dados conforme o destino. Atualmente, quem usa esse tipo de serviço geralmente precisa instalar um novo perfil quando viaja para outro país. A proposta da Airalo é permitir a reutilização do chip virtual em diferentes viagens.
A empresa também permitirá comprar ou recarregar pacotes mesmo depois que o anterior expirar, sem exigir uma conexão Wi-Fi ou outro eSIM ativo. Segundo a Airalo, será possível ainda testar a conexão antes da viagem.
A plataforma prevê pacotes com duração de 1 a 30 dias para a maioria dos destinos, além de planos globais com validade de até 365 dias. A disponibilidade e as condições variam conforme o destino e o pacote escolhido.
A migração ocorrerá por etapas. Até receberem a atualização, os clientes continuarão usando o serviço normalmente.
O eSIM de viagem é uma das opções para acessar a internet fora do Brasil, mas não a única. Vivo, Claro e TIM, por exemplo, oferecem roaming internacional, serviço que permite usar a linha brasileira em redes de operadoras parceiras no exterior. Dependendo do plano, o roaming pode já estar incluído na mensalidade ou exigir a contratação de um pacote adicional.
Outra opção, também popular, é comprar um chip físico ou eSIM de uma operadora local no país de destino. O serviço da Airalo, no entanto, é uma alternativa para quem prefere acertar a internet separadamente, já que o cliente contrata um pacote de dados separado, válido para determinado país ou região.
