articles.title: Cyberattaque : après les frigos des supermarchés, vos appareils ménagers seraient la prochaine cible
articles.text:
Après les infrastructures essentielles, ce sont potentiellement les Français qui pourraient être attaqués chez eux à l'avenir. C'est en tout cas une crainte bien réelle du côté de l'UE !
L'enquête sur l'attaque contre les frigos de supermarché en France, qui avait entraîné de grosses pertes alimentaires, s'oriente dorénavant vers la piste iranienne. Mais plus globalement, cette attaque a servi d'électrochoc quant à la vulnérabilité de nombre de nos infrastructures. Et les spécialistes vont encore augmenter nos inquiétudes vu ce à quoi ils s'attendent à l'avenir.
Protégez votre entreprise gratuitement pendant 30 jours
Découvrez Bitdefender Ultimate Small Business Security et protégez votre activité contre les cybermenaces. Aucune coordonnée bancaire requise.
Les appareils ménagers pourraient être les prochaines cibles d'une grande cyberattaque
Si les cyberattaques émanant d'acteurs étatiques peuvent tomber sur nos infrastructures aujourd'hui, à l'avenir, ça pourrait même toucher directement nos foyers. C'est en tout cas l'avis du directeur exécutif de l'agence européenne de cybersécurité (Enisa), Juhan Lepassaar.
« La sécurité ne devrait pas et ne doit pas être reléguée au second plan. Aujourd’hui c'était les frigos, demain ce pourraient être les routeurs, et après-demain les appareils ménagers domestiques, et ainsi de suite » a-t-il ainsi pronostiqué. Et ici, il s'agit d'un problème qui est moins technique que politique.
Une question essentielle : combien veut-on mettre pour la cybersécurité ?
En effet, nous sommes en mesure de nous protéger en Europe, mais pour cela, il faut y mettre les moyens. « Tous les incidents peuvent être évités, mais la question est de savoir si nous sommes prêts à investir pour cela » a-t-il ainsi expliqué, ajoutant que « la cybersécurité n'est pas bon marché. »
Mais il faudra bien à un moment ouvrir largement les coffres, vu la configuration de l'ensemble des appareils avec lesquels nous vivons aujourd'hui. « Chaque service dont vous dépendez en tant que citoyen, en tant qu'être humain, comporte une couche dans laquelle intervient un élément numérique, un morceau de code qui, s'il n'est pas protégé, peut être piraté » rappelle-t-il. Et dans la configuration géopolitique actuelle, avec une plus grande fragmentation et des guerres hybrides qui se multiplient, ce sont autant de points de vulnérabilité qui seront nécessairement à combler à un moment.
Source : Le Télégramme

articles.title: GitHub Makes Agentic Workflows Generally Available with Isolation and Budget Controls
articles.text:
GitHub has made GitHub Agentic Workflows generally available. The open-source project runs coding agents inside GitHub Actions for repository tasks such as issue triage and continuous integration (CI) failure analysis. Agents start with read-only permissions, and any changes they propose are applied by separate jobs that hold their own write tokens.
That separation has limits. The project's FAQ says the protections do not automatically extend to direct write permissions or to custom jobs a workflow author adds, so the safety of a workflow depends on how it is configured. Authors can also add a GitHub Environment protection rule to require a reviewer before a write job runs.
Developers describe the work in natural-language Markdown, with YAML frontmatter for configuration. The project compiles that definition into a standard Actions workflow, which reuses existing runner groups and policy constraints, and teams can use Copilot or bring another coding agent. According to the general availability announcement, agents run in a sandboxed container behind the Agent Workflow Firewall, and a threat-detection job scans proposed changes before they are applied. The project entered public preview in June 2026.
Since the preview, GitHub has added support for Actions Runner Controller (ARC), its Kubernetes operator for self-hosted runners, with Docker-in-Docker (DinD). DinD runs a Docker daemon inside the runner pod so the agent can start its sandbox containers. The project's guide notes that ARC runs the DinD sidecar as a privileged container by default, a privileged component sitting alongside an agent designed around least privilege.
Spending is capped by default. GitHub's documentation prices AI Credits (AIC) at $0.01 each and sets a cap of 1,000 AIC ($10) per run. The project's enterprise controls reference adds defaults of 5,000 AIC a day, 400 AIC per threat-detection run and a 20-minute timeout on the agent step, all of which organisations can override. The gh aw forecast command, no longer experimental, estimates monthly AI credit spending, including threat detection.
In the announcement, Ben Alton, senior manager in Accenture's Strategy, Architecture & Innovation team, said: "One of our leads saved an estimated 29 hours a week on his development work alone." The announcement does not explain how that figure was measured.
Engineers testing the project have taken a more cautious line. In a walkthrough of an issue-triage workflow, Sascha Mirow-Stanitzok, team lead for middleware at freenet, judged the default budget far too generous for triage and capped his runs at 100 AIC, 15 turns and 10 minutes. He also wrote that telling the agent to ignore instructions in issue text does not protect a workflow by itself, and said he would not use the same pattern for workflows that change code or open pull requests.
GitLab takes a different route with its Duo Agent Platform flows, which run on runners under a composite identity that pairs a service account performing the actions with the human user who started the request. Its triggers, such as a mention or an assignment, must come from a human user, so one flow cannot start another. That rule stops agents from chaining work across flows without a person starting it.
GitHub's FAQ says conventional Actions remain the right choice for reproducible builds and tests, with agent workflows suited to tasks that need interpretation or generation. The project is available on GitHub Free, Team and Enterprise on github.com, and the default Copilot CLI engine requires a Copilot licence.

articles.title: Semantic diffing of formal policies with anti-unification | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Semantic diffing of formal policies with anti-unification
When reviewing code, you start with a diff. You wouldn’t compare two 3,000-line files by eye and hope to spot every change. Formal policies can be even harder to compare because a textual diff often highlights syntactic changes that don’t affect meaning. Reorder two conjuncts, swap the arguments of an equality, or use an equivalent predicate, and much of the file might appear changed. A real change in behavior, such as an Or where the requirement says and, can get lost in that noise.
A semantic diff shows what two policies have in common and where they disagree. The open source engine used in this post computes this diff using anti-unification, which finds a most specific common pattern for two expressions. Plotkin’s 1970 paper gives the classical formulation. The engine works over an e-graph, which keeps track of expressions known to be equal. We supply the algebraic laws and domain rules that justify those equalities, such as equating an external destination with one that isn’t internal. The result shows the shared parts once and keeps both versions of each differing part for review. If no differences remain, the policies are equivalent under those laws and rules. When the rules or the search are incomplete, a remaining difference might reflect an equivalence the engine has not found.
One use case is autoformalization. Autoformalization translates natural language into a formal language. Suppose you want to turn requirements into SMT-LIB, the standard input language for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers such as Z3 and cvc5, or into Cedar or Dogwood to control authorization in your software system. A large language model (LLM) generates the formal artifact from the prose. The model writes the artifact. It plays no part in computing the diff. Run the model twice, and it might produce two different formalizations, with no ground truth to identify the correct one. A semantic diff shows where they agree and where they differ. Generate more candidates by varying the model, prompt, or sampling temperature. Comparing them shows which parts stay the same and which vary. Review the varying parts first.
Requirements can also become OpenShell sandbox policies or Common Expression Language (CEL) expressions. OpenShell uses YAML to describe an agent’s filesystem and network access. CEL is embedded in applications to evaluate expressions, including policy conditions. These languages and formats differ in what they express, but translations into any of them can disagree about a condition, a scope, or an event. The following table gives illustrative disagreements:
| Language or format | Policy focus | Example disagreement | 
| Cedar | Who can perform an action on a resource, under which conditions. | One translation requires ownership and approval. Another accepts either. | 
| Dogwood | Authorization involving the current request and recent event history. | One translation checks a successful prior response. Another checks a request event. | 
| OpenShell policies | An agent’s filesystem and network access, including rules for particular binaries. | One translation permits repository-scoped GET. Another permits organization-scoped POST. | 
| CEL | Conditions evaluated over inputs supplied by a host application. | One translation requires production for both allowed ports. Another requires it for only one. | 
In each worked example, we compare translations of the same requirement within one policy context. We encode the relevant syntax as terms and declare the equalities used in the comparison. The engine reads these encodings. It doesn’t import native policies from the four formats.
The idea is a formal-methods analogue of semantic entropy, described by Farquhar et al. in Nature (2024). That approach samples several natural-language answers, clusters those that entail one another, and reports a single number. For formal outputs, anti-unification preserves more information. It identifies the shared structure and each divergence instead of returning only a score.
Counterexamples help explain the consequences of a disagreement. An SMT solver can find a concrete assignment that satisfies one formula and violates the other. A reviewer can then trace that assignment through the formulas to understand the conflicting decisions. The anti-unifier gives a different view: it organizes the shared structure and the fragments that differ, without issuing an SMT query. A solver or policy validator can help resolve those fragments. We assume you can read S-expression syntax, as in SMT-LIB, and know what an authorization policy is. E-graphs and anti-unification are explained as they come up.
        When several translations agree on part of a requirement, the diff shows that part once. Where they disagree, it keeps the alternatives visible for review.
How semantic diffing represents disagreement
Say a policy-generation pipeline hands you two candidate rules for this requirement: sensitive data sent to an external destination must be encrypted.
| Rule A | Rule B | 
| sensitive(data) ∧ external(dst) → encrypted | ¬internal(dst) ∧ sensitive(data) → audited | 
Whether these are the same rule isn’t obvious. The conditions are reordered, external is expressed indirectly as not internal, and the conclusions do not match. The engine computes a most specific anti-unifier for these terms. In its input language, the two rules are S-expressions.
The complete program first declares the vocabulary:
It then adds one function line for each predicate (sensitive, external, internal) and constant (data, dst, encrypted, audited). Here, And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent, as the next section explains:
The engine answers with a single term:
The reordering doesn’t appear in the result because And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent. Two Variants nodes remain, each marking a place where the inputs disagree, and only one of them is a difference in meaning. The difference between (external dst) and (Not (internal dst)) is a difference in vocabulary. Both express the same domain fact. The engine can’t infer that from syntax alone. State the domain fact as a rewrite, run it to saturation (until no rule adds a new equality), and diff again:
After saturation, the engine answers:
One Variants node remains: Rule B audits where the requirement demands encryption. A textbook presentation would put a fresh variable at that spot. The engine instead writes (Variants encrypted audited): a node that holds both readings. Select the first child of every Variants node and you reconstruct rule A, up to the declared algebra and rewrites. Select the second child and you get rule B. The anti-unifier is a lossless merge of both terms: Shared structure appears once, and every genuine disagreement is a localized, reviewable node.
Three fields describe the result: :size, :cr, and :completion. The :size field counts the concrete nodes (a Variants marker itself isn’t counted, but both of its children are, so structure can’t hide inside one).
The :cr field reports the compression ratio (s - a) / b, where s is the result size and a and b are the smaller and larger input sizes. For each input, we use its smallest known equivalent form in the current e-graph. A score of 0 means full agreement under the declared equalities.
After the preceding rewrite, both inputs have seven nodes and the result has eight, giving (8 - 7) / 7, or approximately 0.1429. Keeping both complete policies in a single Variants node would use fourteen nodes, giving (14 - 7) / 7 = 1. This is the reference value for no sharing.
A score of 1 is a reference value, not an upper bound. The search might use larger equivalent forms than the smallest known inputs. A result larger than their combined sizes therefore scores above 1. For example, if both smallest input forms have ten nodes and a result has twenty-three, the ratio is (23 - 10) / 10 = 1.3.
The :completion field reports exact when the search space was exhausted and budget when the default anytime search (a Monte Carlo search, described in the implementation section) reached its playout limit before exhausting the search space.
A low :cr means the inputs share more structure under the declared equalities. It doesn’t establish correctness: two candidates can share the same mistake. An entropy score summarizes variation in one number. The full semantic diff also identifies where the candidates disagree and retains both alternatives in Variants nodes.
A semantic diff ignores only the differences covered by the declared equalities. A plain syntactic anti-unifier would also have reported the reordering in this example. The next three sections show how to declare the algebra and add domain identities.
        The anti-unifier stores shared structure once and marks each disagreement with a Variants node. Selecting one side of every node reconstructs the corresponding input, modulo the declared equalities.
Run a semantic diff in 5 minutes
The engine requires only a pinned Rust toolchain to build from source. Its formal-verification annotations, covered in the implementation section, compile away under plain rustc. These commands pin the revision used for the worked examples:
It prints a single (anti-unify ...) term.
The command-line interpreter reads one S-expression file (.egg by convention). You declare sorts and operators, define two terms with let, optionally add rewrite rules and run them to saturation, and issue antiunify. Two mechanisms tell the engine which syntactic changes do not affect meaning: annotations that assign algebraic properties such as associativity, commutativity, and idempotence to operators, and explicit rewrite rules for everything else. Here is the algebraic part of the signature used in the worked example:
And and Or are variadic, associative, commutative, and idempotent, and each has a Boolean neutral element. Eq is commutative. Every reordering, regrouping, and duplication of conjuncts therefore counts as the same term. Nothing else is assumed: Only the stated laws hold, and any further identities must be written as explicit rewrites. The :identity element is what lets the diff align a conjunct that one input has and the other lacks: The missing conjunct is paired with (Lit true) rather than causing the entire And expression to fail to align. Both case studies rely on this identity alignment.
        :assoc-comm-idem makes reordered, regrouped, and duplicate operands equivalent. :identity lets the diff align a missing operand with the operator’s neutral element.
Worked example with two policy bugs
The running example ships with the repository as egraph/examples/au_policy_divergence.egg. Consider one policy sentence:
        A cross-Region replication request is permitted only if the source bucket has versioning enabled and the destination bucket lies in an approved Region. If the object is tagged confidential, the destination and source accounts must be the same and server-side encryption with a customer managed key must be in effect. Objects up to the multipart threshold are copied directly. Larger objects require a multipart copy.
Two people, or two independent runs of the same model, produced formalizations of it (formulaA and formulaB in the file):
| Encoding A | Encoding B | 
Five things differ textually. Three are presentational: The conjuncts are reordered, the Eq arguments are swapped, and approvedRegion is explicitly expanded into two AWS Regions (us-east-1 and eu-west-1). Two involve different operators: An And became an Or in the confidential clause, and Lte became Lt at the size threshold. A unified diff of the two encodings marks 18 of their 28 lines as changed (Figure 1, textual-diff pane) and gives no indication of which of the five differences change meaning. The exact anti-unifier of the two encodings follows:
Two of the five differences disappear. The conjunct reordering is absorbed because And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent (ACI). The swapped Eq arguments have the same printed order in both readings because :comm canonized them. Neither changes meaning, so neither is reported.
The confidential clause uses Or where the requirement says and. Encoding A requires both the same-account check and server-side encryption with a customer managed key. Encoding B accepts either. The engine aligns A’s conjunction with B’s disjunction through their neutral elements, so the disagreement surfaces as two adjacent Variants nodes. Choose the first child at each node to reconstruct A: The Or collapses onto the plain equality, and sseCmk remains a mandatory conjunct. Choose the second child at each node to reconstruct B: The mandatory sseCmk weakens to (Lit true) and survives only as an alternative inside the Or. Together, the two Variants nodes show that encoding B accepts server-side encryption alone and therefore admits cross-account replication of confidential objects.
You might have expected sseCmk to be shared rather than repeated. However, a first-order anti-unifier can’t generalize the connective itself, so And versus Or forces the split into two alignments. Identity alignment still shares the five-node equality once. The exact solver’s exhaustive search finds no smaller form, and the printed result is one node smaller than holding both clauses whole in a single Variants.
Add the domain rewrite and run the diff again. The Variants node for the Region is not a bug. It reflects missing domain knowledge: In this deployment, the approved Regions are exactly those two. State that as a rewrite, saturate, and diff again:
The Region difference moves into the shared backbone, and :cr drops from 0.5862 to 0.4000. The full result is the semantic-diff pane of Figure 1. Exactly two disagreements remain: the weakened confidential clause and the threshold. B’s Lt is strict, so an object exactly at multipartThreshold is copied directly under A and takes the multipart path under B. The divergence is confined to the Ite condition. Both branches sit in the shared backbone. Both surviving differences are genuine bugs that an authorization reviewer must resolve. The algebra and one domain rewrite account for the other differences. The same file also runs the anytime search, (antiunify formulaA formulaB :algorithm uct :playouts 3000), which returns the identical size-35 term. The whole program completes in well under 100 ms on an Apple M3 Pro laptop (50–60 ms after the binary is warm). That covers parsing, declarations, saturation, five anti-unification queries with their regression checks, and process startup. We measured the wall-clock time of ./target/release/semi-persistent egraph/examples/au_policy_divergence.egg using a release build at Rust 1.97.1 and the shell’s time command over five warm runs. The Get started section shows the same command.
| textual diff: 18 of 28 lines flagged | semantic diff: two disagreements, localized | 
Figure 1: The same pair of encodings under diff and anti-unification. On the left, the textual diff flags 18 of 28 lines (removed, added). On the right, one domain rewrite moves the shared structure into the gray backbone, and the highlighted Variants confine the remaining differences to the weakened confidential clause and the strict threshold. The semantic-diff pane wraps one long line to fit
        After applying the declared algebra and one domain rewrite, the five textual differences reduce to two semantic disagreements: the weakened confidential clause and the strict size threshold.
Semantic diffing for Cedar and Dogwood policies
In an authorization policy, a dropped guard widens what is permitted and can cause the policy to fail open. Cedar is the open source authorization policy language behind Amazon Verified Permissions. Dogwood extends Cedar authorization policies with temporal conditions for runtime verification of AI agents. Its temporal sublanguage uses recorded event history to guard an action. The engine doesn’t evaluate Dogwood policies. It diffs their abstract syntax modulo a declared algebra. Validation (schema checking) and replay (evaluating a policy against a recorded event history) remain Dogwood’s job. The engine’s user guide has a worked chapter that diffs two independently produced Dogwood candidates for one requirement:
        The agent may POST to /deploy, but only if a health check has already come back 200 in the last 15 minutes.
Candidate A keeps both request guards (method and path) but reads the status code from a request event, an event kind that carries no such field. Candidate B uses the correct response event but drops the /deploy path guard. After any matching health check, B also permits a POST to /admin/purge-all. The candidates differ in six additional presentational ways, all of which the declared algebra or a three-rule comparison theory absorbs:
| Presentational difference | Absorbed by | 
| Cedar condition order | eAnd :assoc-comm-idem | 
| temporal conjunction order | tAnd :assoc-comm-idem | 
| predicate field order | args :assoc-comm-idem | 
| method == "POST" versus "POST" == method | eEq :comm | 
| 15m versus 900s | unit rewrite + constant fold | 
| count >= 1 versus 1 <= count | (birewrite (tLte a b) (tGte b a)) | 
The comparison theory consists of three visible rewrites, not a hidden normalization pass:
The anti-unifier of the two candidates (doc/book/examples/20-dogwood-simple.egg in the repository) has size 61, :cr 0.1864, and exactly two disagreements in an otherwise shared policy backbone:
Use the simplest available check for each disagreement. Two binary disagreements give four candidate completions. Dogwood validation resolves the first without human review by rejecting both request completions (“predicate … mentions field output.status_code, which is not declared on that event”). The second disagreement is an identity alignment: Candidate A’s path guard pairs against eTrue, showing that candidate B omitted the guard. The requirement resolves it (keep the guard), and a replay covering two decision points shows the consequence: After a health check, candidate B allows the off-target POST, whereas the repaired policy denies it. Combining B’s event kind with A’s guard produces a policy that neither candidate wrote. Choosing between the candidates would have kept one of the two bugs.
Commutativity has a side condition, and the engine doesn’t check it. Cedar’s && short-circuits, so commuting it is sound only when neither operand can raise an error. The comparison therefore relies on validation to rule out order-dependent errors, such as an attribute access that is safe only behind a has guard. The engine doesn’t re-check that condition.
A canonical printer can remove the presentational differences, but it can’t recover a dropped guard. A canonizing printer plus textual diff can absorb most, arguably all, of the six differences in the table more cheaply. No normalizer can align a two-conjunct condition against a three-conjunct one inside an otherwise matched term. Matching modulo the identity element aligns them by pairing the dropped conjunct with eTrue. In a permit condition, that dropped conjunct exposes the widening that makes the policy fail open.
        For the Dogwood candidates, the algebra and three rewrites remove six presentational differences. The remaining disagreements expose a schema error and a dropped guard. Combining the correct choices produces a policy that neither candidate supplied.
Comparing policy translations: OpenShell and CEL
The next two examples adapt predicates from the OpenShell and CEL articles. For each, we construct candidate translations of the same requirement. These are illustrative encodings, not recorded LLM samples.
OpenShell: Method and path scope. The OpenShell example models network permissions as predicates over a binary, host, port, layer, method, and path. We adapt the article’s reduced SMT-LIB model, whose path condition is a prefix test. We use that vocabulary for this requirement:
        Allow inspected REST requests made by /usr/bin/gh to api.github.com on port 443 when the method is GET and the path begins with /repos/NVIDIA/OpenShell/issues/. Deny all other requests.
Candidate A requires GET and the repository’s issues prefix. Candidate B uses POST and the broader /repos/NVIDIA/ prefix. The other checks appear in a different order. In the encoding, gh, github, and https name the binary, host, and port shown earlier. The names issuePrefix and orgPrefix identify the two prefixes. The exact solver returns:
The binary, host, port, and layer checks are shared. Their ordering disappears because And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent. Two Variants nodes identify the conflicting readings: the permitted operation and the path scope. The requirement settles both choices here. For an ambiguous requirement, the same nodes would give its owner two specific alternatives to resolve.
CEL: The scope of a shared condition. The CEL example exposes a production check lost during refactoring. We reuse the expressions as candidate translations of this requirement:
        Allow a request exactly when it is in production and its port is either 80 or 443.
CEL’s && binds more tightly than ||, so candidate B applies the production check only to port 80. We encode the expressions with supplied Boolean and integer inputs, using isProd, port80, and port443 for the corresponding input and literals:
The port-80 branch is shared. In the port-443 branch, (Variants isProd (Lit true)) shows the missing production condition. At is_prod = false and port = 443, A denies the request and B allows it. The diff directs the review to one part of the sentence: whether “in production” applies to both alternatives.
This example assumes that is_prod is supplied as a Boolean and port as an integer. Under these assumptions, neither expression raises an error. The encoding doesn’t model CEL errors or unknown values, and the engine doesn’t check these input assumptions.
CEL-Java’s verification framework can check equivalence and policy invariants with Z3. Such checks can provide evidence when resolving a disagreement. The anti-unifier itself doesn’t decide which translation matches the requirement, and a mistake shared by both candidates would remain shared.
Implementation and performance
The algorithm runs over an e-graph, a data structure that stores a term together with everything it is known to equal. E-graphs (equivalence graphs) come from congruence-closure procedures in theorem provers and were popularized for compiler optimization by equality saturation, as described by Willsey et al. in “egg: Fast and Extensible Equality Saturation” (POPL 2021). This engine’s e-graph adds native canonization for associative and commutative operators.
Anti-unification over e-graphs is also used for abstraction learning and program compression in babble (Cao et al., POPL 2023). Earlier implementations didn’t scale beyond small examples. Our saturation-based prototype also stalled there. Native AC canonization, AC-aware matching over distinct children, and direct search made subsecond queries practical. Semi-persistence reduced the cost of repeated queries.
Native AC canonization. Associativity, commutativity, and idempotence are not rewrite rules in this engine. They are properties of the data structure. Associative-commutative (AC) operators store their children as canonical sorted multisets (ACI operators as canonical sorted sets) at insertion time. One e-node therefore represents all reassociations and permutations of a term and, for idempotent operators, treats duplicate children as one. Equality modulo the declared laws is structural equality. The rewrite-based alternative floods the e-graph with an exponential family of equivalent copies before real work starts.
AC-aware matching over distinct children. Pattern matching against multiset nodes uses maximum-partition semantics: It branches over the distinct children of a node rather than enumerating multiplicity splits, so heavily repeated arguments do not cause a combinatorial blowup.
Direct search instead of rewriting. Anti-unification itself isn’t encoded as rewrite rules either. An exact dynamic programming solver (:algorithm exact) solves the joint-decomposition problem optimally. Optimal here is relative to its size-first objective, the current e-graph, and the configured cycle policy. An anytime Monte Carlo graph search (:algorithm uct, the default) returns its best answer for any playout budget. On the worked example’s pair, 3,000 playouts reproduce the exact optimum. Both optimize first for result size and then, among equal-size answers, prefer those that retain more structure in the shared backbone.
Semi-persistence. The e-graph supports (push) and (pop) snapshots recorded as sparse diffs rather than deep copies. Restoring a state therefore costs work proportional to what changed because the snapshot, plus the cost of repairing derived indexes. Proportional-cost restore lets the engine compare many candidates over one shared graph. A backtracking search can restore an earlier state without copying the full graph.
A verified core and its scope. The e-graph’s underlying container layer is verified in Verus, a verifier for Rust. The verified property is that restore reproduces the state at the matching (push) (1,703 verified conditions, 0 errors). The anti-unification crate proves its objective-order and lower-bound lemmas, but the full solver doesn’t yet have an end-to-end refinement proof. The engine can log a justification for every equivalence it derives (--proofs). As the repository notes, these records aren’t yet independently replay-checked certificates. All of these claims, with evidence tiers and retractions, are in the repository’s claims inventory (doc/claims.md).
        Native canonization avoids materializing equivalent AC terms. Distinct-child matching controls multiplicity, direct solvers avoid encoding anti-unification as rewrites, and semi-persistence reduces the cost of repeated queries.
Using semantic diffing in a pipeline
The same method extends from two candidates to a larger sample. Generate N candidate formalizations of the requirement. Load them into one shared e-graph, saturate under your domain rules, and cluster them using pairwise equality checks. In the user guide’s larger Dogwood study, five samples collapse into three clusters. Candidates that differ only in presentation join the same equivalence classes during construction. Anti-unify the cluster representatives pairwise. Then, in a layer built on top of the engine’s output, group recurring Variants nodes by their position in the shared backbone. In the study, three pairwise diffs reduce to exactly two review items. Use the simplest available check for each item: schema validation, replay, example I/O pairs, or human review.
With (push) and (pop) snapshots, you can test a proposed resolution without rebuilding the graph. Temporarily assert one branch of a Variants node as a domain fact, run the diff again, and roll back. A tool built on top of the engine could select and repair a full candidate against hard and soft constraints, for example with a MaxSMT solver over the variant space. MaxSMT (maximum satisfiability modulo theories) seeks a solution that satisfies all hard constraints while satisfying as many soft constraints as possible, or maximizing their total weight. Section 8 of Programming Z3 describes this form of optimization. That capability is not part of the current engine. Figure 2 summarizes the pipeline.
Use a semantic-diff budget in continuous integration (CI). The command (checkau A B :max_size N :algorithm exact) prints nothing on success and causes the program to fail when the anti-unifier exceeds the budget. Every printed result in the user guide is pinned this way, so the guide and the engine can’t drift apart. The same command can serve as a regression gate. Set a maximum result size for a reference formalization and a regenerated one, and fail the pipeline when the anti-unifier exceeds it. The binary follows standard shell conventions: Results go to stdout, diagnostics (ok --- N nodes) go to stderr, and the process exits non-zero if any check fails.
The diff can also guide a follow-up prompt or a question to the requirement owner. Mean pairwise :cr across samples gives a disagreement score for each requirement. A Variants node already contains the alternatives needed for a specific clarification, such as “did you mean strictly less than the threshold, or at most?”
        With several candidates, cluster equivalent outputs, compare the cluster representatives, and resolve recurring disagreements with validation, replay, examples, or human review.
Get started
Build the engine at the revision used for this post, then run the policy examples. These commands select the revision containing the OpenShell and CEL examples from pull request 103:
The engine is Apache-2.0 on GitHub. The user guide progresses from basic terms to the policy case studies, and the test suite runs every program in it directly from the repository. Annex B documents the antiunify and checkau commands. If your artifact language has an abstract syntax tree (AST) and an equational theory, you can diff it: Declare the algebra, state the domain identities as rewrites, and ask for the most specific anti-unifier. If your policies are Cedar, whether handwritten or generated for Amazon Verified Permissions, the same recipe applies to them. The OpenShell and CEL examples show how to encode other policy constructs and compare candidate readings of a requirement.

articles.title: Linux kernel reviewer steps down from memory management duties due to influx of AI slop patches — 'the amount of time wasted on AI slop is already too much, and we're only at the start of this,' volume of submissions coupled with low manpower forces the step back
articles.text:
Linux kernel reviewer steps down from memory management duties due to influx of AI slop patches — 'the amount of time wasted on AI slop is already too much, and we're only at the start of this,' volume of submissions and low manpower forces the step back
"Nowadays it's pretty much half of what I see, if not more."
The Linux Kernel is probably one of the best ecosystems to observe regarding the impact of AI in programming. The critical importance of its code and its maintainers' quality standards mean that patches, including but not only AI slop, go through rigorous review and are often discarded. Still, the amount of AI-produced code is often far higher than what the human reviewers can deal with. Lorenzo Stoakes, a lead Linux reviewer for memory management, has elected to step down from some of his former duties for exactly that reason.
Stoakes announced his decision today in a thread on the Linux kernel mailing list (LKML). He'll be leaving the core, reclaim, Rust, THP (Huge Pages), and miscellaneous sections of the kernel memory management section, while staying on for his remaining duties, including KVM. The partial departure appears amicable, and the developer doesn't appear to be angry or bitter. He says that his decision was due to the mounting pressure on his inbox, that he'll wrap up the patch series he's currently working on, and he'll occasionally pitch in regardless.
However, the underlying cause is also clear: "Of course the AI wave has been horrible, and is getting significantly worse. At first it was once in a while that I'd see slop. Then it was at least once a week. Then every few days. Nowadays it's pretty much half of what I see, if not more."
This is a sentiment echoed by many programmers in the open-source community, and the latest in a running series of AI-provoked project departures, submission rules adjustments, and strategic shifts. AI-assisted programming has arguably been both a boon and a curse for open-source software. The project's open nature means that anyone can find a bug and report it or fix it, or add functionality — all of which are good things.
However, that also means that literally anyone can contribute, and in a world ridden with low-effort AI slop and untold amounts of AI agents, that's... suboptimal. Open-source projects are arguably the hardest-hit because they very rarely have the adequate manpower or funds to keep the code up to date, much less deal with the output of a million robotic monkeys on a million digital typewriters.
Linus Torvalds, creator and headmaster of Linux, has taken a pro-AI stance, supported not only by the speed of additional contributions, but also the fact that bots often don't make mistakes that even seasoned developers do. This topic has been the subject of a lot of LKML discussion, and the current stance is that AI-assisted code commits don't need to be marked as such.
The problem, then, has arguably become one of filtering: it's easy enough to be accepting of AI contributions when your day isn't spent waddling through mud to find the one gold nugget, which is what Stoakes was seemingly weary of.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Back in July, he'd already brought up concerns about the "recent wave of slop in [memory management]," adding that "the amount of time wasted on AI slop is already too much and we're only at the start of this." Even as recently as a month ago, he said that "what kills the project is having 1,000 slop submissions that 2 or 3 people have to do something with."
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Cloud hosting firm Railway says recent breach leads to $740,000 in fraudulent AI charges
articles.text:
Cloud hosting firm Railway says recent breach leads to $740,000 in fraudulent AI charges
A zero-day in a cloud provider's infrastructure granted attackers access to paid AI models
- Attackers exploited a zero-day in Railway’s build infrastructure to steal customer AI API keys and cloud credentials
- Stolen keys fueled roughly $740,000 in unauthorized AI usage, likely supporting large-scale model training and automation
- Railway spent 26 hours battling AI-assisted attackers before containing the intrusion and rotating credentials
US-based cloud hosting company Railway said threat actors abused a previously unknown vulnerability to break in, steal user credentials, and rake up hundreds of thousands of dollars in unauthorized AI usage.
The company managed to throw out the criminals and harden its infrastructure, but not before witnessing an epic 26-hour bot-versus-bot battle.
Railway gets attacked
At its core, Railway is a cloud hosting company, but one designed primarily for developers to build, deploy, and run applications without having to manage much of the underlying infrastructure.
Its key services include running websites and APIs, hosting databases and deploying PostgreSQL and MySQL, connecting GitHub repositories and deploying new code automatically, and handling containers, networking and resource allocation.
Similar to other cloud providers, its build infrastructure uses a multi-tenant architecture, meaning a single device hosts multiple builds which should, in theory, be in full isolation from each other on the same virtual machine.
Many of its customers are developers and businesses using AI services, with API keys stored as environment variables on the platform. This allows the hosted applications to communicate with AI models more easily.
Now, in an incident report, Railway said unidentified threat actors used a zero-day vulnerability in its build infrastructure to “partially escape filesystem isolation” and read some of the files stored on the host virtual machines. In these files were apparently credentials the build servers use to authenticate to a subset of internal systems.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
“After they acquired this credential, the attacker attempted but initially failed to use it in a variety of systems,” the report stated. However, they eventually realized the credential allowed access to Temporal, the company’s internal task management system. There they found a copy of Railway’s internal codebase in which they discovered a misconfigured authentication mechanism that allowed them to nab temporary cloud credentials.
With these, they accessed other internal systems, including credentials needed to access a production database with encrypted customer environment variables, as well as information on how to decrypt them.
API keys for AI services
The attackers were apparently mostly interested in API keys of businesses using AI services. Using the keys, they were able to access paid AI services, leaving the victims to pick up the tab.
And quite the tab it was - roughly $740,000 charged for using coding agents and AI training pipelines. Railway believes whoever obtained the keys likely sold them on the black market, possibly to support model distillation.
Model distillation is when a smaller AI model is trained to imitate the capabilities and responses of a larger, more powerful model. This is usually done by sending a large number of queries to the original model, and using whatever it returns as training data for the smaller ones. Although it is impossible to prove, many analysts believe this is how Chinese models are able to compete with US ones.
Railway estimates environment variables of up to 100,000 customer workspaces could have been decrypted during the incident, but stresses the number represents an upper limit rather than a confirmed number of compromised accounts.
The company said the attack started on October 20 at roughly 07:28 UTC, and ended at 09:24 UTC on October 21, some 26 hours later. During that time the engineers, working in shifts, saw the attacker probing many potential routes in parallel, as Railway was hardening them, also in parallel. “The escalating situation became a contest of agent speed, with Railway defending against abliterated models and a harness similar to ARTEX, according to Wiz,” it said in the report.
Railway said it has since closed the exploited vulnerabilities, rebuilt affected infrastructure, and rotated compromised credentials. It is also working with AI providers to refund fraudulent charges, promising to cover losses that the providers refuse to reimburse.

articles.title: Volkswagen respire enfin en Chine, malgré le flop de ses voitures électriques conçues avec Xpeng — Frandroid
articles.text:
Il fut un temps où les marques automobiles européennes avaient pignon sur rue en Chine. C’était tout particulièrement le cas des constructeurs allemands, comme Volkswagen. Mais aujourd’hui, ces derniers se sont laissé distancer par la concurrence locale, qui prend une importance grandissante.
La firme de Wolfsburg en fait les frais depuis quelques années : au troisième trimestre, les livraisons du groupe en Chine ont encore chuté de 38,5 %, à 405 800 véhicules, après un recul de 36,6 % au deuxième trimestre. Mais où en est-on actuellement ? Eh bien, la marque Volkswagen a dévoilé ce mercredi 11 novembre ses ventes de voitures électrifiées en Chine pour le mois d’octobre.
Globalement, c’est plutôt une bonne nouvelle. La marque a livré plus de 28 000 voitures électrifiées (100 % électriques, hybrides rechargeables et à prolongateur d’autonomie) sur ce seul mois en Chine, un record. C’est 4,5 fois plus qu’en octobre 2025, soit une hausse de 346,9 % sur un an. Le tout alors que le marché chinois des voitures électrifiées a reculé d’environ 13 % sur la même période, selon l’estimation de Volkswagen.
Cette progression repose sur des voitures développées pour ce marché, à commencer par le SUV ID. Aura T6, livré à plus de 12 000 exemplaires en octobre, ce qui le place en tête des SUV de taille moyenne selon Volkswagen.
Du 10 au 30 novembre, le LUBA mini 2 AWD 1000 passe à 1 199 € au lieu de 1 499 €, support de lavage offert ! Vision IA tri-caméra, sans fil périmétrique, tonte des bordures, adaptation à toutes les conditions de luminosité… Bref, il a tout pour tondre à votre place !
L’ID. Era 5S plaît aussi, avec 7 100 livraisons en octobre. Cette berline hybride rechargeable (et pas 100 % électrique, donc) est la plus vendue de sa catégorie en Chine, selon Volkswagen. De son côté, la nouvelle Jetta M6, lancée le 24 octobre sous la marque Jetta (filiale à bas prix de Volkswagen en Chine), a dépassé les 1 200 livraisons dès sa première semaine et cumule 17 000 commandes.
Quant à l’ID. Era 8X à prolongateur d’autonomie, commercialisé depuis le 12 octobre, Volkswagen annonce 3 500 livraisons et 10 000 commandes sur son premier mois. Par ailleurs, la marque lance ce jeudi 12 novembre l’ID. Era 5X, avant l’ID. Aura L5 en décembre, deux premiers modèles basés sur VEGA, la base technique développée en interne par Volkswagen en Chine.
Ses voitures électrifiées devraient représenter plus de la moitié de sa gamme dès 2027, puis plus de 75 % de ses volumes en Chine d’ici à 2030.
Ce bond fait entrer Volkswagen dans le top 15 des marques de voitures électrifiées en Chine, alors qu’il pointait jusqu’ici à la 30e place. La marque vise désormais le top 10 en 2027. Sur les 13 nouveaux modèles électrifiés qu’elle dévoile en Chine en 2026, 11 sont déjà commercialisés.
Une forte déconvenue
Sur le papier, tout semble aller bien pour Volkswagen. Mais l’agence de presse Reuters a publié ce mercredi 11 novembre des informations qui nuancent ce tableau. Volkswagen Anhui, la coentreprise dédiée aux autos 100 % électriques que Volkswagen détient à 75 % avec le chinois JAC, rencontre de grandes difficultés.
Entre janvier et septembre 2026, seuls 11 360 exemplaires de la gamme ID. Unyx ont été vendus, selon le cabinet ThinkerCar cité par Reuters. Le tout alors que la coentreprise prévoit d’en produire 33 000 cette année et vise 128 000 ventes en 2027, d’après un document interne consulté par Reuters.
Un objectif difficile à atteindre, d’autant que Volkswagen Anhui n’aurait prévu aucun nouveau modèle en 2027 et 2028, selon deux sources de Reuters. Un crossover était envisagé pour 2028, mais le projet a été mis en pause. Volkswagen China n’a pas commenté sa stratégie produit et se contente d’évoquer quatre modèles en vente et d’autres nouveautés après cette année.
Pourtant, Volkswagen a tout fait pour imposer sa nouvelle gamme dédiée à la Chine, en nouant notamment un partenariat avec Xpeng pour accélérer sur la partie logicielle. Celui-ci a donné naissance à l’ID. Unyx 08, lancé en avril, dont les ventes restent loin des objectifs malgré une baisse de prix temporaire de 17,4 % dès septembre. Un second modèle conçu avec Xpeng, la berline ID. Unyx 09, est arrivé fin octobre. À tel point que le groupe envisage désormais de vendre ses autos chinoises en Europe.
En parallèle, Volkswagen veut lancer 30 nouveaux modèles électrifiés en Chine d’ici à 2029, incluant des modèles à prolongateur d’autonomie. Mais la firme de Wolfsburg reste sous la pression d’une concurrence chinoise de plus en plus présente, qui casse les prix. Ainsi, les clients semblent délaisser les VE du groupe allemand, qui séduit plutôt avec ses autos électrifiées sur ce marché.

articles.title: Flock is asking lawmakers to regulate its cameras, as long as police don't need a warrant
articles.text:
A hot potato: Flock is fighting to improve its reputation. Not an easy task, considering that the surveillance company has been the subject of so many negative stories in recent times. Its latest attempt to placate the public is a bit of a surprise: announcing support for state rules on its license plate-reading cameras. But it draws the line at requiring police to obtain warrants before searching its databases, which is less of a surprise.
As Arizona Capitol Times reports, Flock policy director Andrea Korb told an R Street Institute webinar that the company supports state-by-state legislation governing its camera technology. It expects a wave of bills in 2027, with lawmakers interested even in states that have recently passed restrictions.
"There is a lot of fear and concern about this technology right now and we want people to know ... your legislature has looked at this and here are the safeguards that have been put in place," Korb said. "There shouldn't be unfettered access to all vehicles and all cameras for any reason."
There is, however, a fairly big sticking point, and probably the most contentious element when it comes to Flock searches: warrants. Korb backed independent third-party audits, noting these are already in place in Minnesota, but argued that requiring police to obtain warrants before searching the databases would burden officers and substantially reduce the technology's effectiveness.
Emily Grimmius, a privacy policy analyst at the Libertas Institute, argued that audits identify problems after they happen, whereas warrants could prevent civil rights violations. She is working on Utah legislation that would require warrants except in emergencies, approval before camera installations, regular audits, and stronger penalties for misuse.
"Sometimes this job should be difficult for law enforcement because due process is incredible," Grimmius said.
Flock has already announced changes to its own policies, including reducing its default data retention period from 30 days to seven. But that doesn't mean every image disappears after a week. Existing customers can retain their current retention periods, while an Evidence Mode allows specific records to be preserved for active investigations.
Customers will also be able to restrict which categories of offenses other agencies can investigate using their cameras, including blocking immigration-related searches.
The company also says it will require automated misuse detection and case codes for law enforcement searches by the end of the year. Emergency searches can bypass the code requirement but will be flagged for review. Another promised safeguard automatically suspends access when activity meets the company's criteria for abnormal behavior, pending an administrator's review.
Whether any of this restores public confidence remains to be seen. It was reported last month that two Flock cameras reappeared in Dayton, Minnesota, after the city canceled its contract and explicitly told the company not to complete work orders. Residents spotted the devices, and police were directed to remove them.
That followed a similar incident in Grass Valley, California, where Flock blamed an automated maintenance process for replacing cameras the city had deliberately removed.

articles.title: Dile adiós a reservar vuelos con una IA: esta aerolínea comienza a bloquear las compras hechas por agentes
articles.text:
United Airlines ha comenzado a bloquear la compra de billetes de avión a través de agentes de IA. La aerolínea anunció este miércoles que no permitirá la realización de transacciones automatizadas a través de sus sistemas. Esto no se limita a las que se realicen a través de su página web oficial, sino también a través de sitios de terceros como agregadores o agencias de viajes.
La principal preocupación que ha expresado United Airlines al momento de tomar esta decisión responde a cuestiones de privacidad. Sin embargo, no se limita a ello. La compañía sostiene que permitir que un agente o asistente de inteligencia artificial concrete la compra de un pasaje puede acarrear problemas regulatorios.
Para ser más precisos, United Airlines habla sobre posibles violaciones de las normativas estipuladas tanto por la Administración Federal de Aviación (FAA) como por el Departamento de Transporte (DOT) de Estados Unidos. El ejemplo presentado por la aerolínea es que hacer el check-in de un vuelo requiere de que un humano reconozca explícitamente que no lleva sustancias prohibidas en su equipaje. Si una IA se encarga de completar el proceso sin que una persona intervenga, puede terminar informando algo incorrecto y generar un incidente en el aeropuerto, o tal vez peor.
En lo que corresponde a los potenciales riesgos de privacidad por el uso de agentes de IA, United Airlines expresó lo siguiente: "Compartir las credenciales de una cuenta con asistentes personales de inteligencia artificial de terceros puede exponer información confidencial. Además, las acciones realizadas por estas herramientas podrían derivar en compras no deseadas, modificaciones en la cuenta o el uso de millas MileagePlus".
United Airlines bloquea la compra de billetes de avión mediante agentes de IA
El bloqueo de United Airlines a las compras de billetes realizadas con agentes de IA implica la adopción de cambios en distintos niveles de sus sistemas. Es por ello que la firma va a actualizar su política de reservas, al igual que la de emisión y distribución de pasajes aéreos.
El comunicado oficial no incluye detalles respecto de qué modificaciones técnicas requerirá esta medida. Tampoco se menciona si United Airlines ha notificado con antelación a las principales empresas de IA sobre su plan, o si ha solicitado su ayuda para evitar violaciones a las nuevas políticas que pretende implementar.
United Airlines incluso menciona que sectores como el comercio minorista y la banca personal han comenzado a bloquear el uso de agentes de IA. Es por ello que la firma insta a más empresas a tomar acciones similares para evitar que la automatización de tareas mediante agentes de IA se vuelva una pesadilla.
Aún no se sabe cuándo comenzará a regir la medida de United Airlines. Tampoco, si otras aerolíneas pretenden tomar determinaciones similares en lo inmediato. The Wall Street Journal reporta que los agentes de IA podrán continuar navegando y observando los precios de los billetes en la web de la línea aérea, pero que quedará totalmente bloqueada la opción de avanzar con la compra sin que un humano esté de forma activa detrás de la pantalla.

articles.title: Apple is shuttering its 28-year-old online community forum
articles.text:
Apple’s online community forum will close on November 20.
On Tuesday night, Apple posted a message to the Apple Support Community announcing the forum’s closure:
The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.
You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site.
We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.
For 28 years, the forum has provided Apple users with a way to get quick technical advice about their products. That advice usually came from fellow users, though Apple employees occasionally chimed in. As with any community forum, the helpfulness and accuracy of the advice varied.
Apple reportedly told MacRumors that it is shutting down the forum after evaluating its support strategy and customer needs.
The Apple Support Community dates to 1998, when the online forum was known as Apple Tech Exchange. Two years later, Apple renamed the community forum to Apple Discussions. In 2011, Apple revamped the forum, adding dedicated communities for specific devices and the ability to track responses to posted questions, while renaming it Apple Support Communities. By 2022, the forum was called Apple Support Community, as MacRumors noted this week.
Based on yesterday’s announcement, it seems Apple now prefers that its customers rely on official Apple employees for technical support. The forum may also have become less popular as rival forums grow, including Reddit and the technical support communities on the MacRumors and AppleInsider forums.

articles.title: Meta is losing its longtime head of infrastructure | TechCrunch
articles.text:
A key figure in Meta’s growth into a social media and tech industry powerhouse is leaving the company.
Santosh Janardhan, the company’s longtime head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, will be stepping down, Meta told TechCrunch. He will be replaced by Dave Brown, who joined the company as vice president of infrastructure earlier this year, the company added. Previous to coming aboard at Meta, Brown spent 19 years at Amazon, where he focused on compute, cloud, and AI, his LinkedIn shows.
It sounds like Janardhan will remain at Meta for a little bit, although he is expected to leave next year. “Santosh will stay on for transition and he is moving into an advisory role on Meta Compute,” said a Meta representative.
Janardhan, who originally joined the company in 2009, helped the firm grow into the massive internet presence that it is today. Bloomberg originally reported Janardhan’s departure, citing an internal memo that had recently been circulated. It’s unclear why Janardhan is stepping down from the role. The memo did not specify the reasons for his departure and Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for clarity on the issue. However, Janardhan’s memo apparently cited the need to “pass the baton.”
In recent years, the company’s investment in infrastructure has exploded, as it seeks to keep up with its competitors in the AI race. Earlier this year, Janardhan was tasked with leading Meta Compute, the company initiative to scale its data center investments and strategy.

articles.title: SpaceX-Strategiewechsel: Anthropic ersetzt NASA als Top-Kunde
articles.text:
Anthropic ist jetzt der größte Einzelkunde von SpaceX. Das berichtet die Finanznachrichtenagentur Bloomberg unter Berufung auf eine anonyme Quelle. Die soll bestätigt haben, dass sich hinter „Kunde B“ im jüngsten Geschäftsbericht von SpaceX, das sich inzwischen auch „SpaceXSI“ (für „SpaceX Super Intelligence“) nennt, die KI-Firma verbirgt. Auf sie entfällt demnach rund ein Drittel des Umsatzes. Grundlage sei eine milliardenschwere Partnerschaft, die Anthropic im Frühjahr mit SpaceX geschlossen hat. Dabei sicherte sich das Unternehmen einen Großteil der KI-Rechenkapazitäten von xAI – Musks KI-Firma, die inzwischen in SpaceX aufgegangen ist. Auch deshalb konnte das Unternehmen nach dem Rekordbörsengang erstmals einen Milliardengewinn verbuchen.
Braucht SpaceX die Nasa nicht mehr?
Die Zahlen untermauern eine Entwicklung, die das US-Technikmagazin Ars Technica kürzlich in einer ausführlichen Reportage beschrieben hat: Mehr als ein Jahrzehnt lang hing Musks Raumfahrtfirma am Geld der US‑Regierung. Inzwischen ist es andersherum: Die Nasa ist beim Transport von Menschen ins All komplett auf SpaceX angewiesen, während sich das Unternehmen immer weiter von ihr abwendet.
So soll die Raumkapsel Crew Dragon nur noch bis 2030 Astronautinnen und Astronauten ins All bringen. Die Trägerrakete Falcon 9 könnte laut dem Bericht schon 2028 ausgemustert werden. Um lukrative Regierungsaufträge bewirbt sich SpaceX demnach nicht mehr in jedem Fall.
Geld soll künftig aus der KI kommen
Bloomberg und Ars Technica kommen übereinstimmend zu dem Schluss, dass SpaceX sein Geld künftig vor allem mit KI verdienen will. Das riesige Rechenzentrum in Memphis, das an Anthropic vermietet ist, ist dabei nur der Anfang. Musk will KI-Rechenzentren in großem Stil ins Weltall verlagern, weil dort „kostenlose“ Energie durch die Sonne zur Verfügung steht. Ob das technisch funktioniert, ist allerdings umstritten.
In der Raumfahrt setzt SpaceX nun alles auf das Starship. Die Riesenrakete soll deutlich mehr Nutzlast transportieren als bisherige Systeme. Ars Technica weist jedoch darauf hin, dass es kaum Hinweise darauf gibt, dass SpaceX noch an einem Aussetzmechanismus für große Nutzlasten arbeitet – also an der Technik, die Satelliten im All freisetzt. Der bisherige Mechanismus eignet sich für Starlink- und Rechenzentrumssatelliten, nicht aber für große Weltraumteleskope, wie die Nasa sie braucht.

articles.title: Así es como está Nintendo frenando la piratería y las emulaciones en PC de sus juegos
articles.text:
Nintendo cerró de forma oficial la puerta a uno de agujero de seguridad que estaba permitiendo la emulación de sus juegos en PC. Con la actualización de firmware 23.5.0 para Nintendo Switch 2 neutraliza el primer jailbreak público de la consola y bloquea la posibilidad de extraer y modificar juegos sin autorización.
La vulnerabilidad llevaba apenas unas semanas en circulación. Había sido difundida en octubre por el desarrollador Sammy Hajhamid, conocido como “pepsipu”, bajo el nombre ns2jb, y permitió a miles de usuarios ejecutar código con privilegios elevados en sus consolas.
Qué permitía hacer el jailbreak antes del parche
El exploit aprovechaba una falla en la versión de firmware 23.01 y abría la puerta a lo que se conoce como aplicaciones homebrew: software casero no autorizado por Nintendo.
Con esa brecha, los usuarios podían ejecutar programas propios, hacer copias de seguridad de partidas guardadas y extraer archivos digitales de los juegos sin modificar el hardware de la consola.
También permitía introducir modificaciones dentro de los propios videojuegos. Un caso mencionado fue el de Mario Kart World, en el que se llegaron a incorporar personajes mediante herramientas de inteligencia artificial como OpenAI Codex.
El impacto se sintió especialmente en la escena de modding y preservación: gracias a la extracción de archivos, títulos como Zelda: Ocarina of Time resultaron jugables en computadoras desde el lanzamiento de la consola.
Cómo actúa la actualización 23.5.0 en Nintendo Switch
El investigador de seguridad conocido como OatmealDome confirmó en una publicación en X que el fallo del sistema operativo utilizado en el jailbreak fue corregido en la versión 23.5.0.
Según explicó, volver a extraer y modificar juegos será imposible a partir de esta actualización, con la excepción de algunos títulos en formato cartucho (y eventualmente sus actualizaciones) que se lancen en el futuro cercano.
El especialista precisó que exploits dentro de juegos específicos, como SmileBASIC y Civilization VII, continúan existiendo. Sin embargo, ya no es posible “escapar” de esos juegos para tomar el control del sistema operativo completo.
Esto implica que las capacidades del homebrew quedan limitadas a lo que el propio juego ya permite hacer de forma nativa, es decir, prácticamente nada en comparación con lo que el jailbreak ofrecía.
En Alemania, el sitio especializado que cubrió el caso añadió que los puntos de entrada dentro de los juegos no desaparecieron, pero que desde el firmware 23.5.0 los usuarios ya no pueden salir del entorno restringido de cada título para operar sobre el sistema.
Qué pasa con los cartuchos físicos y las claves de cifrado
La cuenta especializada SwitchTools matizó el alcance real de la actualización en una publicación en X. Según detalló, el firmware 23.5.0 no incluye ninguna clave maestra de cifrado nueva.
En términos prácticos, esto significa que, por el momento, todavía es posible extraer los cartuchos físicos que se publiquen, siempre que no se trate de GameKeyCards.
Las GameKeyCards no almacenan el juego completo dentro del cartucho: funcionan como una llave de descarga vinculada a la tienda digital de Nintendo, por lo que no equivalen a una copia física tradicional.
Los juegos digitales, las actualizaciones y los contenidos descargables (DLC) no pueden descargarse ni extraerse sin acceso a Nintendo Switch Online, algo que el bloqueo del jailbreak impide en consolas ya actualizadas.
Esta distinción resulta relevante: mientras los cartuchos convencionales siguen expuestos a la extracción mediante métodos ya conocidos, todo el contenido que depende de los servidores de Nintendo queda protegido tras el parche.
Nuevas funciones que llegan junto al parche de seguridad
Nintendo no hizo referencia oficial a la seguridad en las notas de la actualización 23.5.0, que se centraron en cambios de accesibilidad y nuevas funciones para los usuarios.
La novedad más relevante es la posibilidad de regalar títulos comprados en la tienda digital a otro miembro del mismo grupo familiar de una cuenta Nintendo, función que entrará en vigencia el 17 de noviembre.
La actualización también incorpora ajustes de accesibilidad directamente en la etapa de configuración inicial de la consola, según detalló la compañía en las notas oficiales del lanzamiento.

articles.title: IBM Quantum announces upcoming Nighthawk r3 processor designed to execute 10,000 operations - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
IBM Quantum announces upcoming Nighthawk r3 processor designed to execute 10,000 operations
IBM Corp. today announced the Quantum Nighthawk r3, its next-generation processor designed to tackle larger, more complex computations at high speed while maintaining quality.
The company also said that in 2027, IBM plans to link two r3 quantum processors into a single system capable of running up to 10,000 quantum operations, scaling to more than 1,000 qubits between them.
“Useful quantum computing hinges on whether results can be delivered with accuracy and speed, both are fundamental,” said Director of IBM Research Jay Gambetta. “IBM Nighthawk is already showing us what that looks like today.”
The new r3 chip follows the introduction of Nighthawk r2 in September, which supports more than 7,500 quantum operations on 120 qubits.
Qubits are the fundamental unit of logical information in a quantum computer, similar to a classical computer’s bit. Unlike classical bits, which can be a 0 or 1, qubits can be 0, 1 or a “superposition” of both at the same time. Using this property, quantum processors such as IBM’s Nighthawk can do rapid, complex parallel calculations.
The r2 chip introduced a groundbreaking high-speed qubit reset architecture that lets developers and researchers quickly prime qubits after measurements. Under normal circumstances, after a quantum circuit runs and the result is measured, the qubits must return to the ground state before the next program can run; this process can take hundreds of milliseconds, meaning the chip remains idle during that time. With the new technology, this wait period can be reduced from about 200 milliseconds down to roughly 25 nanoseconds without disturbing neighboring qubits.
Scaling to more than 1,000 qubits
Building on lessons learned from Nighthawk r2 and the technology built into it, IBM said r3 will extend the same high-speed architecture to larger quantum systems to support 10,000 operations on 520 programmable qubits with 2,034 physical quantum components.
A physical qubit is the actual, hardware-level quantum device that stores the quantum information. In Nighthawk, the qubits are superconducting and arranged in a square lattice. The programmable qubits are the measurable, active quantum data units, while additional quantum components support them, including couplers and reset elements.
IBM said it has already demonstrated two critical technologies that will make combining two r3 chips. This year, the company connected two Nighthawk r1 processors using four l-couplers, or “long-range” quantum interconnects. These act as a physical bridge between separate processors to create a larger machine.
In the demonstration, the couplers achieved a 99.4% transfer fidelity, progressing towards the target of 99.9% fidelity. The company also connected cryogenic modules into a single system.
In 2027, IBM intends to progress using these modularity advances to scale Nighthawk into a larger quantum system. By connecting two Nighthawk r3 processors into a single 1,040 system, IBM will extend this high-performance architecture to tackle larger and more complex computations.
“As we scale this architecture to larger and more powerful quantum computers, the capabilities of quantum computation will reach new levels as we integrate more closely with classical resources and march ahead to fault tolerance,” added Gambetta.
Bridging quantum and classical on a single platform
IBM also announced that its cloud-based service for researchers and developers, IBM Quantum Platform, will bring high-performance classical and quantum computing together in a single managed environment.
Users can now integrate quantum workflows directly with HPC and classical resources on the platform, or with classical compute on their laptop or any number of the world’s most powerful supercomputers.
Integrating quantum and classical computing permits traditional computers to orchestrate algorithms and computations on specialized central processing units and graphics processing units, while the quantum computer runs parallel computations. Users are already seeing promising results, including Cleveland Clinic using the platform to process 2.6 million samples up to three times faster to model biological structures.
Direct integration of quantum and classical systems will also help drive breakthroughs in quantum error correction. Error correction is fundamental to handling the noise that can destabilize individual qubits, creating a high chance of errors rising out of computations. Quantum Platform is launching pulse-level access to give researchers precise control over how they can detect, understand and correct errors within quantum and classical architectures.
IBM recently launched a new quantum error-correction platform that addresses this, in collaboration with Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and the Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The build physically colocates Nighthawk processors with next-generation AMD GPUs and CPUs.

articles.title: Boulanger brade l'iPad Air 13 M3 1 To à -40 % pour le Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
Dans la gamme Apple, l’iPad Air occupe une position bien précise : plus musclé que l’iPad d’entrée de gamme, moins élitiste que l’iPad Pro. La version 13 pouces offre un grand écran, toujours animé par la puce M3, avec 8 Go de RAM et ici 1 To de stockage. Compatible avec l’Apple Pencil Pro et le Magic Keyboard, elle peut se transformer en station de travail portable, même si ces accessoires restent onéreux à l’achat. Pour le Black Friday, Boulanger propose cette configuration haut de gamme avec 680 euros de réduction à la clé.
Les atouts de l’iPad Air 13 M3
- Puce M3 : performances solides pour la créativité et le multitâche
- Grand écran LCD 13 pouces, 2732 × 2048 pixels, 264 ppp
- 1 To de stockage et connectivité 5G intégrée
Lancée à 1 769 euros par Apple et généralement affichée à 1 669 euros chez les revendeurs, cette version 1 To 5G de l’iPad Air 13 M3 est disponible pour 989 euros sur Boulanger.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant l’Apple iPad Air 13 M3. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un grand écran pour travailler sérieusement
Treize pouces, ça change tout à l’usage. La dalle IPS affiche une définition de 2 732 x 2 048 pixels pour une densité de 264 ppp : le texte est net, les illustrations précises, les vidéos confortables à regarder même en plein jour. Le format 280,6 x 214,9 mm autorise un vrai espace de travail, que ce soit pour annoter des PDF à l’Apple Pencil Pro ou pour ouvrir deux applications côte à côte en Split View.
Honnêtement, le principal point qui fait tiquer à ce prix, c’est le 60 Hz. Pas de ProMotion ici – c’est une limitation claire par rapport à l’iPad Pro, et ça se sent quand on fait défiler de longs documents ou qu’on dessine avec le Pencil. Le design, lui, n’a pas bougé : les bordures sont un peu larges et le châssis est identique à celui de l’iPad Air M2, le premier Air à passer au 13 pouces en 2024. Rien de rédhibitoire, mais à noter si vous venez d’un modèle récent.
La puce M3 et 1 To : une tablette qui ne se limite pas
La puce M3 embarquée ici est la même que celle qui équipe certains MacBook. Sur tablette, ça signifie que les applications créatives – retouche photo, montage vidéo, illustration – tournent sans accroc, même en multitâche avec plusieurs fenêtres ouvertes. Les 8 Go de RAM font le travail, et le 1 To de stockage évite de penser à ce qu’on archive ou pas. Pour de la vidéo 4K ou des bibliothèques de photos volumineuses, c’est franchement appréciable.
La connectivité 5G s’ajoute au Wi-Fi 6E pour travailler partout sans dépendre d’un point d’accès. Côté autonomie, Apple annonce jusqu’à 9 heures – raisonnable pour une journée de travail, sans être exceptionnel. La tablette tourne aujourd’hui sous iPadOS 27 (sorti le 14 septembre) et gère Apple Intelligence. Procreate, Final Cut Pro ou LumaFusion y tournent en versions natives qui tirent vraiment parti de la puissance disponible.

articles.title: 11.11: iPhone 17 (256 GB) registra alta queda de preço na Amazon • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
11.11: iPhone 17 (256 GB) registra alta queda de preço na Amazon
iPhone 17 (256 GB) traz câmeras de 48 MP e tela OLED de 120 Hz; celular custo-benefício da Apple sai 36% mais em conta em oferta no Pix
O iPhone 17 de 256 GB está saindo por R$ 5.273 no Pix na Amazon. O smartphone da Apple, com câmeras de 48 MP e tela OLED de 120 Hz, recebe desconto de 36% no 11.11 sobre o preço base atual de R$ 8.299, reajustado recentemente.
O iPhone 17 é um celular custo-benefício equipado com uma tela OLED de 6,3″ com ProMotion de 120 Hz e brilho máximo de 3.000 nits. Tal combinação permite reproduzir imagens com cores excelentes e alta fluidez, além de garantir a visibilidade em qualquer lugar.
Seu chip Apple A19 e os 8 GB de RAM dão conta de apps em multitarefa, games e soluções do Apple Intelligence localmente. Os 256 GB de espaço interno são adequados para guardar fotos e vídeos.
O kit principal de câmeras inclui wide com OIS e ultrawide com ângulo de 120º, que captam belas cenas ao ar livre, ambas de 48 MP. A frontal de 18 MP tira ótimas selfies na horizontal, mesmo segurando o celular em pé. Todas filmam em 4K a 60 fps.
O corpo de alumínio do iPhone 17 é revestido de ambos os lados pelo vidro Ceramic Shield 2, resistente a arranhões e pancadas. A certificação IP68 adiciona proteção em cenários como ambientes empoeirados e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 3.692 mAh tem autonomia de até 30 horas de vídeo, segundo a fabricante. O suporte a MagSafe e carregamento rápido de 40 W o permitem receber uma carga de 50% em apenas 20 minutos, ideal para quem não tem tempo a perder com tomadas.
O iPhone 17 de 256 GB (R$ 5.273 no Pix) foi atualizado para o iOS 27 e receberá pelo menos mais cinco updates do sistema operacional. O celular da Apple possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, Ultra Wideband (UWB), NFC e comporta eSIM.
11 de novembro é o “Dia dos Solteiros” na China, data em que lojas locais oferecem gadgets com descontos e condições especiais, similar à campanha da Black November; por aqui, a data é tão forte quanto a Black Friday, que ocorre em 27 de novembro de 2026.
