articles.title: Isaac Casado, malagueño que estudia en Suecia: “España está bien para ir de vacaciones, pero para estudiar prefiero Europa”
articles.text:
Isaac Casado tiene 23 años y está haciendo un máster en Liderazgo para la Sostenibilidad en la Universidad de Malmö (Suecia). “España es un país ideal para estar de vacaciones, pero para estudiar prefiero Europa”. Aunque reconoce que hay buenas universidades en España, destaca el enfoque de los centros escandinavos.
En su opinión, la formación está “mucho más orientada al mundo laboral y a la práctica profesional” y hay menos teoría que en España. Además, apunta que es un tipo de formación más cercana a la práctica. “Me encanta aprender cosas nuevas, pero me cuesta leer textos demasiado largos”. Con esta trayectoria cree que podrá desarrollar su carrera profesional en entornos ligados a la UE.
Desde los 16 años empezó a dar pasos en este sentido. Estaba en 4.º de ESO en el colegio Manuel Siurot de Málaga. En esa época participó en un Erasmus+ en Países Bajos. Viajó “con todos los gastos pagados” y formaba parte de un proyecto de su centro subvencionado por la Unión Europea.
Los padres de Isaac tenían dudas. Su madre es ama de casa y su padre trabaja de vigilante de seguridad. Al final, él y su profesor consiguieron convencerlos. Vivir y trabajar con gente de otros países le llevó a pensar en seguir los estudios en el extranjero. “Me apasiona estar rodeado de personas de otras culturas”.
De la FP en Málaga a la universidad danesa
Tras acabar la ESO, optó por la FP. Realizó un grado medio de Comercio y Marketing en el instituto Santa María de los Ángeles (Málaga). También hizo prácticas en Praga. Tras acabar el ciclo, estuvo una temporada en EE. UU.
Volvió a los estudios y realizó un ciclo superior de Agencia de Viajes y Gestión de Eventos. En esta ocasión hizo las prácticas en Cracovia (Polonia). Después regresó a Málaga y realizó otro ciclo superior de formación para ser guía turístico. También aquí hizo prácticas en su ciudad. El ciclo duró un año, según su relato.
El siguiente paso fue el de VIA University College, en Dinamarca. Allí realizó un “bachelor top-up” de Diseño y Empresa. Este programa de un año y medio sirve para completar los estudios anteriores y obtener el título de grado.
En esta fase también contó con una ayuda pública. Estaba relacionada con tener un trabajo. Según cuenta, recibió 800 euros al mes. Para ello tenía que trabajar diez o doce horas a la semana. Podían ser en limpieza, comercio o reparto. “Puede que sean empleos poco cualificados, pero no te roban mucho tiempo y te permiten obtener la beca”. También aprendió a valorar más las cosas.
El sistema de ayuda danés para estudiantes europeos que trabajan es personalizado. La administración requiere, en general, que tengan un mínimo de diez o doce horas de trabajo a la semana. Además, deben mantenerlo al menos diez semanas seguidas. Y deben mantener el trabajo en todo el periodo en el que cobran la ayuda. Los 800 euros son los que cuenta que recibió él.
Vivir en Copenhague y estudiar en Malmö
El idioma no ha sido un problema. Ha tenido que demostrar que tiene un nivel C1. En diciembre de 2025 acabó el “bachelor”. Uno de sus profesores le recomendó el máster de Liderazgo para la Sostenibilidad de Malmö. En agosto de 2026 comenzó este curso.
Vive en Copenhague. Calcula que tarda unos 50 minutos en llegar a la universidad sueca. Está en un piso compartido con su mejor amigo. Este es ingeniero informático por la Universidad de Málaga. Ahora está en la capital danesa realizando un máster de ciberseguridad.
También puede volver. “Espero seguir formándome, aunque también me quiero quitar la espinita de estudiar en Málaga. A lo mejor termino matriculándome en otro máster en mi ciudad”.

articles.title: Kunal Shah’s big plans for WhatsApp; Gaurav Munjal steps down as Unacademy CEO
articles.text:
Kunal Shah’s big plans for WhatsApp; Gaurav Munjal steps down as Unacademy CEO
WhatsApp is gearing up for a future beyond messaging. In other news, Gaurav Munjal is stepping down as CEO to become the executive chairman of Unacademy. Akhilendra Kumar will take over as CEO.
Dear Reader,
Gaurav Munjal is stepping down as CEO to become the executive chairman of Unacademy. Akhilendra Kumar will take over as CEO.
Munjal, however, would stay involved in operations every day, work alongside the new CEO, and help with upGrad’s IPO. The leadership change comes two months after upGrad completed the acquisition of Unacademy for over $200 million.
In other news, the Indian government has prohibited the export of lithium-ion battery black mass, a key intermediate material recovered during battery recycling.
Reversing the earlier policy that allowed shipments overseas, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade has notified an amendment banning shipping of unsorted waste, scrap, and spent primary cells, primary batteries, and electric accumulators. The move, which is expected to strengthen domestic recycling, comes just a week after the Cabinet approved a Rs 2,814 crore scheme to promote critical mineral processing.
Meanwhile, IBM has halted sponsorship of work visas and green cards for most positions in its consulting division in the US, reflecting the growing impact of the Trump administration’s tightening immigration policies on the tech industry.
Lastly, in a high-profile IPL trade, all-rounder Hardik Pandya has moved to Punjab Kings from Mumbai Indians for a fee of Rs 18 crore, up from 16.35 crore. PBKS traded pacer Arshdeep Singh for Pandya, making it the biggest exchange of players in IPL history.
In today’s newsletter:
- Kunal Shah’s plans for WhatsApp’s next phase
- The Tamil Nadu startups that showcased their innovations to PM Modi
Here’s your trivia for today: What is the meaning of the Latin phrase ‘caveat emptor’? (Scroll down for the answer)
Corporate
Kunal Shah outlines plans for WhatsApp’s next phase
WhatsApp is gearing up for a future beyond messaging. Its next phase involves making conversations richer and more expressive, bringing everyday transactions into the app, and using AI for practical tasks. The app would evolve voice notes, groups, stickers and video as communication habits change.
CEO Kunal Shah set out these priorities in a post on X, more than four months after succeeding Will Cathcart as WhatsApp’s global head. “The best technology saves you time, so you can get back to the connections that matter,” said Shah.
What’s in store:
- Simplicity will be the core of what WhatsApp stands for. “We want anything you do on WhatsApp to be as simple as sending a message,” Shah wrote.
- The second priority is to make everyday tasks easier to complete within a chat. WhatsApp is working with financial services and telecom partners to reduce the steps involved in bill payments, borrowing and staying connected while travelling.
- AI is the third strand. The technology would find information, manage routine tasks, and help users avoid missing bookings or appointments. UPI payments within AI-assisted chats would also be introduced.
In-focus
Meet 8 Tamil Nadu startups that showcased their innovations to PM Modi
When Prime Minister Narendra Modi travelled aboard the Chennai Metro with Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay last month, the journey also provided an unusual platform for entrepreneurs from the state to present their ideas to the PM.
Key takeaways:
- Many startup founders from Tamil Nadu showcased their innovations from fields spanning spacetech, aviation, healthcare, agriculture and urban finance.
- The Chennai startups included Dream Aerospace Technologies, which makes propulsion systems for satellites, spacecraft and re-entry vehicles; Blunav Technologies, which is developing software to manage airport operations; and FarmwiseAI, which applies AI and geospatial analytics to agriculture and land management.
- Tirunelveli-based Thazhal Geospatial Analytics uses satellite imagery, drone data, and IoT sensors to monitor physical assets and assess environmental risks. Grahaa Space (Karur), Diagno Intelligent Systems (Chennai), MEDxAI Innovations (Kancheepuram), and Munify Datatech (Chennai) were the others.
News & updates
- PLI scheme: The Indian government has invited fresh applications under its Rs 2,700-crore Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for medical devices and extended the programme till 2035-36. The scheme guidelines have also been simplified and made more investor-friendly to promote ease of doing business.
- AI readiness: India ranks among the world’s ‘Rising Contenders’ in artificial intelligence, a tier of economies with high readiness to use AI but lower exposure to its disruption, Boston Consulting Group said in a report. India’s strength lies in ‘skills’, with a large pool of AI specialists and a skilled IT-services workforce.
- EV push: The Finance Ministry has asked ministries and departments to make electric vehicles the default and preferred choice for staff cars, and has set a price cap of Rs 20 lakh for procurement of these vehicles.

articles.title: Ceci n'est pas un lecteur CD externe : ce mini-PC ultra fin combine une puissante puce Panther Lake à 64 Go de RAM
articles.text:
Fin, mais costaud ! Le constructeur FEVM a dévoilé son nouveau FNPH1. Derrière l’austérité de ce nom, un mini-PC ultra-fin d'à peine 2 cm d’épaisseurd’à embarquant une puissante puce Intel Panther Lake et jusqu’à 64 Go de mémoire vive. Présentations…
Connu sur le segment mini-PC, le constructeur chinois FEVM dégaine cette semaine son nouveau FNPH1 : l’un des modèles les plus fins et compacts du marché, avec seulement 20 mm d’épaisseur pour 0,4 litre et 450 grammes sur la balance. Proche d’un vieux lecteur CD en termes de look, l’appareil se dote pourtant d’une fiche technique récente et haut de gamme.
BenQ iScreenBar : la barre lumineuse qui s’accorde avec l’iMac
Des lignes en harmonie avec celles de l’ordinateur d’Apple, une conception rigoureuse, des matériaux sélectionnés, rien n’a été laissé au hasard, tout comme le service qu’elle rend une fois allumée !
Panther Lake aux manettes
On y retrouve en effet l’une des meilleures puces de la gamme Intel Panther Lake, avec un Core Ultra X7 358H aux manettes. Lancée début 2026, cette puce gravée en 1,8 nm (Intel 18A) regroupe 16 cœurs (4 cœurs hautes performances, 8 cœurs haute efficacité énergétique et 4 cœurs basse consommation) et 16 threads cadencés à un maximum de 4,8 GHz.
On y trouve également 18 Mo de cache pour un TDP compris entre 15 et 80 W… mais sa caractéristique la plus intéressante est à chercher sur le plan graphique. Cette référence embarque un gros iGPU Intel B390 (12 cœurs Xe3 à 2,5 GHz) délivrant à lui seul jusqu’à 122 TOPS de puissance de calcul vouée à l’IA locale (qui s’ajoute aux 50 TOPS du NPU). Cette partie graphique intégrée offre peu ou prou les performances de certaines cartes graphiques dédiées d’ancienne génération, comme la RTX 3050, permettant de jouer confortablement en Full HD (voire plus) avec des réglages élevés et un framerate solide.
Un prix encore flou
Dans le cas présent, ce Core Ultra X7 358H est couplé à un maximum de 64 Go de mémoire vive LPDDR5X-9000. Bien que limitée sur la bande passante mémoire, cette configuration est suffisante pour la gestion locale de LLM de 20 ou 30 milliards de paramètres (MoE de préférence), par exemple.
Pour le reste, le FEVM FNPH1 regroupe deux ports USB4 type-C, deux ports USB-A 3.2 Gen 2, une sortie HDMI 2.1, une sortie DisplayPort 2.1, une prise Ethernet 2.5G, une prise OCuLink (pour connecter un GPU externe au besoin) et une prise casque. L’appareil dispose enfin d’une connectivité Wi-Fi 7.
Fraîchement annoncé, le FNPH1 n’a pas encore de tarif ou de date de lancement. Le doute est d’ailleurs permis quant à une sortie en dehors du marché chinois, mais l’import devrait être possible d’ici quelques mois… À condition d’y mettre le prix. Dans sa configuration Core Ultra X7 / 64 Go de RAM, et compte tenu de la pénurie de RAM en cours, nous voyons mal ce modèle arriver sur le marché à moins de 2000 ou 3000 euros.
Source : NotebookCheck

articles.title: Audi A2 e-tron, Lancia Gamma, Leapmotor B10… les voitures électriques que vous allez payer moins cher grâce à l'éco-score
articles.text:
Depuis le 1er juillet 2025, le bonus écologique a changé de nom et de financeur. L’aide à l’achat d’une voiture électrique neuve s’appelle désormais prime « coup de pouce », et ce sont les fournisseurs d’énergie qui la paient, via les certificats d’économies d’énergie. Le gouvernement vient d’allonger la liste des voitures qui y ont droit dans un arrêté publié au Journal officiel ce mardi 10 novembre. Au total, 31 versions de 11 marques ont ainsi validé leur éco-score (note minimale de 60 sur 80).
De la Twingo au Model Y, qui entre dans la liste ?
Les 31 versions couvrent presque toutes les tailles de voitures, de la citadine à moins de 20 000 € au SUV sept places.
- Citadines : deux versions de la Renault Twingo, que Renault vend à partir de 19 490 €, et une version de sa jumelle, la Nissan Pixo, dont le prix n’est pas encore connu.
- Citadines polyvalentes : deux versions de la Nissan Micra, cousine de la Renault 5, et la Volkswagen ID. Polo avec sa batterie de 37 kWh, en 116 ch et en 135 ch, affichées à partir de 24 995 et 29 920 €.
- Compactes et SUV compacts : l’Audi A2 e-tron (cinq versions, de 170 à 326 ch), le Mercedes GLA 200 (quatre versions), le Leapmotor B10, le Mitsubishi Eclipse Cross, les Volkswagen ID.4 et ID.5 Pro de 286 ch, ainsi que les Audi Q4 e-tron et Q4 Sportback e-tron performance.
- Familiales et grands SUV : une version du Peugeot e-3008 et deux de l’e-5008, le Citroën ë-C5 Aircross, la Lancia Gamma (quatre versions) et une version du Tesla Model Y.
Figurer dans l’arrêté ne garantit pas la prime pour autant. Le plafond de 47 000 € reste le filtre décisif pour les versions les plus puissantes, comme l’Audi A2 e-tron de 326 ch ou les Audi Q4 e-tron performance, dont le prix exact de la configuration fera la différence. L’éco-score conditionne aussi, pour les entreprises, l’abattement de 70 % sur l’avantage en nature des voitures de fonction électriques.
Leapmotor, marque chinoise dont Stellantis est actionnaire, fait aussi son entrée dans la liste. Le SUV B10 a décroché le précieux sésame grâce à sa production dans l’usine du groupe à Figueruelas, près de Saragosse en Espagne. Les voitures assemblées en Europe et équipées d’une batterie européenne touchent en plus une bonification de 1 200 à 2 000 €, selon le ministère de l’Économie.
Comment vérifier que votre version y a droit
Demandez au vendeur le code TVV exact de la version commandée et comparez-le à ceux de l’arrêté, consultable sur Légifrance. Faites la demande de prime avant de signer le bon de commande, comme l’exige le dispositif. Les 31 versions ajoutées ouvrent droit à l’aide à partir de ce jeudi 12 novembre.

articles.title: Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
Silent data corruption (SDC) happens when hardware, such as a GPU, returns a wrong but plausible number and raises no error. In distributed training, the wrong number can flow into the gradients and weights of every replica. Loss can still look normal for hours, and by the time a team notices an unexplained divergence or a weaker model, the compute is spent. It happens at scale: during a 54-day period of Llama 3 405B pre-training on up to 16K H100 GPUs, Meta attributed 6 of 419 unexpected job interruptions to silent data corruption, and those were only the cases that interrupted the job and were traced to SDC.
Amazon SageMaker HyperPod already replaces nodes that report a fault: the health-monitoring agent watches for GPU errors, deep health checks stress-test nodes, and automatic node recovery swaps out bad hardware. SDC slips past all of these features, because the hardware never reports anything. Detection has to come from the training job itself.
In this post, we add three checks to a PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) training loop to detect SDC. When a check fires, we map the suspect rank to its node, contain the corruption, and have SageMaker HyperPod replace the node. Each check covers a different place where a fault can land:
- A non-finite gradient check catches NaN, Inf, and overflow in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step it happens, and NaN or Inf that the gradient all-reduce introduces.
- A ring replay audit catches finite wrong values. On audit steps, every GPU recomputes a micro-batch from another node and compares the loss bit for bit and the gradients by fingerprint.
- A weight fingerprint comparison catches corruption in the optimizer step and in stored weights, by comparing every replica’s weights after the update.
We tested the checks with software-injected faults on a SageMaker HyperPod cluster with 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs), and repeated every test on three instances, the minimum the checks need. The full code of this solution is available in the accompanying GitHub repository.
How silent data corruption happens and why the usual checks miss it
SDC comes from manufacturing defects (marginal transistors that slip past vendor screening) and silicon aging in a specific compute unit, most often a multiply-accumulate lane in a tensor core, which is exactly the hardware model training hammers. That marginal circuit computes correctly most of the time and wrong only under stress: high temperature, voltage droop, or specific operand patterns. Because the arithmetic logic path has no ECC or parity (unlike memory), the wrong result, say 4.0001 instead of 4.0000, is never flagged, and it flows through activations and gradients into every replica’s weights.
The reason it is so hard to catch is that SDC is in the compute path, and every integrity check you already have guards a different boundary:
| Check | What it guards | Why it misses SDC | 
| ECC | memory | Catches bit flips in memory, not wrong math. There is no ECC on a tensor-core result. | 
| Xid errors (NVRM) | GPU driver/hardware faults | The GPU raises an Xid when it detects a fault. SDC by definition raises none, so nothing lands in /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/ HMA logs. | 
| DCGM deep health check | hardware faults | Misses defects that need your workload’s operands, thermal state, or timing. Runs on an idle node, outside your job. | 
| NVLink / PCIe / EFA checksums | transport | Verify bytes arrived as sent, not that they were computed correctly. | 
| Checkpoint checksums | storage round-trip | A poisoned-but-consistent checkpoint checksums fine. | 
The way to catch SDC is to check the result of the computation itself.
Solution overview
The loop has four steps. Your training job does the first two, and the last two use Kubernetes and SageMaker HyperPod features:
Step 1. Detect: Three checks in your training loop name a suspect GPU by comparing data-parallel replicas.
Step 2. Localize: On SageMaker HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), the Kubernetes node name contains the instance ID, so mapping a suspect rank to a node is a lookup.
Step 3. Contain and correlate: Stop the job, cordon the node, and look at its GPU metrics in the SageMaker HyperPod observability dashboards.
Step 4. Confirm and recover: Confirm when the alarm is ambiguous, replace the node after review, and resume from a checkpoint saved before the suspect window.
It helps to see the loop as layers, each adding something different:
| Layer | Source | What it adds | Catches truly silent SDC? | 
| 1. Non-finite gradient check | Your training script | Names a GPU whose local gradient is NaN or Inf, before the all-reduce, and stops the step if the reduced gradient is NaN or Inf | Only faults that become NaN, Inf, or overflow | 
| 2. Ring replay audit | Your training script | Every GPU recomputes another node’s micro-batch and compares the loss bits and gradient fingerprints | Yes, for finite compute-path faults that change the loss or a gradient, on audit steps | 
| 3. Weight fingerprint comparison | Your training script | Names a replica whose weights differ from a strict majority after the update | Yes, for optimizer-step and stored-weight faults on one copy. Blind to compute-path faults and to sharded weights | 
| 4. Localization | Your training script, using SageMaker HyperPod node names | Maps a suspect rank to an instance ID from the Kubernetes node name | n/a: it localizes | 
| 5. DCGM correlation | HyperPod observability add-on | The suspect GPU’s DCGM metrics around the alarm | It confirms faults only where they also appear in hardware counters. Clean telemetry doesn’t clear a node. | 
| 6. Deep health check | StartClusterHealthCheck (DCGM L4) | An on-demand hardware diagnostic on the suspect node | It catches hardware defects its own test patterns trigger. Triage, not proof | 
| 7. Repeat-offender history | A query you build over retained alarms and telemetry | Nodes that alarm repeatedly | Partly: it surfaces nodes worth checking early | 
Layers 1–3 are the only layers that detect silent SDC, and they live in your training code. Layer 4 turns their alarm into an instance ID, and the HyperPod layers corroborate the alarm and close the loop.
Prerequisites
To follow along, you need:
- A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS, with at least three GPU nodes. The ring audit needs three different nodes for every comparison it settles, and the weight comparison needs three copies of each weight to name the odd one out. See Orchestrating SageMaker HyperPod clusters with Amazon EKS.
- A PyTorch DDP training job in which every replica runs its own optimizer step, with a data pipeline that can rebuild any rank’s micro-batch for a given step, such as a seeded sampler.
- Checkpoints on shared storage, Amazon FSx for Lustre or Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). Replacing a node destroys its root and secondary volumes, including anything on local NVMe.
- The SageMaker HyperPod observability add-on for the correlation step. Turn on advanced DCGM metrics if you want ECC, NVLink, and throttling counters.
- Access to the cluster through kubectl, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for sagemaker:StartClusterHealthCheck and sagemaker:BatchReplaceClusterNodes. See Manually quarantine, replace, or reboot a node.
Step 1: Detect with three checks in your training loop
Data parallelism trains several copies of the model, called replicas, at the same time. Each replica trains on a different slice of the batch. After each backward pass, an all-reduce averages the replicas’ gradients, and every replica applies that same average in optimizer.step(). Here’s one weight across three replicas, with a learning rate of 0.1:
|  | replica 0 | replica 1 | replica 2 |  | 
| weight at start | 0.500 | 0.500 | 0.500 | same | 
| local gradient | 0.20 | 0.40 | 0.30 | different (different data) | 
| averaged gradient | 0.30 | 0.30 | 0.30 | same, after the all-reduce | 
| weight after step | 0.470 | 0.470 | 0.470 | same | 
Local gradients differ, because each replica sees different data. And after the optimizer step, the weights must be identical, bit for bit.
Where a fault lands decides which check can see it. If replica 1 computes a local gradient of 4.00 instead of 0.40, the all-reduce spreads that error to every replica: all three apply the same wrong update, and their weights still match. Only replica 1’s local gradient looked different, and only before the all-reduce. If instead replica 1 corrupts a weight during or after the optimizer step, its weights no longer match the others. There’s one exception: a NaN or Inf in one replica’s weights reaches every replica through the next all-reduce, and after that the replicas agree again. A fault inside the all-reduce itself, such as a GPU that adds a partial sum wrong, also reaches every replica identically.
So compute-path faults must be caught before the optimizer step, while the bad gradient can still be discarded, and faults in the update or in stored weights after it. Finite wrong values need recompute: comparing gradient norms across replicas catches only NaN and Inf (see Why not compare local gradient norms?). That gives three checks on every DP rank, in a fixed order within each training step:
- Non-finite gradient check – Before the all-reduce, flag any rank whose local gradient is NaN or Inf. This catches values that blow up in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step they happen, and names the GPU. After the all-reduce, check the reduced gradient for NaN or Inf too, before the update.
- Ring replay audit – On audit steps, before the optimizer step, every rank recomputes the micro-batch of a rank on another node. It compares the loss bit for bit and, with deterministic kernels, every parameter’s gradient fingerprint. This catches finite wrong values in the compute path.
- Weight fingerprint comparison – After the optimizer step, every N steps and before every checkpoint, compare every replica’s weight fingerprints. This catches faults in the optimizer step and in stored weights.
The code in this step is for PyTorch DDP. For tensor, pipeline, or context parallelism, see Beyond DDP.
Order of execution
Why not compare local gradient norms?
A natural first design, and the one we started with, flags a rank whose local gradient norm is more than k median absolute deviations (MADs) from the median of that step. We recorded every rank’s local gradient norm on every step of the three fault-free runs on 4 instances (22,800 steps, see Fault-free runs) on 32 H100s training a 953-million-parameter model, and the test doesn’t work:
- The healthy spread is too wide – Each rank sees different data, so healthy local norms already reached 224 MADs in the first 800 steps, and 1,240 MADs over all healthy steps.
- A quiet threshold sees nothing finite – At k = 336, 1.5 times the highest score in the first 800 healthy steps, it raised 11 false alarms in the remaining 22,000 healthy steps. And no finite fault came close: the faulty rank’s score never exceeded 6.9, even with one activation multiplied by 10,000.
Compare by fingerprint
Checks 2 and 3 compare tensors across GPUs. Sending whole tensors would cost too much, so each tensor is reduced to a fingerprint: two 64-bit sums of its raw bit patterns, one plain and one weighted by position. Any change to one or two elements of a tensor changes the fingerprint, for tensors with fewer than 2³² elements of up to 4 bytes each. That covers every weight fault we injected. Larger changes could, in principle, cancel out, so equal fingerprints are strong evidence of equal tensors, not proof. The position-weighted sum matters: in our tests, a swap of two weight values and a compensating change to two values left the plain sum unchanged, and only the weighted sum caught them.
Check 1: NaN/Inf gradients, before and after the all-reduce
A DDP communication hook records each rank’s local gradient before it’s averaged. It stores the squared norm of every gradient bucket and, on deterministic audit steps, the fingerprints of every parameter’s gradient (used by check 2). Then it passes the bucket to PyTorch’s standard all-reduce.
After backward, nonfinite_ranks gathers one scalar from every rank and returns the ranks whose local gradient norm is NaN or Inf. The first rank flagged is the faulty one. If the step were applied, the NaN would reach every rank on the next step.
train() also checks the gradient after the all-reduce. A NaN or Inf produced inside the reduction reaches every replica the same way, so the copies still match and check 3 passes them. Without this check, the NaN becomes NaN weights on every replica, and a checkpoint due on that step is saved with them and tagged as passing. clip_grad_norm_ already computes the norm of the reduced gradient, so the check adds only one one-element all-reduce per step. A finite error in the reduction still passes every check.
If you train with fp16 and a gradient scaler, exclude the overflow steps the scaler already skips. bf16 doesn’t have them.
Check 2: Ring replay, before the optimizer step
Every replica holds the same weights until optimizer.step(). So, between the backward pass and the optimizer step, any rank can recompute any other rank’s micro-batch, and with deterministic kernels it must get the same bits.
On an audit step, every rank r recomputes the micro-batch of rank r + 8: 8 positions ahead, which is one node away on p5 instances. It uses the unwrapped module, so nothing is all-reduced, and it restores the gradients, the module’s buffers, and the random-number state afterwards. A replay blocks the job no matter how many ranks do one, so auditing every rank costs the same wall-clock time as auditing one.
Each rank then appears in two comparisons: its own micro-batch, replayed by a peer, and the micro-batch it replayed for someone else.
- Both comparisons mismatch: That rank computed wrong in both, so it’s the culprit.
- Only one mismatches: Either side could be wrong. confirm settles it in place: the GPU eight positions after the target, on a third node, and the target itself replay the target’s micro-batch again. That also tells a persistent fault, which the target reproduces, from a transient one, which it doesn’t.
The confirmation is only independent if the three GPUs are on three different nodes. check_topology verifies that for every pair before training starts, from each pod’s NODE_NAME, and raises an error otherwise.
Choose the audit mode:
- Default kernels: Compare the loss only. This needs a forward pass whose loss is bitwise reproducible, which held in our tests: healthy replays matched the original loss bit for bit. Gradients can’t be compared this way, because attention’s default backward pass isn’t deterministic. This mode catches forward-pass faults that change the loss.
- Deterministic kernels (deterministic_audits=True): The whole audit step runs with deterministic algorithms and the math attention kernel. Gradient fingerprints then match too, so the audit also catches backward-only faults. An op with no deterministic implementation raises an error instead of producing a false alarm. On our model, a deterministic audit step cost 2.4 times a default one.
Never replay a suspect’s work on the suspect alone. A GPU with a persistent defect can reproduce its own wrong answer.
Check 3: Weight fingerprints, after the optimizer step
After optimizer.step(), every replica’s weights must be identical, so there’s no tolerance to tune. Each rank fingerprints every weight tensor and gathers everyone’s fingerprints.
A rank is named only when its copy of a tensor differs from a strict majority, more than half of the copies. With two copies, or a split with no strict majority, the comparison reports a disagreement without naming any rank.
Run it every N steps and on every checkpoint step. It’s the only check that runs after the update, so it’s the only one that can stop a checkpoint from being written out of a corrupted copy. In our tests, a weight corrupted right after one update was caught at the next checkpoint step, and the save didn’t happen. Without the forced check, the save went ahead from the corrupted copy, and the ring audit noticed only at the next audit, five steps later.
It costs 31.1 ms per check on a 953-million-parameter model: 2 percent of a step when it runs every 10 steps.
Put the checks in the training loop
train runs each step in the order of Figure 2 and stops at the first alarm. It decides whether a step is an audit step before the forward pass, because a deterministic comparison needs the original computation to be deterministic too. When check 1 or 2 fires, it zeros the gradients and returns without clipping or applying the update, so the bad gradient never reaches the weights or the optimizer state, and the exact state is still there for confirmation. After clipping, it checks whether the reduced gradient is NaN or Inf, and if it is, returns before the update. It saves a checkpoint only if nothing fired.
The alarm’s suspect_window is the range of steps since the last pass of the check that fired. A fault that was active on every step since it started began inside it. An intermittent fault can be older, and a fault that no check sees can be in any checkpoint, so treat the tags as a record that the checks passed at that step, not as proof that the saved state is clean.
A training script calls it like this:
The replay depends on these:
- Exact micro-batches: rebuild_batch(step, rank) must return exactly the micro-batch that rank trained on, for example from a seeded sampler.
- Same loss function: compute_loss must be the same function in training and in replay, including autocast, and any randomness inside it, such as dropout, must be seeded per step and rank.
- No collectives or output-affecting state in the model: The confirmation replay runs on only two ranks, the target and the third GPU, so a model that calls a collective inside its forward or backward pass (SyncBatchNorm, for example) hangs on an ambiguous alarm. A buffer that the forward pass both reads and updates makes a healthy replay differ.
- Deterministic setup: Set CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8 before the training process starts, and make sure every op in the model has a deterministic implementation.
- Peer offset: Number DP ranks node by node, so that peer_offset equal to the GPUs per node puts every replayer on another node. check_topology refuses a layout where it doesn’t.
- Untested here: Unused parameters, gradient accumulation, BatchNorm, and forward hooks with side effects. With unused parameters, set deterministic_audits=False, which compares the loss only.
audit_every is the main cost-versus-robustness setting:
- Detection delay: A persistent finite fault is caught within audit_every steps if it also occurs in the kernels the audit runs. Deterministic audits run deterministic kernels and the math attention kernel, so a fault confined to the default kernels used on the other steps is never audited.
- Corrupted updates: Up to audit_every − 1 corrupted updates can be applied before the audit catches it. They’re inside the alarm’s suspect_window.
- One-time faults: A finite fault on a single non-audit step that doesn’t recur isn’t caught at all.
Make ckpt_every a multiple of both audit_every and check_every, so every checkpoint step is audited before its update and fingerprinted after it.
We measured the average step time end to end, over 1,000 consecutive steps per schedule, on the 953M model and 32 H100s. Every schedule with the checks also runs the weight check every 10 steps:
| Schedule | Average step time | Over plain DDP | 
| Plain DDP, no checks | 157.4 ms | — | 
| Checks, no audits | 169.0 ms | +7.4% | 
| Deterministic audits every 10 steps | 211.9 ms | +34.7% | 
| Default-kernel audits every 10 steps | 177.0 ms | +12.5% | 
| Deterministic audits every 100 steps | 173.3 ms | +10.1% | 
| Default-kernel audits every 100 steps | 169.3 ms | +7.6% | 
About 7 percentage points of each schedule’s cost don’t depend on audits: the gradient hook and the two NaN/Inf checks on every step, and the weight check every 10 steps. A reasonable starting point for production is deterministic audits every 100 steps, which cost 10 percent here. They still catch a persistent fault within 100 steps, including a backward-only one, at the price of up to 99 corrupted updates to roll back. Audit every 10 steps when you need faster detection, for example during a burn-in on new capacity or while you watch a suspect node. Measure the cost on your own model: deterministic attention uses the math kernel, whose cost grows with the square of the sequence length.
In the fault-free runs, 15,320 audit steps and 3,080 weight checks raised no alarm, which bounds the false-alarm rate at about 1 in 5,100 audit steps (95 percent confidence).
Step 2: Localize the suspect rank to a node
A rank is a logical ID. To act on it, you need the instance and the physical GPU. On HyperPod EKS, the Kubernetes node name is the instance ID with a hyperpod- prefix. Pass it to your pod with the Kubernetes downward API:
At job start, log a table that maps every rank to its node, instance, and GPU UUID:
If a job is already running without the downward API, you can map a pod to its node from outside with kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}'.
Step 3: Contain the damage and check the GPU metrics
When an alarm fires, stop the job first. Then stop new work from landing on the suspect node by cordoning the node while you investigate:
Then open the GPU health dashboard in the SageMaker HyperPod observability add-on, filter to the suspect node and GPU, and look at the time the alarm fired. A rise in correctable ECC errors, PCIe replays, throttling, or temperature on that GPU raises confidence that the hardware is at fault. A clean panel doesn’t clear the node: pure SDC often leaves no trace in hardware telemetry.
Step 4: Confirm, then replace the node
With the Step 1 checks running, an alarm already names a suspect GPU. When you see a symptom without an alarm, such as a loss spike, or want to rule out software before you replace anything, start with the cheap explanations. Most loss spikes aren’t SDC, and chasing SDC on a data bug wastes days:
The test that separates SDC from software is whether the problem follows the hardware:
- A reproducible failure doesn’t rule out SDC – Meta pinned a failing workload to one core and got the same wrong answer every time for specific inputs.
- Neither does a failure that starts at a software change – Google traced one incident to a correct library update that began using rarely used instructions on defective cores.
- Don’t expect the global loss to point anywhere – A forward fault first changes the faulty rank’s own loss, and the all-reduce then spreads its gradient to every replica. Per-rank checks and replays give you the locality.
Decide what the alarm means
| Alarm | Meaning | Suggested action | 
| check == "weights", suspects == [r] | Rank r’s copy differs from a strict majority after the update | Keep r’s node cordoned. Replace it after review | 
| check == "weights", suspects is None | Copies disagree, but no strict majority | Ambiguous: keep the nodes involved cordoned. Check DCGM and run deep health checks | 
| culprits == [r] | Both of r’s ring comparisons mismatched. This assumes at most one faulty GPU among the GPUs that replay each other (the GPUs with the same local index). With two, a healthy GPU can be named | Keep cordoned. Replace after review, or after the fault repeats | 
| Verdict persistent | The target reproduced its own wrong answer, and a third GPU agreed with the replayer | Keep cordoned. Replace after review | 
| Verdict transient | The target’s retry came out right and agreed with the third GPU. An intermittent fault can look the same | Keep cordoned until an audit with the node as the target, or a deep health check, passes. Replace it if it happens again | 
| Verdict replayer computed wrong | The replaying GPU, not the target, was wrong | Treat the replayer as the suspect, and confirm again | 
| nonfinite set, no mismatched pairs | NaN or Inf in a backward pass that the loss doesn’t show, or a gradient norm too large for float32 (above about 1.8 × 10¹⁹) | Ambiguous: audit with the suspect as the target, or check DCGM and run a deep health check | 
| check == "reduced gradient" | The gradient was NaN or Inf after the all-reduce, although every rank’s local gradient was finite. No rank is named | Ambiguous: keep the job stopped, check DCGM and run deep health checks on every node in the job, and resume from a checkpoint saved before the alarm step | 
| Verdict unattributable or unclear | The three GPUs don’t line up | Ambiguous: check DCGM and run deep health checks on the nodes involved | 
In production, keep a human approval on every replacement until you have evidence of the checks’ precision on your own workload. Synthetic tests like ours don’t establish it.
Confirm an ambiguous alarm
A deep health check is the main tool for ambiguous alarms. Its stress tests catch faults that the hardware reports, and subtle data-dependent faults often pass. To run one on the suspect instance group:
Replace the node
When you’re ready to replace the node, you have two options. Both trigger the same SageMaker HyperPod recovery process, described in Manually quarantine, replace, or reboot a node.
If automatic node recovery is turned on, you can label the node and let SageMaker HyperPod replace it, which is convenient for automation:
To use the API instead, run:
On clusters that use Karpenter for autoscaling, BatchReplaceClusterNodes terminates the node but creates a replacement only if pending pods need one. After the replacement joins, the training job restarts through the SageMaker HyperPod training operator or the job’s restart policy, and your training script resumes from the newest checkpoint saved before the alarm’s suspect_window starts. Call find_divergent_ranks right after loading it, before the first step. Replacement destroys the node’s root and secondary volumes, so keep checkpoints on shared storage.
Automating the workflow
The manual steps are for understanding. In production, wrap them in a small controller that runs in your own cluster and account:
- Trigger: The training job reports the alarm as a Kubernetes event, a small custom resource (for example SDCReport{rank, job, step, check}), or an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on metrics such as sdc_nonfinite_grad, sdc_replay_mismatch, and sdc_divergent_tensors.
- Resolve: The controller maps rank → pod → node through the Kubernetes API, then node → instance ID by stripping the hyperpod- prefix.
- Contain: It cordons the node.
- Decide: It applies the table in Step 4. The ring audit has already confirmed ambiguous pairs in place, so the alarm carries the verdicts. For an ambiguous result, it runs one node-scoped deep health check.
- Recover: For a replacement, it asks a human to approve, then calls BatchReplaceClusterNodes, or sets the node-health label if automatic node recovery is turned on. Then it relies on the training operator and your checkpoint reload, and records every step in CloudWatch.
Build it as a lightweight Kubernetes operator, or as an Amazon EventBridge rule on the CloudWatch alarm that invokes an AWS Lambda function.
Use case: Testing the checks on SageMaker HyperPod
We ran the tests twice on one SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS, using 4 and then 3 ml.p5.48xlarge instances with 8 NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 GPUs each, and PyTorch 2.9.0 (CUDA 13.0) from the AWS Deep Learning Containers training image. The model was a 953-million-parameter Llama-style decoder with 16 layers, a hidden size of 2,048, 16 attention heads, a 32,000-token vocabulary, and 2,048-token sequences. Each GPU processed 2 sequences per step (131,072 tokens per step on 32 GPUs), with fp32 weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and bf16 autocast for compute. We trained with AdamW at a learning rate of 3 × 10⁻⁴ after a 100-step linear warm-up, with betas of (0.9, 0.95), weight decay of 0.1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. The data was synthetic: a copy task with Zipf-distributed tokens whose first half repeats, seeded per rank and step so that any micro-batch can be rebuilt.
Fault scenarios
Faults were injected in one layer, the MLP down-projection of the eighth of 16 decoder blocks, on a chosen rank and step:
- Forward faults change the layer’s output but keep its gradient path, like a wrong multiply in the forward pass.
- Backward-only faults change the gradient of the layer’s input or weight.
- Weight faults change one GPU’s copy of the stored weight right after the optimizer step: a bit flip, a swap of two values, or a compensating change to two values.
- A persistent fault recurs in everything the faulty GPU computes, including the replays it runs for other ranks. A transient fault fires once.
Every scenario restarts from a snapshot taken after 400 warm-up steps, and step numbers count from it. Unless noted, audits ran every 10 steps with deterministic kernels, weight checks every 10 steps, and a checkpoint every 20. The table shows the 4-instance results. On 3 instances, every scenario raised the same alarm, at the same step, from the same check, naming the same ranks. Only the peer ranks changed.
| Injected fault | Result | Caught by | 
| NaN in one element of rank 13’s forward output, on step 25 only (not an audit step) | Fired on step 25 and named rank 13. The ring replay also ran. Confirmation by rank 21 and rank 13: transient on rank 13. Step 25 wasn’t applied. Suspect window: steps 21–25 | Check 1 | 
| One element of rank 13’s forward output ×1,000, on every step from step 23 | Steps 23–29 passed check 1 and were applied. The audit at step 30 mismatched (13, 5) and (21, 13) and named rank 13. Step 30 wasn’t applied. Suspect window: steps 21–30 | Check 2 | 
| The same ×1,000 on audit step 30 only | One pair mismatched, (13, 5). Confirmation by rank 21, on a third node, and by rank 13: transient on rank 13 | Check 2 | 
| The persistent ×1,000 on rank 5, which replays rank 13’s micro-batch | Pairs (13, 5) and (5, 29) mismatched. Named rank 5. A single replay of rank 13 by rank 5 would have blamed the healthy rank 13 | Check 2 | 
| Other forward faults on rank 13, every step from step 23: one element ×10,000, 10% multiplicative noise on the whole output, bit 3 flipped in one bf16 element, and one output column ×1.1 | Each named rank 13 at step 30. The bit flip and the ×1.1 column were also caught with default-kernel audits | Check 2 | 
| One element of the gradient flowing into rank 13’s layer, or of its weight gradient, ×1,000, every step from step 23 (backward only) | Each named rank 13 at step 30, from the gradient fingerprints alone | Check 2 | 
| The weight-gradient fault above, with default-kernel audits | No alarm in 50 steps. The checkpoints at steps 20 and 40 were tagged with passing audits and weight checks, because the loss was unaffected and every copy had applied the same corrupted updates | Not caught | 
| The persistent forward ×1,000 on ranks 13 and 22 at once | Pairs (13, 5), (21, 13), (22, 14) and (30, 22) mismatched. Named ranks 13 and 22 | Check 2 | 
| Bit 22 flipped in one fp32 weight element on rank 0 after the step-31 update, with a checkpoint every 5 steps | The forced weight check at checkpoint step 35 named rank 0, and the save didn’t happen. Suspect window: steps 31–35 | Check 3 | 
| The same, with check_on_checkpoint=False | The save at step 35 went ahead from rank 0’s corrupted copy. Its tags showed the last passing weight check at step 30. The ring audit named rank 0 at step 40, from pairs (8, 0) and (0, 24) | Check 2 | 
| Two values swapped, or +4,096 and −4,096 added to the bit patterns of two values, in one weight tensor on rank 0 after the step-31 update, with no audits and weight checks every 10 steps | Each named rank 0 at the step-40 weight check, although the tensor’s plain bit sum hadn’t changed | Check 3 | 
| Bit 22 flipped in one attention weight on rank 7, after restoring the snapshot (a stand-in for loading a checkpoint) | find_divergent_ranks, run before the first step, named rank 7 | Check 3 | 
Fault-free runs
To measure false alarms, we trained without faults on both cluster sizes, with three schedules each. Every schedule ran the weight check every 10 steps and saved no checkpoints, and each run’s length was fixed in minutes, so the two schedules that audit every step contribute most of the audit steps:
| Instances | Audits | Minutes | Steps | Audit steps | Weight checks | Alarms | 
| 4 | Deterministic, every step | 45 | 4,600 | 4,600 | 460 | 0 | 
| 4 | Default kernels, every step | 22.5 | 5,400 | 5,400 | 540 | 0 | 
| 4 | Deterministic, every 10 steps | 45 | 12,800 | 1,280 | 1,280 | 0 | 
| 3 | Deterministic, every step | 15 | 1,600 | 1,600 | 160 | 0 | 
| 3 | Default kernels, every step | 7.5 | 2,000 | 2,000 | 200 | 0 | 
| 3 | Deterministic, every 10 steps | 15 | 4,400 | 440 | 440 | 0 | 
| Total |  | 150 | 30,800 | 15,320 | 3,080 | 0 | 
With 0 alarms in 15,320 audit steps, the rule of three puts a 95 percent upper bound of 3 / 15,320, about 1 in 5,100, on the false-alarm rate per audit step. The NaN/Inf checks didn’t fire on any fault-free step either. The gradient-norm analysis in Why not compare local gradient norms? uses the 4-instance runs only.
Beyond DDP
The weight comparison isn’t limited to DDP. find_divergent_ranks takes any data-parallel group, so it also applies to tensor, pipeline, and context parallelism, HSDP, and mixture of experts, which are all layouts that keep independent copies of each weight. It can’t help under ZeRO-1 or full FSDP sharding, where each shard’s update is computed on only one rank. We tested the checks and the training loop in this post only with DDP.
To use it in another layout, call find_divergent_ranks with the group that holds copies of the same shard. With only two copies, it can detect a disagreement but can’t name the faulty copy.
If you’d rather have the service check your nodes for you, SageMaker HyperPod also offers the MultiNodeTraining deep health check. It runs a short, fixed distributed training job across a batch of GPU nodes, with no code changes, and replaces nodes whose training loss turns NaN or Inf, diverges, or doesn’t finish in time. Select it alongside InstanceStress and InstanceConnectivity when you create an instance group, or run it on demand with StartClusterHealthCheck. It complements the checks in this post: use it to screen new and replacement nodes before your job lands on them, and the in-job checks to catch wrong values in your own training that never become NaN or Inf. For details, visit SageMaker HyperPod Deep Health Checks.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete what you created for testing. If you created a HyperPod cluster, delete it with aws sagemaker delete-cluster --cluster-name <cluster-name>. That removes only the HyperPod resources. Delete the EKS cluster, its add-ons, and any Amazon FSx volumes separately, after the HyperPod cluster. See Deleting a SageMaker HyperPod cluster.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to detect silent data corruption in data-parallel training and how to hand a suspect node to SageMaker HyperPod for replacement. Three checks cover the three places a fault can land: a NaN/Inf check on each rank’s gradient and on the reduced gradient, a ring replay that compares every GPU’s work with a GPU on another node, and a weight fingerprint comparison after the update. Run the first two before the optimizer step, don’t apply a step that failed a check, and compare weights before every checkpoint. Node names on SageMaker HyperPod EKS clusters turn the suspect rank into an instance ID. Then quarantine the node, roll back to a checkpoint from before the suspect window, and let the node-health label or the Replace API complete the recovery.
To get started, review the SageMaker HyperPod resiliency features for Amazon EKS, and try the companion repository. To go deeper, see deep health checks and the observability add-on.

articles.title: JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents
articles.text:
JioHotstar evaluated six approaches to helping AI coding agents navigate large codebases, finding that structural code search performed well on clearly defined engineering tasks, while semantic retrieval helped more with ambiguous requirements. The evaluation also found that adding retrieval layers did not consistently improve task completion or reduce token consumption.
Abhishek Bansal, Senior Staff Engineer at JioHotStar, compared filesystem tools, Sourcebot, Graphify, CocoIndex Code, Repowise, and an in-house retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. The team evaluated the approaches using subsets of SWE-bench and CodeScaleBench, alongside a custom question-answering harness for JioHotstar's codebase. The experiments used Claude Sonnet as the solving model and measured task accuracy, token consumption, agent turns, and tool usability.
JioHotstar’s benchmark setup for evaluating code retrieval approaches for AI coding agents. (Source: JioHotstar Blog Post)
The filesystem baseline, which relied on locally checked out repositories and standard search and file operations, remained competitive on concrete tasks. Sourcebot, which provides indexed text search, symbol definitions, references, and file reads, performed better than the baseline on harder SWE-bench Verified tasks while also costing less. On simpler SWE-bench Lite tasks, retrieval generally added overhead without consistently improving results.
CodeScaleBench showed a different pattern. Semantic retrieval helped more when agents had to interpret ambiguous problem descriptions and map them to implementation details that were not obvious from exact text or symbol searches. The findings suggest that retrieval approaches should be selected according to task characteristics rather than treated as interchangeable solutions.
The report also highlighted the importance of tool design. Agents frequently preferred familiar developer operations such as searching text, reading files, and locating symbols over higher-level abstractions that required additional verification.
Tool call breakdown by category across coding agent knowledge base approaches. (Source: JioHotstar Blog Post)
Siddharth Vaithinathan raised a broader architectural question in a LinkedIn post discussing the study:
Whether coding agents should understand not only the code but also the company that produced it. He argued that repository indexing alone cannot capture why architectural decisions were made, which constraints shaped them, or what earlier incidents taught the engineering team.
Vaithinathan suggested extending agent knowledge beyond code and documentation to include architecture, constraints, decisions, rationale, incidents, and outcomes. Such context could help agents evaluate existing design choices before proposing changes, particularly in systems where historical operational experience influences architectural decisions.
Tarun Bhargava raises a relevant question for benchmark interpretation, particularly when evaluations use limited subsets and probabilistic models.
Cost/accuracy numbers with multiple runs of the same setup.
JioHotstar's evaluation did not identify a single retrieval approach that performed best across all tasks. Instead, JioHotstar recommends retaining filesystem tools as a baseline, using structural search for concrete, code-focused problems and semantic indexing for ambiguous or cross-cutting requirements. JioHotStar engineering team also emphasizes measuring tool-use traces alongside task accuracy to determine whether retrieval reduces unnecessary exploration. The findings highlight the importance of matching retrieval capabilities to the programming task and how the agent navigates the codebase.

articles.title: A radio-wave trick from the 1980s could keep fusion reactors running continuously
articles.text:
Why it matters: A fusion power plant only makes sense if it can run for days on end, much like the coal and gas plants it would replace. Most tokamaks, however, still work in bursts, because the giant magnet coil driving their plasma current eventually has to stop and reset. Physicists in San Diego have now shown that radio waves can carry some of that load instead, using a trick that every experiment in the 1980s failed to pull off.
The coil in question, a central solenoid, works a lot like a transformer. It keeps ramping up its own current to induce one in the plasma, but it eventually runs out of room to ramp. Those stop-start cycles also wear on the machine over time, so engineers would much rather run a reactor in steady state.
The new method, called helicon current drive, gets around that by beaming 476 MHz radio waves into the plasma, where they nudge electrons along and keep current flowing without the coil's help. Bob Pinsker, a General Atomics physicist on the new paper, was among those who tried it back then. He told the American Nuclear Society that the theory predicted a very weak effect in '80s-era plasmas, so researchers were "kind of hoping for a miracle."
That miracle never showed up, so the idea sat on the shelf for decades. These days, though, DIII-D can produce plasmas that come fairly close to reactor conditions. On top of that, General Atomics built a "comb-line" antenna with 30 radiating elements, more than twice as many as earlier tokamak antennas carried, to launch the waves more efficiently.
The team has now published the results in Physical Review Letters. In each test, the antenna coupled roughly 370 kW into the plasma for a full second. That was enough to drive around 20 kA of current near the core. Comparison shots using microwave heating of similar strength showed no such effect, so heat alone doesn't explain it.
Even so, the plasmas in these tests carried around 1 MA of current in total, so the helicons supplied only about 2% of it. Realistically, then, helicons won't let anyone retire the coil anytime soon. Instead, they could become one of several current drive tools a future reactor uses at once. That matters because every watt a plant spends keeping its current going is a watt it can't sell to the grid.
Meanwhile, China's EAST, which held a plasma for a record 1,066 seconds last year, and France's WEST already sidestep the coil on long runs using lower hybrid waves. But those waves struggle in dense plasma, so in a power plant they'd mostly be useful near the edge. Helicon waves aren't expected to hit that density wall at all.

articles.title: IBM to offer access to a dual-processor quantum system in 2027
articles.text:
IBM’s Quantum Developer’s Conference is being held this week, and the company is using the gathering to provide an update to its roadmap: It is aiming to make error-corrected quantum computers before the decade is out.
The changes greatly expand the scope of its next-generation Nighthawk general-use processors by adding a version with over 500 programmable qubits. At the same time, it’s stepping back a bit on its plan to link multiple Nighthawk processors together, dropping the intended number of linked systems from nine to two.
The total number of qubits planned for next year will remain the same; how the company is getting there, however, will be different.
Meanwhile, the company is touting the performance boost achieved via a major change that was made in the generation of Nighthawk processors released in September: hardware-based qubit resets.
Parallel roadmaps
IBM’s most recent roadmap to error-corrected quantum computing has two parallel tracks. One is focused on technical development, with the company testing technologies it will need to build error-corrected hardware, but that may not be useful outside of that context. The other is public-facing, focused on delivering high-performance processors for people interested in testing algorithms on quantum systems today.
The reason for this split is that IBM plans to use an error-correction “code” that requires a specific number of hardware qubits connected in a specific geometry, along with additional hardware qubits needed to perform operations on that code. You could potentially run some algorithms directly on this hardware without error correction, but it wouldn’t necessarily be optimal. So IBM is also offering a more general-purpose processor in parallel, called Nighthawk.
For past generations of its processors, the company has often developed revisions that improve performance in various ways. So while the roadmap lists only one processor labeled Heron, there were two subsequent revisions to Heron after its release. Throughout 2028, however, the company’s public-facing track will see nothing but revisions to the current generation of processors, called Nighthawk, which started with 120 hardware qubits and the expectation of performing about 5,000 gate operations before errors become too likely to rely on its output.

articles.title: Pour rester en France, ChatGPT et Gemini pourraient devoir passer un examen
articles.text:
La commission « IA générative et vulnérabilités » a remis mardi 10 novembre à Emmanuel Macron un rapport de 177 pages, fruit de 55 auditions menées depuis février. Ses neuf experts, emmenés par la chercheuse en IA Serena Villata et les psychiatres Raphaël Gaillard et Amine Benyamina, y formulent 18 recommandations. Le document s’intitule « Protéger sans empêcher ».
Un examen d’entrée inspiré du médicament
La mesure la plus lourde conditionnerait la mise sur le marché des systèmes d’IA générative grand public, puis leur maintien, à une évaluation pluridisciplinaire préalable de leurs impacts. La mesure vise les seuls services destinés au grand public, ChatGPT et Gemini en tête ; les outils professionnels y échapperaient. Amine Benyamina assume la filiation pharmaceutique en défendant une véritable « autorisation de mise sur le marché ».
Le rapport réclame aussi un accès des autorités et de chercheurs agréés aux données d’entraînement, d’usage et de monétisation des modèles, ainsi qu’un « protocole national de réponse aux crises informationnelles liées à l’IA ». Les auteurs assurent ne pas « vouloir mettre un boulet au pied de l’économie française ni européenne » et pressent le chef de l’État de « prendre des décisions ». Celui-ci jugeait la veille, dans un entretien, qu’il fallait « interdire » l’IA partout où elle présente un risque pour les enfants.
« L’affaiblissement cognitif », première crainte des psychiatres
« Le premier enjeu est l’affaiblissement cognitif. C’est attractif, on y délègue des compétences. Puisqu’on y délègue des compétences, on ne les acquiert pas », résume Raphaël Gaillard, qui y voit un problème pour les jeunes comme pour le reste de la population. Son confrère Amine Benyamina parle d’une « dette cognitive », contractée à force de confier réflexion, décision et esprit critique à la machine.
La flagornerie des agents conversationnels, cette propension à flatter l’utilisateur au détriment de la vérité, figure parmi les mécanismes à encadrer dès la conception, au même titre que l’anthropomorphisme. « On crée un registre de relations émotionnelles qui peut avoir vocation à se substituer à l’interaction » humaine, décrit Raphaël Gaillard. Le psychiatre y voit « un système disponible en permanence, qui n’a pas d’autre intention que de vous garder en ligne ». Le rapport demande en parallèle des protections dédiées aux mineurs et un durcissement de la répression des contenus sexuels non consentis et pédocriminels générés par IA.
33 millions de personnes ont utilisé l’IA générative en France en début d’année, d’après le document, qui situe le pays au cinquième rang mondial des usages. Le rapport avancerait aussi que 73 % des Français s’informent désormais par ce biais, face à des contenus jugés 50 % plus persuasifs qu’un article de presse. Attendues pour mai dans la lettre de mission, ces conclusions auront mis six mois de plus à aboutir. « Si on ne prend pas ces décisions », prévient Raphaël Gaillard, l’externalisation cognitive, la dépendance affective et les dérives informationnelles, « on les subira ». Aucun arbitrage n’a été annoncé à ce stade.

articles.title: Olaf Sakkers is betting he can beat the emerging-manager squeeze | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Entering into the world of venture capital has never been easy, especially as a first-time fund manager. But it’s especially daunting right now.
According to PitchBook data, firms raising their fourth fund “or later” captured a whopping 88.2% of U.S. VC fundraising dollars through the first three quarters of this year, while first-time funds captured a measly 4.5%. Just 81 first-time funds closed in the first nine months of 2026. That puts the year on track to be the worst for first-time managers in at least a decade, according to PitchBook’s estimate.
Olaf Sakkers has spent the past five years proving that difficult doesn’t mean impossible. He founded his firm RedBlue Capital in 2021 and closed its first fund with roughly $5 million in capital commitments in 2023. He has now held a first close on a second fund that he says will total at least $50 million.
Raised in South Africa, he studied anthropology at Princeton, focusing on global health and health policy, and wrote his thesis on HIV in his home country. He moved to Israel after graduating and was drafted into the Israel Defense Forces, where he says he had a desk job liaising with the U.S. military, and where he became interested in autonomous vehicles.
An introduction led to Michael Granoff, founder of the venture firm Maniv Mobility and an early backer of electric-vehicle startup Better Place. Granoff, who had money to invest, hired him on the spot, Sakkers says. Neither had been a venture investor at that point, so they built a fund “almost by accident,” learning as they went. Sakkers says he ran the investment process day to day, backing Israeli founders who were bringing cybersecurity skills into the automotive world, and later expanding to the U.S. and other markets.
By 2021, Sakkers says, he was an equal partner in Maniv’s economics, but he wanted something different — more formal and scalable — so struck out on his own. Today, RedBlue backs what he calls the “real economy,” including robotics, logistics, manufacturing and energy.
Getting to this point has been a test of endurance as much as salesmanship, seemingly. Sakkers says that institutional limited partners, outfits like endowments and pension funds, have been the toughest to win over because his checks are small (and theirs are comparatively huge) but also because their risk model is built to “avoid getting a zero,” which is why they tend to gravitate toward established brands.
Says Sakkers, it’s akin to founders who come to be seen as “inevitable,” after they’ve previously founded another company. Meanwhile first-time founders often battle against the “gravity of perception,” meaning a more dominant brand can bend how people perceive a newer one.
His answer has been to let the results speak, but it takes time. “It’s a long-term game of building trust, demonstrating performance over time,” Sakkers says.
The first fund was a proof of concept, backed by LPs he had known for a while, including family offices. The second draws on family offices and institutions.
RedBlue writes small checks, $50,000 to $100,000, mostly joining deals led by other investors rather than leading them. That lets it do more deals and be “the last investor that they take” on by promising practical help, including introductions to lead investors like Andreessen Horowitz and Thrive Capital, and to customers. Founders expect little from VCs, in Sakker’s view, so RedBlue tries to overdeliver on the support part.
By his account, the results are strong. Of 28 investments, he says that 15 have been marked up, and he cites a net internal rate of return of “significantly above 50%.” There has been just one exit — an acqui-hire — so most gains from the tiny fund remain on paper and unrealized.
Public records support part of Sakker’s story. HappyRobot, which RedBlue backed early, raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.2 billion valuation in August. Westmag, which makes motors for drones and robots and which Sakkers backed at pre-seed alongside Nat Friedman, emerged in June with an $11 million seed led by Andreessen Horowitz. Flai, an AI startup for car dealerships, followed its 2025 seed with a $27 million Series A. And Humble Robotics, a driverless-truck startup in whose $24 million seed round RedBlue participated, announced a $51 million Series A led by Obvious Ventures earlier this month.
Sakkers argues that discipline is his edge. RedBlue publishes thesis essays, such as one on robotics, and runs on a custom database that he built with Claude Code to log relationships, meeting notes and introductions.
That lets him and his lone full-time principal, based in New York, work asynchronously. AI agents, he says, are “useless if they just have to guess,” so everything gets written down. He contrasts that with Benchmark’s more artisanal model, which he says suits a firm with a record he lacks. Long exit timelines for physical-world companies don’t worry him, either: even a $50 million to $100 million fund, he says, can sell stakes on the secondary market.
The data isn’t uniformly grim. Smaller venture capital funds between $1 million and $10 million consistently outperform larger funds of $100 million or more at the top end of net TVPI (total value to paid-in capital, which compares a fund’s total value to the money invested in it) across recent vintages tracked by the software outfit Carta.
In the meantime, Sakkers is out there knocking on doors, making introductions between disparate parties, and calling up reporters like this one to tell his story. It’s not easy to make a mark in a world where the spoils accrue to the few, but he says he never seriously considered a safer job. “Life is short, and regrets last forever,” he says.

articles.title: AMD is running over 100 servers at 50% DRAM capacity with MEXT — company claims 95% performance of full-DRAM server, plans to expand to 2,000 servers in 2027
articles.text:
AMD shares how it can retain 95% of server performance with just half the DRAM, sidestepping memory shortages with MEXT — tech powers over 100 servers already running, with plans to expand to 2,000 servers in 2027
MEXT offloads cold memory pages to flash storage and serves them up with a predictive AI model.
In June, AMD overtook the predictive memory engine known as MEXT, which claims to offer upwards of 99% of the performance of a system with full DRAM capacity while running with as little as 25% of the physical DIMMs. The technology offloads cold memory pages to flash storage and uses an AI model to serve pages before they’re needed, and AMD says it plans to extend the tech across a wide swath of its IT infrastructure next year.
The pitch behind MEXT seems too good to be true. According to AMD and MEXT founder Gary Smerdon, the technology can cut the physical DRAM required in a server by 20% to 75% depending on the application and performance target. That missing memory still registers as installed DRAM to the OS. Instead of DRAM, however, MEXT uses relatively inexpensive flash storage to offload cold pages, flying them back in as they’re needed with an AI model. In some of AMD’s internal workloads, such as Synopsys PrimeTime, the company says it’s able to achieve 95% of the performance of a full server while running at 50% DRAM capacity with MEXT.
AMD has deployed MEXT internally on 145 servers, which it says will expand to 2,000 servers next year. In addition, the company has announced a partnership with HPE to bring MEXT to customers. Currently, we’re in phase 1 of the rollout, with some EPYC Venice servers carrying a “MEXT Ready” badge and a dedicated NVMe drive or bay for the offload. Phase 2 brings MEXT licenses out to these servers, as well as the RAM View application. AMD hasn’t said when Phase 2 will begin.
The AI-driven DRAM pricing surge impacts more than just gaming PCs, with enterprises also feeling the brunt of price increases, even if they aren’t running AI workloads. If MEXT is able to achieve what AMD claims, it could be transformative given the current market. Because of that, it’s worth understanding what exactly MEXT is, as well as what AMD claims it can do.
Although MEXT is exciting in concept, it’s obvious that AMD is taking a conservative approach to the rollout. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, after all. The applications of MEXT are currently narrow, though AMD says it’s expanding the workloads it’s using MEXT on with promising early results.
DRAM, Flash and an LLM
The basic setup of MEXT is simple in concept: cold pages go to flash, AI brings those pages back as needed, and it’s as if the memory was never missing in the first place. The main problem should be obvious. Flash is orders of magnitude slower than DRAM, so streaming pages back into memory from flash as they’re needed isn’t feasible. MEXT’s trick is using an AI model to predict the pages you’ll need. And, as long as the model is able to stay ahead by at least the transfer latency from the SSD, it’s as if the physical DRAM was installed the whole time.
This isn’t a crazy concept considering how a transformer-based LLM, which MEXT uses, operates. If you’re unfamiliar with the inner workings, this open-source visualization breaks down the concept of a transformer AI model cleanly. The foundational concept is next token prediction, which underpins the design of modern LLMs. Given a set of tokens, the LLM determines which token (word, portion of a word, etc.) is most likely to come next. It makes a prediction. In the case of MEXT, it’s predicting what page is needed next, not what word comes next.
Memory offloading to flash isn’t a new concept, but MEXT founder Gary Smerdon says that AI is the critical difference in this technology. MEXT itself is deployed as a Linux kernel module that works with any Linux distro. It uses an “ensemble of AI models,” with the primary transformer-based LLM driving the technology. And critically, it doesn’t come pre-trained.
Instead, AMD says that MEXT trains in under a second when first deployed, operates on one EPYC core without a GPU, and continually trains as the workload progresses. This approach makes sense given the varied workloads that MEXT may apply to. The idea is that it would learn the access patterns of the application in order to drive that prediction engine.
MEXT isn’t perfect, but it doesn’t need to be perfect in every situation. For instance, the order of stored pages isn’t important. With text, an LLM needs to predict the correct text in the correct order, but with MEXT, the order doesn’t matter. As long as the page is in DRAM when it’s needed, that’s fine.
In order to understand the application of MEXT to different workloads, AMD has developed RAM View to go alongside the tech. It’s a memory utilization tool that shows which pages are hot and which have gone cold. As you can see from the example above, a system with 1.5 TB of memory shows near-full utilization across the full workload, but around half of the pages stored in memory haven’t been touched in five minutes or more at any given time.
AMD provided this generalized example and didn’t clarify what workload it was testing. That’s very important, as the utilization breakdown will look vastly different depending on the application(s) running on the server. Initially, AMD is applying MEXT to critical EDA applications it uses internally, such as Synopsys PrimeTime, but the company says it has focused on optimizing agentic AI, database, and media and entertainment workloads as well.
This is important not only because memory access patterns change between applications, but also because performance in those applications reacts differently when a system doesn’t have enough memory. The “memory wall,” as AMD calls it, should be a familiar concept regardless of whether you’ve ever touched a server. With MEXT, AMD says it’s trying to extend this memory wall, which may look different for different applications.
For instance, the company is confident that many workloads can reduce capacity by around 20% to 25%. As the reduction increases, however, the applications become more specialized, and the performance delta becomes greater.
AMD’s internal MEXT results
AMD has shared some internal MEXT results, which look impressive, though as usual, it’s always smart to handle first-party benchmarks like this with skepticism. Starting with PrimeTime, where AMD has focused much of its attention on MEXT up to this point, it says servers running at 50% capacity retain 95% of the performance of a full server, and going down to as little as 25% capacity still maintains 80% of the application’s performance.
PrimeTime demands a lot of memory for large designs. There are some applications where performance is nearly identical, according to AMD. In a 3-node cluster running in Azure with 5th-gen EPYC CPUs, AMD says MEXT offers 99% of the performance of the full cluster while running at 50% DRAM capacity with the Spark SQL workload from the TPC-DS benchmark. SQL databases try to cache as much data as possible in memory to prevent I/O bottlenecks, creating a golden opportunity for tech like MEXT that wants to free cold pages.
Perhaps the most applicable workload at the current moment, however, is agentic AI, and AMD says MEXT has similar applications there. Across a five-agent concurrent geomean, AMD claims 99% of the performance of a full server with 50% memory capacity, and 85% of the performance with 25% capacity. With a “memory-hungry” agent, AMD claims 90% and 88% performance for 50% and 25% capacity, respectively.
The slide you can see above has footnote tags. However, AMD has not shared the footnotes with us yet, so we don’t have a view into how these tests were run. Naturally, we assume AMD has, at minimum, represented the performance of MEXT in the best light possible. We can’t do a full analysis without knowing how the tests were run, however.
What is interesting is AMD’s cautious approach to rolling out MEXT. It’s an EPYC-exclusive feature right now, though AMD left the door open for support on future products (consumer devices, such as Strix Halo) far down the road. It will be sold as a license, bundled with the RAM View software, but we don’t have a timeline on when that will happen. And, despite a partnership with HPE to push out “MEXT Ready” servers, we still don’t know when MEXT itself will be ready for deployment beyond AMD’s walls.
Given that conservative approach, there are likely pitfalls to MEXT that we’re not seeing yet, and it’s hard to imagine it will be broadly applicable to every server, at least at the 50% and 25% DRAM capacity levels that AMD showed off with its benchmarks.
However, even being able to trim 25% of a server’s DRAM capacity represents a massive cost savings in the current supply-constrained environment. If some workloads can push that to 50% capacity, that’s even better. Of course, we’ll need to see how MEXT holds up once it’s available broadly, but if AMD’s claims hold water, it could become a defining technology in data centers that can’t seem to get enough memory.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.
