articles.title: Démarchage téléphonique : trois mois après l’interdiction, pourquoi votre téléphone sonne toujours
articles.text:
Pour chacun des 3 377 appels qu’elle avait passés dans la rénovation énergétique, où le démarchage téléphonique est interdit, une entreprise de Haute-Garonne a payé 75 euros d’amende, loin du plafond de 375 000 euros prévu par la loi. Trois mois après l’interdiction du démarchage sans votre accord, des sénateurs s’inquiètent de voir les appels continuer.
« Plusieurs mois après l’entrée en vigueur de la loi, les pratiques perdurent ! Certains concitoyens signalent encore près de cinq appels indésirables par jour », a dénoncé devant le Gouvernement le sénateur de la Haute-Saône Olivier Rietmann, rapporteur de la loi, le 20 octobre. Depuis le 11 août, une entreprise n’a plus le droit de vous appeler pour vous vendre quelque chose sans votre accord préalable. Selon la répression des fraudes (DGCCRF), 43 000 signalements de démarchage ont été déposés entre début août et fin septembre. D’après l’enquête du Parisien, le démarchage reste très rentable pour les entreprises.
75 euros par appel, loin du plafond de 375 000 euros
La loi prévoit jusqu’à 375 000 euros d’amende par manquement pour une entreprise, et 75 000 euros pour une personne physique. En juillet 2025, la DGCCRF a infligé 253 275 euros à la société CB Performance, en Haute-Garonne, pour 3 377 appels passés dans la rénovation énergétique, soit 75 euros par appel.
Les dossiers mettent aussi du temps à aboutir et on vous en rapporte quelques uns régulièrement sur Clubic. Le Betef, une entreprise de Sarcelles, a écopé le 3 septembre de 92 107 euros d’amende pour des appels passés dans la rénovation énergétique entre janvier 2024 et mars 2025. Moins de deux semaines plus tard, l’opérateur Syma Mobile, filiale d’Altice, a reçu une amende de 1,1 million d’euros pour avoir appelé des personnes inscrites sur Bloctel et dépassé le plafond de quatre appels par mois et par personne.
Toutes ces sanctions portent sur des appels passés avant le 11 août. En 2025, la DGCCRF a contrôlé 6 300 établissements et notifié 11 millions d’euros d’amendes pour l’ensemble du démarchage téléphonique, alors que les Français déposaient 287 000 signalements.
Une partie des démarcheurs appelle depuis l’étranger
Au Maroc, les centres d’appels réalisent plus de 80 % de leur chiffre d’affaires avec la France, et le démarchage pèse encore 15 à 20 % de leur activité. Selon l’AFP, entre 40 000 et 50 000 emplois du royaume pourraient être touchés par l’interdiction française.
Installée à l’étranger, une entreprise n’est pas pour autant intouchable. La société Merrios, basée à Dublin, a écopé de 6,03 millions d’euros d’amende pour avoir appelé en masse des personnes inscrites sur Bloctel, au nom de la marque Délices & Gourmandises. Mais il faut d’abord identifier la société qui appelle, et le député de l’Ain Xavier Breton a demandé au gouvernement comment sanctionner les plateformes de démarchage installées à l’étranger.
Interrogé au Sénat en avril, le gouvernement a mis en avant une autre mesure. Depuis le début de l’année, un appel venu de l’étranger avec un numéro de mobile français non authentifié s’affiche en numéro masqué sur votre téléphone.
Les fraudeurs usurpent des numéros français
Certains appels frauduleux affichent un numéro français qui n’appartient pas à l’appelant. Depuis 2020, la loi oblige les opérateurs à authentifier le numéro de l’appelant. Selon l’Arcep, le gendarme des télécoms, les signalements d’usurpation de numéro sont malgré tout passés de 531 en 2023 à plus de 19 000 en 2025 sur sa plateforme « J’alerte l’Arcep ». Le régulateur a ouvert en janvier une enquête administrative auprès de l’ensemble des opérateurs.
Les fraudeurs disposent aussi de nouveaux fichiers. Juste avant la fermeture de Bloctel, le service a confirmé qu’un pirate avait utilisé le compte d’une entreprise abonnée pour récupérer environ 3 millions de numéros de téléphone, qui peuvent servir à des campagnes de démarchage illégal ou à des SMS frauduleux.
Votre opérateur ou votre assureur garde le droit de vous appeler
Une partie des appels que vous recevez sont parfaitement légaux, car la loi prévoit deux exceptions. Une entreprise peut vous appeler si vous lui avez donné votre accord, ou si vous êtes son client et que l’appel concerne votre contrat. Comme l’explique la DGCCRF, elle peut alors vous proposer des produits ou des services « afférents ou complémentaires à l’objet du contrat en cours », et vous rappeler pour renouveler votre abonnement. Les éditeurs gardent aussi le droit de vous proposer par téléphone un abonnement à un journal ou à un magazine.
Vous pouvez retirer votre accord quand vous le souhaitez. En dehors de ces cas, vous pouvez signaler l’appel sur SignalConso, avec le nom de l’entreprise, la date, l’heure et le numéro affiché, et bloquer sur votre smartphone les numéros réservés au démarchage.
Au Sénat, Hervé Reynaud a demandé au gouvernement le nombre de signalements enregistrés depuis le 11 août et les contrôles engagés par la DGCCRF contre les entreprises qui démarchent toujours sans consentement.
- Simple d'utilisation et rapide pour faire un signalement.
- Permet d'obtenir dans la plupart des cas une résolution au problème.
- Totalement gratuit.

articles.title: SA fintech startup Lumepay raises $6m pre-seed round - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African cross-border payments startup Lumepay has raised US$6 million in pre-seed funding, alongside US$10 million in capital float, as it builds institutional-grade payment infrastructure for African businesses.
Led by CEO Harry Huang, Lumepay provides cross-border payment solutions for SMEs, corporates and institutions. Its rail-agnostic platform combines traditional finance and stablecoins to enable fast, cost-effective and transparent B2B transfers within and across African jurisdictions.
The startup launched Lumetrade, its digital asset and stablecoin trading venue, in April, before rolling out its payments platform in June, and has now raised US$6 million in pre-seed funding. The round was backed by founder-led angels and South African fintech investors. The US$10 million capital float was secured to give clients access to deep, reliable liquidity.
“The future of cross-border payments isn’t traditional finance or stablecoins; it’s a combination of both, backed by the FX depth to make them work for real businesses,” said Huang. “Our integrated approach addresses the real drivers of friction: fragmentation, liquidity inefficiency and execution risk.”
Lumepay is now live in Nigeria, Ghana, Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique and Kenya, as well as the West and Central African CFA franc zones, and is awaiting further regulatory approvals to expand its payment capabilities in these markets.
Last month, the startup received regulatory clearance from the Central Bank of Kenya, marking its entry into East Africa. Businesses in Kenya can now use Lumepay to pay international suppliers in currencies including Chinese yuan, US dollars and Indian rupees, and to move money across intra-African trade corridors.
“In the months since the raise, we’ve turned plans into working products: diversified and reliable liquidity; a platform that handles cross-border payments end to end; a growing network of partners and payment rails; and regulatory clearance in South Africa and Kenya,” said Luc Varejes, Lumepay’s COO.
In South Africa, Lumepay works with Nedbank as its Third-Party Payment Provider (TPPP) sponsoring bank, while sister business Lume Trade, an authorised financial services provider covering crypto asset intermediary services, banks with Standard Bank.
“Working with Nedbank and Standard Bank across our two businesses reflects the compliance standards we have built from day one,” said Tatenda Nhemachena, Lumepay’s chief legal and compliance officer.
The pre-seed funding has been used to build out Lumepay’s core infrastructure, including its payment rails, banking relationships, regulatory approvals and licensed partner network. The startup is now focused on expanding its regulatory footprint across Southern, West and Central Africa, with Malawi, Mozambique and the CFA franc regions key targets, as it lays the groundwork for a Series A round.

articles.title: AirEarth Pitch Event 2026: Clean Air and Climate Innovators to Face Investors
articles.text:
AirEarth Pitch Event 2026: Clean Air and Climate Innovators to Face Investors
AirEarth’s November 12 online event will see climate innovators pitch to investors and experts, with winners chosen by panel and audience.
AirEarth.org, which works on clean air and climate action, will hold its first Pitch & Partnership Event online on November 12, bringing together innovators, investors and experts in the field.
The AirEarth Pitch & Partnership Event 2026 is scheduled to run from 11:30 am to 2:30 pm IST. According to the organisers, the event aims to connect innovation, capital and expertise to speed up the development of solutions for clean air and climate action.
Six categories, two formats
Presenters have been grouped into six categories: clean energy; industry, construction, dust and urban air; waste and circularity; carbon capture, markets and emerging solutions; promising solutions; and grant and policy support nominees.
The format differs between the groups. Presenters in the first four categories will get three minutes to pitch, followed by three minutes of questions and feedback from the panel. Those in the last two categories, promising solutions and grant and policy support nominees, will have two minutes each and no Q&A round.
How winners will be selected
The organisers said the event will open with an introduction to AirEarth, the investor and expert panel, and the evaluation process. After each pitch, both panellists and audience members will submit feedback through a form. A live audience poll will follow each category.
Feedback and poll results will be consolidated at the end of the session, after which the final winners will be announced. The organisers have not yet disclosed the names of the panellists or the presenting startups, or whether winners will receive funding, grants or other forms of support.
Beyond the pitches
The organisers said that, beyond the pitches, the event is meant to build connections, open up opportunities and bring together people working towards clean air and climate action. The closing session will cover next steps for collaboration among participants.

articles.title: Active ScreenConnect attacks breach MSPs, impact dozens of organizations
articles.text:
Update 11/11/26: Added additional information from ConnectWise and Huntress.
ConnectWise is investigating an active malware campaign targeting managed service providers (MSPs) that uses compromised ScreenConnect environments to deploy rogue remote-access clients to customer devices.
As part of its investigation, ConnectWise has disabled five third-party ScreenConnect extensions across approximately 400 partner environments as a precaution, warning that they may be associated with the attacks.
The campaign was first discovered Wednesday by cybersecurity firm Huntress, which says it has identified six compromised MSPs and 286 affected endpoints across 47 organizations, and that the number of victims continues to rise.
"Our SOC is working an active campaign that started around 17:47 UTC today targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances," Huntress posted to Reddit.
"We are currently tracking 6 compromised MSPs and 286+ endpoints, and those numbers are climbing. ConnectWise is engaged and working this with us."
ScreenConnect is a remote access and support platform used by MSPs and IT teams to remotely manage and troubleshoot customer devices.
According to Huntress, attackers are using ScreenConnect's Run Command functionality to deploy rogue ScreenConnect clients on managed endpoints, providing remote access outside of the legitimate MSP's ScreenConnect environment.
The researchers also warned of a potentially more dangerous technique in which attackers can compromise an MSP technician's workstation when they initiate a ScreenConnect session with an infected customer device.
Spike Brandt, Principal Threat Intelligence Incident Commander at Huntress, told BleepingComputer that the activity appears to involve abusing legitimate functionality rather than exploiting a software vulnerability.
"This appears to be abuse of legitimate functionality, aided using custom-built tooling that is, in some cases, compiled on the fly on the victim’s computer," Brandt told BleepingComputer.
"We have no information about how a “patient zero” computer or machine would have initiated this attack."
Huntress said it began receiving alerts when rogue ScreenConnect clients appeared on monitored endpoints and subsequently retrieved attacker scripts that were still accessible to analyze how the attacks worked.
However, the precise mechanism allowing malware to spread from an infected endpoint to a technician's workstation has not been publicly explained.
ConnectWise disables third-party extensions
In a security advisory published Wednesday night, ConnectWise confirmed unauthorized access to ScreenConnect partner accounts and the installation of unauthorized remote-access software in customer environments.
As part of its investigation, the company discovered five independent third-party extensions that may be associated with the attacks and disabled them across approximately 400 partner environments as a precaution.
ScreenConnect extensions are installed through its built-in Extensions marketplace via the ScreenConnect administration interface.
The extensions are:
- Labtech Plus
- RMM Plus
- RMM+
- RMM Plus Password Link
- RMM+ Password Link
"Our initial assessment leads us to suspect the threat actor deployed additional remote-access software through independent 3rd party extensions that partners may have added to their environments," ConnectWise said.
The company stressed that having these extensions installed does not necessarily mean that a network was compromised and that the attacks remain under investigation.
"Disabling these 3rd party extensions is a precautionary containment measure. It does not establish that unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already present on affected devices has been removed," explained ConnectWise
While ConnectWise has disabled the extensions in affected cloud-hosted environments, it warned that on-premises ScreenConnect customers must disable them manually, as the company cannot do so from their end.
Partners were also instructed not to re-enable or reinstall the extensions until further guidance is available.
ConnectWise warned that disabling the extensions does not remove malicious software, persistence mechanisms, or unauthorized access that attackers may have already established on compromised endpoints.
The company advised partners to review authentication logs, extension installation records, administrative activity, Run Command history, and Toolbox records for suspicious activity.
It also urged technicians to avoid initiating interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially compromised devices and instead use separate security tools to investigate.
ConnectWise also said it has received reports of technician workstations being compromised during interactive ScreenConnect sessions, but these reports are still being confirmed.
The company added that it has no reason to believe partners that have not deployed the five identified extensions are impacted by this incident, but encouraged all partners to remain on heightened alert.
Huntress has not determined how the attackers are gaining access to affected MSP environments, but says its current telemetry points to compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions.
Huntress also warned that sequential identifiers used by the attackers suggest additional MSPs may have been previously compromised.
"Sequential attacker-assigned tags suggest other MSPs may have been compromised earlier, so ScreenConnect users should check their Run Command history even if they haven’t received alerts," Huntress told BleepingComputer.
Huntress also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations identify malicious activity, including rogue ScreenConnect client IDs and infrastructure used by the attackers.
The indicators include:
- Attacker relay: 185.99.255[.]28 (hostname: screen)
- C2 domains: newnewnew.gotdns[.]org, soxnewwork.homedns[.]org
- Possible additional C2: cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com
- Secondary C2: sc.payproofkit[.]com (155.94.150[.]39, hostname: WIN-FB5CKHMU4E1)
- Stager: hxxps://ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4
- Rogue ScreenConnect client IDs: 2588ef5c15954b10, ed630cc2c873b091
- Installer pattern: /Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi?...&c=Exploited<N>
- Attacker name: Addmin
- Files: Panel-Lateral.ps1, runnew.cmd, ToolboxRelayUploader.exe, Run-Lateral-Full.bat
The researchers are urging MSPs to review their environments for signs of compromise and avoid initiating interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially infected endpoints.
Huntress also told BleepingComputer that its researchers have contacted ConnectWise, the VPS provider hosting the attacker's infrastructure, cloud providers whose dynamic DNS services were used in the attacks, and the broader MSP community.
Earlier malware activity linked to rogue ScreenConnect identifier
BleepingComputer found an earlier malicious batch script that references one of the rogue ScreenConnect client IDs listed by Huntress, suggesting that the ID was used in malicious activity months before the current attacks were disclosed.
The script, named SSA-2026-STATEMENT-15518787.bat (VirusTotal), appears to impersonate a Social Security Administration statement and was first uploaded to VirusTotal on July 25, 2026.
The batch file attempts to add Microsoft Defender exclusions and creates persistence through the Windows Startup folder and the Run registry key.
It then contacts amexsafekeyupdate.com to retrieve installation commands for two separate installers.
VirusTotal sandbox activity associated with the sample includes downloads of ScreenConnect MSI installers from cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com and cyberrexdesign.screenconnect[.]com, with cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com also listed by Huntress as a possible C2 domain.
After launching the second installer, the script uses PowerShell to search running processes and Windows services for ed630cc2c873b091, one of the rogue ScreenConnect client IDs identified by Huntress.
If the identifier is found, the script considers the installation successful and sends a notification to the attackers through Telegram.
The earlier script also appears designed for a different distribution campaign, with its Social Security-themed filename suggesting it may have been used in phishing attacks.
Asked about the earlier activity, Huntress declined to comment on the specific July incident but said it has observed a significant increase in attacks using legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software as an initial payload in 2026.
The relationship between the July malware activity and the current ScreenConnect attacks remains unclear.

articles.title: ¿Cuándo ha pasado el Xiaomi TV Box S 3rd Gen a costar casi el doble? Era la mejor alternativa al Fire TV Stick pero ya no lo es tanto
articles.text:
Ha pasado poco más de un año desde que Xiaomi lanzó en España su TV Box S (3rd Gen) y desde entonces hemos visto una subida de precios en muchos dispositivos; buena culpa la tiene la crisis de la memoria RAM. Y este dispositivo en concreto parece que no se ha salvado, ya que en la tienda oficial de Xiaomi hemos notado un gran incremento en su precio: ahora cuesta nada menos que 119,99 euros.
Una subida de precio muy grande
Cuando la marca lanzó oficialmente el Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen), al menos en España, otras tiendas como Powerplanet ya lo estaban vendiendo (incluso le dedicamos un artículo). El precio oficial de esta generación era de 74,99 euros, pero como decimos Powerplanet lo estaba vendiendo de oferta a un precio inferior de 57,50 euros.
Teniendo en cuenta la rebaja que pudimos ver en aquel entonces, el dispositivo ha subido 62,49 euros con respecto al precio de Powerplanet y de 45 euros con respecto al precio de la tienda oficial de Xiaomi. Es una gran subida de precio, sobre todo porque, por su precio, esta era la mejor alternativa que podíamos encontrar a los Fire TV Stick, sobre todo tras el paso de Amazon de cambiar el sistema operativo apostando por VegaOS. Además, estos dispositivos también subieron de precio hace poco tiempo.
Tiendas como Powerplanet tienen este dispositivo por un precio más elevado que hace un año, ya que esta tienda en concreto lo tiene de oferta por 84,49 euros. ¿Lo podemos encontrar más barato? Sí, AliExpress, por ejemplo, lo tiene por 64,74 euros, aunque con el cupón ESD1103 se queda por 61,74 euros.

articles.title: Isabel Ocaña, administradora de fincas: “Un propietario no debe conectar el vehículo a un enchufe comunitario por iniciativa propia”
articles.text:
“Un propietario no debe conectar el vehículo a un enchufe comunitario por iniciativa propia”. Así se pronuncia Isabel Ocaña, administradora de fincas y vicepresidenta primera del Colegio Profesional de Administradores de Fincas de Madrid. Se trata de la situación en la que se quiere utilizar el tomacorriente de la comunidad (por ejemplo, en el garaje) para la recarga de un vehículo eléctrico. En este caso, los dueños de los vehículos no pueden enchufar por su cuenta a los tomacorrientes de la comunidad.
El asunto tiene que ver con nuestro bolsillo. Si utilizamos el suministro comunitario para la recarga, los consumos se contabilizan en la comunidad. Recordemos que la toma de corriente y el suministro son servicios comunes.
En este caso hay que contar con el acuerdo de la comunidad y establecer un sistema de individualización de consumos. Es decir, que la comunidad disponga de un sistema que permita cuantificar el consumo de cada uno de los usuarios y que su coste se le cobre. Si se instala un punto privado en una plaza individual, los costes de instalación y de consumo de electricidad corren por completo a cargo de los interesados (artículo 17.5 de la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal).
En estos casos no es necesario un acuerdo de la junta. Es suficiente con informar a la comunidad de antemano. Hay que destacar que esto es aplicable a los puntos de recarga privados en plaza individual.
Por otra parte, la instalación ha de cumplir con el Reglamento electrotécnico para baja tensión. En concreto, en la instrucción técnica que regula la recarga de vehículos eléctricos, se regulan las infraestructuras relacionadas con la recarga de vehículos (también en aparcamientos colectivos). No basta con informar de la realización de la obra a los vecinos.
Es recomendable que la comunicación se realice de forma escrita, según Ocaña. Además de la información sobre la instalación (esquema o memoria), conviene indicar cómo va a ser la trayectoria de la canalización. También es conveniente indicar quién es la empresa instaladora. Una vez finalizada la instalación, es bueno entregar a la comunidad toda la documentación de legalización que se exija. También el certificado de instalación eléctrica.
Cómo llevar la electricidad hasta la plaza
Que no haya una infraestructura específica en el garaje no quiere decir que no puedan instalarse puntos de recarga. Por ejemplo, se puede llevar una línea desde el suministro individual de la vivienda hasta la plaza (si técnicamente es posible y cumple con el reglamento) y se podría crear un suministro específico para la recarga.
También se puede pensar en una infraestructura común a la que posteriormente se van a ir conectando los puntos individuales. Estas soluciones están previstas en diferentes esquemas de la instrucción técnica mencionada. Hay que adaptar la solución a las características de la instalación. El tema es cómo llevar la electricidad al cargador y cómo asignar los consumos (sin llevarlos a los gastos generales del edificio).
En el caso de que haya varios propietarios con vehículo eléctrico (o vayan a adquirirlo), es especialmente recomendable la infraestructura común.

articles.title: Face aux incendies de voiture électrique, des ingénieurs chinois testent une mesure radicale : éjecter la batterie
articles.text:
La scène tient en quelques secondes : un SUV à l’arrêt expulse son pack de batterie sur le côté, à plusieurs mètres, au premier signe d’emballement. Tournée en Chine et apparue en ligne à l’automne 2025, la démonstration ressurgit régulièrement depuis, entre fascination et moqueries. Elle répond pourtant à un problème de sécurité bien réel, sur lequel deux industriels français ont pris des chemins nettement plus discrets.
Catapulter le danger, une idée qui revient
Le principe emprunte à l’airbag : un générateur de gaz chasse le pack hors de son logement, en une seconde environ. Le bloc retombe à 3 à 6 mètres du véhicule, loin de l’habitacle qu’il menaçait d’embraser. L’origine exacte du montage reste floue : l’équipementier Joyson Electronics et le constructeur iCar, un temps cités, ont démenti toute implication.
Lire aussi : Incendies de Volkswagen ID.Buzz en France : le rappel de 100 000 véhicules était-il suffisant ?
Restait une question sans réponse publique : l’endroit où retombe un bloc de plusieurs centaines de kilos éjecté en pleine ville. Le logiciel censé interdire le tir hors des zones dégagées n’existait pas encore au moment de la démonstration. L’idée, elle, circule bel et bien dans l’industrie : Hyundai et Kia ont déposé dès 2024 un brevet voisin, pensé pour un véhicule à l’arrêt et déclenché manuellement, par un levier.
Toute cette ingéniosité vise le même ennemi, l’emballement thermique, cette réaction en chaîne qui fait monter une cellule en température jusqu’à embraser ses voisines. Une étude américaine publiée en août 2026, après l’incendie volontaire de 18 véhicules électriques, conclut qu’aucune technique d’extinction ne stoppe le phénomène une fois lancé. La Chine impose d’ailleurs, depuis juillet 2026, une norme radicale : un pack ne doit plus ni s’enflammer ni exploser, même quand une cellule s’emballe.
Noyer plutôt qu’éjecter : les réponses françaises
En France, la réponse déployée à grande échelle fait le chemin inverse : elle fait entrer l’eau au cœur du pack. Le Fireman Access de Renault, mis au point avec les sapeurs-pompiers, ajoute au carter de la batterie un opercule qui cède sous la pression de la lance, ouvrant un accès direct aux cellules. L’extinction tombe à quelques minutes, contre plusieurs heures autrement, avec environ dix fois moins d’eau. Le dispositif équipe tous les véhicules électriques et hybrides rechargeables de Renault, Dacia, Alpine et Mobilize ; la licence en est offerte à l’ensemble des constructeurs depuis le 18 février 2025.
Stellantis explore une voie médiane, décrite dans une demande de brevet repérée cet automne : des fixations pyrotechniques larguent le pack au sol sous la voiture, laquelle s’éloigne ensuite sur sa seule batterie 12 volts. Sur le papier, l’approche évite le projectile, le bloc restant à plat sur la chaussée pendant que l’habitacle s’écarte du foyer.

articles.title: The iOS Crash We Could Not Reproduce
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Intermittent production crashes often need controlled fault isolation when logs and local testing cannot identify the failing path.
- A lower overall crash rate does not prove that the root cause is fixed. Unrelated changes can simply change the timing of a concurrency defect.
- One device that reproduces a failure probabilistically can turn speculative debugging into testable engineering work.
- HTML import through NSAttributedString has a main-thread requirement that is easy to miss when the call sits inside asynchronous screen preparation.
- A shared main-actor abstraction is a stronger safeguard than asking every call site to remember a framework threading rule.
Some production crashes announce themselves with a clean stack trace. This one did not. It appeared in a large-scale consumer iOS application, affected only some executions, and resisted every local reproduction attempt. The final code change was small, but reaching it required turning a vague SIGBUS report into a controlled set of experiments. This article walks through the investigation and the threading contract behind HTML import in NSAttributedString.
The Crash That Refused to Reproduce
Most production crashes I investigate start with a familiar routine. I read the crash report, look for the stack frame closest to the failure, try to reproduce the path, and then work backward toward the root cause. This incident did not fit that pattern.
The crash showed up in a large-scale consumer iOS application. It affected only a subset of executions and appeared at unpredictable times. Exact production metrics are confidential, but the incident was serious enough to require a focused investigation and an expedited hotfix.
Neither developers nor QA engineers could reproduce it consistently. We could repeat the customer flow without seeing anything unusual. The crash report included a SIGBUS signal and Foundation frames related to attributed string processing, but it did not point to a clear line in our Swift code.
SIGBUS is a low-level invalid memory access signal, not a diagnosis. It can come from several conditions, so it would have been wrong to assume from the signal alone that a specific variable had been released or reused. The evidence narrowed the search area, but it did not establish the cause.
That left a wide search space. I considered object lifetime, SwiftUI view model ownership, shared mutable state, unsynchronized work, and Foundation behavior. Management needed an answer quickly, and I initially had about a week to investigate and prepare a fix.
Starting With the Expected Suspects
I started with the checks that usually help with this kind of failure. I enabled Zombie Objects, added exception and symbolic breakpoints, reviewed ownership around the affected screens, and inspected the asynchronous paths that prepared their data.
I also made defensive improvements while I was in that part of the codebase. I tightened observable object ownership, reviewed whether several reference types really needed identity semantics, clarified synchronization, and made UI-related concurrency more explicit with async and await and MainActor isolation.
Those changes improved the code. The first hotfix also produced a noticeable reduction in the overall crash rate. But the original crash signature continued to appear in production, and customers were still reporting the behavior tied to the incident.
Why the First Hotfix Misled Us
The initial improvement looked encouraging because the aggregate crash rate moved in the right direction. It did not prove causation. Changes to lifecycle handling and synchronization can affect task scheduling, object retention, and timing. A timing-sensitive failure can become less frequent even when the underlying contract violation is still present.
That distinction became central to the investigation. We had improved the application, but we had not shown that we had removed the defect. The target crash still existed, and the remaining investigation window had narrowed to only a few days.
A Reproducible Device Changed the Investigation
The turning point was not another breakpoint or a more detailed stack trace. A QA engineer who also used the production application found that she could trigger the crash by repeating the affected flow. It was still intermittent and sometimes took four or five attempts, but that was enough.
For the first time, I had a practical test oracle. If a new build still crashed on that device, the change had not addressed the problem. If repeated attempts stopped producing the failure, the change deserved deeper validation. The device changed the work from production forensics into an experiment.
Turning Debugging Into an Experiment
My first experiments still focused on the screens closest to the visible failure. I cleaned up their code, adjusted ownership, reviewed asynchronous work, generated an IPA, and sent it to the QA engineer.
After several attempts, that build crashed again. The result was negative, but it was useful. Until then, I had been making reasonable changes without a reliable way to know whether they mattered. A reproducible failure made every rejected hypothesis informative.
The loop became simple: change one area, build an IPA, install it on the affected device, repeat the customer flow, and record whether the crash returned. Across the investigation, I shared roughly nine or ten experimental builds.
I also explored potential solutions through developer communities, including Stack Overflow, the Apple Developer Forums, and LinkedIn iOS development groups. However, the application's source code and internal debugging artifacts were confidential under company policies, so I could only discuss the problem at a general technical level without sharing proprietary information. While these communities offered opportunities to explore possible causes, they could not directly inspect or conclusively diagnose the issue. I therefore continued investigating through controlled experiments within our development environment.
Systematic Fault Isolation
I changed the question. Instead of asking which code looked suspicious, I asked which code had to remain for the crash to survive. I removed one view or behavior at a time, generated a new build, and tested the same flow on the affected device.
After six or seven elimination builds, the failure surface narrowed to one file. Nothing in that file looked obviously unsafe, so I repeated the process inside it. Several more experiments reduced the problem to one operation.
The line converted HTML data into an attributed string:
let attributedString = try NSMutableAttributedString(
    data: data,
    options: [
        .documentType: NSAttributedString.DocumentType.html
    ],
    documentAttributes: nil
)
The code had no force unwrap, unsafe pointer, manual memory management, or obvious shared state. At the call site, it looked like a normal Foundation conversion. That ordinary appearance had kept it low on the original list of suspects.
The Disclosure Code Path
The affected flow involved two important views of the application. Each view displayed a static disclosure section near the bottom, containing legal and informational text formatted as HTML. Although the content itself was static, it included interactive elements such as hyperlinks and phone numbers that users could tap to open external web views or initiate phone calls.
The application received this disclosure content as HTML and converted it into an attributed string before rendering it on the screen.
Because the disclosure section was relatively small and worked correctly during most executions, it initially appeared unlikely to be responsible for the crash. Attention naturally focused on the larger architectural components and asynchronous screen-loading operations.
The critical issue was that HTML-to-attributed-string conversion could be invoked from an asynchronous screen-preparation path without an explicit guarantee of main-thread execution. This mattered because Foundation's HTML importer has a threading constraint that was not enforced at the call site.
The Hidden Threading Contract
Apple documents an important constraint for HTML import through NSAttributedString: when the options specify HTML as the document type, the importer should not be called from a background thread. Apple says the method may try to synchronize with the main thread, fail, and time out. The broader attributed string documentation also notes that WebKit handles HTML conversion, which matters because this path is not just a pure data transformation.
Our problem was therefore not that the screens displayed attributed text. The unsafe condition came from creating HTML-backed attributed strings from an execution context where the main thread was not guaranteed.
The API did not make that requirement obvious at the call site. It accepted a Data value and returned an attributed string, so it looked like a straightforward transformation. The implementation carried a platform constraint that the surrounding asynchronous architecture had to enforce.
Why the Failure Appeared Random
Timing-dependent defects can survive many successful executions. Two users may receive equivalent HTML and call the same Swift function, yet reach the importer under different scheduling conditions. One execution may occur safely while another reaches the same code from background work during screen preparation.
This also explained why the defensive hotfix reduced the observed frequency without removing the signature. Lifecycle and synchronization changes changed timing. They did not eliminate the unsupported execution context.
The practical lesson was clear: changing the probability of a concurrency failure is not the same as removing its cause. For this incident to be considered resolved, the targeted crash signature and the reproducing flow both had to confirm the fix.
Turning the Fix Into an Application Wide Guarantee
The immediate repair was to perform the HTML conversion on the main actor. Fixing only the original call site would have addressed the visible incident, but it would not have prevented the same mistake elsewhere in a large codebase.
I searched for every place where the application converted HTML into an attributed string. Then I introduced a shared helper that made the execution requirement part of the API instead of an instruction each developer had to remember. The following code is a simplified and anonymized representation of that design:
enum HTMLAttributedStringRenderer {
    @MainActor
    static func render(from data: Data) throws -> NSAttributedString {
        try NSMutableAttributedString(
            data: data,
            options: [
                .documentType: NSAttributedString.DocumentType.html
            ],
            documentAttributes: nil
        )
    }
}
The UI-facing caller also stayed isolated to the main actor:
@MainActor
func updateDisclosure(from data: Data) throws {
    disclosureText = try HTMLAttributedStringRenderer.render(from: data)
}
Existing call sites were routed through this helper. The design centralized the Foundation dependency, reduced duplication, and created one place to document and test the threading contract. More importantly, it turned the requirement from a convention into a code-level boundary.
This did not mean all screen preparation moved to the main actor. Networking, decoding, and other suitable work could remain asynchronous. Only the operation with the framework constraint, along with the UI state that consumed its result, needed explicit main-actor isolation.
Validating the Complete Fix
I sent the corrected build to the QA engineer and asked her to repeat the flow on the device that had exposed every earlier attempt. The failure no longer appeared. I then asked for additional testing across both affected views and nearby behavior before promoting the change to the hotfix branch.
After release, production monitoring showed a dramatic reduction in the targeted crash. Exact figures cannot be disclosed, but this outcome differed from the first hotfix in the way that mattered: the specific production signature no longer appeared at a meaningful rate.
The investigation ended with three validations rather than one. The known device stopped reproducing the issue, every related call site used the shared helper, and production monitoring confirmed the expected change.
What the Incident Changed
The most useful lesson was broader than one Foundation API. When evidence is incomplete, a debugging process has to create new evidence. A device that reproduced the crash intermittently was more valuable than a long list of plausible code changes because it allowed each hypothesis to fail clearly.
The incident also changed how I evaluate framework abstractions. A Swift initializer may look safe while hiding behavior inherited from Objective-C, Foundation, UIKit, WebKit, run loops, or older platform design. Swift concurrency makes execution context easier to express, but it does not automatically make every underlying API safe for concurrent use.
Finally, a successful repair should make the same defect harder to reintroduce. The shared helper mattered because it protected future call sites, not only the two views involved in the incident.
A Practical Investigation Checklist
- Treat a signal such as SIGBUS as evidence about the failure category, not as proof of one memory-management cause.
- Track the specific crash signature separately from the overall crash rate so unrelated improvements do not create false confidence.
- When one device can reproduce the issue intermittently, preserve that environment and use it as a controlled test target.
- Change or remove one area at a time, and keep a record of which build accepted or rejected each hypothesis.
- After identifying a framework contract, search the full codebase and enforce the rule through a shared abstraction when possible.
- Validate the fix through targeted reproduction, regression testing, and post-release production monitoring.
Conclusion
The final code change was small. The hard part was reaching it through incomplete crash information, an unreproducible flow, misleading early improvements, time pressure, and proprietary artifacts that could not be shared outside the organization.
Once a single device reproduced the failure, the investigation stopped depending on intuition. Repeated builds narrowed the problem from two screens to one file and then to one ordinary-looking Foundation call. The root cause was HTML import running without the main-thread guarantee required by its implementation.
When a stack trace cannot identify the bug, the next step is to design an experiment that forces the code to reveal it. In this incident, systematic fault isolation provided the evidence that ordinary debugging could not.

articles.title: Vodacom’s 250m customers: How Safaricom is fueling growth
articles.text:
Vodacom, a pan-African technology group, is now generating growth beyond its South African home market, with Egypt, Kenya and other international markets outpacing its more mature domestic business.
The acquisition of a controlling stake in Safaricom, East Africa’s biggest telco, brings M-Pesa, Safaricom’s mobile money platform, and its vast financial services ecosystem into the group, strengthening Vodacom’s ambition to evolve beyond traditional mobile connectivity.
Vodacom reported revenue of R102.5 billion ($6.2 billion) for the six months ended 30 September 2026, a 25.6% year-on-year increase, boosted partly by the consolidation of Safaricom, according to its interim financial results on Tuesday
The results reveal a relatively mature South Africa, where growth is harder to extract, and faster-expanding markets where mobile connectivity and financial services are opening new revenue opportunities.
Egypt delivered 36.3% service revenue growth in local currency, while Safaricom grew service revenue by 13.1%. Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Lesotho also recorded strong performances. Vodacom’s international business achieved normalised service revenue growth of 13.7%, with Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) increasing 15.9%.
In South Africa, Vodacom returned its prepaid business to growth, supported by higher data consumption, while cost optimisation lifted its EBITDA margin to 37.4%, its highest level in several years.
Shameel Joosub, Vodacom’s chief executive officer, said the group had delivered one of its strongest six-month performances. “We exceeded our medium-term growth target on service revenue, EBITDA, and operating free cash flow, while also reaching the milestone of serving a quarter of a billion customers across Africa,” he said.
Vodacom added 26 million customers over the past 12 months, taking its total customer base to 250 million across Africa.
The Safaricom acquisition is becoming central to Vodacom’s ambition to diversify beyond traditional mobile connectivity and accelerate its financial services business. Vodacom increased its shareholding to 55%, consolidating Safaricom as a subsidiary from June 30. The transaction gives it greater exposure to Kenya’s mobile money ecosystem and one of the continent’s most established fintech platforms.
Vodacom and Safaricom both generated pro-forma financial services revenue of R43.1 billion ($2.6 billion) over the last 12 months. Their platforms served 108 million financial services customers, who accessed and initiated more than $575.5 billion in transaction value over the same period.
Financial services revenue grew 99% to R15.9 billion ($966 million) in the reported half-year, although that figure reflects Safaricom’s consolidation for only one quarter. On a pro-forma basis, including Safaricom in the comparative period, growth was 19.2%.
Joosub said M-Pesa is key to Vodacom’s ambition to build a business that earns money from more than calls, data and connectivity. Beyond payments, the opportunity includes savings, investments, credit and other digital financial products.
“The combination of Vodacom and Safaricom creates one of the continent’s largest FinTech platforms,” he said, adding that the platforms are expanding access to formal financial services and enabling greater economic participation for millions of people and businesses.
Financial services, fixed connectivity, digital and Internet of Things (IoT) services now account for 27.4% of Vodacom’s service revenue. Following the Safaricom acquisition, the group has raised its 2030 target for these businesses from 30% to more than 32%, demonstrating how central diversification has become to its growth strategy.
For shareholders, the interim performance has brought a handsome payout. Vodacom declared an interim dividend of 355 cents per share, up 7.6%, supported by headline earnings per share growth of 25.7% to 587 cents. Headline earnings rose 25.6% to R11.3 billion ($685 million).
The group also invested R13.3 billion ($806 million) in capital expenditure during the half, up 41%, expanding network capacity and adding infrastructure to support rising data consumption and digital services.
Joosub said Vodacom was on track to exceed its medium-term growth targets as it pursues its Vision 2030 ambitions.

articles.title: Il utilise son Renault Scénic comme groupe électrogène pendant 30 heures, l’impact sur la batterie est bluffant
articles.text:
Un Renault Scénic E-Tech alimente une maison pendant une coupure électrique de 30 heures : voici l’exploit de la technologie V2L
Privé d’électricité pendant 30 heures après une tempête en Angleterre, un journaliste a alimenté son logement de vacances grâce à son Renault Scénic électrique, perdant seulement quelques pourcentages de batterie.
Si rares sont encore les voitures électriques capables d’alimenter directement tout le compteur d’une maison, beaucoup proposent déjà le V2L, une fonction toute simple qui permet d’y brancher des appareils du quotidien. Fin octobre, le journaliste d’Automotive News Europe, Nick Gibbs, en a fait l’expérience avec son Renault Scénic E-Tech dans le Lake District, en Angleterre, lorsqu’une violente tempête a privé d’électricité sa maison de location pendant 30 heures.
Un adaptateur qui transforme le Renault Scénic en prise domestique de secours
Face à cette panne rarissime outre-Manche, Nick Gibbs s’est souvenu d’un petit sac bien pratique fourni avec son Renault Scénic E-Tech, qu’il avait pris en option pour 400 €. À l’intérieur, un adaptateur capable de convertir le port de recharge du véhicule en une prise domestique délivrant jusqu’à 3,7 kW de puissance.
Le manuel du constructeur déconseillant de raccorder plusieurs rallonges bout à bout, la famille a concentré son installation de secours dans la cuisine à l’aide d’un unique câble. Durant la panne, le dispositif a ainsi permis de faire fonctionner simultanément deux réfrigérateurs, plusieurs lampes sur pied, une station de recharge pour téléphones et même un grille-pain.
En revanche, impossible d’allumer le four électrique, trop gourmand pour la limite de 16 ampères (3,7 kW) imposée par la voiture. “Les plans pour le dîner se sont vite rabattus sur des plats préparés sur la plaque de cuisson au gaz”, raconte le journaliste, qui estime malgré tout que ces 3,7 kW sont “proches de la limite pratique de ce qui est supporté par une rallonge standard”. Certains modèles chinois, comme le Chery Tiggo 9 hybride rechargeable ou le pick-up BYD Shark, auraient cependant pu sauver le coup grâce à leur puissance de 6,6 kW, permettant ainsi d’alimenter un four ou une pompe à chaleur (à condition d’utiliser des câbles bien plus épais).
Le plus fou dans l’histoire, c’est que l’utilisation de cette technologie V2L durant les 30 heures de panne n’a consommé qu’environ 8 % de la batterie de 87 kWh du Renault Scénic E-Tech, soit près de 7 kWh. Seul petit couac : une fois les frigos arrivés à bonne température, ils ne tiraient presque plus de courant. Pensant que plus rien n’était branché, la voiture s’est alors mise en veille et a coupé l’alimentation toute seule.
Pour parer à de futures tempêtes hivernales, le journaliste prévoit désormais d’investir dans une rallonge d’extérieur renforcée “pour améliorer à la fois la sécurité et la flexibilité en cas de future coupure de courant”, mais aussi de maintenir au maximum la batterie de sa voiture chargée à 100 %, “au cas où il faudrait à nouveau faire appel à elle pour maintenir le courant”.

articles.title: Robots de Google hacen más de 200 tareas: desde servir comida hasta manipular objetos de laboratorio
articles.text:
Google DeepMind presentó Gemini Robotics 2.5, un modelo de inteligencia artificial que permite a los robots aprender más de 200 tareas nuevas en semanas en lugar de meses y ejecutarlas en fábricas reales con un 96% de éxito.
El sistema combina visión, lenguaje y acción, lo que en la práctica significa que el robot ve un objeto, entiende qué se le pide y mueve brazos y manos para lograrlo, sin que un programador le indique cada movimiento paso a paso.
Qué tareas pueden hacer estos robots
Gemini Robotics 2.5 fue evaluado en más de 200 tareas distintas, desde servir comida con pinzas hasta atar un lazo en una caja de regalo o manipular líquidos con una pipeta.
Gemini Robotics 2.5 es el modelo de Google DeepMind que combina visión, lenguaje y acción para que un robot interprete una orden, reconozca un objeto y lo manipule de forma autónoma, con mejoras de hasta el cien por ciento en la tasa de éxito frente a su versión anterior. Esa capacidad lo acerca a actividades que antes requerían la destreza manual de una persona.
Según las pruebas de la compañía, el modelo logra entre un 30% y un 100% más de éxito que la versión previa, dependiendo del tipo de tarea, y completa esas tareas entre un 20% y un 30% más rápido.
El modelo funciona en distintos cuerpos robóticos. Uno de ellos es el humanoide Apollo 2, de la empresa Apptronik, que incorpora una mano de cinco dedos con 22 grados de libertad llamada SharpaWave. También opera en la plataforma Franka Duo, equipada con pinzas de dos dedos.
La prueba en las fábricas de Mercedes-Benz
Para comprobar si el sistema funciona fuera de un laboratorio, Google DeepMind lo llevó a líneas de producción activas de Mercedes-Benz en Kecskemét, Hungría, y en Sindelfingen, Alemania.
Allí, los robots Apollo 2 realizaron de forma autónoma una tarea conocida como kitting: tomar piezas sueltas de contenedores a granel y ordenarlas en bandejas, en la secuencia exacta que necesita cada vehículo de la línea.
Es un trabajo repetitivo y físicamente desgastante que, al quedar en manos de los robots, libera a los técnicos humanos para concentrarse en el ensamblaje de mayor complejidad.
El robot usa un modelo de razonamiento para seguir el flujo de trabajo y el modelo de acciones para controlar brazos y manos, con capacidad de corregir desvíos sin intervención humana. El resultado fue una tasa de éxito del 96%.
Para esto fue para lo que construimos Apollo: para realizar un trabajo útil junto a las personas en entornos industriales reales, afirmó Jeff Cardenas, cofundador y director ejecutivo de Apptronik. El directivo agregó que, al combinar Apollo 2 con Gemini Robotics, los modelos mejoraron de forma notable en pocas semanas de entrenamiento posterior y mantuvieron ese rendimiento al pasar a la producción real de Mercedes-Benz.
Cómo entrena la inteligencia artificial a estos robots
Detrás del avance está Gemini 4 Argon, uno de los modelos más recientes de Google, que funciona como motor de simulación para acelerar el entrenamiento.
Argon genera miles de ensayos simulados a partir de una escena grabada con cámaras reales y construye lo que la compañía llama un gemelo digital de alta precisión. Combinado con demostraciones reales, esto permite que el robot aprenda a manejar objetos y escenas nuevas con mayor rapidez.
El modelo también ayuda a los investigadores a identificar por qué falla una tarea a partir de la grabación de video, y a poner a prueba mejoras tanto en simulación como en robots físicos.
A esto se suma un entrenamiento basado en un sentido del tacto compartido entre varios robots, construido con un conjunto de datos de origen chino que reúne 5.000 horas de manipulación. Esa base táctil común permite que distintos robots trasladen lo aprendido por uno de ellos a tareas que nunca habían enfrentado.

articles.title: PlayStation 5 passes 100 million sales as GTA VI prepares to give it another boost
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Sony just revealed that the PlayStation 5 has officially sold more than 100 million units since its launch almost exactly six years ago. The PS5 is now just a few million units behind the seventh-place Wii and sixth-place PlayStation on the list of best-selling consoles ever, but it will likely soon outsell those machines as GTA VI's upcoming release boosts sales.
Sony wrote on its website that its latest console generation has sold over 100 million units as of November 10, 2026. That means it's still around 17 million units shy of the PS4 and slightly behind the original PlayStation (102.4 million), but ahead of the PS3 (87.4 million) and the PSP (76.4 million). Nothing comes close to the best-selling console of all time, the PlayStation 2, which sold more than 160 million units.
The figures reveal that Sony has sold another 2.1 million PS5 consoles since its previous financial quarter ended on September 30.
Reaching 100 million sales in six years is impressive considering the PS5 launched during the Covid pandemic in November 2020, when buying one was a near impossibility without paying scalpers a fortune. It took just over two years after release – January 2023 – before Sony announced that PS5 shortages were effectively over and the consoles should be much easier to find at retailers globally.
The PS5 was also the subject of some substantial price hikes this year as the memory crisis pushed up costs of numerous devices. The console became between $100 and $150 more expensive, with the PS5 Pro reaching $899.
But the PlayStation 5 has seen an uptick in sales recently that's being driven by one big factor: GTA VI. One of the most anticipated games of all time won't be on the PC when it arrives on November 19. Its console-only launch has led to many people buying a PS5 for this one reason alone. The game's also on Xbox Series X/S, but Sony's machine is a lot more popular.
Elsewhere in Sony's report, the company writes that cumulative worldwide software unit sales for the PS5 and PS4 combined have passed 1.795 billion. This includes physical and download-only titles, PS VR games, and software bundled with PS4 and PS5 consoles. There are also 127 million PlayStation monthly active users.
We still don't know when the PlayStation 5's successor will arrive. A previous report revealed that Sony itself still hasn't decided when the PlayStation 6 will launch. Some analysts had predicted a 2027 release, but the memory crisis could push its arrival further back.

articles.title: Critical Xen Orchestra Flaws Exploited in Attacks
articles.text:
A threat actor has been exploiting a critical-severity authentication bypass and a zero-day in Xen Orchestra, software maker Vates warns.
A web-based backup, management, and disaster recovery solution for XCP-ng and XenServer virtualization environments, Xen Orchestra operates as an agentless control center across hosts, VMs, storage, and pools.
The critical flaw exists in the REST authentication mechanism, where an authentication token is turned into {} and then treated as an unfiltered lookup, leading to the first token being returned by token collection. If the token is not expired, the provider authenticates as its owner.
This opens a route that exposes reusable login token IDs, allowing unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and gain administrator privileges.
“Xen Orchestra compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root,” Vates says.
The security defect impacts Xen Orchestra releases before 6.9.2 (stable) and 6.10.1 (latest), and Xen Orchestra Appliance, which contains Xen Orchestra.
Vates warned that the same threat actor has been exploiting this bug and a zero-day vulnerability that requires administrator privileges. The zero-day allows malicious VM imports that could compromise XCP-ng hosts, and a fix is still being developed.
According to the company, the attacker initially operated from 91.211.251.112:8001 and via the Tor network. No CVE identifier has been assigned to the security defects.
The company warns that unauthorized access is not logged, but has shared indicators of compromise (IoCs) associated with the observed attacks, and warns that they are limited to this specific campaign.
“Exploitation of the vulnerability by other threat actors using different TTPs and infrastructure cannot be ruled out. The absence of these IoCs alone is not sufficient to conclude that no compromise has occurred,” Vates notes.
The company recommends placing Xen Orchestra instances behind a dedicated network, blocking IP addresses and domain names associated with known malicious activity, blocking the empty token in a WAF rule, and rotating all potentially compromised credentials.
“In case of a confirmed compromise, a full reinstallation is recommended as cleanup alone cannot guarantee the removal of all backdoors left by the attacker,” Vates says.

articles.title: Dois terços das empresas investem em IA sem calcular o retorno financeiro • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Dois terços das empresas investem em IA sem calcular o retorno financeiro
Ainda assim, perspectiva é positiva para 67% das companhias do Brasil.
Quase 64% das empresas brasileiras assumem que fazem investimentos em inteligência artificial mesmo sem saber se terão um retorno positivo ou não. É o que aponta o levantamento AI Reality Report, realizado pela consultoria Avanade. A percepção geral é positiva: 67% das companhias percebem uma vantagem no investimento, índice superior à média global, que é de 59%. Apesar disso, o retorno financeiro de fato é mais tímido: apenas 51% dos entrevistados entendem que os gastos se justificam economicamente.
Outro ponto importante levantado é o treinamento de equipes na área: 77% das empresas dizem ver a necessidade com urgência, enquanto mais da metade (51%) veem dificuldades relacionadas a cibersegurança e privacidade com atenção. Essa informação casa com o entendimento da maioria (79,6%) de que as companhias dizem estar mais avançadas no setor do que estão de fato.
A pesquisa foi realizada entre agosto e setembro com 230 profissionais em posições de liderança no país e considerou empresas com faturamento anual superior a US$ 500 milhões (aproximadamente R$ 27,5 milhões).
Apesar da avaliação geral ser positiva em relação aos investimentos em IA, chama atenção que o retorno financeiro seja pouco considerado. Com 64% das empresas assumindo que não calcularam os ganhos a nível econômico e apenas 51% percebendo alguma vantagem econômica, o cenário é de incerteza nesse aspecto. Ainda assim, o aumento de produtividade dos funcionários é um dos principais destaques entre os que veem a IA de forma positiva.
Para o presidente da Avanade Brasil, Adriano Picchi Neves, a situação é positiva no Brasil. Segundo ele, as empresas nacionais “já estão capturando valor relevante com inteligência artfiicial”, entre o retorno financeiro e outros ganhos percebidos pelos profissionais. Ele afirma ainda que esse é o primeiro passo, e que a etapa seguinte “exige ir além de aplicar IA aos processos existentes”, sendo importante “repensar modelos, fluxos e formas de trabalhar”.
Há ainda uma preocupação geral em relação ao preparo dos funcionários para uso de IA: 77% entendem que é necessário aprimorar os treinamentos, além dos próprios sistemas (70,9%), que ainda não conseguem acessar todos os dados disponíveis. Considerando as preocupações relacionadas a cibersegurança e privacidade, 51% entendem que há desafios na área que precisam ser superados.

articles.title: Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal
articles.text:
Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.
Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.
More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn’t have critical vulnerabilities.
Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind’s Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.
“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.
The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

articles.title: Congress to call Jensen Huang in to answer for alleged Chinese spy affair | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Congress is gearing up to subpoena Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to answer their questions about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Bloomberg reports, citing two House Republicans.
The report comes a week after House Republicans Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford sent a letter to Huang asking him to appear before their committees for a joint, closed-door briefing in regards to his relations with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy.
House China committee Chairman Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that Huang has until the end of the day to respond to the request. If he doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed, said Moolenaar.
Mast, who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee, on Wednesday said his committee is preparing a subpoena for Huang to send if he doesn’t respond.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

articles.title: Elon Musk wants to build a s $24 billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Texas company town — massive 10 gigawatt site goes up for approval in December, but could face headwinds from new governor
articles.text:
Elon Musk wants to build a s $24 billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Texas company town — massive 10 gigawatt site goes up for approval in December, but could face headwinds from new governor
Building a data center in a company town could mean less resistance.
Starbase, Texas, which hosts SpaceX’s Starship rocket program, has just posted a notice of a public hearing for a gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility within the corporate limits of the city. The project has an initial cost of $24 billion and will apparently be owned by SpaceX. Bloomberg reports that the project could face resistance from incoming Texas governor Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned against approving new data centers until the state's legislature has enacted stronger protections against potential harms from those projects.
Until now, Elon Musk's SpaceXSI has been building out its Colossus I and Colossus II data centers near the Mississippi-Tennessee border, but those projects have faced backlash, attracting a lawsuit from area residents that aims to curb the pollutants produced by the large number of gas turbines required to power those facilities.
Now, it seems that SpaceXSI wants to build another site in Texas that would lie in a city that mostly sits on land owned by SpaceX and whose population mostly comprises its own employees. The project might face reduced local opposition compared to the company's Memphis facilities, as Starbase is essentially a company town for SpaceX. But Hinojosa's arrival in the governor's office could trump that seemingly permissible local regulatory climate.
The project would seem to be a part of SpaceX’s push to build 10 gigawatts of compute in 2027 alone, and the $24 billion budget for this new facility could make it one of the biggest and most expensive data center projects focused on a single site. The company's announcement also notes that the $24 billion outlay it foresees was only for the “initial phases of the projects” and that it could “include future expansions.” That suggests that SpaceXSI could invest in more capacity in Starbase, Texas, going forward, assuming the favorable regulatory climate the company likely hoped for in the area holds.
Beyond its new terrestrial ambitions in Starbase, SpaceX also remains hard at work on launching data centers into space. Musk has already laid out the plans for a first-generation AI1 compute satellite with a 150kW peak compute payload, and submitted a proposal to build a 1-million-satellite Orbital Data Center System to the FCC. That work could accelerate after data center measures lost big in the poll in the recent U.S. midterm elections. In a post-election post on X, Musk ventured that “data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

articles.title: Schlafanalyse: Wie eine Open-Source-KI deinen Schlaf auf die Sekunde genau auswertet
articles.text:
Schlafanalyse: Wie eine Open-Source-KI deinen Schlaf auf die Sekunde genau auswertet
Forschende der FH Aachen haben das KI-Modell AnySleep zur Schlafanalyse von Menschen entwickelt. Das Modell soll Schlafphasen besonders fein analysieren können, indem es schon kurze Veränderungen in der Gehirnaktivität erkennt. Die Forschungsergebnisse wurden kürzlich im Fachjournal npj Digital Medicine, das zum Nature Portfolio gehört, veröffentlicht. Künftig könnte das Werkzeug dabei helfen, Muster, die für bestimmte Krankheiten typisch sind, aufzuspüren.
KI-Modell zur Schlafanalyse
Bei Schlafanalysen wird die Gehirnaktivität meist per Elektroenzephalografie (EEG) aufgezeichnet. Für die Auswertung teilen Fachleute die Daten einer Nacht üblicherweise in 30-Sekunden-Abschnitte ein und ordnen jedem Abschnitt ein Schlafstadium zu. Das Ergebnis ist ein stufenförmiges Bild des Schlafverlaufs. Mit dem Modell AnySleep ist es laut den Forschenden nun möglich kürzere Intervalle abzubilden und entsprechend kürzeste Veränderungen der Gehirnaktivität im Schlaf festzustellen. Dafür verarbeitet das Modell die nächtlichen Messdaten und erstellt ein detailliertes Gesamtbild der verschiedenen Phasen des Nachtschlafes.
„Kurze Wachereignisse beispielsweise, die oft nur wenige Sekunden andauern, können in der Schlafforschung wichtige Hinweise liefern. Ist das Auswertungsintervall zu lang, werden diese Veränderungen nicht ausreichend berücksichtigt und das Ergebnis wird ungenau“, sagt Stephan Bialonski, Autor der Studie. Für das Training der KI griffen die Wissenschaftler:innen auf die Schlafdaten von etwa 20.000 Proband:innen zu. Deren Alter, Lebensumstände und Gesundheitszustand variierten laut der Forschenden stark.
Potenzial für die Medizin und Schlafforschung
Durch den genauen Einblick in die Schlafstadien sei es schon gelungen Unterschiede in den Schlafstrukturen von gesunden Menschen und Menschen mit Krankheiten zu erkennen. Der Studienautor Bialonski räumt jedoch ein, dass das KI-Verfahren noch nicht dazu geeignet sei, Krankheitsdiagnosen auszusprechen. „Aber AnySleep liefert bereits jetzt Hinweise auf bestimmte Krankheitsbilder und hilft uns, mehr über den Schlaf zu lernen“, sagt er. Nach Angaben der Forschenden wird das Projekt in Kooperation mit mehreren Kliniken fortgesetzt.
Open Source und lokale Installation
Der Quellcode von AnySleep ist öffentlich zugänglich und kann theoretisch auf jedem Rechner installiert werden. Zusätzlich bietet die FH Aachen die Browser-Oberfläche SomnoBot an, mit der sich das KI-Tool auch ohne Coding-Kenntnisse nutzen lassen soll. „Die sensiblen Daten verlassen dabei zu keinem Zeitpunkt den lokalen Computer, was die Arbeit auch im strengen klinischen Forschungsumfeld datenschutzsicher macht“, heißt es in der Pressemitteilung.

articles.title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
articles.text:
What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
Climate finance and fossil fuels top the formal agenda at COP31.
It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.
COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.
This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.
In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.
This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.
Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”
So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.
Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.)
The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).
Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.
Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.
One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there.
The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.
With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.
