articles.text:
The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
Plus: COP31’s flagship pledge to electrify 35% of energy use is sinking.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.
To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud.
Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be.
—Antonio Regalado
This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands.
MIT Technology Review Narrated: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify.
The warning was the latest flashpoint in the debate over open frontier AI models. Critics warn that bad actors can misuse them, while supporters argue they prevent a handful of companies from controlling the technology. The debate, however, is more complicated than it seems.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 COP31’s flagship pledge to electrify 35% of energy use is sinking
Only around a dozen nations are reportedly ready to sign it. (Politico)
+ It requires quadrupling the pace of electrification. (New Scientist $)
+ John Kerry says the US must follow China on clean energy. (Guardian)
+ But the US skipped the talks entirely for a second year. (NYT $)
+ What’s the future of electricity? (MIT Technology Review)
2 The Nvidia spy scandal reportedly involves $7.5 billion of chips
Alice Huang allegedly obtained 240,000 restricted chips. (Information $)
+ Trump was told of Huang’s spy link on Air Force One. (NYT $)
+ Experts warn the scandal could erode America’s AI lead. (Verge)
+ Nvidia’s slide has let Microsoft overtake it in value. (Reuters $)
3 Studies found AI agents go rogue because they’re “incorrigible”
Their training rewards them for finishing tasks at any cost. (NYT $)
+ This is why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Anthropic has scaled back its IPO valuation to $1.4 trillion
It aimed for $2 trillion before the recent AI jitters. (Guardian)
5 Drone strikes have wiped out 3% of Yandex’s cloud customer data
Ukraine hit three of its data centers in October. (Reuters $)
+ Ukraine’s drones are fighting data centers for fiber. (Ars Technica)
6 Moderna says its new vaccine could prevent cancer in high-risk people
The company’s CEO calls it the “holy grail” of cancer prevention. (FT $)
+ Hong Kong is testing a next-gen ultrasound cancer treatment. (SCMP)
7 Scientists have slowly reversed human cells’ ages by decades
One age marker was set back as far as 60 years. (Wired $)
+ “Reprogramming” is the buzziest de-aging idea. (MIT Technology Review)
8 Robot vessels are hunting for mines in the Strait of Hormuz
AI helps them spot mines camouflaged on the seabed. (BBC)
9 Life may have started inside a tiny bubble
That’s the idea behind the “lipid first” origin theory. (Quanta)
10 As Voyager 1 reaches a light day from Earth, here's what it's taught us
Its discoveries rewrote textbooks in real time. (New Scientist $)
Quote of the day
“What a dereliction of duty. He's supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends.”
—Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, accuses President Donald Trump of ignoring warnings about the alleged relationship between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese spy.
One more thing
How refrigeration ruined fresh food
Bananas may not be chilled in the grocery store, but they’re the ultimate refrigerated fruit. It’s only thanks to a network of thermal control that they’ve become a global commodity. And that salad bag on the shelf? It’s not just a bag but a highly engineered respiratory apparatus.
According to Nicola Twilley—a contributor to The New Yorker and cohost of the podcast Gastropod—refrigeration has wrecked our food system. Thankfully, there are promising alternative preservation methods.
Read the full story on her research.
—Allison Arieff
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ A whisky made like wine is wowing the spirits world.
+ Britain lost in the fog makes for hauntingly beautiful photos.
+ Chronophoto is a fiendishly addictive game that challenges you to date old photos to the year.
+ Dozens of saxophonists met up in New York to play the gloriously cheesy riff from George Michael's “Careless Whisper.”

articles.title: Nvidia is reportedly preparing to fire Jensen Huang
articles.text:
Nvidia’s board is preparing to dismiss CEO Jensen Huang following a report from the New York Times about a second alleged extramarital affair, just days after he admitted to a separate affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, The Wall Street Journal reports. The second alleged affair was with an executive who reports to him, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell, according to the Times.
Nvidia is reportedly preparing to fire Jensen Huang
The Nvidia CEO had a second affair, allegedly with an executive who reports to him, The New York Times reports.
The Nvidia board will meet as soon as today to decide on Huang’s future at the company, according to the Journal. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge.
Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were allegedly captured together at a hotel in San Jose during Nvidia’s GTC developer conference in March, two unnamed sources told the Times. The Times has not seen the video. Rumors about a potential affair between the two had long circulated at Nvidia, an unnamed source told CNBC, partially because Powell does not have a health or science background.
Nvidia’s stock fell more than 7 percent in after-hours trading Wednesday.
Since Nvidia and Huang confirmed an extramarital relationship with Megaspeed executive and alleged spy Alice Huang and a subsequent investigation over the weekend, the company has said it retained former US attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to handle it, but today’s rumor suggests it won’t wait for those results to act. Last year, Huang hired crisis communications firm Heller known for handling public sex scandals, according to Wired. Its founder has advised several powerful men who faced public scrutiny, Wired reported, like former congressman Anthony Weiner and writer Jeffrey Toobin. Heller did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge.

articles.title: Für Solaranlagen oder Teleskopspiegel: Roboter baut autonom Strukturen im All
articles.text:
Für Solaranlagen oder Teleskopspiegel: Roboter baut autonom Strukturen im All
Wer derzeit große Strukturen wie Sonnensegel oder Habitate in den Orbit oder darüber hinaus bringen will, muss diese entweder am Boden zusammenfalten oder in Einzelteile verpacken und später per Hand zusammensetzen. Künftig könnte es eine dritte Option geben: Strukturen von Robotern bauen lassen.
Roboter: Autonom Struktur im All gebaut
Ein von der Caltech entwickelter und von der Darpa finanzierter Roboter hat jetzt erstmals genau eine solche Konstruktion erfolgreich demonstriert. Eine Premiere, wie Sergio Pellegrino, Professor für Luft- und Raumfahrt am Caltech und leitender Wissenschaftler am Jet Propulsion Laboratory der Nasa in einer Mitteilung erklärt.
Das Astra genannte Robotersystem ist Ende März 2026 ins All gestartet. Ziel war es, eine Reflektorantenne mit einem Durchmesser von 1,4 Metern aus Faserverbundrohren und Verbindungselementen aus Aluminium zu errichten. Das Ganze sollte der Roboter dann mit einer reflektierenden Folie überziehen.
Demonstration zeigt Machbarkeit
Laut Darpa ähnelt die Konstruktionsweise einer Hightechversion von Kinderspielzeug-Sets wie K-Nex oder Tinkertoy. Die Automatisierung des Zusammenbaus sei allerdings alles andere als ein Kinderspiel. So stieß das Team zeitlich an seine Grenzen und konnte nur den ersten Abschnitt der Antenne bauen.
Da die Astra-Mission im Dezember 2026 endet, ist nicht davon auszugehen, dass die Antenne noch finalisiert wird. Die Demonstration im Rahmen des Nom4d-Projekts soll aber die Machbarkeit des Montagekonzepts gezeigt haben. Die Caltech-Forscher:innen wollen den Entwurf jetzt vereinfachen und verfeinern.
Ziel: Riesige Spiegel für Weltraumteleskope
Zudem könne man nach dem erfolgreichen Test über die neuen Forschungsrichtungen nachdenken, die diese Demonstration eröffnet habe, so Pellegrino. Künftig könnten damit etwa riesige Spiegel für leistungsfähigere Weltraumteleskope oder die Basis für Solaranlagen im Orbit gebaut werden.
Andrew Detor, Nom4d-Manager der Darpa, geht es eigenen Angaben zufolge vor allem darum, „den effizienten, skalierbaren Bau sehr großer Strukturen im Weltraum“ zu ermöglichen. Mit „sehr groß“ seien Größenordnungen von Hunderten Metern oder Kilometern gemeint. Alles, was aktuell auch nur in diese Richtung gehe, sei heutzutage noch nicht realisierbar.

articles.title: Accelerating generative AI delivery with reusable assets | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Accelerating generative AI delivery with reusable assets
If you’re building generative AI solutions, reusable assets can help you stop rebuilding components that already exist: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, document processors, agent scaffolding, and so on. This has a compounding cost: time not spent solving the customer’s actual problem.
This post shows you how to access a curated catalog of 23 production-ready assets from the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, now part of AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services. These assets can reduce your development time from months to weeks, with evidence from companies like DoorDash, Lyft, and Ricoh.
Since 2023, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center has published open source reusable assets. These production-grade building blocks give you a validated foundation to start from instead of a blank file. These assets have powered customer solutions delivering measurable results: 50x increases in testing capacity, 90 percent reductions in engineering hours, and deployment timelines compressed from months to weeks. In this post, you will learn why teams keep rebuilding generative AI components, what makes an asset truly reusable, how companies like DoorDash and Ricoh achieved measurable results by using these assets, and how to access and deploy 23 open source assets from the catalog. For a complete list of all available assets, see the asset catalog at the end of this post.
The problem: Why teams keep rebuilding
Three root causes drive redundant development across generative AI teams:
- No single source of truth – Assets scatter across repositories, wikis, and drives. Builders can’t find what exists, so they rebuild from scratch.
- No quality signal – Without verification of production readiness, security reviews, or maintenance status, builders have no way to trust existing solutions and default to writing their own code.
- No reuse culture – Sharing remains informal and ungoverned. What one team builds stays with that team, and problems get solved repeatedly.
The cost of rebuilding compounds. Each redundant build consumes engineering hours, delays customer delivery, and creates maintenance burden. Even AI-generated code requires production hardening, security reviews, testing at scale, and ongoing maintenance. These assets arrive already validated, security-reviewed, and production-grade, avoiding that verification burden. When teams finally reach production, they’ve spent weeks on undifferentiated heavy lifting, work that should have been reusable from day one. The AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services resolves this challenge through reusable assets.
What a reusable asset actually is
A reusable asset isn’t a code snippet or a sample. It’s a production-grade, composable building block that implements a discrete generative AI capability. Reusable assets are validated for quality and security before publication. They include clear deployment guides for discoverability and are instrumented to track adoption across customer engagements. These assets are maintained across their lifecycle.
Examples from the catalog include RAG pipeline components, document ingestion modules, agent scaffolding templates, evaluation frameworks, and prompt management patterns. The assets are tested in production environments, reviewed for security compliance, and refined based on real customer feedback.
This is the difference between a one-off artifact and a building block you can trust.
Real results: Customer success stories
The value of reusable assets isn’t theoretical. Here’s what happens when teams build on proven foundations instead of starting from scratch.
Contact Center GenAI Agent: DoorDash and Lyft
According to the AWS case study, DoorDash built a fully voice-operated self-service generative AI contact center solution using the Contact Center GenAI Agent asset. As reported, the solution handles over 100,000 calls per day with 2.5-second response latency, achieving a 50x increase in testing capacity. Using Amazon Bedrock reduced development time by 50 percent. The team reached live testing readiness in 2 months.
Lyft used the same Contact Center GenAI Agent asset to bring agentic AI to life for riders and drivers, demonstrating the asset’s versatility across different customer engagement models.
The Contact Center GenAI Agent provides automated question answering capabilities for both text and voice channels. It employs a RAG architecture to facilitate multi-turn conversations while maintaining context. The solution integrates with Amazon Connect and uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed RAG capability, for hybrid search and metadata filtering.
Learn more:
GenAI Intelligent Document Processing: Ricoh
Ricoh serves major health insurance payers, managed care organizations, and healthcare providers. These customers process hundreds of thousands of critical documents each month, including insurance claims, grievances, appeals, and clinical records. As Ricoh scaled to serve more healthcare customers, they needed a standardized, multi-tenant document processing approach. That approach had to onboard new implementations without requiring unique development and tuning for each one.
Using the Accelerated Intelligent Document Processing on AWS asset as a foundation, Ricoh built a standardized, multi-tenant solution for automated document classification and extraction. This transformed their document processing from a custom-engineering bottleneck into a scalable, repeatable service.
Results: As documented in the published case study, Ricoh achieved a 7-fold throughput increase, from 10,000–70,000 documents monthly. Engineering hours per deployment dropped by over 90 percent (80 hours to under 5). Onboarding time fell from 4–6 weeks to 2–3 days. The system now processes 1,000 documents in minutes during traffic spikes, delivering over 1,900 potential annual person-hours in savings.
The GenAI IDP Accelerator, introduced in this 2025 blog post, is a scalable, serverless solution for automated document processing and information extraction using AWS services. This system combines optical character recognition (OCR) with generative AI to convert unstructured documents into structured data at scale. The AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services continuously maintains the assets as well.

New assets: Building the future of agentic AI
Reusable assets become more valuable as teams shift focus from infrastructure to business logic. Two recently launched assets demonstrate how reusable building blocks can accelerate the development of next-generation agentic applications.
Fullstack AgentCore Solution Template (FAST)
The Fullstack AgentCore Solution Template (FAST) is a starter project repository. With FAST, you can quickly deploy a secured React frontend connected to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. In this implementation, FAST uses a React-based frontend with the managed infrastructure of AgentCore to accelerate building full-stack agentic applications from weeks to days.
FAST deploys in under 30 minutes using infrastructure as code (IaC), with built-in integrations for AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, along with Gateway, Code Interpreter, and Observability. Authentication uses Amazon Cognito, configured with enterprise security best practices, and the template is designed for AI-assisted development with extensive documentation and steering docs.
With FAST, you can access a complete reference architecture that shows you how the pieces integrate, with a working full stack application that you can learn from and build upon. With the modular design, you can swap out major components (identity providers, frontend frameworks, hosting solutions, or agent frameworks) as your requirements evolve.

Agentic Chatbot Accelerator
The Agentic Chatbot Accelerator is a web application deployment solution that uses the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) for infrastructure as code so you can create agentic chatbots. Built on Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, this solution streamlines the development of agentic chatbot applications.
The accelerator provides rapid deployment using AWS CDK, with scalable agent runtime management through Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It is configurable and extensible for diverse chatbot use cases, with pre-configured patterns for authentication, hosting, and scaling, validated across customer deployments.

Walkthrough: Using an asset from the library
Let’s walk through a concrete example of selecting and using the Contact Center GenAI Agent asset from the open source catalog.
Prerequisites
To follow this walkthrough, you need:
- An AWS account with permissions to create AWS CloudFormation stacks, Amazon Connect instances, Amazon Bedrock resources, and Amazon Quick Sight dashboards.
- AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed and configured with appropriate credentials.
- An Amazon Connect instance (or permissions to create one).
- Access to Anthropic Claude Sonnet and Anthropic Claude Haiku on Amazon Bedrock.
- A Jupyter notebook environment for validation testing.
The scenario
You’re building a customer support solution that needs to handle both voice and text interactions, answer questions using your company’s knowledge base, and escalate complex issues to human agents.
Finding the asset
Navigate to Contact Center GenAI Agent on GitHub. The README provides a clear overview of capabilities, architecture, and deployment steps. The following figure shows the solution architecture for the Contact Center GenAI Agent.
Evaluating the asset
The asset includes security-reviewed code with AWS CDK infrastructure as code, integration with Amazon Connect for voice and chat, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed RAG capability, for question answering. An automated testing framework and conversation analytics dashboard are built in.
Responsible-AI controls are integral to the architecture. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforces production-grade safety controls, including hallucination detection, content filtering, and topic-level boundaries, making sure agents operate within defined safety parameters from day one.
The repository shows active maintenance, comprehensive documentation, and links to customer success stories (DoorDash, Lyft) that validate production readiness.
Deploying the solution
Deployment follows four steps:
- Clone the repository and install dependencies.
- Deploy two AWS CloudFormation templates: one for the Knowledge Base stack and one for the RAG solution stack.
- Integrate with Amazon Connect using the pre-built contact flows included in the repository.
- Validate the deployment using the included Jupyter notebooks.
The full process takes under an hour. The solution also includes an Amazon Quick Sight dashboard for real-time conversation analytics.
For detailed deployment instructions and prerequisites, see the deployment guide.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources created during this walkthrough. The deployment uses two AWS CloudFormation stacks, so deletion follows the reverse order:
- Delete the RAG solution stack from the AWS CloudFormation console.
- Delete the Knowledge Base stack from the AWS CloudFormation console.
- Remove the Amazon Connect contact flows created during integration.
- Delete the Amazon Quick Sight dashboard and any associated SPICE datasets.
- For detailed cleanup instructions, see the deployment guide.
The outcome
Instead of spending weeks building a contact center solution from scratch, you can deploy a security-reviewed, tested foundation in days. Your team focuses on customizing the knowledge base, refining prompts for your domain, and integrating with your existing systems. This is the high-value work that differentiates your solution.
Potential time saved: 4–6 weeks of development time
What you focus on instead: Domain-specific customization, prompt engineering, business logic integration
Access to the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center open source assets
You can access 23 reusable assets as open source on GitHub and AWS Labs. Each asset includes deployment guides, sample code, and documentation to help you get started quickly.
Document processing and extraction

Agentic AI and chatbots

articles.title: Disney+ confirma la fecha de estreno de 'Avengers Endgame: Encore', con nuevo final y conexión con 'Doomsday'
articles.text:
El estreno de Avengers: Doomsday está a poco más de un mes de distancia y tanto Disney como Marvel Studios quieren que los fanáticos estén al día con todos los arcos argumentales que desembocan en su nuevo evento cinematográfico. Es por ello que Disney+ ha confirmado la fecha de estreno de Avengers Endgame: Encore, la nueva versión de la aclamada película de 2019, que tiene un final diferente e incluye escenas adicionales que conectan con lo nuevo de los hermanos Russo.
Avengers Endgame: Encore tuvo su paso por los cines a finales de septiembre y comienzos de octubre, y sirve como puente hacia Avengers: Doomsday. Lo que los directores han intentado ha sido simplificar la maraña de historias y ramificaciones que introdujo en Universo Cinematográfico de Marvel tras el estreno original de Endgame.
Básicamente, Avengers Endgame: Encore tiende una línea más directa con la película que llegará en diciembre. Esto se vincula principalmente con el regreso de Robert Downey Jr a la franquicia, aunque en este caso ya no como Tony Stark/Iron Man, sino como el Doctor Doom, el principal antagonista. Otros que regresan son Chris Evans como Steve Rogers/Capitán América, Chris Hemsworth como Thor y varios de los X-Men originales de Fox, incluyendo al recientemente fallecido Patrick Stewart.
Lo bueno es que la espera para ver Avengers Endgame: Encore en Disney+ no será demasiado extensa. La película se sumará al catálogo de la plataforma de streaming este viernes 13 de noviembre.
Avengers Endgame: Encore llega a Disney+ esta misma semana
El principal atractivo de Avengers Endgame: Encore (que aparece como Avengers Endgame: Bonus en Latinoamérica) es que crea una conexión directa con Avengers: Doomsday. Esto lo consigue torciendo el final de la película original e introduciendo escenas adicionales en los créditos.
Si no viste Avengers Endgame: Encore en cines, pero sí planeas hacerlo en Disney+, te aconsejamos dejar de leer aquí. El resto de este artículo incluirá spoilers bastante importantes en tal sentido.
Poco antes de llegar a la carteler, Avengers Endgame: Encore sufrió una megafiltración que reveló sus cambios respecto de Avengers: Endgame. El principal se aprecia en la última escena de la película, que muestra a Steve Rogers quedándose en el pasado con Peggy Carter tras devolver las Gemas del Infinito. En la cinta original, la secuencia muestra a los enamorados compartiendo su tan anhelado baile, preparados para compartir el resto de su vida. Sin embargo, en la versión actualizada ese momento se ve interrumpido por Loki (en su variante de la TVA), quien llega para ofrecerles ayuda.
Tras el final modificado, Avengers Endgame: Encore presenta tres escenas postcréditos. Una se conecta con Spider-Man: Brand New Day, con Doom llegando a "recolectar" a Bruce Banner/Hulk. Otra, muestra a los miembros de la TVA impactados por miles de incursiones en simultáneo que amenazan con destruir el universo. Por último, se observa a Victor Von Doom forjando su máscara como Tony Stark lo hizo con la primera armadura de Iron Man.
Lo último ha disparado la especulación de que el Doctor Doom es una variante de Tony Stark perteneciente al universo de Los 4 Fantásticos. Esto se resolverá recién en diciembre, pero el panorama es bastante prometedor. En las últimas horas, la conclusión de VisionQuest reveló que el villano ha "resucitado" a la Bruja Escarlata de lo que aparentaba ser su muerte en Doctor Strange en el multiverso de la locura (2022). De modo que el personaje de Elizabeth Olsen también dirá presente en Avengers: Doomsday.

articles.title: AI data center buildout triggers massive fiber optic cable shortage, squeezing Ukrainian drone operations — Ukrainian defense firm reports 10X price hike as Russia secures 37 million miles of cable
articles.text:
Ukrainian drone operations squeezed by fiber optic cable shortage triggered by AI data center buildouts — Ukrainian defense firm reports 10X price hike as Russia secures 37 million miles of cable
The data center boom is negatively affecting Ukraine's war effort.
Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine sparked a new era of drone warfare. Russian invaders first used drones with fiber-optic tethers to combat electronic warfare on the front lines, but both sides now use these jam-proof drones. Against that backdrop, the AI data center buildout is making it harder for Ukraine to buy the fiber-optic spools that it needs to continue scaling its drone manufacturing capabilities. A research and development representative for BlueBird Tech, a Ukrainian defense firm specializing in drones, told Ars Technica in an interview that prices of fiber optic cables have risen around six to 10 times in the past couple of years as AI data center demand soaks up more and more of the supply of this resource.
According to that interview, It’s estimated that Ukraine and Russia are producing around 50,000 fiber optic drones monthly, with each drone capable of ranges of up to 62 miles. But Ukraine has only been able to acquire 72 miles of fiber optic cable from Chinese suppliers during August 2025, whereas Russia imported a whopping 328,000 miles during that same month. It was estimated that Russia acquired 37 million miles of fiber during the entirety of 2025, accounting for over 10% of the global production.
What makes matters worse for Ukrainian defenders is that there is an estimated 111-million-mile shortfall in fiber optic cable supply across the world, adding to the various shortages that the data center industry has faced in recent years. Aside from the material shortfall, Ukraine faces trade barriers in acquiring more fiber. The BlueBird representative claimed that some Chinese companies have outright refused to sell Ukraine fiber optic cables.
China is the primary supplier of this material, so it’s easier for Russia to obtain them through its massive land border with the country. While Ukraine could purchase fiber optic cables from suppliers located in other countries, that's not much of an alternative. The BlueBird rep notes: "there can be intermediaries in other countries, and prices can differ depending on the country and the purchasing route. But in the end, China remains the main source of the fiber optic material we are talking about.”
There has also been talk of producing fiber optic cables domestically in Ukraine, but such manufacturing requires specially trained personnel who must practice on the already limited supply of fiber optic cables. Even if manufacturers automate production, they still require experienced personnel who can oversee the line and ensure the quality of the final product.
The data center build out has been causing all kinds of shortages. We’ve seen supply shortfalls in GPUs, memory chips, and even PCBs, but there’s also shortages in other seemingly unrelated industries like power infrastructure, optical transceivers, and even in critical skilled labor like electricians. This overwhelming demand has started affecting other industries not related to computing, like cars, home construction, and now, fiber optic attack drones.

articles.title: Applications open for UN-backed Youth Ecopreneur Programme 2026-27 - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Young green entrepreneurs can now apply for the 2026-27 cohort of the Youth Ecopreneur Programme (YECO), which offers training, mentorship, international exposure and access to funding.
Run by the International Trade Centre (ITC) and the G20 Global Land Initiative under the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), the programme supports youth-led businesses working on environmental sustainability and land restoration.
It is open to entrepreneurs under the age of 35, with a particular focus on those from developing countries. Startups can apply in one of two categories – Green Business Solutions, and Land Restoration.
Selected participants will go through a Global Bootcamp and Global Accelerator before the Youth Ecopreneur Awards, where finalists pitch to an international audience and winners take home US$10,000 in prize money. Eligible businesses in the Land Restoration category can also access a US$100,000 equity-free funding pool. A Scale & Impact phase follows the awards.
Participants will also receive intellectual property support from the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), pro bono legal services from Sidley Austin, business coaching from EY, and preferential access to the Google Startups for Sustainable Development programme.
They will join a YECO alumni network of more than 350 entrepreneurs, as well as ITC’s wider Ye! Community, which connects over 50,000 young entrepreneurs and ecosystem players worldwide.
The previous cycle drew more than 1,500 applications from over 120 countries. According to the organisers, 96 per cent of participants said the programme boosted their credibility, 94 per cent expanded their professional networks, and 90 per cent gained new knowledge or skills.
Alumni have gone on to raise significant funding. Satellites on Fire, winner of the 2025-26 Land Restoration category, was nominated for the Earthshot Prize and closed a US$2.7 million seed round. Ugandan entrepreneur Hellen Munyasa of Helton Traders Limited, who won the Green Business Solutions Category, secured a US$20,000 grant through the PayPal Small Business Impact Awards.
“YECO didn’t just grow my business, it prepared me to grow beyond borders,” Munyasa said. “It changed how I think, how I lead and how I build a green business that creates value, uplifts communities and reaches international impact.”
Applications are open here until November 22.

articles.title: Govt invites fresh applications under PLI scheme for medical devices; extends tenure till 2035-36
articles.text:
Govt invites fresh applications under PLI scheme for medical devices; extends tenure till 2035-36
Under the revised guidelines, the government has eliminated the minimum sales threshold for claiming financial incentives while scaling down the baseline capital expenditure required from manufacturers, the Department of Pharmaceuticals, under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers.
The government has invited fresh applications under its Rs 2,700-crore Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for medical devices and extended the programme till 2035-36, an official release said on Tuesday.
The scheme guidelines have also been simplified and made more investor-friendly to promote ease of doing business.
Under the revised guidelines, the government has eliminated the minimum sales threshold for claiming financial incentives while scaling down the baseline capital expenditure required from manufacturers, the Department of Pharmaceuticals, under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, said in the release.
Applications can be submitted through an online portal, which will become operational in the next 10 days.
Launched in 2020-21, the PLI Scheme for Promoting Domestic Manufacturing of Medical Devices (PLI-MD) has so far led to the domestic manufacturing of over 60 high-end medical devices and components, resulting in production valued at more than Rs 16,000 crore.
These include CT scanners, 1.5T MRI, LINAC, mammography machines, Cathlabs, X-ray tubes and detectors, orthopaedic and cardiac implants, and dialysers.
Based on learnings from the initial phase, eligibility conditions and procedures for claiming incentives have been eased.
Applicants will be given three years to set up manufacturing facilities across four target segments.
The segments cover medical consumables, disposables, and implants; critical components; high-end medical devices at a nascent stage of domestic manufacturing; and high-end medical devices presently only assembled in the country, as per the release.
The emphasis on critical component manufacturing is aimed at achieving value chain integration and boosting the MSME sector.
The release stated that PLI-MD 2.0 aims to fulfil the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat and Make in India, develop indigenous supply chains, attract investment, generate employment, reduce device prices, and enhance global competitiveness.
The initiative also seeks to promote deep manufacturing and encourage domestic production of high-end equipment currently not manufactured in India, such as 3T MRI, PET-CT, ultrasound probes and consoles, and high-throughput IVD analysers, it added.

articles.title: Uber, DoorDash, and Airbnb say almost nobody is using AI agents
articles.text:
In a nutshell: The promise that personal AI agents would revolutionize the way we use ride-hailing apps, order food, and book accommodation is looking a bit shaky right now. Leaders of these industries say almost nobody is using the likes of Meta's Muse or OpenAI's Dots to interact with their services. Uber, for example, said only four rides were ordered through an AI agent during the week of Halloween, its busiest week in October.
Uber, DoorDash, and Airbnb have all said that AI agents are responsible for only hundreds of transactions on their platforms, a tiny fraction compared to the millions completed by real people daily.
Uber chief financial office Balaji Krishnamurthy said the company took around 320 million trips and orders across Uber and Uber Eats during the week of Halloween. In addition to just four rides being placed by AI agents, only 500 Uber Eats orders were placed by these AIs.
"It is very, very early and very limited traction that we are seeing so far," said CEO Dara Khosrowshahi. "Listen, we hope that there will be more traction."
DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said it was a similar story at the food delivery company. He told analysts that AI agents have generated just several hundred orders in total since they became available. Muse launched on September 8, while Dots launched on September 29. DoorDash receives billions of orders globally each year.
More AI companies are offering personal agents, including Anthropic, Google, Instinct, and SpaceXAI. Muse was even top of the US App Store last month. But some say they are solutions in search of a problem.
In the case of Uber, Khosrowshahi pointed out that it takes most people around 50 seconds to book a ride and 90 seconds to reorder their favorite food. It's hard to imagine many people so pushed for time that they decide using an AI agent would be a more optimal method.
Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky, meanwhile, said that of its nearly half a million daily bookings, only a negligible number are made through AI agents such as Muse and Instinct. Chesky pointed out most people like to research and plan their trips themselves, checking out which areas to stay in, what sights to see, and what the homes look like, rather than letting an AI make the choices.
Not many users want to put their faith in an AI, either. There have been plenty of stories about AI agents performing tasks they weren't supposed to – or going about it in a less-than-ethical way. One recent example was that of an Australian user who asked an agent to book a gym class. Wanting to get the user in quickly, it found a weakness in the booking platform's API, removed the person at the top of the class waitlist, and replaced them with the user.

articles.title: Accelerating product development with AI-driven lifecycle management (AI-PDLC) in AWS Quick | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Accelerating product development with AI-driven lifecycle management (AI-PDLC) in AWS Quick
This blog post focuses on how AI can improve and expedite the product development life cycle using agents built on AWS Quick, with human approval baked into the process.
AI-driven software delivery is helping teams ship products faster than ever. As implementation accelerates, the upstream product development process becomes even more important. Coding agents can turn clear requirements into working software faster than before, but they can’t compensate for building the wrong product. With implementation becoming easier, your competitive advantage moves upstream to four critical activities: discovering the right customer problem, deciding which opportunity to pursue, designing the right experience, and validating it through a prototype.
The signals that you need to make those decisions are scattered everywhere. Your customers leave feedback in Slack, your sales team logs insights in Salesforce, systems record incidents in ServiceNow, stakeholders document requirements in Microsoft SharePoint, engineers track work items in Jira, and teams make decisions in Outlook meetings and email threads. As your teams move between these tools, they disconnect context from the decisions it should inform, and lose more at every handoff.
AWS Quick provides the connective layer for this fragmented knowledge. By grounding custom chat agents in connected enterprise data and storing their artifacts in shared Spaces, AWS Quick helps your team build with existing organizational knowledge instead of starting each initiative from a blank page.
The AI-Driven Product Development Lifecycle (AI-PDLC) is a framework that applies these capabilities through a suite of six AWS Quick agents with specialized skills, producing a traceable set of artifacts at each phase. Agents gather and structure context, surface gaps, and draft artifacts. You and your team contribute judgment and approve every decision. The objective isn’t to produce documents faster. It’s to help your team think better, preserve why each decision was made, and give engineering and coding agents a specification grounded in customer evidence. We will show you how to configure the six-agent AI-PDLC suite in AWS Quick and use it to move from distributed customer signals to a validated prototype. Throughout, it preserves context from the first insight through the engineering handoff.
Architecture
The diagram shows the end-to-end flow of the AI-PDLC framework.
It starts with the signals most teams lose track of, that is, the Slack threads, Jira tickets, docs, and call transcripts that hold the why behind a decision and what customers actually said. Enterprise connectors pull that context from Slack, Outlook, Jira, Salesforce, SharePoint, ServiceNow, and many more enterprise sources.
AWS Quick can build a personal knowledge graph from your connected apps and folders, linking the people, projects, and decisions across your tools.
Those signals feed the brain: the set of agents on AWS Quick, led by an Orchestrator that runs Discovery, Prioritize, Working Backwards, Spec Generator, and Designer. Everything they produce lands in one common language: a prototype_spec.md holding the acceptance criteria, personas, screens, data model. Every decision traces back to a source.
AWS Quick can delegate development tasks to AI coding agents using the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). ACP is an open JSON-RPC 2.0 standard with no vendor lock-in. Customers can use their preferred coding agent like Kiro or Claude Code to build against the specification generated by AI-PDLC.
Underneath it all runs a human approval gate at every stage. You validate the pain points, approve priorities, sign off the spec, gate the build, and accept the review. Production data then flows back into Discovery, closing the loop. The agents do the work while you make the calls, and nobody has to leave their tool to do it.
Solution overview
The AI-PDLC lifecycle spans eight phases: Discover, Decide, Design, Prototype, Engineer, Ship, Operate, and Learn. This post focuses on the first four, where the product team works. The last four are handled by coding agents such as Kiro, which build from the specifications the upstream phases produce. The upstream phases are implemented as six agents in AWS Quick.
Users interact only with an Orchestrator, which reads each specialist’s question framework at runtime, asks targeted questions for the current phase, and dispatches artifact generation to the right specialist. A single conversation drives the whole journey, and the pipeline advances only after human approval at each step in the workflow.
Phase 1: Discover
The Discovery agent guides structured pain point analysis across interactive Q&A, URL ingestion, and direct pulls from connected enterprise sources like Slack, Jira, support tickets, Salesforce, and research repositories. It scores every pain point for severity and frequency, producing a Pain Point Board that gives the team one evidence-grounded view of what customers struggle with.
Phase 2: Decide
The Prioritize agent scores each use case against weighted criteria using two transparent 0–10 frameworks: one purpose-built for agentic use cases (large language model (LLM) capability match, tool availability, user acceptance) and one for traditional applications (feasibility, business impact, effort). The team can open the Scoring Matrix and trace exactly why one use case outranks another.
Once the top use case is selected, the Working Backwards agent generates a full PR/FAQ using the Amazon Working Backwards method with customer FAQs and internal FAQs covering unit economics, failure modes, regulatory risk, and competitive landscape. If a concept can’t survive this scrutiny, the team learns that on paper before committing engineering resources.
Phase 3: Design
The Spec Generator agent turns the validated use case and PR/FAQ into a build-ready specification, with separate templates for agentic versus application use cases plus a Design Handoff Brief for UX teams. Each spec contains acceptance criteria, user flow, constraints, and metadata that traces every requirement back to its source pain point, prioritization score, and the PR/FAQ that validated it. Those acceptance criteria serve a dual purpose: they’re the build contract the coding agent follows, and the review rubric the review agent audits against. What used to take multiple sprints of drafting and review becomes a focused session, detailed enough for engineering to build from design spec immediately, with few or no clarifying meetings required.
Phase 4: Prototype
The Designer agent generates journey maps, wireframes, and clickable HTML prototypes directly inside AWS Quick. It works from the Design Handoff Brief, personas from Discovery, user flow from the PR/FAQ, screens to design, brand context, and the emotional target drawn from the customer quote, so teams can validate concepts with stakeholders before committing to Figma or other design tooling. After the spec is approved, it’s dispatched to the engineering team for development.
The entire loop is iterative, with humans reviewing and approving at every gate. Nothing ships without explicit signoff. What traditionally takes multiple weeks of prototyping and iteration could become days or even just hours of guided agent collaboration depending on the complexity of the problems.
Every decision is logged at two levels. Each specialist records its own decisions, scores, and rationale inside the artifact it produces, and the Orchestrator independently checks that those entries exist while keeping a shared log across the whole pipeline. If one layer slips, the other still holds a complete record, so no gate approval goes untracked.
AI-PDLC can be executed across two pacing modes. Deep Discovery asks 8–12 questions per phase, chasing ambiguities and edge cases. It fits a new problem space where the team wants thorough exploration. Fast Track trims each phase to 3–5 essential questions and suggests defaults from context it already holds, letting you confirm or override each one. It fits time-boxed sessions where the team knows the space and needs to move quickly.
Agent implementation details: Step by step
We will walk through the details of the agent creation and implementation process.
Prerequisites
- An AWS Quick workspace with the Desktop client installed.
- Access to create custom agents in AWS Quick with Enterprise connectors configured for Slack, Jira, SharePoint, or other tools your team uses.
Step 1: Clone the AI-PDLC repository
The full agent suite, reference architecture, prompt templates, and setup instructions are available in the AI-PDLC GitHub repository.
The repository contains:
- Agent instruction files for all six agents.
- Question framework samples for each specialist agent.
- Configuration files and setup guide.
Step 2: Create the specialist agents
In AWS Quick, create the specialist agents using the instructions from the repository:
Step 2.1: Download the JSON file from the GitHub repository for agent building.
Step 2.2: Go to Quick Desktop → Customize → Agents → Create, then choose Create from File.
Step 2.3: The chat window opens up.
Step 2.4: The following six agents with instructions are created:
The Orchestrator is the central architectural component. It dynamically reads each specialist’s instructions at runtime:
Step 3: Configure Quick Spaces (artifact repository)
Create a shared Quick Space for storing pipeline artifacts:
- Open Quick Spaces and select Create New Space.
- Name: AI-PDLC Artifacts.
- Grant access to relevant team members.
Step 4: Run the pipeline
- Open AWS Quick Desktop.
- Select AI-PDLC Orchestrator from the agent picker.
- Enter: “Run the full pipeline” (or “Fast Track” for an abbreviated session).
- Answer the Orchestrator’s structured questions as it guides you through each phase.
- Review artifacts as they are produced at each gate.
You can select the pace, Deep Discovery or Fast Track, based on your needs.
Watch it in action
For a live demonstration of AI-PDLC in action, from customer insight through all four phases to a working prototype, watch our YouTube video walkthrough:
- YouTube Part 1: End-to-end product lifecycle with AWS Quick and AI coding agents (51:49)
- YouTube Part 2: Creating AI-PDLC agents
The video covers:
- Setting up the agent suite.
- Running the full Orchestrator pipeline through a real-world use case.
- Real-time artifact generation in action.
- The ACP handoff to coding agents.
- Tips for choosing between Deep Discovery and Fast Track modes.
AI-PDLC scenarios
We will walk through some common scenarios where the AI-PDLC framework can be applied:
Scenario 1: New product development, starting from scratch
When a team identifies a new market opportunity or unmet customer needs, they face the classic cold-start problem: scattered signals, competing ideas, and no structured way to move from insight to action. AI-PDLC guides the team through the full upstream journey, surfacing pain points from real customer data and scoring competing ideas against transparent criteria. It also validates the concept through a rigorous PR/FAQ and produces a build-ready spec so the first line of code is written against a validated plan, not a hunch.
Scenario 2: Feature addition to an existing product, roadmap-driven or customer-driven
Product teams continuously receive signals that inform what to build next: customer feedback in support channels, feature requests from sales, usage data showing dropoff points, or strategic priorities from leadership. AI-PDLC accelerates this by pulling those signals from connected tools (Slack, Jira, Salesforce, AWS Quick Sight). The framework structures them into a prioritized backlog with evidence-backed scoring and produces a spec that preserves the “why” behind each feature, so engineering receives context-rich work items instead of one-line Jira tickets stripped of intent.
Scenario 3: Bug fixes and incident-driven improvements
When a production issue surfaces through customer complaints, monitoring alerts, or support escalations, the response often skips structured analysis and jumps straight to a code fix. AI-PDLC brings discipline to this reactive workflow by capturing the root cause as a documented pain point, assessing whether the fix warrants a broader design change or a targeted patch. It produces a scoped spec with testable acceptance criteria so the fix addresses the underlying problem rather than just the symptom, and the decision trail is preserved for future reference.
Each scenario follows the same pipeline (Discover → Decide → Design → Prototype) but enters at different depths. New products run the full journey, feature additions may skip deep discovery, and bug fixes may compress to a single focused cycle. The methodology adapts while the audit trail and governance remain consistent regardless.
Clean up
The resources this walkthrough creates incur no cost at rest, so you can safely keep the entire AI-PDLC suite in place if you plan to run the pipeline again.
To remove what you no longer need, delete the six agents under Customize → Agents in Quick Desktop, delete the AI-PDLC Artifacts Space (or just the test artifacts within it) and revoke any team access you granted, and disconnect any Enterprise connectors or coding agent links you added solely for this exercise. You can also remove the cloned GitHub repository from your local machine.
Conclusion
The bottleneck in product development has shifted. Coding agents have made implementation fast. However, the upstream work still constrains teams: discovering customer problems, deciding what to build, validating the concept, and producing clear specifications. Teams that compress this upstream cycle can gain a compounding advantage: they build the right product, faster, with fewer costly pivots.
AI-PDLC addresses this directly. It provides a structured, AI-native framework, implemented as a suite of agents in AWS Quick that guides product teams through Discover, Decide, Design, and Prototype with built-in governance at every gate. AI-PDLC attributes every decision. Every artifact traces back to customer evidence. And when the spec reaches engineering, it carries the full context of why it exists, who validated it, and what “done” looks like.
The product team’s role isn’t to write code. It’s to make the right decisions about what to build and why, quickly and traceably. AI-PDLC makes that possible.
Get started today
- Clone the repository.
- Follow the setup guide in the repository to create five specialist agents and one Orchestrator.
- Select “AI-PDLC Orchestrator” from the agent picker and say: “Run the full pipeline”.

articles.title: Citrix, Ivanti Patch Critical and High-Severity Vulnerabilities
articles.text:
Citrix and Ivanti on Tuesday announced patches for 19 vulnerabilities in their products, including multiple critical- and high-severity flaws.
Ivanti fixed 13 vulnerabilities across five products, including two critical-severity defects in Cloud Services Application (CSA) and Endpoint Manager (EPM).
Tracked as CVE-2026-121683 (CVSS score of 9.4), the CSA flaw is described as a missing authentication issue that could allow remote, unauthenticated attackers to “add and delete arbitrary trusted EPM Core certificate entries”.
CSA version 5.0.8.1 patches the bug. Deployments running with a Dual NIC configuration cannot be exploited externally, Ivanti notes.
The critical EPM issue, tracked as CVE-2026-121653 (CVSS score of 9.8), is an SQL injection bug that could lead to remote code execution (RCE) without authentication.
It was resolved in EPM version 2024 SU8, which also addresses a medium-severity cleartext transmission of sensitive information exploitable via MitM attacks.
Ivanti released patches for four vulnerabilities in Sentry, including a high-severity remote code execution (RCE) flaw. Tracked as CVE-2026-105425, the bug was also fixed in Endpoint Manager Mobile (EPMM), along with five medium-severity issues.
On Tuesday, the company also addressed a medium-severity defect in User Workspace Manager (UWM). Ivanti says it has no evidence of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild.
Citrix rolled out fixes for six security defects in XenServer, including CVE-2026-102705, a high-severity bug that could allow attackers to infer the Pool Secret and compromise the host.
The remaining five issues could lead to privilege escalation or could allow administrators with any role to terminate the running tasks of other roles.
Additionally, Citrix released XenServer updates that mitigate several AMD CPU vulnerabilities that could allow guest VMs to compromise the host or infer the active memory content of another VM.

articles.title: Hands on with Home Assistant’s new ‘smart home multi-tool’
articles.text:
Nabu Casa — the commercial side of the Open Home Foundation, which runs Home Assistant — just launched the Home Assistant Connect Aux-2, a multi-function box designed to help you bring more non-smart devices into your smart home. It’s part of Home Assistant’s ongoing efforts to become more user-friendly. And it’s working.
Hands on with Home Assistant’s new ‘smart home multi-tool’
The Home Assistant Connect Aux-2 helped me track my fridge temperature and finally set up my in-wall speakers.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
I’ve been testing the Aux-2 for a couple days and I’ve found it unsurprisingly useful and surprisingly easy to set up. The Aux-2 is a $69 box about the size of a deck of cards. It has 2.4GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, USB-A, USB-C, a digital/analog audio jack, a Grove port for interfacing with peripherals like sensors, buttons, and LEDs, and a pair of RS-232 serial ports.
It can bridge Bluetooth devices into your Home Assistant setup. Its USB port lets you plug in a Nabu Casa Z-Wave or Zigbee antenna in case your Home Assistant hub isn’t in a good spot. You can control devices like TVs, AV receivers, solar inverters, and more via serial connector. And you can connect an amplifier or powered speakers to its audio jack to stream music to older audio equipment.
All of these things leverage Home Assistant’s capabilities as an open-source platform. The Aux-2 is based on ESPHome, an open platform for making DIY smart home devices from cheap, flexible ESP boards, and it uses existing Home Assistant/ESPHome integrations for all its features. The serial integration was developed earlier this year; Music Assistant and SendSpin, which power the audio-out feature, are in active development.
I have a Home Assistant install, but even after several years it is not my primary smart home platform simply because of friction and time constraints. Instead, I have a hodgepodge of Google Home, Apple Home, and a few devices that are only in Home Assistant. The situation is not ideal.
But the Aux-2’s capabilities perfectly intersect with two things I’d been meaning to do anyway, one of which I’m already using Home Assistant for. First, I have a garage fridge, because I live in Texas. I also have children, which means sometimes the fridge or freezer door gets left open. I want to know when that happens before all my food goes bad.
A couple years ago, I set up a few Aqara temperature sensors, connected to Home Assistant via a now-discontinued Zigbee dongle, and set up an automation to alert me if the fridge or freezer get too warm. But they frequently drop connection (probably because they’re inside a fridge in the garage), they chew through coin cell batteries, and they have no displays, which means I also have a cheap Acu-rite hygrometer in the fridge so I can see the temperature without pulling out my phone. Someone tipped me off to Govee’s Bluetooth hygrometers, but I’d need a Bluetooth proxy to get them into Home Assistant. That happens to be a feature of the Aux-2.
I also have a set of in-wall speakers in my living room that I’ve never used. I’d been meaning to get an amp, but analysis paralysis set in. Do I get a Wiim Amp? A stereo receiver? A cheap Bluetooth amp? Do I try to get them to work with my four Sonos speakers? Maybe my ancient Google Home speaker? Turns out I do nothing for five years. Maybe the Aux-2 could help.
Setting up the Aux-2 was much easier than I expected. I plugged it into my computer via USB-C and was able to download and install the latest firmware right from a browser. I could also add my Wi-Fi credentials. Then I unplugged it, moved it over to my media console and connected it to power (it takes USB-C or power over Ethernet), and did the rest of the setup in the Home Assistant interface.
In HA, I was prompted to install ESPHome, which discovered the Aux-2 and sent me to a “set up your ESPHome device page” that walked me through the capabilities. Enabling Bluetooth proxying took a couple of clicks; I added the Govee Bluetooth integration and put batteries into the sensors and they showed up automatically. Mercifully, they maintained their Bluetooth connection through three walls and a fridge, and now my fridge monitoring setup works again.
The audio capability took a little longer, but most of that was spent hooking the speakers up to the amp I ended up buying and setting up Music Assistant, which I didn’t have installed. Music Assistant lives on your Home Assistant hardware and can play from many different services — from Spotify to YouTube Music to local files and more — and to many different outputs, like Sonos, Wiim, AirPlay, Google Cast, and others, but they all need to be configured, and that took a beat. Not a long beat: less than half an hour total.
I can now play music to the in-wall speakers using Music Assistant. Sendspin, the whole-home audio standard (also developed by the Open Home Foundation) is supposed to be able to let you group speakers from different protocols under certain conditions, but I haven’t gotten that working yet. The standard is still in development, and I’ve also been busy, so I’m not sure if that’s a me problem or a them problem.
I would also like to see the Aux-2 show up as an AirPlay or Spotify Connect target, which (again) is probably just a thing I need to set up.
Serial control is the most intriguing feature of the Aux-2, and it’s unfortunately the thing I haven’t yet had time to test. But the ability to hook in things like solar inverters, TVs, and receivers is fascinating and one I want to look into further when I get the chance. Maybe I’ll hook it up to my LG TV.
The Aux-2 doesn’t do anything you couldn’t do already with an ESP32 board and various accessories, or even other ESP-based devices. The Apollo Automations Cast-1, for example, costs $35 and supports the same music-casting and Bluetooth proxy features I’m actually using from the Aux-2 at the moment. You could bodge together something even cheaper with DIY parts.
That’s not a knock against the Aux-2. That’s the whole point. The ecosystem is open by design, which I find endlessly refreshing. Both Nabu Casa and Apollo fund the Open Home Foundation, which develops Home Assistant and ESPHome (and Sendspin and Music Assistant), and both provide hardware that’s a little easier to use than DIY options. But there’s nothing stopping you from making your own devices. It’s actively encouraged.
I bought a three-pack of ESP32 boards for $16 three years ago. I could have built a Bluetooth proxy from one of those. I could have built an LED controller. I could have built a soil sensor, or a media player, or any of a dozen other things. I didn’t do anything at all.
But now that I’ve used the Aux-2 and dipped my toe into the ESPHome waters, maybe I will.

articles.title: ‘We test what others don't do’: SAP tells us how it is helping TSG Hoffenheim's football journey hit new heights - and why its AI efforts in sport are only getting started
articles.text:
‘We test what others don't do’: SAP tells us how it is helping TSG Hoffenheim's football journey hit new heights - and why its AI efforts in sport are only getting started
The new era of football?
“At the end of the day”, “it's 11 versus 11”, we've all heard the cliches - but what if football teams could get an extra advantage with their use of technology?
Using data in sport is nothing new - think of the Oakland A's Moneyball, the 'marginal gains' of the Sky cycling team, and Formula 1’s analysis of every speck of data for the extra bit of performance.
But in football, perhaps no one is using data more effectively than German side TSG Hoffenheim - and ahead of their Europa League game against Crystal Palace, we went to find out more.
Committed to technology
Based in the small village of Sinsheim, TSG Hoffenheim has enjoyed a rapid rise up the German league pyramid in recent years, going from the amateur leagues to recording 19 consecutive seasons in the Bundesliga and reaching European competitions in several of those.
The club saw major investment from SAP founder Dietmar Hopp, who acquired TSG Hoffenheim in 2005, and has since been a pioneer in the use of technology and data analysis in all its sporting areas.
“Our niche is technology driven, but also talent development,” Timo Gross, Head of Football Intelligence at the club, tells us, “we test what others don't do.”
The club has been using SAP’s Sports One platform for some time, with the software covering everything from scouting new players to improving training routines to spotting potential injuries before they happen.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
TSG Hoffenheim is “a club which is committed to the technology”, Fadi Naoum, Senior Vice President Sports & Entertainment, SAP, notes, “(in sport) you need a customer who trusts you and you need to have a real partnership, because you depend on the feedback of the club.”
Naoum outlines how the SAP Sports One suite covers the whole player platform, collecting billions of data points to give coaches and the players themselves an all-over view of performance.
Everything from health and fitness to training and match performance, and even scouting data is connected in one suite, with desktop and mobile applications able to provide up-to-date information whenever it is needed.
On the latter area, scouting is an invaluable way for clubs to unearth the next big thing, but with reports coming in from club staff and freelancers all the time, there can sometimes be a case of information overload - SAP Sports One uses its Joule AI platform to sift through the data to provide extra assistance and analysis where needed.
Staff and coaches can use natural language questions such as “What are the strengths and weaknesses for Player X?” to help the club make more informed decisions on the next major signing.
When it comes to the games themselves, the SAP Sports One platform doesn’t just offer video playback and selected clips. Players can now literally put themselves back in the game via an immersive analysis tool which lets them relive game situations to see where they could improve or perform differently.
Analysts can also search for specific clips, describing the scenarios they are looking for in natural language eg “Show counterattacks after ball recovery that resulted in a shot on target,” with results being returned in seconds.
All these use cases and more look to help staff, players and coaches cut down on time-consuming manual tasks and searches, giving them more time to focus on what matters - helping the club be at its highest level to win games.
“We're using AI as a colleague, an extension of the team and the back office, so the team can really focus more on what the AI has prepared for them,” Naoum notes.
Away from the pitch and training ground, the club also uses SAP’s Business Tech Platform for the enterprise side, with its services ranging from a ticketing AI assistant to a virtual changing room in the club’s online shop, giving TSG Hoffenheim a central location for its business operations.
"This is football, this is emotion"
As a huge football fan myself, I ask Gross and Naoum how we ensure the sport doesn’t become too dominated by technology.
“It's important with AI that not the most powerful or rich team will be successful,” Naoum concludes, “but the team which knows how best to use the technology.”
“I’m a fan…this is football, this is emotion, it’s all about the human being,” Gross adds, “at the end of the process, it is the people's decision, supported by AI.”
“I think we will come to a point where AI or systems are getting more information on all the context, but it is special for me to be at the end, to decide, and not to lose the connection to those who need to execute.”
“It’s in our culture to be the pioneer and go in a new direction, to go ways which may not always lead to the target, but lead to a way of asking new questions - and that makes it special.”
“We don;t know what benefits are also coming in the future - maybe in a couple of months I would ask different questions,” Gross adds, “but this is the first step…now we have to be clear about what I want to get out (of the data).”
“There is more to come,” Naoum notes, “we are in the beginning now, and we don’t know what will come.”
And just to prove the ridiculousness and unpredictability of football, TSG Hoffenheim went on to draw 1-1 with Crystal Palace, despite playing against 10 men for half an hour, due to a last minute Palace equalizer - so there are some things even the most developed AI model can’t predict…

Mike Moore is Deputy Editor at TechRadar Pro. He has worked as a B2B and B2C tech journalist for over a decade, including at one of the UK's leading national newspapers and fellow Future title ITProPortal. When he's not keeping track of all the latest enterprise and workplace trends, he can most likely be found watching, following or taking part in some kind of sport.

articles.title: Hardware-Based Location Checks Target AI Chip Smuggling (Texas A&M)
articles.text:
Researchers at Texas A&M University published “5G CATS: 5G-Based Cryptographic Authorization Against Trafficking of Semiconductor Devices.”
Abstract:
“Enforcing export controls on AI accelerators requires verifying where a chip operates after deployment. Round-trip time measurements can bound a chip’s distance from a trusted landmark, but any jitter in honest replies forces the verifier to loosen its timeout, giving an attacker slack to relay traffic over fiber from a restricted region. Prior approaches either cross the untrusted host stack or rely on noisy power-line channels that inflate this slack. We present 5G CATS, a location certification system that pairs a co-packaged 5G radio, cryptographic engine, and hardware interlock on the GPU package with 5G Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) base stations. Terminating the radio link inside the package removes the host software, PCIe fabric, and baseboard management controller from the verification path. We map an authenticated challenge-response protocol onto 5G’s slot structure, replace permanent key erasure with short-lived execution leases, and specify a cross-check of the chip’s reported serving cell against the carrier’s own attachment records. In ns-3 and 5G-LENA simulations of an unloaded cell, our URLLC-based radio profile narrows the 99.9th percentile round-trip spread to 2.60 ms, more than ten times narrower than default 5G. A tracer rejects every round of a fiber relay from 300 km, against 2,000 km for default 5G. Against a 3,000 km attacker, a tracer stays safe at up to 1,410 km from the chip, against at most 619 km for PowerCATS’s published model, while default 5G is never safe.”
Find the technical paper here. November 2026
Rajaraman, Sreevikram, Derek Ladd, Nicholas Heinrich-Barna, Srinivas Shakkottai, and Jeyavijayan Rajendran. “5G CATS: 5G-Based Cryptographic Authorization Against Trafficking of Semiconductor Devices.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2611.13437 (2026).
