articles.title: Une platine Blu-ray 4K à 2 000 € offre-t-elle vraiment une meilleure image qu'un modèle à 200 € ?
articles.text:
Alors que Sony abandonne son dernier lecteur Blu-ray 4K au Japon, Magnetar vient de faire certifier THX deux platines affichées jusqu'à près de 3 800 euros. Mais à l'heure où un lecteur à 200 euros suffit déjà pour profiter des disques UHD, que gagne-t-on vraiment à dépenser autant ?
Le 22 octobre, nous apprenions que Sony mettait fin aux expéditions de son dernier lecteur Blu-ray 4K au Japon, l'UBP-X700/K. Une décision qui intervient après les retraits de Samsung en 2019 et de LG en 2024. Si Sony n'a annoncé aucun arrêt mondial, Panasonic demeure l'un des derniers grands fabricants encore présents sur ce marché.
À l'autre extrémité du secteur, Magnetar poursuit son offensive. Le 3 novembre, le spécialiste annonçait la certification THX de ses lecteurs UDP800 MKII et UDP900 MKII, proposés respectivement à 1 999 et 3 799 euros chez certains revendeurs. Des tarifs qui contrastent avec celui d'un Panasonic DP-UB150, disponible autour de 200 euros.
Ces appareils lisent pourtant les mêmes Blu-ray UHD. Alors, qu'est-ce qui justifie une telle différence de prix ? Et surtout, cette montée en gamme se voit-elle réellement à l'écran ?
Des écarts réels, mais pas proportionnels au prix
Un lecteur Blu-ray UHD haut de gamme ne produit pas automatiquement une image plus détaillée qu'un modèle abordable. Les données vidéo présentes sur le disque sont numériques : à flux et traitements équivalents, deux appareils peuvent délivrer un résultat identique en HDMI. Une platine à 2 000 euros ne peut pas inventer des détails absents du disque, pas plus qu'un câble HDMI coûteux ne peut améliorer un signal numérique transmis sans erreur.
Il existe néanmoins une première différence concrète entre les lecteurs : leur compatibilité avec les formats HDR. Le Panasonic DP-UB150 prend en charge le HDR10 et le HDR10+, mais pas le Dolby Vision. Les deux Magnetar sont compatibles avec ces trois formats. Sur un disque proposant du Dolby Vision, le Panasonic se rabat donc sur le HDR10, tandis que les Magnetar peuvent exploiter les métadonnées dynamiques du Dolby Vision, à condition que le téléviseur soit également compatible.
Alors que les grands fabricants se retirent progressivement du marché, le Blu-ray 4K a-t-il encore un avenir ? Dans notre dernière vidéo consacrée au sujet, nous revenons sur les décisions de Sony, les atouts du disque face au streaming et les raisons pour lesquelles le support physique conserve une place à part chez les passionnés de home cinéma.
Selon le film et l'écran, le rendu des hautes lumières et des scènes sombres peut changer. Mais nul besoin d'investir dans une platine audiophile pour profiter de ces formats. Le Panasonic DP-UB450, affiché autour de 230 euros, prend déjà en charge le Dolby Vision et le HDR10+. Quant au DP-UB820, disponible à partir de 430 euros environ selon les offres, il ajoute notamment le processeur HCX et un optimiseur HDR permettant d'adapter le rendu aux capacités du diffuseur.
Les autres différences se jouent dans les traitements vidéo. Le tone mapping HDR, l'upscaling des DVD et des Blu-ray 1080p vers la 4K, la conversion de chrominance ou encore le désentrelacement peuvent produire des résultats différents selon les lecteurs. Dans une comparaison publiée par TechRadar, le DP-UB820 délivrait notamment une image plus fine et moins bruitée que le DP-UB154 lors de l'upscaling de sources de définition inférieure à la 4K. Il s'agit toutefois d'une appréciation visuelle, et non de mesures démontrant une supériorité systématique des appareils plus coûteux.
Magnetar met également en avant un moteur vidéo retravaillé sur sa série MKII, avec des améliorations annoncées sur la fidélité des couleurs, le contraste, la réduction du bruit et l'upscaling. Faute de mesures comparatives indépendantes, difficile toutefois d'établir leur avantage face aux Panasonic. D'autant que sur un téléviseur OLED ou MiniLED récent, certains traitements peuvent être réalisés directement par l'écran, parfois avec davantage de pertinence que par le lecteur.
Ce que les Magnetar apportent vraiment
C'est en réalité sur d'autres aspects que les Magnetar prennent tout leur sens. Leur première particularité est d'être des lecteurs universels : contrairement à de nombreuses platines traditionnelles, ils lisent aussi les SACD et les DVD-Audio. Pour un collectionneur qui possède des concerts, des albums haute résolution et des films sur différents supports physiques, un seul appareil peut ainsi remplacer plusieurs sources.
L'autre intérêt concerne la restitution audio analogique. L'UDP800 MKII dispose de sorties stéréo RCA et XLR symétriques, associées à une électronique dédiée. Cela permet notamment de le relier directement à un amplificateur hi-fi, y compris dépourvu d'entrée HDMI, en confiant la conversion numérique-analogique au lecteur. Une possibilité intéressante pour exploiter une installation stéréo de qualité. Précisons toutefois que le Panasonic DP-UB820 possède déjà deux sorties HDMI et des sorties analogiques 7.1 : la différence ne se résume donc pas à la présence de connecteurs, mais tient surtout à la conception de l'étage audio.
Les Magnetar vont également plus loin dans la gestion des bibliothèques musicales dématérialisées. Tous deux sont certifiés Roon Ready, ce qui permet de les intégrer comme lecteurs réseau dans une installation utilisant Roon. L'UDP900 MKII peut aussi servir de DAC USB pour un ordinateur grâce à son interface XMOS acceptant jusqu'au PCM 768 kHz et au DSD512. La connectique USB 3.0 bénéficie par ailleurs d'une alimentation isolée, destinée à améliorer la stabilité avec les supports de stockage externes. On dépasse ici largement le simple usage d'un lecteur de films.
| Médias supportés | UHD Blu-ray Blu-ray Blu-ray 3D DVD-Vidéo DVD-Audio AVCHD SA-CD CD Kodak Picture CD CD-R/RW DVD±R/RW DVD±R DL BD-R/RE | 
| 4K/UHD natif | Oui | 
Cette polyvalence intéressera aussi les collectionneurs de disques importés. Des versions multirégions et multizones, proposées séparément par certains revendeurs, permettent de lire des DVD et Blu-ray provenant de différentes régions du monde. Pour une installation home cinéma entièrement intégrée, la compatibilité avec les systèmes de contrôle Control4 et Crestron, ainsi que la fonction Wake-on-LAN, facilitent également le pilotage à distance et l'automatisation des équipements.
Magnetar pousse même cette spécialisation à l'extrême avec son Ultima, un lecteur Blu-ray UHD présenté en septembre 2026, dont le prix annoncé atteint 12 990 euros. Particularité étonnante : malgré son tarif, il ne possède ni DAC ni sorties audio analogiques. Destiné aux installations déjà équipées de processeurs audiovisuels ou de convertisseurs externes, il mise sur une alimentation séparée assistée par batterie, une horloge de référence à 10 MHz et une construction particulièrement élaborée. L'objectif affiché est de préserver l'intégrité du signal numérique. Un exemple extrême qui illustre combien le prix d'une platine peut dépendre de son architecture et de son usage, plutôt que de sa qualité d'image.
Enfin, la construction participe au positionnement tarifaire. L'UDP800 MKII pèse déjà 6,8 kg, contre environ 15 kg pour l'UDP900 MKII. Châssis métallique, mécanismes de lecture soignés, isolation des composants et réduction des vibrations visent notamment à limiter le bruit mécanique et les interférences. Ce soin peut avoir un intérêt dans une salle de projection silencieuse ou une installation hi-fi exigeante, même s'il ne garantit pas, à lui seul, une meilleure qualité d'image.
L'écart entre les deux Magnetar est d'ailleurs révélateur. L'UDP900 MKII coûte environ 1 800 euros de plus que l'UDP800 MKII, sans offrir davantage de formats vidéo. Il adopte en revanche un double châssis en aluminium, des alimentations séparées et deux convertisseurs ESS9038PRO pour les sorties stéréo et multicanal. Il propose ainsi des sorties analogiques 7.1, là où l'UDP800 MKII se limite à la stéréo analogique. Ce supplément prend donc surtout son sens pour celui qui souhaite exploiter l'électronique audio du lecteur, plutôt que transmettre directement le son en HDMI à un amplificateur home cinéma.
Reste la certification THX, obtenue par les deux modèles. Selon les informations publiées par le média allemand Area DVD, les contrôles portent notamment sur la fidélité des couleurs, le gamma, les niveaux de luminosité, l'upscaling et la restitution audio.
Quel lecteur pour quel usage ?
Le choix dépend finalement moins du budget maximal que de ce que l'on attend de son installation. Les différents paliers de prix permettent de distinguer assez clairement les besoins :
- Vers 200 € – Panasonic DP-UB150 : pour regarder ses Blu-ray 4K en HDR10 ou HDR10+ sans fonctions superflues. Une porte d'entrée suffisante pour profiter de ses films sur un téléviseur compatible.
- Vers 230 € – Panasonic DP-UB450 : pour profiter également du Dolby Vision, sans augmenter sensiblement son budget. Un choix particulièrement pertinent avec un téléviseur récent.
- Vers 500 € – Panasonic DP-UB820 : pour bénéficier de traitements vidéo plus élaborés, notamment de l'HDR Optimizer, intéressant avec certains téléviseurs et vidéoprojecteurs.
- À partir de 2 000 € – Magnetar UDP800 MKII et UDP900 MKII : pour réunir films, SACD, DVD-Audio, bibliothèque musicale dématérialisée et intégration hi-fi ou home cinéma dans un même appareil.
Nous détaillons ces différentes références, leurs avantages et leurs limites dans notre comparatif des meilleurs lecteurs Blu-ray 4K en 2026.
En définitive, une platine Blu-ray UHD à 2 000 euros peut être un meilleur appareil qu'un modèle à 200 euros, sans produire systématiquement une meilleure image. Pour profiter d'un film en 4K HDR sur un téléviseur moderne, un lecteur abordable fait déjà très bien le travail. Les Magnetar se justifient autrement : par leur polyvalence, leurs capacités audio et leur aptitude à prendre place au cœur d'une installation plus ambitieuse. Encore faut-il avoir l'usage de ces prestations pour que l'investissement prenne tout son sens.

articles.title: Nigerian agri-tech startup Bridge Merchant connects smallholder farmers to institutional buyers - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian agri-tech startup Bridge Merchant is combining a network of rural agents, storage infrastructure and its own technology platform to link smallholder farmers more efficiently with processors, manufacturers and other institutional buyers.
Founded in 2020 by CEO Chinwendu Nweke, Bridge Merchant began as an agricultural trading and aggregation business before evolving into a tech-enabled supply chain company. It is now led by a four-person founding team, with six core employees and a network of more than 1,300 rural agents, around 65 per cent of whom are women.
“Bridge Merchant was established after I saw first-hand how much value farmers were losing, not necessarily because they could not produce, but because the infrastructure between production and the market was fragmented,” Nweke told Disrupt Africa.
The startup’s platform, Aladinn Agro, is used alongside its field network to onboard and verify farmers, map farms, aggregate produce, manage quality and traceability, and coordinate logistics. Bridge Merchant works mainly with staple commodities such as maize, soybeans, paddy rice, sorghum, millet and beans, as well as selected export and agricultural by-product value chains.
“We realised that Nigeria does not necessarily have a production problem alone; it also has a significant market-access and agricultural infrastructure problem,” said Nweke. “A farmer can produce successfully and still lose income because there is inadequate storage, fragmented demand, poor logistics, quality inconsistencies or no reliable buyer available at the right time.”
At the other end of the chain, processors and large buyers struggle to source consistent volumes of traceable, quality-controlled commodities from thousands of fragmented smallholders. Bridge Merchant aims to solve both problems at once.
Nweke said the startup faces competition from other agricultural marketplaces, aggregators, commodity traders and supply chain technology companies. It differentiates itself by integrating the digital and physical layers of the supply chain rather than solving only one part of the problem.
“The real challenge is building a system that works reliably in rural communities where connectivity, storage, logistics and trust remain major constraints,” Nweke said.
Bridge Merchant has engaged more than 10,000 farmers and aggregated more than 20,000 tonnes of agricultural commodities to date. It has access to around 3,000 tonnes of partner warehousing capacity and has deployed three solar-powered storage units in northern Nigeria.
“The strongest indication of uptake for us is repeat demand. Farmers and agents continue to work with us because we provide access to structured markets, while institutional buyers return because they need reliable aggregation, quality control and fulfilment at scale,” said Nweke.
The startup makes most of its money from commodity aggregation and trade, earning a margin between procurement and final sale on transactions where it acts as principal. On larger transactions it facilitates without taking ownership of the commodity, it earns commissions of between two and five per cent.
The startup has grown mainly through operating revenue, founder capital, grants and non-dilutive funding, and has received support from organisations including Acumen, Heifer International, Standard Chartered Foundation, Access Bank and Sahara Group Foundation. It is now progressing towards institutional debt financing to boost its working capital for commodity aggregation.
“Agricultural commodity transactions are capital intensive. A business can have farmers ready to supply and buyers ready to purchase but still be unable to execute the transaction because it does not have enough capital to bridge procurement and buyer payment,” Nweke said.
Bridge Merchant has built a presence across 16 Nigerian states over time, and is currently focusing its expansion on major production corridors in Kaduna, Niger, Benue and Nasarawa states. Nweke said the immediate priority is to deepen operations in Nigeria, but the model could eventually extend to other West African markets facing similar challenges.
“Our ambition is to build agricultural supply-chain infrastructure that can work across borders while remaining deeply connected to local farming communities,” Nweke said.

articles.title: Le nouveau rover lunaire de la NASA n'aura pas besoin du Soleil : il roulera au nucléaire
articles.text:
Au pôle Sud de la Lune, la nuit dure quatorze jours terrestres et certains cratères n’ont jamais reçu la lumière directe du Soleil. La NASA y prépare pourtant sa future base, et elle a détaillé le 7 novembre, depuis le centre spatial Kennedy, la mission robotique chargée d’en dresser l’inventaire. Un rover à six roues baptisé PROMISE y forera le sol à partir de fin 2028, alimenté par un générateur nucléaire, pour une mission prévue sur dix-huit mois.
Un rover lunaire né dans les réserves martiennes
Le véhicule sera assemblé au Jet Propulsion Laboratory à partir de pièces de vol de rechange et de modèles d’essai de Curiosity et de Perseverance, les deux rovers martiens de l’agence. Son acronyme se traduit par « rover polaire d’observation, de cartographie et d’exploration in situ ». La bête embarque spectromètres, caméras et capteurs de température et de radiations, ainsi qu’une foreuse capable d’entamer le régolithe jusqu’à un mètre de profondeur et un ordinateur de bord durci conçu pour naviguer en autonomie.
Lire aussi : 164 395 dollars par an et une base sur la Lune : la NASA recrute ses futurs astronautes, mais pas n’importe qui
La NASA parle d’une alimentation nucléaire sans en préciser le modèle. Les générateurs qui équipent Curiosity et Perseverance donnent l’ordre de grandeur : 4,8 kg de dioxyde de plutonium 238 y produisent environ 110 watts d’électricité au lancement, pour au moins quatorze ans de service. La chaleur excédentaire maintient au passage les instruments à bonne température. Le principe tient de la pile atomique plus que du réacteur, sans réaction en chaîne ni pièce mobile : la chaleur de la désintégration devient du courant, que la nuit tombe ou non. Blue Origin livrera l’engin au pôle Sud à bord de son atterrisseur Mark 1, pour un contrat de 94 millions de dollars assorti d’une option de performance pouvant atteindre 140 millions.
VIPER, le précédent à 450 millions
VIPER devait déjà cartographier la glace d’eau du pôle Sud, avec des panneaux solaires et une batterie incapables de tenir loin des zones éclairées. La NASA a annulé la mission le 17 juillet 2024, après environ 450 millions de dollars dépensés, avant de la relancer en septembre 2025 avec Blue Origin pour un alunissage désormais visé en 2027. Sa feuille de route plafonnait à une centaine de jours terrestres, là où PROMISE promet dix-huit mois, nuits lunaires comprises.
L’annonce arrive au milieu d’une rafale de contrats pour le programme Moon Base, qui vise une base opérationnelle à l’horizon 2032. Huit entreprises, dont SpaceX et Blue Origin, se partageront jusqu’à 10 milliards de dollars de livraisons lunaires sur dix ans, et 1,3 milliard de commandes de lancement a déjà été réparti. Le patron de l’agence résume la méthode d’une formule : la Lune se construit « mission par mission », pour que les astronautes arrivent sur un chantier déjà entamé.
Côté européen, l’atterrisseur Argonaut de l’ESA n’est pas attendu avant 2030 sur une Ariane 64. Il testera d’abord des technologies de survie à la nuit lunaire avant d’embarquer, à terme, sa propre source à radioisotopes. La carte de la glace d’eau que dressera PROMISE pèsera donc sur l’emplacement de la base, et sur tout ce qui suivra. L’eau, c’est de l’oxygène et du carburant que personne n’aura à lancer depuis la Terre.

articles.title: Beyond code generation: Five lessons on AI, reliability, and recovery
articles.text:
Beyond code generation: Five lessons on AI, reliability, and recovery
At a TechSparks 2026 roundtable hosted by OPPEX, technology leaders discussed the challenges of maintaining AI-generated code, managing risk, and responding when production systems fail.
AI is speeding up software development, allowing teams to build in days what once took weeks. But writing code faster does not necessarily make it easier to understand, maintain, or fix. As codebases grow, engineers must deal with failures in systems they may not have built or fully understood, often under pressure during an incident.
At TechSparks 2026, OPPEX hosted a roundtable titled ‘AI Can 10X Your Engineers. Can It 10X Your Ability to Fix What They Build?’, bringing technology leaders together to discuss the challenges of maintaining, troubleshooting, and recovering software systems built faster with AI.
The discussion brought together Abhishek Dwivedi, VP Engineering, Cimpress; Amit Khanna, Global Head of Engineering, Amadeus; Anand Rangarajan, VP Engineering, Google DeepMind; Ashish Chandra Tewari, Vice President of Engineering, Razorpay; Dheeraj Khanna, VP Engineering, Global Logic; Jaya Krishnan, VP Engineering, Coforge; Roopasree Ranganna, SVP, Workplace Technology and Service Delivery Leader, Synchrony; Ruby Tomar, Vice President & Head Agentic Firmware, Ascendion; Sarath Gollapalli, VP Engineering, Broadridge; Saurabh Kumar, VP Engineering, Capillary Technologies; Sridhar Jonnala, Chief AI Scientist, Distinguished Engineer, CTO -AI Strategy & Delivery, IBM; Sudhir Tiwari, Global Head, Digital Engineering Center, Thoughtworks; Trilok Ramakrishna, Site lead and Head of Engineering, dbt Labs; and Vasanthi Ramesh, Vice President & Engineering Site Leader, NetApp.
OPPEX was represented by Prasun Kumar, Founder and CEO. The discussion was moderated by Madanmohan Rao, Research Director at YourStory.
Here are five key takeaways from the discussion.
Faster code does not mean faster business results
AI has accelerated code generation, but testing, validation, deployment, and downstream systems have not necessarily kept pace. As a result, code may be ready long before the rest of the system can support it.
Participants cautioned against confusing output with outcomes. Writing 10X more code does not mean customers will see a tenfold improvement. What matters is whether AI helps deliver better business results. Several leaders also suggested that teams should be willing to use AI to remove unnecessary code, rather than simply generate more of it.
Match AI autonomy to the level of risk
Participants agreed that AI agents should not have the same level of autonomy across all systems.
Tasks that are easy to reverse, such as restarting a stateless service or adding capacity, can be handled autonomously. But changes involving money, patient data or physical manufacturing require closer oversight because errors can have consequences that are difficult or impossible to reverse.
Many teams are classifying applications and data according to risk, giving agents greater freedom in low-risk areas while retaining human oversight of critical code. In regulated sectors, participants stressed the need to establish controls before expanding autonomy, along with clear procedures for handling errors made by agents.
Context is critical to making AI agents effective
AI agents need access to the right information to work effectively. In many organizations, knowledge about legacy systems, service dependencies, and past incidents rests with a few experienced employees. These are often the people teams turn to when something goes wrong.
To reduce this dependence, teams are using knowledge graphs, memory layers, and shared repositories to document how systems interact, what has failed before, and what each service is expected to deliver. This can help preserve institutional knowledge when employees leave or move to other roles.
However, making more information available to agents also has a cost. Large prompts increase token usage, making it important to retrieve relevant information efficiently rather than feed agents everything available.
Human accountability remains essential
As AI-generated changes become larger and more frequent, there is a risk that engineers may approve code they do not fully understand.
Instead of requiring people to review every line, participants discussed systems in which agents indicate their confidence levels and escalate decisions when confidence is low. Human oversight remains particularly important in regulated environments, where organizations may need to explain decisions to regulators or customers.
Participants also emphasized the need to track incidents caused by AI-generated changes and use those findings to improve development and review processes. Several noted that many organizations have yet to establish this feedback loop.
Let agents investigate, but leave critical decisions to people
Incident response was identified as one of the most promising near-term uses of AI agents.
Agents can collect logs, trace dependencies, examine recent deployments, filter false alarms, and bring together information that engineers need to investigate failures. This can save on-call teams time and help them identify problems without having to gather evidence from scratch.
For critical incidents, however, appropriate teams must be alerted immediately, even while agents continue investigating.
Participants also pointed to the additional cost and complexity of monitoring AI agents, along with unresolved questions about accuracy, drift, and the value they deliver. They stressed that product managers, analysts, and other roles should also be involved in the process of building with AI.
The roundtable highlighted common concerns among technology leaders across industries, particularly around reliability, oversight, and incident response. Participants called for greater investment in stability, security, and recovery alongside AI-driven development.
As organizations generate more code with AI, they must also ensure they have the systems, processes and people needed to maintain it and respond when things go wrong.

articles.title: Un vecino de Salamanca se puso a lanzar bolas de papel mojado desde un sexto piso. Ahora se enfrenta a una multa publicada en el BOE
articles.text:
Todavía recuerdo las clases donde más de uno y más de dos mojaban una bolita de papel, la introducían en el tubo vacío de un boli y, a modo de cerbatana, la proyectaban sobre el cuello o la mochila de algún cándido estudiante que ni sabía por dónde le había llegado el ataque. Ahora imagina esto a escala más “industrial”.
Hace un par de meses, una patrulla de la Policía Local de Salamanca vio a alguien lanzar bolas de papel mojado desde la terraza de un sexto piso. Las bolas caían cerca de la terraza de un bar y salpicaban. Ahí quedó la cosa, ¿no? No: semanas más tarde, el Ayuntamiento publicó en el BOE una propuesta de sanción al vecino, cazado con 751 euros. No es ninguna broma y tiene un precedente jurídico.
Qué pasó. El lanzamiento partió de una vivienda en la calle Bordadores. Las bolas llegaron a las inmediaciones de la terraza de un establecimiento de hostelería. Este estaba en la calle Condes de Crespo Rascón. La notificación no precisa cuántas fueron, no habla de heridos ni daños y no cita a vecinos o peatones afectados. Pero la broma fue cazada por la Policía Local, quienes advirtieron la escena e identificaron al presunto autor. Hasta hay un precedente de 200 euros por una situación análoga.
Y si hubiera caído algo más duro. El Código Civil prevé otro tipo de multa para quien arroja objetos más contundentes. Su artículo 1910 dice que quien habita una casa responde de los daños causados por las cosas que se arrojen o caigan de ella. No hablamos de banderas ni de tejas, que casi siempre son fruto de accidentes. Hablamos de un “agua va” malintencionado o sortear de milago como por desgracia me consta, un pañal bomba. El Supremo lo aplica a propietarios, inquilinos e incluso negocios. Aquí nadie reclama por daños, pero deja meridianamente claro por qué tirar objetos desde un piso nunca es un juego.
Por qué una multa. El Ayuntamiento aplica el artículo 11 de su Ordenanza Municipal de Limpieza Urbana y Gestión de Residuos. Prohíbe arrojar a la vía pública “todo tipo de residuos u objetos de pequeña entidad”. Una bola de papel encaja porque la ley de residuos define como residuo cualquier objeto que su poseedor desecha o tiene intención de desechar. Mojado o no, da igual. Y ojo porque la ordenanza califica la conducta de grave.
Por qué 751. Aquí está el dato curioso: la Ley de Bases del Régimen Local permite a los ayuntamientos sancionar el incumplimiento de sus ordenanzas, pero establece un techo económico. Las multas leves llegan hasta 750 euros. Las graves, hasta 1.500. Las muy graves, hasta 3.000. Por eso las graves arrancan en 751. Un euro más que la leve más cara, porque no se aprecia reincidencia ni agravantes, pero sí malas intenciones.
Qué decide la gravedad. La ley estatal siempre fija los criterios generales, gradúa las infracciones según la intensidad de cuánto se perjudica a la salubridad o qué daños se infringen al ornato público. Pero cada ordenanza concreta qué conducta cae en cada escalón. En Salamanca, tirar algo de pequeña entidad ya es grave. Getafe, por ejemplo, prevé hasta 1.500 euros por tirar pipas, chicles o colillas, al techo de lo grave.
Cuándo sería muy grave. La ley reserva el multazo de hasta 3.000 euros a perturbaciones relevantes de la convivencia. Por ejemplo, las que afectan de forma grave, inmediata y directa a la tranquilidad o a los derechos de otras personas. Pintarrajear un escaparate o reventarlo ya es delito. En cualquier situación, los ayuntamientos solo pueden sancionar así cuando no existe una norma sectorial específica que ya regule la materia.
Las fechas. Los hechos son del 3 de septiembre y el informe se emitió el 28 de septiembre. Entretanto, la comisión de Medio Ambiente lo ha estado analizando. Como la notificación no pudo entregarse en el domicilio indicado, el Ayuntamiento recurrió al BOE. También es de Salamanca el vecino que montó una piscina en un patio de luces sin pedir permiso y también se hubo de recurrir al BOE. Es lo que prevé la Ley de Procedimiento Administrativo cuando no se localiza al interesado. Entre los hechos y el análisis en comisión han pasado casi dos meses: ahora el vecino tiene 10 días para presentar alegaciones. Pasado el plazo llegará la resolución.
¿Multa firme? No, no que se publicó es una propuesta dentro de un expediente sancionador. El vecino puede alegar, aportar pruebas o negar los hechos. La misma ley contempla reducciones: si el infractor reconoce su responsabilidad o paga de forma voluntaria antes de la resolución, la sanción baja. Cada reducción es de al menos el 20 %, y se pueden sumar. En este caso, 751 euros quedarían en unos 601 con una de ellas y en unos 451 con las dos. Poca cuantía, papel mojado.

articles.title: Javier Calvo: “A la gente le llama la atención que una película como La bola negra se haya podido hacer con menos de 15 millones de euros, pero se ha podido hacer porque tiene dos directores”
articles.text:
“La han podido hacer dos personas”, contesta Javier Calvo cuando alguien le pregunta por qué se ha podido rodar “La bola negra” con un presupuesto inferior a los 15 millones de euros. El director atribuye la posibilidad de rodarla con ese presupuesto a trabajar en pareja con Javier Ambrossi. Podían cubrir las necesidades. Ambrossi se encarga de esto y Calvo de aquello. Y así van avanzando.
Un director no podría ocuparse solo de todo ese trabajo porque tiene muchas otras cosas que hacer. Ocurre, por ejemplo, con la selección de figurantes.
A los extras los han ido seleccionando uno a uno. Ellos querían que fueran diferentes en las tres líneas de la historia. Han visto vídeos y han hecho castings. Han seleccionado a miles de personas. Mientras Ambrossi estaba haciendo esto, Calvo estaba preparando el día siguiente con la dirección de fotografía.
Dos directores para una película en tres épocas
La acción transcurre en tres momentos distintos (1932, 1937 y 2017), según la ficha oficial del Festival de Cannes. Está basada en parte de la obra inacabada de Federico García Lorca y en “La piedra oscura” de Alberto Conejero. Se ha rodado en 12 semanas en España y Grecia.
También es fácil verlo en las escenas colectivas. Una secuencia con Penélope Cruz ha tenido 500 figurantes. En Granada se han utilizado hasta 250 disfrazados de la época para recrear la ciudad de 1932.
Además de Penélope Cruz y Glenn Close, el reparto está formado por Guitarricadelafuente, Miguel Bernardeau, Carlos González, Milo Quifes y Lola Dueñas. Las productoras detrás son Suma Content Films, El Deseo, Movistar Plus+ y Le Pacte (info de la productora).
En cuanto al presupuesto, hay que detenerse en algunas cuestiones. Los 9,9 millones de euros que aparecen en la resolución de ayudas del Instituto de la Cinematografía y de las Artes Audiovisuales corresponden a la parte española de la coproducción. Es decir, no es el total del coste de producción y de promoción y distribución.
La taquilla y la venta de derechos
El 27 de octubre de 2026 tenía 34,3 millones de euros de taquilla. Además, había vendido más de cinco millones de entradas en España y se situaba en el cuarto puesto de recaudación de las películas españolas en salas nacionales.
El primer día de taquilla fue de 1,32 millones. También creció en el segundo fin de semana sobre el primero. El 17 de octubre, en su cuarto fin de semana en cartel, tenía un acumulado de 28,6 millones.
El salto internacional empezó con Netflix, que compró los derechos para Norteamérica después de su paso por Cannes (los Javis han ganado el premio de dirección ex aequo). Se ha calculado que la venta ha sido de unos cinco millones de dólares.
También ha sido galardonada por el público en Toronto y Sídney. Mantener los pies en la tierra y ser metódicos es lo que ha defendido Calvo después de recibir el Premio del Público en San Sebastián. Por su parte, Ambrossi ha dicho: “Estamos los dos juntos en esta aventura y eso siempre lleva a casa”.

articles.title: Le patron de la cybersécurité européenne prévient, le piratage de votre électroménager est la prochaine étape
articles.text:
Piratage des frigos de supermarchés : pourquoi vos appareils électroménagers sont les prochaines cibles
Après les cyberattaques ayant visé des réfrigérateurs de supermarchés en Europe, le chef de la cybersécurité de l’UE alerte sur la vulnérabilité de nos appareils électroménagers.
En octobre et novembre, les supermarchés d’au moins douze pays européens, dont la France, ont été frappés par une vague de cyberattaques. Mauvaise nouvelle, ce ne serait que le début. Mardi 10 novembre 2026, Juhan Lepassaar, directeur exécutif de l’agence européenne de cybersécurité (ENISA), a prévenu que les failles exploitées sur ces réfrigérateurs pourraient bientôt toucher les routeurs et appareils électroménagers de nos logements.
L’IA au service des hackers et une pénurie de talents qui impacte l’Union européenne
Des failles PHP aux attaques contre les frigos de supermarchés ou les banques de sang, les récents incidents mettent en lumière les lacunes opérationnelles des États membres de l’UE. Souvent causées par des logiciels obsolètes, ces brèches prouvent que “la sécurité ne devrait pas et ne peut pas être une préoccupation secondaire”, comme l’a souligné le chef de la cybersécurité européenne, Juhan Lepassaar. Il avertit par ailleurs que “aujourd’hui, ce sont les frigos, demain cela pourrait être les routeurs, après-demain les appareils électroménagers, et ainsi de suite”.
Bien que l’IA permette aux entreprises de corriger leurs failles de manière proactive, elle offre aussi aux pirates des outils redoutables pour les attaquer. Les hackers l’utilisent en effet de plus en plus pour repérer des vulnérabilités à grande échelle et concevoir des campagnes de hameçonnage ultra-réalistes grâce aux deepfakes. Selon l’agence, le délai entre la découverte d’une faille et son exploitation malveillante est désormais proche de zéro. “Quand nous regardons le paysage des menaces, le tableau n’est pas si rose”, s’inquiète Juhan Lepassaar, qui rappelle l’urgence d’un “partage d’informations et d’une coordination réactive”.
Au-delà des évolutions technologiques, la géopolitique dicte le rythme des attaques. En 2025, près de 57 % des incidents étaient motivés par des raisons idéologiques, tandis que 29 % relevaient d’intérêts financiers, le rançongiciel restant la menace la plus dévastatrice pour les entreprises. Face à cela, Bruxelles déploie un arsenal réglementaire, à l’image de la directive NIS2 ou du Cyber Resilience Act. Pourtant, un obstacle majeur subsiste : de nombreuses sociétés confient encore la gestion de leurs infrastructures connectées à de simples équipes de maintenance, ignorant les enjeux de cybersécurité.
Enfin, l’Europe fait face à une pénurie critique de compétences. Près de 45 % des organisations peinent à recruter des experts, un déficit qui favorise les entreprises les plus riches au détriment des autres. L’ENISA exhorte donc les États membres à investir massivement dans la formation pour combler ce vide. Un effort financier inévitable selon son directeur, qui conclut : “Tous les incidents peuvent être évités, et la cybersécurité n’est pas donnée. La question est : sommes-nous prêts à investir pour que cela se concrétise ?”

articles.title: Nigeria’s active mobile subscriptions hit 200m in two years
articles.text:
Nigeria’s active mobile subscriptions rose 29% in two years to 200.3 million in September 2026, recovering from the sharp decline that followed the enforcement of the National Identification Number (NIN)-SIM linkage policy.
The rebound, however, remains concentrated among two operators, with MTN and Airtel accounting for about 86% of active connections, leaving Globacom and T2 with a much smaller share of the market.
MTN had 104.6 million active subscriptions in September, while Airtel had 68 million. They collectively accounted for about 172.7 million out of the 200.1 million recorded across the four operators. Globacom had 23.5 million, while T2 had 3.6 million, according to the latest data from the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC).
The 200 million mobile subscriptions refer to active phone lines, not that 200 million people own or use mobile phones. One person can have multiple SIM cards, and active connections also include SIMs used in routers and other devices.
The figure marks a new milestone since the full enforcement of NIN-SIM linkage in 2024, which led to a sharp reduction in reported connections. The policy required mobile subscribers to link their phone lines to verified national identity numbers. The policy was introduced in 2020, but its enforcement intensified in 2024 as operators completed the verification and disconnection of lines without valid NIN records.
In its 2024 year-end performance report, the NCC said active subscriptions fell from 224.7 million in 2023 to 164.9 million in 2024, a loss of 59.8 million connections or 26.6%. The commission attributed the decline to removing SIM cards not linked to verifiable NINs and correcting a major discrepancy in one mobile network operator’s subscriber figures.
By August 2024, the regulator said more than 153 million SIM cards were linked to NINs, representing 96% compliance. It subsequently set September 14, 2024, as the final deadline for operators to complete the exercise.
Rising mobile subscriptions
The rise in mobile subscriptions has also been accompanied by higher data consumption, which grew by about 51% year-on-year in September 2026 to 1.73 million terabytes. However, the shift towards faster networks remains uneven. 4G accounted for 54.37% of mobile connections, while 5G represented just 5.05%. Older technologies, 2G and 3G, still accounted for 36.42% and 4.16%, respectively.
As demand for connectivity grows, the NCC’s figures also show an expansion in fixed broadband infrastructure. Fibre-to-the-X subscriptions, which cover connections to homes, offices, streets and hubs, increased by about 67% between the first and third quarters of 2026, pointing to growth in fibre access beyond mobile networks.
These developments come as telecommunications accounts for a larger share of Nigeria’s economic activity. The sector contributed 9.72% to GDP in the second quarter of 2026, up from 9.20% in the corresponding period of 2025. The NCC noted that figures for late 2024 and early 2025 were affected by the National Bureau of Statistics’ GDP rebasing.

articles.title: UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents
Teams building AI agents on AWS use a range of frameworks, including LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Each framework records agent execution in its own way, so the structure of messages, tool calls, and handoffs between agents differs from one to the next. Evaluation tooling tends to follow the same boundaries: teams build metrics, scoring logic, and result storage against a single framework’s trace format, and they must rebuild them when they switch frameworks or run agents on more than one.
This coupling makes a basic development question harder to answer: did a change to the prompt, model, or tools improve the agent? Answering it requires consistent metrics across versions of an agent and a shared record of past results to compare against. Agent quality also spans several dimensions that a single accuracy score does not capture: tool calling, response quality, responsible AI, performance, multi-turn conversation, multi-agent coordination, and reasoning.
In this post, we introduce the Universal Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF). Customers across 12 organizations in the telecom, healthcare, and financial services industries used UAEF to evaluate their AI agents with one consistent set of metrics and compare agent versions before release. UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system: it uses adapters to convert traces from each framework into a common format, then scores those traces with 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions. It stores the results in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and generates reports and insights that inform the next iteration of the agent. This post describes how UAEF works, provides a playbook for choosing metrics and preparing datasets, and points to runnable notebooks for each supported framework.
UAEF: One evaluation layer for agent frameworks
UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system for AI agents. It takes the agent a team already has and scores it the same way across supported frameworks and runtimes. UAEF takes two inputs: the agent under test and a dataset to run it on. The dataset provides the inputs for each test case, and it can also include ground-truth answers, the expected output for each input. Ground truth is optional, and only metrics that compare the agent’s response against a reference use it. To evaluate tool calling, the ground truth must also include the expected tool calls for each test case: which tools the agent should call, in what order, and with what arguments. Everything after that happens inside the UAEF.
Figure 1 shows the path a single evaluation takes, from the inputs to the reports and insights. First, an adapter reads the agent’s native execution, its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs, and normalizes it into one canonical trace, so that the steps that follow are identical no matter which framework produced the agent. Next, UAEF screens the trace for personally identifiable information (PII), such as email addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers, before data is stored. The evaluation engine then scores the trace on a selection from 36 built-in metrics across 7 quality dimensions. When you persist a run, UAEF records it as an experiment in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3: Amazon DynamoDB holds the per-experiment metadata used for listing and comparison, and Amazon S3 holds the full results. With runs stored, a team can compare an agent version against a baseline to detect regressions and generate reports and insights that explain what changed and why. Those reports close the loop: the team evaluates the agent, learns what regressed or improved, changes the prompt, model, or tools, and evaluates again.
The rest of this section follows that flow in order: the adapters that make UAEF framework-agnostic, the evaluation engine and its metrics, PII detection, experiment storage and comparison, and the reports that close the loop.
Canonical trace and adapters
Adapters are what make UAEF framework-agnostic. An adapter reads the record of an agent’s run, including its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs. It converts that record into one canonical representation called the AgentTrace, which is the only thing the rest of UAEF scores. Because of that conversion, UAEF works with the agent, whatever SDK it was built with (such as LangGraph, LangChain, or Strands Agents). It can run locally, behind an HTTP endpoint, or on a managed runtime such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with traces in Langfuse or not captured at all. UAEF provides an adapter for each of these, and they produce the same AgentTrace, so metrics, scores, and comparisons stay consistent across every one of them.
A trace reaches UAEF two ways. If one already exists, from a past run, a log, or an observability store, it is handed to UAEF and the matching adapter normalizes it. If not, UAEF invokes the agent for you: given a runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) or an HTTP endpoint, it calls the agent on each dataset input, collects the response, and adapts it in one step. Either way, the output is the same AgentTrace.
Because every metric, mode, and report operates on the AgentTrace rather than on a framework native format, the scoring that follows is identical no matter where the trace came from. That separation, normalization first and scoring second, is what lets a team compare an agent built on one framework against an agent built on another on a single scale.
Evaluation engine
The evaluation engine scores a canonical trace across 7 quality dimensions, each capturing a distinct aspect of agent behavior that a single accuracy number would hide. Tool calling measures whether the agent selected the right tools, called them in a sensible order, and passed valid arguments. Response quality measures whether the final answer is relevant, complete, accurate, and grounded in the provided context rather than hallucinated.
Responsible AI measures safety, bias, toxicity, and resistance to prompt injection. Performance measures operational cost in latency, token use, and throughput. Multi-turn measures how well the agent sustains a conversation, including context retention, coherence, and goal completion across turns. Multi-agent measures coordination in systems of cooperating agents, such as task delegation and the division of work. Reasoning measures the internal logic of the agent’s chain of thought, including consistency and freedom from fallacies.
Each dimension is computed by one or more of 36 built-in metrics, and every metric returns a normalized score in the interval [0, 1], where 1 is best, so dimensions and the overall result share one scale. Metrics come in two families. Deterministic metrics compute a score directly from the trace and the ground truth and reproduce exactly on repeated runs. Large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge metrics score qualities that resist a closed-form definition, such as response relevance or safety, by prompting a judge model on Amazon Bedrock. You can also add your own custom metrics or draw on the RAGAS and DeepEval integrations.
Because judge metrics feed an agent’s own output back into a prompt, that content is treated as untrusted input: an agent that can influence its judge can influence its own scores. The rubric is sent separately from the content, and the content is escaped so it cannot break out of its delimiter and be read as instructions. Each judge response is parsed strictly and must cite a verbatim span of the content it scored. A score whose evidence is not found is rejected rather than recorded. Judge scores are evaluation signal, not a safety decision, and should not gate a security control. For runtime enforcement on the agent itself, apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails in its own invocation path. The full model is in SECURITY.md.
Experiment management and comparison
UAEF records each evaluation as an experiment, so results from different agent versions can be compared later. Calling evaluate() or batch_evaluate() with persist=True creates a new experiment, identified by an optional name and objective, and writes it to two stores with complementary roles. Amazon DynamoDB holds one row per experiment with the metadata used for listing and comparison: evaluation count, the average score per metric, and an overall average. Amazon S3 holds a JSON file with the full evaluation results, including per-metric scores and the judge’s reasoning. Teams that handle sensitive data can turn on PII redaction for the stored copy.
The Python library also models a finer-grained structure. An experiment contains runs, and each run records the agent design under test: framework, model, tools, system prompt, and parameters. A run can also record a configuration snapshot and a Git commit. You can mark one run as the baseline for its experiment. This ties each score to the change that produced it, whether a new prompt, a different model, or an added tool.
Comparison works on the stored per-metric averages. For each metric that two runs have in common, the comparison engine calculates the absolute and percentage change. It then classifies the metric as a regression, an improvement, or unchanged, using a configurable threshold with a default of 5 percent. Several runs can be compared against a single baseline in one call. The regression detector also assigns a severity to each regression: minor (5–10 percent), moderate (10–20 percent), or severe (over 20 percent). It groups regressions by dimension, which shows, for example, whether a prompt change affected tool calling but not response quality.
In the web UI, the Compare tab lists stored experiments and filters them by framework or dataset. You select two or more experiments. The first is used as the baseline, and the UI shows per-metric scores with regressions and improvements highlighted. The UI calls the same library comparison engine, so results match what the Python API returns.
Report and insight generation
After an evaluation is stored, UAEF reports on it at three levels, each answering a different question. How did this run perform? Why did it score that way? How does it compare with earlier versions?
Results view. When an evaluation finishes, the web UI shows a summary of the experiment: the overall score, the number of test cases evaluated, the framework, and queries that failed to run. Per-metric averages appear with a dimension radar chart and a metric bar chart. A table lists every test case with its query, the agent’s response, the expected answer, and the score. Expanding a row shows the full response with its dimension and metric scores. For a multi-turn conversation, it shows each turn with its own scores and the tools the agent called.
Detailed report. From the results view or the experiment list, you can generate a statistical report on demand. UAEF loads the stored results from Amazon S3 and opens the report in a new browser tab. The report breaks results down by dimension and by metric. It shows confidence intervals and outliers for each metric, score distributions, correlations between metrics, a responsible AI summary, and test cases that reported failures. It closes with recommendations that point to the lowest-scoring dimensions and the metrics that vary most across test cases. The report is computed from the scores alone, without an LLM, so the same results produce the same report.
LLM-generated insights. In the Python library, you can pass a report to a model on Amazon Bedrock for analysis. For a single run, the analysis covers strengths, critical weaknesses, hypotheses about root causes, and prioritized recommendations. For a comparison of several runs, it covers the overall trend, likely causes of regressions and improvements, the risk each regression carries, and next steps. These insights suggest what to change in the prompt, model, or tools before the next evaluation.
Two ways to use it
You can run UAEF two ways over the same engine. With the Python library, you can evaluate agents in code from notebooks, scripts, and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines. You can use the deployable AWS service to evaluate agents through a low-code web interface. You upload your dataset, select a framework and metrics, run the evaluation, and review the scores. Both paths run the identical evaluation engine and write to the same stores, so a result does not depend on which path produced it. You can start in the interface and move to code without changing how your results are scored or compared.
Evaluating agents with UAEF: A playbook
Knowing what UAEF can measure is different from knowing what you should measure. A travel-booking agent and a policy Q&A agent fail in different ways, and scoring both on every dimension wastes time and Amazon Bedrock invocations. Use this playbook to pick the metrics that match your agent, then add more as new questions come up.
Getting started
UAEF is open source under the Apache 2.0 license in the awslabs/uaef GitHub repository. It includes the Python library, framework adapters, built-in metrics, AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) infrastructure for the deployable service, the web interface, and runnable notebooks for each supported framework. The Installation Guide covers requirements, installing from a built package, and the development setup.
The service deployment guide covers deploying UAEF as a service with the web interface, the config reference, and teardown.
See it in action
A complete evaluation in the UAEF web interface, from ground-truth upload to per-dimension scores.
Choosing the metrics
Start from your scenario, not the metric list. Find the column that matches your agent and begin with the metrics checked in it. The Needs ground truth column shows which metrics compare against a reference answer or expected tool calls.

|  |  |  | RAG / knowledge Q&A | General Q&A | Tool-using agent | Multi-turn conversation | Reasoning | Safety and compliance | Multi-agent | Production monitoring | 
| Response Quality | answer_relevance |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | accuracy |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | completeness |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | hallucination_score |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | ragas_faithfulness |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | ragas_context_precision |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | ragas_context_recall |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
| Tool Calling | tool_selection_accuracy |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | tool_sequence_correctness |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | parameter_quality |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | mcp_compliance |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
| Multi-Turn | context_retention |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | coherence |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | conversation_completeness |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | user_satisfaction |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

| Responsible AI | safety_score |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

The table shows recommended starting metrics for each scenario. For the complete list of supported metrics, see the metrics catalog.
Pass the metrics you picked as the metrics argument to evaluate() or batch_evaluate(). For a worked example, see the Example notebooks section that follows. Deterministic metrics, such as tool calling and performance, are computed directly from the trace, whereas others call an LLM judge. UAEF automatically skips metrics that need a reference answer when no ground truth is present, so partially labeled datasets and unlabeled production traffic are still worth evaluating.
Choosing the pipeline
Metrics decide what you measure. Six independent choices decide how the evaluation runs. Use the question in each row to settle it.
| Choice | Ask yourself | Then use | In code | 
| Passive or active | Do I already have traces, or do I need to generate them under controlled conditions? | Passive: evaluate a trace you already have. Active: call an invoke_* helper so UAEF runs the agent. | evaluate(trace=recorded, adapter=“langgraph”) or raw = invoke_http_agent_for_framework( ENDPOINT, query, “strands”) | 
| One trace or a dataset | Am I debugging one case or measuring a release? | Use evaluate() for one trace or conversation. Use batch_evaluate() for a dataset. | evaluate(trace=trace) or batch_evaluate(traces=traces, max_workers=4) | 
| Single-turn or multi-turna | Does any test case depend on an earlier turn? | Multi-turn: add session_id and turn_id to the dataset and pass every turn to the adapter, which assembles each conversation. | sessions = adapter.transform_to_canonical( turn_payloads) batch_evaluate(traces=sessions) | 
| Single-agent or multi-agent | Does more than one agent handle a single request? | Nothing to configure. The adapter returns an AgentTrace or MultiAgentTrace, and UAEF selects the matching evaluator. | adapter = get_adapter(FRAMEWORK) trace = adapter.transform_to_canonical(raw) | 
| Offline or online | Am I testing before release or monitoring production? | Offline: a prepared dataset in development and CI. Online: live conversations, scored turn by turn. | batch_evaluate(…) or OnlineEvaluator().evaluate_response( trace=trace) | 
| Ephemeral or persistedb | Will I compare this run with a later one? | Persisted: set persist=True with an experiment name. Otherwise, use the returned result. | batch_evaluate(traces=traces, persist=True, experiment_name=“Support agent v2”) | 
a Multi-turn – For details, refer to the multi-turn evaluation workflow guide.
b Only persisted runs can be compared.
Preparing your dataset
Provide one row per test case in a CSV or XLSX file. Only Question is required.
| Column | Required | Purpose | 
| Question | Yes | Input sent to the agent | 
| Answer | No | Expected response | 
| context | No | Reference documents for retrieval-style evaluation | 
| expected_tool_calls | No | Expected tool calls as a JSON array | 
| session_id | Multi-turn only | Groups rows into one conversation | 
| turn_id | Multi-turn only | Orders turns within a conversation, starting at 1 | 
Question and Answer are matched case-insensitively and accept common aliases such as Query and Expected_Output, so existing test files usually work without renaming.
Multi-turn datasets. Rows that share a session_id are sent in order to a single agent session, so later turns can depend on earlier ones. Your agent endpoint must maintain its own conversation state, because UAEF sends each turn with its session ID rather than replaying history. Use lowercase session_id and turn_id. Otherwise, the file is evaluated as single-turn.
Protect sensitive data. Before sharing or persisting a dataset drawn from real traffic, use uaef.security.PIIDetector to detect and redact personally identifiable information such as email addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers.
Example notebooks
If you want to see more examples, check our notebooks/ folder. The notebooks cover scenarios such as batch evaluation, multi-turn conversations, multi-agent, and experiment management across frameworks including LangGraph, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
| Notebook | What it covers | 
| 00_langgraph.ipynb | LangGraph: single, batch, multi-turn, and multi-agent evaluation | 
| 02_langchain.ipynb | LangChain agents | 
| 04_json.ipynb | Custom frameworks, through the generic JSON adapter | 
| 05_strands.ipynb | Strands Agents, including multi-agent | 
| 06_agentcore.ipynb | Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, including multi-agent | 
| 07_langfuse.ipynb | Traces already collected in Langfuse | 
| 01_langgraph_ragas_deepeval.ipynb | RAGAS and DeepEval integrations | 
| 08_experiment_management.ipynb | Experiments, baselines, and regression detection | 
| 10_reporting_pipeline.ipynb | Reports and dashboards from stored results | 
| 11_pii_detection.ipynb | PII detection and redaction in traces | 
Clean up
Running the library creates nothing on its own, but persisting a run writes experiment metadata to Amazon DynamoDB and full results to Amazon S3. Delete both when you no longer need the saved experiments. The default names are uaef-experiments and uaef-results, overridable through the UAEF_DYNAMODB_TABLE and UAEF_S3_BUCKET environment variables. The bucket has to be emptied before it can be deleted.
If you deployed the service, the service deployment guide has the teardown sequence for both deployment modes. Read its retained-resources note before you assume teardown is complete: the DynamoDB tables, S3 buckets, and Amazon Cognito user pool are created with a retain policy, so deleting the stack leaves them, and their contents, in place. That is deliberate, so a teardown does not destroy saved experiments, but it means the storage keeps costing you until you remove it yourself.
Conclusion
UAEF separates agent evaluation from the framework that produced the agent. Adapters convert traces from LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Langfuse into a common format, and a generic JSON adapter handles other frameworks. The same 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions then apply regardless of how a team built the agent. UAEF evaluates individual traces or runs batch evaluations over historical traces, then stores results per experiment in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3. Teams can then compare runs across agent versions, detect regressions, and use the generated reports and insights to decide what to change in the next iteration. The web UI and the Python library share the same evaluation engine, so teams can start low-code and move to code without changing how scoring or storage works.
To get started, see the open source repository.

articles.title: Why Nvidia gave OpenShell to the CNCF
articles.text:
Why Nvidia gave OpenShell to the CNCF
Nvidia this week donated OpenShell, its open-source runtime for securing and governing AI agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. The teams that run it in production already work with Kubernetes and the CNCF’s other projects, says Ali Golshan, Nvidia’s senior director of AI software, who leads the project.
The company announced the move on Tuesday at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City. OpenShell, which Nvidia launched at its GTC conference in March, joins the CNCF as a Sandbox project, the foundation’s entry-level tier for early-stage projects. The CNCF formally accepted the project in late September.
The CNCF currently hosts 262 projects, including 155 at the Sandbox level, but it wasn’t the only possible home for OpenShell. The CNCF’s parent organization, the Linux Foundation, also runs the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), which hosts agentgateway, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol. Last month, the AAIF also took in OpenSandbox, a sandbox platform for AI agents that Alibaba contributed.
“Securing and creating trust around AI is really infrastructure. That’s really where you need to start.”
But as Golshan tells The New Stack, “Securing and creating trust around AI is really infrastructure. That’s really where you need to start.” That, he says, is what made the CNCF the logical place for the project to land.
The platform team is the user
OpenShell runs an agent inside a sandbox and enforces policies on which files, networks, credentials, and model endpoints that agent can reach. That enforcement happens in the infrastructure around the agent, according to the CNCF, and the project is adopting Cedar, another CNCF project, as its policy language.
Golshan says that securing agents takes a full stack solution and that Nvidia couldn’t build that stack one piece at a time.
“We can’t go build OpenShell and then go build the next pieces of it,” he says. “And a lot of those pieces, from an infrastructure standpoint, already existed in CNCF.” He cites Kubernetes itself, as well as the lightweight K3s distribution and service meshes, as examples of adjacent projects.
While building OpenShell, it also became clearer who would operate it, Golshan says. The profile matched the DevSecOps engineer who already stands up the rest of a company’s infrastructure.
He points to SAP as a company where DevOps and infrastructure teams stand up large agent environments.
The people who work with the agents may be engineers or researchers, he says, but the operators are “the same teams that are spinning up Kube and Linux and that whole stack.”
Ideally, those end users never see OpenShell. “You don’t really see Kubernetes,” Golshan says. “You just get that environment.”
When Jonathan Bryce, the CNCF’s executive director, thinks about where a technology should live, he tells The New Stack, the question to ask is “where are the people who are going to be making the decision about deploying, using, contributing to a specific technology?”
Agents started with people running OpenClaw on Mac Minis at home, Bryce says, but long-running, SaaS-style agents look more like other software run in a data center. Before OpenShell joined the CNCF, he adds, much of its early uptake came from neoclouds, GPU cloud providers that want to govern the workloads their customers run on their infrastructure.
Since OpenShell plugs into Kubernetes and other ecosystem projects, Bryce says, teams that already run that stack can easily add it to the workloads they want to contain.
Where agent projects live
Agents will exist throughout the entire stack, Bryce says, and the open-source projects that support them will spread across several foundations, each with a different kind of contributor.
The PyTorch Foundation, home to PyTorch, vLLM, DeepSpeed, and Ray, is where the engineers with deep AI expertise work. Bryce likens them to “the people who write Postgres.”
The CNCF, he says, is “the very broad set of folks who understand how to take mature systems and deploy, scale, observe, secure them.”
The AAIF, with protocols like MCP and A2A, is oriented toward the front-end experience of agents, Bryce says. He compares those protocols to HTTP and JavaScript, the standards that made millions of web apps possible.
The foundations are “Venn diagrams” and not silos, Bryce says, “and I think that’s good.” He points to KubeRay, which runs Ray workloads on Kubernetes, and to llm-d, which pairs vLLM with Kubernetes. The AAIF’s agentgateway works with Kubernetes, too.
The CNCF also tends to be flexible about where a project lands and lets maintainers “choose their own adventure to some extent,” he notes.
Meanwhile, Bryce says Nvidia’s visibility into how people run AI workloads is “unparalleled,” and the company brings new projects built on that experience to each KubeCon. “Some of those end up in a foundation,” he says. “Some of them don’t.”
Governance and a security committee
Golshan joined Nvidia in 2025, when the company acquired Gretel, the synthetic data startup he co-founded. Before that, he also co-founded StackRox, the Kubernetes security company Red Hat acquired in 2021.
He says the people who started OpenShell had been contributors to CNCF projects and knew its governance model from the inside.
That model fit what the team wanted, he says: a single mission for OpenShell and a place within a larger ecosystem.
Security governance, he says, is still being worked out. OpenShell is a Sandbox project for now, and Golshan says the team is “spending a bunch of time thinking through” how to put an independent security committee around it.
“One of the things that I think becomes very important is how do you manage things like disclosures, vulnerabilities,” he says. If OpenShell is going to become a critical piece of infrastructure, he adds, it needs contributions from many participants, “not necessarily us.”
Nvidia’s engineers will keep working on the project’s core, but Red Hat, Docker, and Canonical have been core contributors alongside Nvidia since the start.
When Nvidia opened OpenShell for early access in March, roughly 10 to 15 companies were contributing, Golshan says. The project dropped its alpha label with the 0.1.0 release in September, and the CNCF’s project page now lists about 380 contributing organizations.
“There are a lot of people who will engage at a certain level without it being in neutral governance,” Bryce says. “But once it makes that move to fully neutral governance, then that engagement gets a lot deeper.”
Adoption cycles that used to take two or three years now play out in six to 12 months, Bryce says, and he describes neutral governance as “rocket fuel” for integration and adoption.
“llm-d came into CNCF in March of this year, and they now have their 1.0 release,” Bryce says of the distributed inference framework, “and they have a whole set of companies that are actually running it in production, including some of the neoclouds.”
What Nvidia wants from the community
Golshan says OpenShell needs an ecosystem of tools around it before it can run at scale in production. About 50 to 60 companies, from startups to large vendors, have built on it so far, he says. OpenShell now has defined extension points for compute, credential management, inference providers, and policy enforcement, and he hopes the CNCF community will use them as a blueprint for tying OpenShell into the rest of the cloud native stack.
“It would be amazing if within the next six months we could support everything from Istio to Envoy to K3s for edge,” Golshan says.
Since the 0.1.0 release, early adopters that are moving agents from research into production have asked for recommendations on security, privacy, and observability tooling that works natively with OpenShell, he says. They also want help optimizing the agents and harnesses that run inside it.
Golshan describes a recent conversation in Berlin with someone who already knew Datadog and distributed tracing well. “I don’t even know what to observe for an agent,” he recalls the person saying.
Golshan wants what the community learns from those edge cases to flow back into the OpenShell core, the way it did for Kubernetes. “It’s pretty easy these days to say I’m going to bet my company on Kube,” he says. “Nobody’s going to get fired for that.” He hopes OpenShell will get there too.
An unsettled agent stack
The stack for training models is clear, and the one for inference is pretty settled, Bryce says, but for agents it’s “not at all.”
“If there’s not a clear stack, then the industry can’t come together on the most significant problems and actually make really fast, rapid progress,” he says.
Over the next six to 12 months, he expects experimentation to settle into answers on how OpenShell integrates with Kata Containers, gVisor, Agent Substrate, and existing OpenTelemetry projects. Once that happens, he expects agents to take off the way inference has over the last eight months.
Two of those projects are new to the CNCF. Google contributed Agent Substrate, its framework for running long-lived agents on Kubernetes, and the gVisor sandbox runtime at this week’s KubeCon. Nvidia says it’s working with Google on an integration between OpenShell and Agent Substrate.

articles.title: 30 heures de panne d’électricité : il branche sa maison sur son Renault Scénic et ne perd que 8 % de batterie
articles.text:
Quand on parle de la batterie d’une voiture électrique comme réserve d’énergie, on pense surtout au vehicle-to-grid (V2G), qui renvoie du courant vers le réseau pendant les pics de consommation, ou au vehicle-to-home (V2H), qui alimente directement une maison. Pour la plupart des propriétaires de véhicules électriques, ces deux usages restent relativement abstraits car ils sont peu développés.
En revanche, le vehicle-to-load (V2L), lui, est déjà répandu. Ce mode transforme le port de recharge en prise électrique, et il peut vraiment dépanner en cas de coupure de courant. Nick Gibbs, journaliste d’Automotive News Europe, l’a vérifié à ses dépens pendant ses vacances et raconte son expérience dans un article publié ce mardi 10 novembre. Privé d’électricité pendant 30 heures, il a branché sa maison de location sur son Renault Scénic électrique.
Le V2L du Renault Scénic à la rescousse
Fin octobre, une tempête a frappé le Lake District où la famille louait une maison, mettant à mal les installations électriques et coupant le courant. Les coupures sont rares au Royaume-Uni, et Nick Gibbs reconnaît que la panne l’a d’abord inquiété. Puis il s’est souvenu d’un petit sac livré avec la voiture. Dedans, il y avait un adaptateur (vendu 400 € en accessoire) qui se branche sur le port de recharge et la transforme en prise domestique. Une fois une rallonge branchée, la maison a retrouvé 3,7 kW de puissance électrique.
Seuls les appareils à portée de la rallonge étaient alimentés. Alors que le manuel de Renault déconseille de brancher plusieurs rallonges bout à bout, le journaliste britannique n’a pas voulu tenter le diable pour étendre son réseau de fortune. La famille a donc tout regroupé dans la cuisine : deux réfrigérateurs, plusieurs lampes sur pied, une station de recharge pour les téléphones et même le grille-pain au petit-déjeuner.
Pourquoi le four est resté éteint ?
En relisant le manuel, Nick Gibbs a découvert que le système est limité à 16 ampères. Sur le réseau britannique en 230 volts, ça correspond aux 3,7 kW maximum délivrés par le Scénic. Or, au Royaume-Uni, les fours électriques sont en général raccordés directement à l’installation de la maison, avec un interrupteur dédié, parce qu’ils tirent trop de puissance pour une prise classique. Le dîner s’est donc fait en mode camping, sur la plaque au gaz.
Certains modèles chinois vont plus loin. Le pick-up hybride rechargeable BYD Shark peut fournir jusqu’à 6,6 kW en V2L, de quoi faire tourner un four, une douche électrique et même une pompe à chaleur. Mais il faudrait alors des câbles bien plus adaptés pour supporter une telle charge sans danger.
Pour Nick Gibbs, les 3,7 kW du Scénic sont donc proches de la limite utile avec une rallonge standard. En Europe, les constructeurs vendent d’ailleurs surtout le V2L comme un accessoire de camping, tandis que les fabricants d’utilitaires le présentent comme un remplaçant du groupe électrogène sur des chantiers isolés.
Une panne qui n’a presque rien coûté à la batterie
En 30 heures, la famille a utilisé environ 8 % des 87 kWh du Scénic, soit à peu près 7 kWh. Le seul accroc est venu de la voiture elle-même lorsque le Scénic a coupé automatiquement le courant quand la demande est devenue trop faible. Nick Gibbs explique que son réfrigérateur ne consommait presque plus rien une fois arrivé à température, ce qui a laissé croire à la voiture que plus aucun appareil n’était branché.
Ce qu’il faut prévoir avant la prochaine coupure
Avant de brancher quoi que ce soit, lisez aussi la partie du manuel qui donne la puissance maximale. D’après le journaliste, le seul achat utile est une rallonge d’extérieur renforcée, plus sûre et plus pratique qu’un câble domestique. Pour l’hiver à venir, il compte faire attention à maintenir régulièrement son Scénic chargé à 100 % en cas de coups durs.

articles.title: Notion says Fireworks breach exposed customer AI chat transcripts
articles.text:
Notion, the digital workspace platform, disclosed that a security breach at its AI infrastructure provider, Fireworks AI, exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in a small number of workspaces.
The disclosure comes shortly after Fireworks AI confirmed that an attacker accessed its development environment via a third-party cloud provider on October 23 and compromised resource metadata, billing information, model weights, and datasets for some customers.
Fireworks AI experienced another breach in early October, when hackers accessed environment variables containing API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts.
Notion learned about the exposed chat transcripts after receiving an alert from Fireworks on November 2 about an exposed dataset that contained only synthetic test data.
Notion responded by cutting off traffic to Fireworks, deleting all data from the vendor’s systems, and halting training runs by November 3.
However, Fireworks confirmed on November 8 that customer data had been accessed, including that of Notion users.
Notion is a cloud-based workspace used for note-taking, document creation, internal wikis, project management, and task tracking. It includes an AI assistant that can answer questions, summarize content, and help draft text.
Fireworks AI enables Notion to run some of the open-weight models available through Notion AI and analyze stored conversations for Insights, a feature that gives workspace administrators visibility into how their teams use AI.
The exposed transcripts came from the Insights dataset specifically, which has now been disabled.
“Upon analysis of the dataset Fireworks AI gave us on November 8, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable,” Notion stated in an update.
"Unattributable means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results.”
Notion has also published a FAQ page about the incident, highlighting that Fireworks had contractually committed to zero data retention for Notion data.
According to the company, less than 1% of its users are impacted by the incident. Potentially affected workspace owners should review the data through Security incident review in Notion’s desktop web interface and share a link with members that lets them download their own transcripts.
Notion advises affected users to rotate any passwords, API keys, or other credentials entered into affected chats.
If neither a user nor their workspace owner has received a notice, Notion says no action is needed for now, and they are most likely not part of the impacted subset.

articles.title: AMD launches Zen 6 Epyc 9006 series with up to 256 cores, 512 threads, and TSMC N2
articles.text:
Highly anticipated: AMD has fully pulled back the curtain on its first Zen 6 CPU lineup. Debuting with Epyc server chips, the new architecture offers up to 256 cores and 512 threads at the top end, and AMD has promised substantial upgrades in AI, GPU hosting, and per-watt performance.
AMD's first Zen 6 Epyc processors, labeled the 9006 series and codenamed Venice, are now shipping to server clients, with SP7 systems arriving first and SP8 following in the first half of 2027. The company recently published the full technical specs for every SP7 and SP8 CPU in the lineup, mainly promoting their usefulness for AI workloads.
As expected, AMD's new flagship Epyc 9996 raises the maximum core count to 256, with 512 threads, clocked at up to 4.1GHz. With 1GB of L3 cache, it sits at a 2.55GHz base clock and defaults to 600W, though it can be configured down to 400W.
AMD's rack-density comparisons also reference a 400W, 256-core 9956, but that chip isn't on the published list. According to AMD's internal benchmarks, the 9996 at least doubles the Intel Xeon 6980P's performance in some tasks and more than triples it in others.
Early independent testing backs up the scale of the gains: Tom's Hardware measured a dual 9996 server at up to 93% faster than a dual Epyc 9965 in SPEC CPU 2026's intrate test. AMD lists the top-end chip at $14,904, but the lineup also scales all the way down to the eight-core, 16-thread Epyc 9016, at just $700.
Shifting to TSMC's N2 process node grants Epyc Venice up to a 2.6x improvement in performance per watt. AMD also claims 1.87x as many AI agents per CPU dollar compared to recent Intel Xeon processors.
With a 5.3GHz maximum boost clock on its high-frequency host-node parts, Venice also supposedly delivers up to 1.8x the LLM inference output of the previous Epyc generation. PCIe 6.0 doubles CPU-to-GPU I/O bandwidth, with up to 128 lanes in dual-socket SP7 systems and on SP8.

Since AMD recently declared itself a data center-first company, it remains unclear exactly when Zen 6's architectural advantages will filter down to consumer-grade products.
