articles.title: Broken: LearnArk’s mission to make tech truly accessible
articles.text:
When Adedolapo Oguntayo-Williams arrived at a conference hosted by one of Nigeria’s premier banks in 2024, she was pushing her daughter in a stroller. There was no ramp. If a multi-billion-naira financial institution could overlook something as fundamental as a wheelchair pathway, what chance did persons with disabilities have inside Africa’s digital economy? She stopped waiting for corporate panels to figure it out. From childhood dreams of the cockpit and washing dishes in Cyprus on a state scholarship, to negotiating vendor contracts for Ruff ‘n’ Tumble and running global cybersecurity compliance remotely from Abule Egba, Lagos, Adedolapo’s career has never followed a straight line. Now, she is using that enterprise playbook to bootstrap LearnArk Inclusion Academy—a tuition-free tech training engine designed to move deaf, blind, and physically impaired talent from the margins into high-value tech roles. “Inclusion had to go beyond conversations and good intentions,” she tells TechCabal. “It had to translate into access, opportunities, and the ability for people to build independent lives.” In this edition of My Life in Tech, JOHN ADOYI charts Adedolapo Oguntayo-Williams’s journey from industrial engineering to building digital ramps for Africa’s most overlooked talent.
In 2024, when Adedolapo Oguntayo-Williams, an inclusion educator and technology advocate, arrived at a conference hosted by one of Lagos’s leading commercial banks, she was pushing her daughter in a stroller. There was no accessible pathway for them.
An industrial engineer by training, she had spent years in business analysis and product management, learning to scrutinise operational problems and understand whom they affect. The experience stayed with her. “If a leading financial institution could overlook something as fundamental as an accessible pathway, what would the situation be like in many other public spaces?” she remembers thinking.
The incident prompted her to examine physical and digital accessibility wherever she went. More often than not, she observed that persons with disabilities were largely overlooked. She began asking what she could do to change that.
“I knew I could not solve Nigeria’s wider accessibility challenges on my own, but I could contribute in an area I understood: education and technology,” she says.
Her answer was the LearnArk Inclusion Academy, a free technology training programme for persons with disabilities offered through her edtech platform, LearnArk. “For me, inclusion had to go beyond conversations and good intentions. It had to translate into access, opportunities, and the ability for people to build independent lives.”
It is the latest chapter in a career that began with a very different ambition.
From a childhood dream to Cyprus
Oguntayo-Williams once aspired to become a pilot, drawn to aviation and the prospect of seeing the world from a distinct vantage point. At the time, women were rarely seen in the cockpit, which made the career path even more compelling. “I wanted to be the different one. I wanted to go into a field where there were not a lot of women,” she says.
By her fifth year in secondary school, she and her mother had begun researching aviation colleges in Nigeria. They found one in Zaria, Kaduna State, in north-west Nigeria, but the tuition was well beyond what her family could afford. She pivoted towards petroleum engineering and applied to the University of Lagos, but was offered an alternative course instead.
“You know how the Nigerian university thing is, where you apply to study something and they offer you something else. Obviously, I wasn’t having it,” she says.
An alternative route emerged through her pastor’s wife, whose son had secured admission to a university in Cyprus. She shared the institution’s prospectus with Oguntayo-Williams’s mother; industrial engineering was the closest discipline to petroleum engineering on offer.
“As God would have it, I gained admission to Eastern Mediterranean University to study industrial engineering,” she says. In 2012, at the age of 16, she left Nigeria for Cyprus.
“My university experience was honestly amazing,” she says.
In 2013, she was awarded the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) State Scholarship, which included a monthly stipend. That same year, she enrolled in business administration as a second major, eventually graduating top of her class in her department.
University also afforded her the latitude to explore broader entrepreneurial pursuits. During her second year, Oguntayo-Williams founded Deroy Consults, organising entrepreneurship seminars to encourage undergraduates to look beyond traditional degrees and build viable enterprises.
“Looking back, I am particularly proud that I did not limit my university experience to writing examinations and graduating,” she says. “I genuinely took advantage of the opportunities around me.”
Studying abroad also transformed her outlook on education and equity. Engaging with peers from diverse backgrounds in an unfamiliar academic environment demonstrated how access to quality education can expand what individuals believe they can accomplish.
“Most importantly, it gave me the confidence to see myself as someone who could contribute beyond my immediate environment,” she says.
She began reflecting on young people in Nigeria who possessed the intellect and drive to excel, but lacked comparable access to global opportunities. Although she was not yet certain how to act on that realisation, the thought remained with her.
“I left university with a broader understanding of what was possible, and a strong conviction that education should not merely prepare you for employment; it should equip you to create opportunities, solve systemic problems, and make an impact.”
Finding her footing in the workplace
After graduating in 2016, Oguntayo-Williams moved to the United States, working as a paralegal secretary in Brooklyn, New York. By 2017, however, she had returned to Nigeria.
A friend establishing a management consulting practice hired her as its director of marketing on a salary of ₦50,000 a month (around $140 at the prevailing 2017 exchange rate). She remained there for nine months.
“I didn’t want to stay at home, and I didn’t want to be a broke babe. Imagine being exposed to a lot of money in Cyprus and America, then coming back with no money,” she says.
In 2018, she left and joined Ruff ‘n’ Tumble, a Nigerian children’s fashion and apparel brand, first as an executive assistant and later as a buyer. The company had vendors in Turkey, and its founder, Adenike Ogunlesi, was looking for someone who could speak Turkish.
Oguntayo-Williams says she had learned the language while studying in Cyprus, where she lived on the Turkish side of the island.
“While I was in school, I took jobs in cafes as a dishwasher and waitress. Interacting with local people helped me pick up the language quickly,” she says.
At Ruff ‘n’ Tumble, she worked directly with Ogunlesi, whose approach shaped how she approached business. She recalls how the founder reacted whenever she came to her office without a pen and notebook.
“Sometimes I would go to her office without a pen and a book, and she would shout at me. She would say, ‘Your brain is not to jot down notes; your brain is to think.’ That scared me. I made sure I always had a pen and a book with me,” she says.
Ogunlesi also taught her to read beyond the subjects she naturally enjoyed and introduced her to negotiation. Those lessons have remained useful throughout her career.
“The skills I learned while working with Mrs Ogunlesi have been instrumental in everything I do,” she says. “Whether I am hiring, doing business or working in my current role at ShortPoint.”
Moving into technology
In 2019, Oguntayo-Williams left Ruff ‘n’ Tumble to join AXA Mansard as a business transformation analyst. A contact at the insurance and asset management group informed her of its transformation programme, which targeted first-class graduates, and urged her to apply.
“He told me, ‘Girl, you are a first-class graduate. I think you are perfect for this job.’ I said, ‘Put me on.’ I sent my CV, attended the interview, and got the job,” she says.
At AXA, she worked on core internal restructuring, replacing legacy manual workflows with automated digital systems. She describes the remit as an intersection of business analysis, product management, and process optimisation.
The company invested heavily in professional development, and she complemented internal training by pursuing external technical certifications independently.
“Beyond the training they provided, I took more courses, earned certifications, and kept improving myself,” she says.
AXA provided her initial formal grounding in enterprise technology and delivered her first industry credential, clarifying the operational landscape across the digital economy.
In August 2020, Oguntayo-Williams left AXA and joined ShortPoint, a global software company that develops tools for building and customising corporate intranet websites, as an associate product manager. Her experience in business transformation, alongside the additional courses and certifications she had pursued, helped her secure the role, and she worked remotely from her mother’s home in Abule Egba, Lagos.
“I would never have thought that I could be in Lagos and be working for someone in another continent,” she says.
Within a year, she was promoted to product manager, directing software development cycles from conception to release. By 2023, she transitioned into cybersecurity and compliance, taking charge of the company’s governance and information security operations.
The pivot carried significant regulatory responsibilities, but her grounding in product design and systems architecture gave her the requisite technical foundation.
“Cybersecurity and compliance deepened my focus on what allows organisations to innovate responsibly: protecting information, managing risk, and building trust,” she explains.
In January 2026, she broadened her remit further by assuming responsibilities as human resources manager.
“My experience has really been amazing. I’ve learned a lot, and I’ve been able to excel working with colleagues from diverse countries and nationalities. My interpersonal and leadership capabilities have matured considerably,” she says.
Building LearnArk
The conceptual framework for LearnArk originated during Oguntayo-Williams’s undergraduate years in Cyprus. Experiencing how an international academic environment unlocked professional mobility made her consider the millions of young Africans unable to study abroad who nonetheless warranted high-calibre instruction.
Her initial model was an online portal where accredited universities could deliver subsidised or tuition-free courses to African students. She initiated discussions with Rutgers University, while Eastern Mediterranean University agreed to supply curriculum content. She hired a software engineer and deployed her personal savings to construct the architecture.
“Eventually, I had to pause the project because I could not sustain it financially,” she admits.
In 2023, while on maternity leave, she re-evaluated the concept. Years of informally mentoring aspiring technology professionals had revealed that the primary obstacle was not access to academic theory, but navigating the transition into formal employment.
“People were eager to learn, but finding structured learning opportunities, practical guidance, mentorship, and a clear pathway to employment was difficult,” she says.
That deficit defined LearnArk’s strategic pivot. Shifting away from an academic marketplace, she restructured the venture around practical, industry-aligned technical instruction.
“I wanted to address the gap between wanting to enter technology and knowing how to take practical steps towards a career,” she says. “People can find lots of information online, but they still struggle to understand which pathway fits them, what skills are required, and how to apply what they learn in a commercial environment.”
LearnArk now runs structured cohorts in product management, data analytics, cybersecurity, and emerging technologies, augmented by interview coaching and recruitment placement support.
“LearnArk has trained more than 1,000 learners, which is an important milestone, but I want us to deepen how we track outcomes: whether learners secure roles, apply their skills in the workplace, or advance within their respective disciplines,” she says.
Building an inclusive pathway into technology
Central to this mandate is the LearnArk Inclusion Academy, through which Oguntayo-Williams delivers tuition-free virtual technology instruction to persons with disabilities.
“We designed the academy to make technology education genuinely accessible to individuals with physical disabilities, visual impairments, and hearing impairments,” she says.
Candidates register via the portal, specifying their preferred tracks and accessibility requirements. The operational team and mentors provide specialised support throughout the cohort, while the organisation works to scale up its closed-captioning capabilities and sign-language interpretation.
“I have been bootstrapping the academy from inception. There are real costs attached to providing learner support, upgrading accessibility tools, and expanding our intake,” she says. “We are open to strategic partnerships, institutional grants, and technical resources that will help us scale our reach without compromising our commitment to zero tuition fees.”
Her underlying objective remains straightforward.
“For me, the real measure of success is not simply the number of people we enrol, but whether the academy enables individuals who have historically faced structural barriers to acquire skills, secure viable opportunities, and participate meaningfully in the technology ecosystem,” she says.
Balancing work, family and purpose
For Oguntayo-Williams, one of the hardest lessons of building a career and a business while raising a family was learning that she could not do everything at once.
After experiencing burnout, she realised she could not keep relying on motivation or assume she had to do everything herself to prove her commitment. The experience changed how she approaches work. She now plans her week ahead, prioritises fewer tasks, delegates where possible and sets clearer boundaries.
“I no longer see being constantly busy as proof of impact,” she says. “I want to build things that create real value and can continue to grow without requiring me to sacrifice every other part of my life to keep them going.”
Over the next year, she wants to strengthen LearnArk’s learning pathways, build more industry partnerships and create better opportunities for learners to turn their training into employment and career progression. She also hopes to expand the Inclusion Academy, so more people with disabilities can access technology education, mentorship and opportunities in the digital economy.
Ultimately, Oguntayo-Williams wants to be remembered for more than the positions she held or organisations she built.
“I want to be remembered for the doors I helped open, the systems and policies I helped improve, and the people whose lives became different because I chose to make a contribution,” she says.

articles.title: Más de 30 años: un programador muestra el programa más antiguo que todavía funciona en Windows 11
articles.text:
Si alguna vez te has preguntado hasta dónde llega la compatibilidad de Windows, un desarrollador que firma como Enlyth ha intentado responderlo buscando la aplicación con interfaz gráfica más antigua que todavía arranca en Windows 11 sin emulación ni modificaciones. El autor lo cuenta en su blog, donde apunta a que la búsqueda acabó a principios de los noventa, aunque con un poco de trampa puede llegar a retrasarse más atrás.
Sin sitio para los 16 bits. Windows 11 no puede ejecutar programas de 16 bits. Y es que, según la documentación de compatibilidad de Microsoft, las versiones x64 y ARM de Windows no admiten código x86 de 16 bits de ningún tipo, así que cualquier candidato tiene que ser una aplicación de 32 bits. Eso lleva a los inicios de Windows NT, cuya primera versión, Windows NT 3.1, salió el 27 de julio de 1993 como sistema de 32 bits.
Un solitario de 1993. Pero hay un atajo que adelanta un poco el reloj. Como explica en la misma entrada, en un foro anónimo alguien le habló de Win32s, unas bibliotecas que permitían ejecutar aplicaciones de 32 bits sobre Windows 3.1, o sea que hacían de puente entre las dos épocas. Las primeras versiones de Win32s traían el FreeCell, y la copia que encontró, del 22 de febrero de 1993, funciona en Windows 11 sin tocar nada.
Un reproductor de CD de 1992. El desarrollador siguió buscando en versiones preliminares de Windows NT 3.1 hasta dar con el reproductor de CD de la compilación 347, enlazado el 16 de noviembre de 1992, que también arranca en Windows 11. Eso sí, como su ordenador no tiene lector de CD, al abrirlo aparece un aviso de que no hay ninguna unidad de CD-ROM, así que para comprobar que reproduce música tiró de una pequeña biblioteca que emula la unidad con audio falso, según detalla el propio autor.
Hay un truco para ir más atrás en el tiempo. Para ir más atrás hay que saltarse las reglas del experimento. Con otvdm, una adaptación de Wine para programas de 16 bits que permite ejecutarlos en Windows de 64 bits, Enlyth consiguió jugar en Windows 11 al Reversi de Windows 1.01, fechado el 15 de noviembre de 1985. Es la versión para ordenador de un juego de tablero de la década de 1880 que se atribuye a Lewis Waterman, aunque el autor admite que recurrir a otvdm es como hacer trampas.
Por lo tanto, sin ayudas ni pequeñas trampas el programa más antiguo que ha logrado hacer funcionar en Windows 11 tiene unos 34 años, pero si recurre a la adaptación de Wine que ha utilizado para añadir una capa de compatibilidad la cifra va hasta los 41 años.

articles.title: Microsoft promete hasta un 40% más de velocidad en los Windows 11 con solo 8 GB de RAM
articles.text:
Durante las últimas dos décadas, la receta de Microsoft para hacer que Windows tuviera un comportamiento más fluido era sencilla: instalar más memoria RAM. Sin embargo, cuando la memoria RAM se ha convertido en un bien tan escaso (y sobre todo, caro. Carísimo), a Microsoft no le ha quedado más remedio que hacer lo que tenían que haber hecho desde el principio: optimizar el uso de recursos de Windows.
Por eso, Microsoft ha admitido que les ha tocado arremangarse para resolverlo, haciendo que Windows sea capaz de funcionar de forma más fluida en equipos con 8 GB de RAM.
Más datos en RAM, menos visitas al disco. Pavan Davuluri, jefe de Windows y dispositivos de Microsoft, publicó las cifras de esa mejora. Habla de una mayor capacidad de respuesta y de una multitarea hasta un 40% más rápida en equipos de 8 GB. Las cifras de la mejora suenan muy bien, pero antes de celebrarlas, toca ver cómo se midieron.
El cambio de mayor peso es una compresión de memoria ajustada para 8 GB. Según indicaba el responsable de dispositivos de Microsoft, Windows puede conservar hasta 2 GB más de datos activos en la memoria RAM, mientras que antes se apoyaba en la memoria de almacenamiento. Así, una pestaña o una app que dejaste abierta en segundo plano implica una carga menor para el sistema cuando vuelves a ella.
Hay recortes más pequeños que también contribuyen a esa mejora en el rendimiento. En equipos de hasta 8 GB de RAM, el panel de Widgets solo carga al abrirlo y libera más de 200 MB. Las apps de Office también se han ajustado el cinturón y ahora reducen su consumo hasta 360 MB.
Una prueba con letra pequeña. Tal y como indica la compañía en su escrito, el 40% de mejora en el rendimiento sale de un solo ensayo en un HP OmniBook 3 con Snapdragon X Plus y 8 GB de RAM. Como se puede ver en un vídeo publicado por Microsoft, la prueba consistió en abrir 20 pestañas de Edge, un vídeo 4K y archivos grandes de Office, uno tras otro. Se comparó el tiempo con una versión anterior del sistema. La propia empresa aclara que no es un benchmark en sí mismo, sino una demostración de cómo ha mejorado el sistema al ejecutarlo sobre el mismo hardware.
La mejora del 20% en la experiencia de uso de Windows sale de telemetría que mide los procesos de Inicio, Búsqueda o el Explorador, cuando se usa un equipo con 8 GB de RAM. Es decir, lo razonable en este caso no es esperara una mejora del 40% en su rendimiento, sino tomarlo como el mejor dato que Microsoft ha podido recoger en sus pruebas con un mismo equipo con un software determinado y un escenario de uso acotado. No es un escenario de uso real en el día a día de los usuarios…pero algo es algo.
El trabajo sigue. Los de Redmond preparan menos componentes duplicados entre apps y funciones de Windows para reducir la carga que implica que un mismo componente deba activarse por duplicado cuando dos aplicaciones hacen uso de él. Que haga falta tanta limpieza y optimización dice mucho de lo cargado que estaba el sistema desde el principio.
De hecho, este problema se ha hecho tan evidente que en Microsoft se creó un proyecto interno denominado Windows K2, que tiene como principal objetivo reducir las redundancias y simplificar procesos de Windows para hacerlo más ligero, asumiendo un compromiso por mejorar la calidad de uso de Windows.
La IA a condicionado el cambio. Microsoft ha insistido mucho en que, para garantizar el mejor rendimiento de los equipos, eran necesarios 16 GB de RAM y, de hecho, lo convirtió en un requisito técnico para los PC Copilot+. Es decir, que realmente, quien condicionaba el incremento del consumo de RAM no era el sistema operativo en sí mismo, sino las funciones de IA de Copilot que corrían paralelas al sistema.
La escasez de memoria RAM por la decisión de los fabricantes de priorizar su producción para abastecer las necesidades de memoria de los centros de datos ha provocado que Microsoft deba apretarse el cinturón y poner a dieta a Windows y la forma en la que gestiona esas funciones de IA. Lo que la IA te da, la IA te lo quita.
Un mercado que no se puede ampliar. Además del uso de funciones de IA que los usuarios no habían pedido, hay otro elefante en la habitación al que Microsoft no ha tenido más remedio que mirar a los ojos: quien ya tiene un equipo de 8 GB de RAM y no puede ampliarle la memoria por su precio.
Microsoft amplió hasta octubre de 2027 las actualizaciones de seguridad gratuitas de Windows 10 para consumidores. Ese margen se acaba y Microsoft debe convencer a sus actuales usuarios de Windows 10 que actualizarse a Windows 11 es la mejor opción, y no un castigo que implique gastarse un dineral en ampliar su memoria RAM o en comprar un nuevo equipo. Si la IA de Microsoft va a vivir en Windows, le conviene que esos equipos aguanten su peso para que la compañía no se pegue un tiro en el pie. Sobre todo, tras el lanzamiento de los MacBook Neo con menos requisitos técnicos y con un precio inferior al de la media de portátiles.

articles.title: Expensive accelerators, no workload-level visibility: Introducing Amazon CloudWatch accelerated compute insights
articles.text:
Expensive accelerators, no workload-level visibility: Introducing Amazon CloudWatch accelerated compute insights
Accelerator bills have become one of the largest lines in the infrastructure budget. GPUs have become the most expensive resource in modern computing, and yet most organizations operate them with little visibility. A single training cluster can run for days and cost millions of dollars. Most organizations pool these accelerators across teams on shared clusters to keep them busy. But in these shared environments, platform teams cannot answer basic questions: which team is using which accelerators? Is the inference workload generating tokens efficiently? What is wasting money?
When a workload degrades (a failing accelerator, a thermally throttled node), teams find out only after a run crashes or the bill arrives. The device-level signals needed to find the cause (request traces, kernel logs, memory metrics from the accelerator itself) are not collected or connected. Without a way to isolate the problem to a single accelerator, teams fall back on cycling the entire instance, surrendering seven healthy GPUs to address a fault on one, and often waiting on scarce capacity to get the instance back.
“GPUs have become the most expensive resource in modern computing, and yet most organizations operate them with little visibility.”
Accelerator observability turns those blind spots into answers. It tells you who is using your accelerators, whether they are healthy, and what the waste is costing you, all the way down to a single device. That way, you fix one bad GPU instead of eight, and spend your accelerator budget on real work instead of idle capacity.
Amazon CloudWatch accelerated compute insights, a new capability launched at KubeCon North America 2026, gives you a single operational view of every accelerator in your fleet. It shows platform and AI teams who are using their GPU and AWS AI Accelerators capacity across Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). In this post, we walk through what accelerated compute insights does, how it works on Amazon EKS, and how to get started.
What accelerated compute insights does
Accelerated compute insights gives you a single operational view of every accelerator in your fleet. It shows how each accelerator is being used, detects failures and bottlenecks as they happen, estimates the cost impact of each problem, and connects those findings to the actions that resolve them.
“Accelerated compute insights holds accelerator telemetry, workload boundaries, and pricing data together, a combination that monitoring tools that only see metrics cannot replicate.”
On Amazon EKS, it supports NVIDIA GPUs and NVIDIA GPUs, AWS Trainium and AWS Inferentia. Metrics from NVIDIA GPUs and Inferentia are normalized into a common schema and presented in a single Accelerator Health view, so teams running mixed fleets manage every accelerator type in one place.
Fleet visibility with Kubernetes context
Every accelerator in your EKS cluster is enriched with Kubernetes metadata: pod, namespace, node, node group, and custom labels (team, application). You see utilization by team and workload across your entire fleet.
Accelerated Compute Insights auto-detects MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) partitioned GPUs and shows utilization and memory for each MIG instance, along with the pod using it. It also recognizes other partitioning schemes, including Kubernetes DRA (dynamic Resource allocation) and time-slicing, by reading device labels. No configuration required.
Cost waste identification
Accelerated compute insights connects real-time accelerator telemetry to workload boundary events and AWS pricing data to surface recoverable waste in three categories:
- Right-sizing opportunities: workloads running on more powerful instances than the task requires.
- Training efficiency gaps: low tensor core (MFU) utilization relative to the workload’s own historical baseline, indicating the job is not getting full value from the hardware.
- Inference below hardware capacity: endpoints serving fewer requests than the hardware supports, based on customer-emitted throughput correlated with device utilization.
For each finding, accelerated compute insights identifies the specific workload or node responsible, helping users troubleshoot and optimize. This works because accelerated compute insights holds accelerator telemetry, workload boundaries, and pricing data together, a combination that monitoring tools that only see metrics cannot replicate.
Note: CloudWatch accelerated compute insights is an operational tool, not a billing or chargeback tool. Cost figures are estimates intended to guide operational decisions. For authoritative cost and usage accounting, continue to use AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report.
Device-level remediation
When an inference workload experiences performance degradation or inefficient token generation, accelerated compute insights helps identify GPU bottlenecks, inefficient accelerator utilization, and potential resource waste. By automatically collecting and correlating inference performance metrics, request traces, logs, and accelerator telemetry, it provides end-to-end visibility into workload performance and GPU efficiency. With AI-powered insights and troubleshooting capabilities, customers can quickly identify root causes, optimize token throughput, reduce inference latency, and improve accelerator utilization without disrupting healthy workloads.
“It distinguishes between failure modes that call for different actions. By default, the agent presents a specific, evidence-backed action plan for you to approve.”
You can also route health events to the AWS DevOps Agent for deeper investigation. The agent reasons across accelerator telemetry, CloudWatch logs, recent infrastructure changes, job configuration, and any runbooks you have authored. It distinguishes between failure modes that call for different actions. For example, a node with an accelerating memory-error trend that needs replacement versus a driver issue that clears with a restart. By default, the agent presents a specific, evidence-backed action plan for you to approve. For a faster loop, you can opt in to let it carry out well-understood remediations through AWS APIs on its own.
How it works on EKS
Collection paths converge at the CloudWatch Metrics API. For NVIDIA GPUs, the CloudWatch agent and NVIDIA Exporter collect device-level metrics. The Unified Accelerator Health Layer normalizes GPU and Inferentia collection paths into a common schema and presents them in a single dashboard.
The diagram below illustrates how Amazon CloudWatch accelerated compute insights provides end-to-end observability for AI inference workloads and accelerator efficiency on Amazon EKS. Customers can install the CloudWatch Observability add-on from the CloudWatch console or CloudWatch Omni to collect NVIDIA GPU metrics and inference workload performance metrics, logs, and traces. The telemetry data is ingested into CloudWatch’s centralized storage through the CloudWatch OpenTelemetry (OTLP) endpoint. Customers can monitor inference workload performance and GPU utilization directly in the CloudWatch console or leverage CloudWatch Omni and its AI-powered investigation to troubleshoot performance issues, identify accelerator inefficiencies, and optimize resource utilization.
Getting started on EKS
Install the CloudWatch Observability add-on with OTel Container Insights enabled. The add-on discovers your accelerators and collects everything the dashboard needs. No per-node setup, no agents to manage, no collection pipelines to configure. Your fleet appears in the console within minutes and stays current as nodes join and leave the cluster.
Step 1: Get your data flowing
If you run self-hosted inference on Amazon EKS, install or upgrade the Amazon CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on to v7.0.1 or above. The add-on discovers every NVIDIA GPU and AWS Inferentia device in your cluster and starts sending OpenTelemetry data, with no per-node setup and no collection pipelines to configure.
You can enable the add-on using eksctl, Helm, or Terraform. Check examples with eksctl and Helm below:
Using eksctl
eksctl create addon \
  --name amazon-cloudwatch-observability \
  --cluster your-cluster-name \
  --region your-region
Using Helm
helm repo add aws-observability https://aws-observability.github.io/helm-charts
helm install amazon-cloudwatch-observability \
  aws-observability/amazon-cloudwatch-observability \
  --namespace amazon-cloudwatch --create-namespace
Step 2: Use your data in CloudWatch Omni
Once telemetry is flowing, open CloudWatch Omni. Omni is built for the teams that own the inference code and fix it. Instead of a wall of infrastructure metrics, you get an application-centric view: your inference workloads appear next to the services and AI agents that call them, with accelerator health, utilization, and waste tied to each workload.
When an endpoint shows low throughput or a high time to first token, Omni helps you trace the problem to the workload, node, or single accelerator responsible and shows what to change, whether that’s a configuration update or a code fix. You can go from detection to fix without switching tools.
“Instead of a wall of infrastructure metrics, you get an application-centric view: your inference workloads appear next to the services and AI agents that call them, with accelerator health, utilization, and waste tied to each workload.”
Platform and infrastructure teams who need a fleet-wide view, such as accelerator allocation across many teams, idle capacity, or a cross-account summary, can also see the same data on the accelerated compute insights page in the CloudWatch console.
Ready to see your own fleet? This documentation walks you through getting started.
Where this fits in the Amazon EKS observability stack
Amazon CloudWatch accelerated compute insights builds on the observability foundation we have been shipping for EKS throughout 2025 and 2026: OTel Container Insights for infrastructure metrics, Application Performance Monitoring for application telemetry, and Container Network Observability for the network layer. Accelerated compute insights adds the missing layer, the accelerators themselves. Teams get GPU and Inferentia utilization, cost waste, and device-level health, all enriched with Kubernetes metadata and connected to automated remediation, in the same place they already monitor everything else
- OTel Container Insights for EKS (GA, June 2026) collects infrastructure metrics from your cluster using OpenTelemetry, with up to 150 descriptive labels per metric and PromQL support in CloudWatch Query Studio.
- Application Performance Monitoring enabled by default (February 2026) in the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on gives you application-level telemetry out of the box.
- Container Network Observability (November 2025) provides service maps, flow tables, and network performance metrics for EKS traffic, powered by CloudWatch Network Flow Monitor.
- Observability patterns for AI agents on Amazon EKS (October 2026) documents observability patterns for agentic AI workloads running on EKS.
Getting started today
Amazon CloudWatch accelerated compute insights is available today in all Regions where CloudWatch Omni is available. To get started:
- Install or upgrade to the latest CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on on your cluster.
- Open CloudWatch Omni to see your inference workloads, with accelerator health and waste for each one.
- Troubleshoot and optimize from the workload view, from time to first token down to a single device.
Check out the documentation for more.

articles.title: Así funcionan estos procesadores que anticipan la llegada de un tifón y aumentan el tiempo de reacción
articles.text:
AMD ha presentado la sexta generación de procesadores EPYC, una familia para centros de datos que busca reducir el tiempo necesario para realizar cálculos complejos en áreas como la ciencia, computación o incluso, en la predicción meteorológica.
Los modelos incluyen versiones con hasta 256 núcleos (las unidades internas que ejecutan instrucciones) y están orientados a tareas como inteligencia artificial, servicios en la nube, investigación científica y simulaciones técnicas.
Una de las aplicaciones mostradas por la empresa tecnológica está vinculada con el pronóstico del clima.
En una prueba con simulaciones de trayectorias de tifones en Taiwán, una configuración de 256 núcleos completó una previsión de tres días en 2,66 horas. La plataforma de referencia empleada en la comparación tardó 7,38 horas. Para una proyección de cinco días, el cálculo demoró 4,41 horas, frente a 12,28.
Estos tiempos pueden ampliar el margen para que meteorólogos y autoridades estudien una amenaza y definan respuestas ante fenómenos como tifones, lluvias intensas o vientos fuertes.
El procesador no anticipa el clima por sí mismo: ejecuta las operaciones matemáticas que requieren los programas especializados para elaborar una previsión.
Qué puede hacer un procesador en el pronóstico meteorológico
Un pronóstico meteorológico se construye a partir de grandes cantidades de información. Los modelos reúnen datos sobre temperatura, humedad, presión atmosférica, viento, lluvia y otras variables. Esos registros pueden proceder de estaciones terrestres, radares, satélites, boyas o globos meteorológicos.
El software organiza esa información y aplica ecuaciones físicas para estimar cómo evolucionará la atmósfera durante las siguientes horas o días. Para hacerlo, divide el territorio observado en una cuadrícula formada por zonas pequeñas.
En cada una calcula qué podría ocurrir con el aire, las nubes, el viento y la precipitación. Luego relaciona los resultados de todas las zonas para representar, por ejemplo, el avance de una tormenta o la posible trayectoria de un tifón.
La compañía de hardware utilizó una plataforma denominada WRF para medir el desempeño de los nuevos procesadores. WRF es una aplicación de pronóstico meteorológico empleada en estudios de clima, meteorología y geociencias.
En la demostración se usó un modelo con una resolución de 2,5 kilómetros. Eso significa que el área analizada se dividió en sectores de aproximadamente esa dimensión.
Una cuadrícula más detallada puede ofrecer una representación más precisa de las condiciones atmosféricas en un área. A la vez, requiere una cantidad mayor de cálculos. Cada sector debe intercambiar información con los que lo rodean y actualizar sus resultados de manera constante durante la simulación.
La empresa liderada por Lisa Su indicó que WRF depende en buena medida de la memoria. En términos simples, los núcleos necesitan acceder y modificar datos de forma continua.
Si esa transferencia resulta lenta, una parte de la capacidad de cálculo queda a la espera. La sexta generación incorpora hasta 1,6 TB por segundo de ancho de banda de memoria, una medida que expresa cuánta información puede mover el sistema en un segundo.
Más núcleos, memoria y conexiones para los centros de datos
La plataforma se basa en las arquitecturas Zen 6 y Zen 6c. La firma estadounidense indicó modelos con hasta 256 núcleos Zen 6c, pensados para concentrar una mayor capacidad de procesamiento, y versiones con hasta 96 núcleos Zen 6, destinadas a tareas que necesitan un rendimiento más alto por núcleo.
Los procesadores admiten hasta 8 TB de memoria por socket. El socket es el espacio de la placa base en el que se instala el chip. Esta capacidad permite trabajar con modelos de mayor tamaño y conjuntos de datos más amplios dentro de un mismo servidor.
La nueva familia también incorpora PCI Express 6.0, una tecnología que conecta el procesador con otros componentes del equipo, como sistemas de almacenamiento, redes y aceleradores.
La empresa tecnológica prevé variantes dirigidas al cómputo técnico, los servicios empresariales, la nube, la inteligencia artificial y el diseño de chips.

articles.title: Introducing usage-based pricing for Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Introducing usage-based pricing for Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming
Usage-based metering for bidirectional streaming solves a software billing problem for real-time speech AI. Customers deploying streaming models on Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming pay for the endpoint infrastructure that hosts the model. Separately, model providers listing on AWS Marketplace need a way to charge for what customers consume during a live stream. Today, we’re announcing usage-based metering for Amazon SageMaker bidirectional (bidi) streaming inference, so model providers can report actual usage for the AWS Marketplace software charge. Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges still apply.
Deepgram, the real-time speech AI company, is the launch partner for this capability, bringing usage-based Speech-to-Text (STT) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) billing to AWS Marketplace. This post builds on a series of innovations between Deepgram and AWS. First, we introduced bidirectional streaming for real-time inference on Amazon SageMaker AI, which supports long-lived bidirectional streams between clients and model servers. Then, Deepgram enhanced Amazon SageMaker AI support with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) temporary delegation, simplifying secure authentication for enterprise deployments, and expanded observability with enhanced metrics. Now, with usage-based metering, we further strengthen the foundation for production real-time AI, aligning billing with how customers consume streaming and real-time AI workloads.
Why streaming broke the existing billing model
With AWS Marketplace software metering for SageMaker AI real-time request-response inference, model providers can report a unit count in an HTTP response header. AWS Marketplace uses that quantity for the software charge. This works for request-response APIs where the billable quantity is known when the response is sent.
Bidirectional streaming is different. A client streams audio and receives transcriptions through the SageMaker AI API using an HTTP/2 event stream. SageMaker AI connects to the model server over WebSockets. A session can last 30 seconds or 30 minutes. Usage accumulates as the session runs, and the final total isn’t known until it ends. A response header alone can’t report periodic usage during that live session.
Hourly software pricing can charge customers while a model is available, including quiet periods. With usage-based metering, providers can align the AWS Marketplace software charge with reported usage. SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges remain separate and continue to apply while the endpoint is provisioned.
How companion metadata streaming works
The solution introduces a second WebSocket connection alongside the existing inference stream. When a bidirectional streaming session starts, SageMaker AI establishes two connections to the model server:
- Data connection: carries inference request and response data, the existing bidirectional stream.
- Metadata connection: a companion WebSocket dedicated to metering data.
Model servers opt in by returning one header on the WebSocket upgrade response:
X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Supported: true
SageMaker AI then opens a companion WebSocket to the model server at /invocations-bidirectional-stream-metadata. Both connections carry the same X-Amzn-SageMaker-Request-Id header, which the model server uses to correlate metering records with the active inference session.
The model server sends metering data as JSON text frames on the metadata connection. Send records at a frequency that matches the billing model: incrementally as usage accrues (recommended), either as each unit is consumed or as periodic batches of units consumed since the previous record. Send any final record as soon as the session ends. Each frame contains exactly one metering record, rather than an array of records. The metadata stream has a rate quota of one message per second per connection, with a maximum message size of 512 bytes.
We recommend sending metering records incrementally as usage accrues. This reduces the amount of usage left unreported if a session ends unexpectedly. Transport delivery alone does not establish that usage has been billed. Validate reported units against AWS Marketplace reports and buyer charges.
Metering messages use the inference.count dimension, and ConsumedUnits supplies the quantity for that dimension. If the product charges per second of audio, a record reporting 12 minutes of metered audio carries 720 seconds as ConsumedUnits: 720. The dimension name doesn’t mean one unit per request. The provider defines which audio counts as metered usage, and the AWS Marketplace offer maps the unit to its price. The listing shows one price per unit, labeled per request, with up to three decimal places. The ClientToken field supports idempotency. If a duplicate token arrives on the same connection, SageMaker AI drops the duplicate message silently.
The metadata connection runs over TCP, which provides ordered, reliable delivery at the transport layer. If it fails to establish or drops mid-session, inference continues by default because X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Required defaults to false. Set this header to true when the provider must stop inference if the metadata stream becomes unavailable. This choice trades inference availability for metering continuity. It doesn’t guarantee that malformed or dropped records are billed.
What this means for customers
If you deploy real-time AI models for transcription, contact centers, voice agents, or captioning, the new metering model changes how the AWS Marketplace software charge is calculated. SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges still apply.
Transparent, per-unit billing through AWS Marketplace means usage flows directly into your AWS bill. You get consolidated AWS billing, negotiated rates through private offers, and no separate billing relationship with the model provider to manage.
Pay for audio processed according to the product’s unit definition. If the product charges per second of audio, 12 minutes of metered audio equals 720 billable seconds and ConsumedUnits: 720. An open connection lasting 12 minutes doesn’t, by itself, define the billable audio quantity. The provider’s counting rules determine the metered usage, whereas endpoint infrastructure charges remain separate.
Model providers can offer negotiated per-unit rates or fixed-price contracts through AWS Marketplace private offers.
We recommend discussing directly with your AWS account representative or partner representative.
What this means for model providers
If you’re a model provider listing on AWS Marketplace, you can configure your model server to report usage during streaming inference sessions through companion metadata streaming.
The SageMaker Marketplace Onboarding Agent Skill accelerates onboarding with an opt-in inference metering path. Its starter templates advertise metadata-stream support and build validated, incremental ConsumedUnits frames for the companion WebSocket. Review and production-harden the code before submission.
Align billing with your pricing model by defining what one unit represents and reporting units as the session progresses. AWS Marketplace charges one per-unit price for real-time inference.
The following three-step walkthrough describes how to integrate your model server to report metering data during bidirectional streaming inference sessions.
Step 1: Opt in using data WebSocket response headers
When SageMaker AI opens the data WebSocket connection to your model server, include these headers in your WebSocket upgrade (101) response:
|  | Header | Required | Values | Description | 
| 1 | X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Supported | Yes (to opt in) | TRUE | Signals that your model server supports the companion metadata stream. If absent or not true, no metadata connection is attempted. Without the metadata stream, the session is not metered for the model provider’s software charge. | 
| 2 | X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Required | No | true / false | This header only takes effect when X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Supported is true. If true, inference stops when the metadata connection fails. If false or absent, inference continues in data-only mode. Default: false. Choose true when metering continuity takes priority over inference availability. This setting doesn’t guarantee billing for malformed or dropped records. | 
| 3 | X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Invocation-Path | No | Custom path string | Overrides the default metadata WebSocket path. Default: /invocations-bidirectional-stream-metadata. | 
Step 2: Accept the metadata WebSocket connection
After your model server returns X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Supported: true, SageMaker AI opens a second WebSocket connection to your model server at the default path /invocations-bidirectional-stream-metadata (or the custom path you specified by using X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Invocation-Path).
SageMaker AI includes the header X-Amzn-SageMaker-Request-Id on both the data and metadata WebSocket handshakes. Your model server must do the following:
- Accept the WebSocket upgrade on the metadata path.
- Use X-Amzn-SageMaker-Request-Id to correlate the metadata connection with the corresponding data connection for the same inference session.
Step 3: Send metering messages
Send metering data as a JSON object in a WebSocket text frame on the metadata connection. Each frame must contain exactly one metering record. In this example, the product charges per second of audio, and the record reports 12 minutes of metered audio as 720 units:
Message fields:
|  | Field | Required | Type | Constraints | Description | 
| 1 | Metering | Yes | Object | — | Container for the metering record. | 
| 2 | Metering.Dimension | Yes | String | Must be inference.count | The billing dimension. Must be inference.count. | 
| 3 | Metering.ConsumedUnits | Yes | Number | 0 or greater | The units consumed since your previous record. Each record is billed separately. A value of 0 is accepted but not billed. | 
| 4 | Metering.ClientToken | No | String | Max 64 characters | A unique token (for example, a UUID) for idempotency. If the same ClientToken is sent multiple times on the same connection, only the first occurrence is recorded. | 
Send metering records incrementally as usage accrues to reduce unreported usage if a session ends unexpectedly. Reconcile the reported quantities with AWS Marketplace reports and buyer charges to verify billing, including interrupted-session tests.
Constraints and limits
|  | Limit | Value | Notes | 
| 1 | Maximum message size | 512 bytes | Total size of the JSON text frame | 
| 2 | Maximum send rate | 1 message per second per connection | Exceeding this rate might result in dropped messages | 
| 3 | Maximum Dimension length | 128 characters | — | 
| 4 | Maximum ClientToken length | 64 characters | — | 
| 5 | Messages per frame | Exactly 1 | Don’t batch multiple metering records in a single frame | 
| 6 | Frame type | Text frames only | Binary frames are not supported for metering | 
Error handling and failure modes
The Required header controls what happens when the metadata connection becomes unavailable. Set it to true to stop inference, or use the default false to let inference continue in data-only mode. This is a choice between metering continuity and inference availability. Malformed messages can still be dropped with either setting.
|  | Scenario | Required = true | Required = false (default) | 
| 1 | Metadata WebSocket fails to connect | Data stream is terminated | Data stream continues normally (data-only mode) | 
| 2 | Metadata WebSocket drops mid-session | Data stream is terminated | Data stream continues normally. Metering stops | 
| 3 | Malformed metering message | Message is dropped. Metadata connection stays open | Message is dropped. Metadata connection stays open | 
| 4 | Data connection breaks mid-stream | Metadata stream is closed | Metadata stream is closed | 
List your model on AWS Marketplace
- Register your AWS account as an AWS Marketplace seller. For paid products, complete the tax and banking information.
- Create a SageMaker AI model package from your container in a supported publishing Region, and an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Marketplace can assume to read it.
- In AWS Partner Central, choose Build, Machine learning, then Create machine learning product, and add the model package as the first version.
- Choose per-inference pricing. You set one per-unit price for real-time inference across all instance types, shown per request with up to three decimal places. You also set an hourly price for each batch transform instance type. Choose the pricing model when you create the listing because you can’t switch a released listing between hourly and per-inference pricing.
- After validation, request Public visibility. For enterprise buyers, extend private offers with a negotiated per-unit rate or a fixed-price contract.
Validate billing before release
Validate the integration with a Limited listing and an allowlisted test buyer. Use an appropriate offer, including a private offer where needed, so the test exercises the intended unit and price mapping.
- Run a known-quantity test. For a product priced per second of audio, send 12 minutes of metered audio and check that the reported records total 720 units.
- Reconcile the model-server records with the seller’s usage reports and the buyer’s charges. Allow time for reports to populate and verify the usage type <region code>-SMMP:inference.count.m.i.c (for example, USE1-SMMP:inference.count.m.i.c in us-east-1). Confirm the offer’s unit and price mapping rather than assuming a fixed reporting delay.
- Test normal completion, interrupted sessions, metadata-stream loss, and malformed messages. Compare reported and billed quantities for each case with the SageMaker AI and AWS Marketplace teams before release.
- Delete test endpoints when testing is complete to avoid ongoing infrastructure charges.
Getting started with Deepgram on AWS Marketplace
To deploy Deepgram with usage-based metering on SageMaker AI, follow these steps.
- Subscribe to the Deepgram Voice AI streaming model you need on AWS Marketplace, such as Deepgram Nova-3 Monolingual Speech-to-Text (STT) Streaming.
- Deploy a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint using the Deepgram model package from your AWS Marketplace subscription.
- Connect to the endpoint using the SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming API and stream audio through its HTTP/2 event stream.
Deepgram’s model server calculates metering automatically, and Amazon SageMaker AI and AWS Marketplace process it. You don’t need to configure anything on the client side.
Clean up
When you finish testing, delete the SageMaker AI real-time endpoint and model resource to stop infrastructure charges. If you no longer need the product, remove the AWS Marketplace subscription.
Conclusion
With usage-based metering for bidirectional streaming, model providers can align AWS Marketplace software pricing with reported usage during a live session. Customers pay the software charge for the metered units defined by the product and offer. Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges remain separate and still apply. Learn more about Amazon SageMaker AI.
To get started:
- For customers, subscribe to a Deepgram Voice AI streaming model on AWS Marketplace, such as Deepgram Nova-3 Monolingual Speech-to-Text (STT) Streaming
- For model providers, follow the integration walkthrough in this post to add usage-based metering to your own model server.
Acknowledgements
Special thanks to Kareem Syed-Mohammed (Principal Product Manager), Susmitha Marupaka (Product Marketing Manager), Zhengfei Ji (Software Development Engineer for Amazon SageMaker AI), and EJ Ferrell for reviewing this post and leading the development of this capability.

articles.title: Fortinet Patches Nearly 100 Vulnerabilities
articles.text:
Fortinet on Tuesday dropped 89 new security advisories that address nearly 100 vulnerabilities across its products.
The massive release comes three weeks after the company announced it has integrated frontier AI models into its product security testing and can discover security defects more efficiently.
“This ongoing effort complements the conventional methods we employ to identify and address vulnerabilities. This approach gives customers time to prioritize upgrades before additional technical details become public, which matters even more as AI shortens the time between disclosure and exploitation,” Fortinet says.
Approximately 17 of the newly resolved flaws are critical-severity issues, several of which could be exploited for arbitrary code execution.
Other critical bugs could lead to authentication bypass, LSA broadcast, account takeover, access to other VDOMs and to secure email accounts, IBE webmail session compromise, server-side request execution, malicious/malformed attribute delivery, webmail password resets, and command execution as super admin.
FortiMail received the largest batch of critical fixes, followed by FortiAuthenticator, FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer. New FortiSASE and FortiClient updates also resolve critical issues.
According to Baldur Security principal security consultant Kevin Joensen, the FortiClient bug is exploitable if FortiPAM is enabled and could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code if the victim visits a malicious website.
“The root cause is a CORS misconfiguration that allows attacker-controlled web pages to communicate with a local service and reliably execute arbitrary code,” Joensen says. The researcher named the flaw Fortinet2Shell.
Fortinet also patched nearly 80 high-severity vulnerabilities that could lead to XSS attacks, code execution, code injection, arbitrary file uploads, command execution, denial-of-service (DoS) conditions, MitM attacks, privilege escalation, information disclosure, account takeover, unauthorized access, and other unauthorized actions.
Fortinet makes no mention of any of these security defects being exploited in the wild. Additional information can be found on the company’s PSIRT page.
Related: ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens Flags High-Severity Flaws, Node2Shell Exposure
Related: Threat Actors Exploit Openwave, Cisco BroadWorks Vulnerabilities
Related: Chipmaker Patch Tuesday: Over 200 Vulnerabilities Addressed by Intel, AMD

articles.title: Siri co-founder backs Helix for its voice ID tech | TechCrunch
articles.text:
For years, websites have relied on technology like CAPTCHA to prove that the user on the other end is human. More recently, social media platforms have turned to photos or videos to verify users’ identities. Now, a startup called Helix is betting that voice technology can do the same job, without requiring users to hand over sensitive personal information.
The voice technology, which can run directly on a user’s device, has attracted backing from Siri co-founder Dag Kittlaus, who will also act as an adviser.
The company raised $6.2 million in funding in a round led by Chicago Ventures, with participation from BAM Ventures, Aglaé Ventures, Corazon Capital, Press On Ventures, Tusk Ventures, Yonder Ventures, Rule 30, and Brown Angel Group.
The startup was founded by Alex Oberg, Anna Dorofiyenko, and Mike Hall in 2025. Oberg previously worked at Ticketmaster, which acquired his startup; Dorofiyenko led data science teams at Live Nation and Zillow; and Hall has worked at Nike and Tinder, where he helped develop the initial matching algorithm.
At Ticketmaster, Oberg played a role in creating Verified Fan, which is designed to keep bots out of the platform. As AI advanced, he started thinking along the same lines for a new solution.
“As AI started to come up in the last two years, I was realizing that it’s going to make it increasingly difficult to determine who’s human and who’s not on the internet. Identity on the internet’s always been about proxies for identity, right? It’s your email, it’s your phone, it’s your IP address, it’s your device fingerprint, it’s your device ID,” Oberg said.
He noted that with the rise of AI agents like Instinct and Muse, the industry needs to rethink human identity on the internet and rely on biometric signals like voice, which is where Helix comes in.
Its core technology can run directly on a device to determine whether someone is human and estimate their age. The company is also running pilots to explore whether voice can be used as a biomarker to detect conditions such as drunkenness or distress.
The company can deploy its technology to replace or supplement CAPTCHA and help block bot attacks. Helix said that because its model can run locally even on an iPhone 13, the cost of deploying the technology is minimal. The startup said one of its customers is Zeel, an in-home healthcare provider that uses Helix’s tech to verify the identities of providers visiting customers’ homes.
Oberg said verifying workers, such as cabdrivers, is another use case the startup is exploring. He also said that age-verification regulations for social media platforms around the world are forcing users to trade privacy for access. Helix’s voice technology, he said, could offer an alternative.
“There’s like an avalanche of regulation coming down because essentially society has decided children should not be able to use the internet as adults. That has created a bit of a strawman argument that everyone needs to trade their privacy for the sake of security and child safety. We are that company that’s saying, nope, don’t agree. It’s a four-second voice challenge,” he said.
The CEO also emphasized the limitations of Helix’s technology, noting that it cannot reliably detect whether someone is lying. He added that its voice technology doesn’t identify individual speakers — while verifying them being unique humans — and claimed that even if the company stores a voiceprint, it cannot be used to reconstruct a person’s voice.
AI-powered fraud is also a growing problem in phone calls. But Helix believes its technology isn’t yet capable of reliably detecting AI agents during live calls.
Siri co-founder Kittlaus said that voice-identification technology has finally reached a point where it works reliably, positioning Helix to scale as AI-powered fraud increases. He also said that Helix’s work to compress its models gives the startup a cost advantage.
“What folks at Helix are doing is, instead of teaching computers how to understand speech, these guys are understanding what the speech of the speaker actually means, what’s going on with them, if they are lying, are they impaired? That side of it is fascinating to me within the larger picture that I just described,” he told TechCrunch.

Os registros incluem encontros na China, em Taiwan e na sede da fabricante de chips em território norte-americano.
Porto de Santos reforça segurança após ataque hacker; sistema segue fora do ar
A Autoridade Portuária de Santos montou um Gabinete de Crise para coordenar medidas de resposta ao ataque cibernético que deixou sistemas da companhia indisponíveis. Nesta quarta-feira (11), a entidade informou que a recuperação dos sistemas está sendo feita gradualmente e que não há risco de paralisação das operações portuárias.
Espaçonave da NASA está prestes a atingir 1 dia-luz de distância da Terra
A sonda Voyager 1 foi lançada pela NASA em 5 de setembro de 1977 e tem viajado pelo espaço desde então. Atualmente, ela está a cerca de 25,9 bilhões de quilômetros da Terra e se prepara para alcançar um feito inédito: chegar a um dia-luz de distância do nosso planeta. Isso significa que levaria 24 horas para que os sinais da Voyager 1 chegassem até a Terra e vice-versa. Em sua velocidade atual, a espaçonave deve atingir essa marca na quarta-feira (18), daqui exatamente uma semana.
Alessandro Di Lorenzo é editor do Olhar Digital e formado em jornalismo pela Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS).
André Milhomem integra a equipe de redes sociais do Olhar Digital e do programa Olhar Digital News.

articles.title: 'Good riddance': Apple is closing its Support Community forums after 28 years of service, but not everyone is disappointed
articles.text:
Apple pulls the plug on its Support Community forums after 28 years — hub for iPhone and Mac advice will 'permanently close' on November 20
A sudden end to almost 30 years of support
- Apple is closing its official support forums
- The site will shut its doors on November 20
- You can no longer make new posts or reply to existing threads
If you’ve ever had a problem with an iPhone, Mac or other Apple device, chances are you’ve gone to the official Apple Support forums for help. Well, not for much longer, as Apple has just announced it is closing the message boards with almost immediate effect — marking the end of almost 30 years of people helping each other find solutions to their iDevice issues.
Users visiting the forums are now greeted with the following message from Apple:
“The AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site.”
The post finished by saying: “We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.”
Apple has already barred people from making new posts or replying to existing threads, meaning the support forums are essentially in a state of suspended animation. There was no warning of the move and Apple didn’t give a reason for the closure, making it an abrupt ending for a resource that has existed in one form or another since 1998, when it was known as the Apple Tech Exchange.
A mixed response
For many people, Apple’s official support forums were a good place to find answers to their tech problems. Not only were they frequented by knowledgeable customers, but company representatives often chimed in with helpful advice and suggestions.
Now that’s been suddenly shut down, leaving many people disappointed. “A shame. Some good stuff on there when Googling for help” said one user on Reddit, for example. “There was so much good advice on there” added another.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
However, some Reddit users weren’t sad to see the community go, with many commenting on their poor experiences and the lack of helpful responses they received when turning to the Apple Support forum. "Good riddance" as one commenter put it, while another said the forum was "routinely a useless top hit on Google". While we can’t know Apple’s reasoning for sure, perhaps the forums’ limited utility played into it.
Whatever the case, the official Apple Support community is on the way out. You’ve only got until November 20 to find an answer there before it goes offline for good, taking with it 28 years of tech support knowhow.

articles.title: 3,500 laser-armed AI submarine drones patrol Norwegian salmon farms, killing sea lice and protecting 112 million fish — parasites get zapped by high-tech alternative to harsh chemical baths
articles.text:
3,500 laser-armed AI submarine robots patrol Norwegian salmon farms, killing sea lice and protecting 112 million fish — parasites get zapped by high-tech alternative to harsh chemical baths
Stingray systems are deployed in salmon pens along the Norwegian coast, protecting over 112 million fish.
Submarine AI laser robots have been a surefire success for Norwegian salmon farmers, according to the most recent annual report from the aptly named Stingray Marine Solutions. The Oslo, Norway-based firm now has over 3,500 units deployed around salmon pens along the Norwegian coast, protecting over 112 million fish. Stingray deployments are up by about 1,000 over the last year. This operation has grown to become one of the largest commercial AI deployments in Scandinavia.
These high-tech AI-enhanced submarines protect 20-25% of farmed salmon in the country, according to the latest figures. Using this high-tech AI laser solution to ‘optically delouse’ the salmon means fish don’t have to be passed through harsh chemical baths to prevent infestations of these tiny parasitic crustaceans. The result is improved salmon growth and welfare, and consistently cleaner fish exhibit reduced mortality.
The video above shows a behind-the-scenes peek at the 250-employee-strong Stingray operation. There’s some colorful laser action with two Stingrays seen zapping away in a salmon pen included in the clip. They use AI to recognize and target the sea lice.
Sea lice are a big problem for fish farmers, with the control of these parasites being a central challenge for the industry. Traditionally, measures such as chemical treatments were used to help control the buildup of sea lice. However, while chemicals can treat a large number of fish simultaneously, they can be bad for the environment, can stress fish, lice can develop resistance, and the introduction of any kind of poison or toxin into food production isn’t usually good for humans either.
In contrast, the Stingray AI laser system identifies and targets only sea lice, works continuously 24/7 as the fish go around normally in their pens, and avoids any chemical introduction or resistance issues. The reduction in sea lice around the farming area is better for other wild fish populations nearby, too.
Solutions like Stingray do have a few drawbacks. Primarily, fish farming businesses might look sheepishly at the up-front costs of deployment. Moreover, it might be best used as a preventative measure, keeping localized lice populations low. The Stingray’s range is limited now by its deployment in the salmon pens, so lice can gather in darker, murkier corners and outside their patrol area.

articles.title: Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
articles.text:
Gaming, social media, and e-commerce platforms are facing a fresh wave of sweeping European Union rules that aim to make “your online experience fairer.” The newly proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA) published by the EU Commission on Wednesday is designed to tackle practices that exploit consumers into spending more of their time and money online, including misleading prices or availability, addictive design features like gaming loot boxes, undisclosed influencer marketing, and more.
Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
The proposed Digital Fairness Act seeks to bolster consumer protections for online users.
“The Act will protect consumers of all ages shopping and browsing for goods or services online,” the EU Commission said in a news bulletin. “It will also mean fairer competition for businesses, which are expecting to save EU consumers up to €13.7 billion ($15.1 billion) a year.”
Here’s an overview of what the DFA proposal includes:
- A ban on manipulative marketing practices and so-called “dark patterns” that push consumers into making decisions they might not otherwise make, such as fake claims about a product almost being sold out.
- A requirement to give consumers the choice to turn off addictive features, such as persistent prompts, endless scrolling, and autoplay of videos. Restrictions around addictive design also apply to “AI companions and general conversational chatbots.”
- Restrictions on unfair practices that encourage overspending, such as banning gambling-like features (pay-to-win and pay-to-progress, for example) for minors.
- Requiring influencers to clearly disclose advertising content, and restrictions to prevent them from exploiting the trust of children.
- Restrictions on unfair personalised ads and prices that target minors or take advantage of sensitive data.
- Making subscriptions and digital contracts easier to cancel, with prompts to remind customers about upcoming automatic renewals and free trial periods coming to an end.
- Requiring clear and transparent pricing, especially around dynamic pricing and purchases using virtual in-app currency. When consumers wait in virtual queues for cultural and sports event tickets, companies will have to show the current price in real time and at the highest possible price.
- Giving consumers the right to communicate with a human customer service representative, and clear rights using an AI agent to make purchases.
The scope of the restrictions being proposed is broad, and could have a significant impact on major parts of the online digital landscape, from the “rabbit hole” algorithms across YouTube, TikTok, and Meta platforms, to AI chatbots and apps like DuoLingo that relentlessly nudge users to keep interacting with them. Some gaming organizations have already slammed the DFA proposal, describing its restrictions around virtual currencies, loot boxes, and offering micro-transactions to minors as being “unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate.”
Given this is a draft proposal, the DFA will undergo various approvals through the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union before being passed into law, and its current measures could be changed or removed entirely as part of that process. When (or if) it does come into force, the EU Commission says companies who violate the regulations could see fines of up to six percent of their worldwide annual turnover.
“Our consumer protection rules will help ensure that businesses compete on the merits of their products and services - not on their ability to exploit consumers or evade the rules. We are not making it harder to do business. We are making it harder to do business unfairly,” EU Commissioner Michael McGrath said in remarks following the DFA draft publication. “We cannot have 21st-century consumers protected by rules that have not kept pace with the 21st-century economy.”
