articles.title: Google’s AlphaGenome 2 zooms in on the cellular roots of disease
articles.text:
Researchers at Google DeepMind have unveiled a new AI model designed to unravel how changes in our DNA affect different cells, giving scientists a more detailed view of a notoriously difficult problem that could hold important clues to the causes of disease — and point the way to new treatments.
Google’s AlphaGenome 2 zooms in on the cellular roots of disease
DeepMind’s new DNA model better predicts how mutations affect different cells, potentially opening paths to treatment.
AlphaGenome 2 is the successor to DeepMind’s genome-predicting AI model AlphaGenome, which was released last year. While nearly every cell in the human body carries the same DNA, different types of cells — from heart muscle cells and skin cells to immune cells fighting an infection — switch different genes on and off, and those patterns can change depending on what a cell is doing. As a result, the same genetic variant can have very different effects depending on the type and state of the cell.
The new model is designed to capture those differences, predicting the effects of genetic variants on individual cell types and states. Google said in a blog post published Wednesday that it offers a much finer-grained view than broader models like AlphaGenome, potentially revealing disease-relevant effects in specific cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.
AlphaGenome 2 was trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues to give it that more detailed view. DeepMind says the model effectively turns static cell atlases — huge data repositories that map and catalog individual cells in detail — “into a predictive engine for human genetics.” According to the company, AlphaGenome 2 identifies nearly twice as many variants that can change gene expression in cells than its previous state-of-the-art model.
Notably, the researchers found that AlphaGenome 2 could also make predictions about new types of cells and biological states without needing to be retrained. It could also identify gaps in experimental data, potentially helping scientists decide what to investigate next in the lab.
For Adam Gayoso, a research scientist at Google DeepMind involved in the project, the big breakthrough is “tying human genetics to cell biology.” AlphaGenome 2 gives researchers a way to drill down on genetic variants identified in large populations, to see what effects they may be having on a cellular level, and potentially connect those effects to disease, he told The Verge.
Google DeepMind’s genomics lead Žiga Avsec told The Verge that this specificity is important if you have a goal like figuring out how to treat a particular disease. “When you develop drugs, you’re targeting specific proteins and specific cell types,” he explained, which makes having this kind of granularity vital.
Building a model like AlphaGenome 2 has only recently become possible thanks to new technologies that can capture individual cells and their states at high resolution and create the vast datasets needed to train it, Avsec said. DeepMind is now working to improve its genetics models by generating more data, including for cell states that aren’t represented well today. Avsec said future versions could also potentially be trained on data “across multiple species,” giving the models a broader view of biology. Longer term, he said models like AlphaGenome 2 could feed into efforts to create “virtual cells,” digital simulations designed to mimic biological systems.
Although Avsec said he views AlphaGenome 2 as a successor to AlphaGenome, it isn’t replacing it any time soon. He said its more detailed predictions come at a computational cost and are “more expensive” to produce than those of its predecessor, he said. Those demands would have made it impractical to use AlphaGenome 2 to produce the genome-wide Atlas covering “every possible DNA letter change in the human genome” that DeepMind released in September.
Google says it is making AlphaGenome 2 available for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API from today, with a limited “private preview” for commercial research.
The model is the latest in a growing array of efforts by Google and rival AI labs to use the technology to tackle major problems in science and medicine. Pushmeet Kohli, who heads DeepMind’s AI for science research, has hinted that more impressive scientific results are on the way, and the organization is expected to open an automated materials science lab in the UK soon. Anthropic, meanwhile, has been experimenting with drug design and given Claude a wet lab, while OpenAI has been mowing down an impressive amount of longstanding problems in mathematics and related fields.

articles.title: À peine lancée en France, la Leapmotor B05 s'offre déjà le 800 volts en Chine : pourquoi on risque d’être déçus — Frandroid
articles.text:
Chez Leapmotor, un modèle ne reste jamais longtemps sans mise à jour. En juillet, la marque partenaire de Stellantis a passé au 800 volts deux de ses électriques les plus abordables, le SUV B10 et la berline B01, à peine un an après leur lancement.
La Lafa 5, vendue en France sous le nom de B05, suit le même chemin : le site chinois Autohome affirme qu’une version revue sera lancée au salon de Guangzhou, qui ouvre ses portes le 27 novembre 2026.
En Chine, les clients auront donc une recharge plus rapide et un habitacle mieux équipé. La B05 commandable en France depuis mai, elle, n’en profite pas.
Une recharge plus rapide
Autohome dit tenir ce calendrier de Leapmotor elle-même. Le design ne bouge pas, ni sur la version standard ni sur l’Ultra (la déclinaison sportive lancée en avril, avec jupes, diffuseur et becquet).
Du 10 au 30 novembre, le LUBA mini 2 AWD 1000 passe à 1 199 € au lieu de 1 499 €, support de lavage offert ! Vision IA tri-caméra, sans fil périmétrique, tonte des bordures, adaptation à toutes les conditions de luminosité… Bref, il a tout pour tondre à votre place !
Les nouveautés se trouvent à l’intérieur et dans l’électronique : l’architecture 800 volts, un affichage tête haute en réalité augmentée, un écran central de 17,3 pouces, des sièges « zéro gravité » inclinables et un système audio à 14 haut-parleurs.
Les autonomies annoncées vont de 630 à 660 km selon le cycle chinois CLTC, bien plus généreux que le WLTP européen : nous estimons autour de 530 et 560 km d’autonomie en équivalent WLTP. En août, des documents d’homologation du ministère chinois de l’Industrie évoquaient déjà des moteurs de 180 et 185 kW (245 et 252 ch), toujours avec des batteries LFP (lithium-fer-phosphate, moins chères et plus durables, mais moins denses).
Leapmotor travaille ici sur une compacte qui se vend de mieux en mieux. En Chine, la Lafa 5 s’est écoulée à 9 486 exemplaires en octobre, soit 38 % de plus qu’en septembre. C’est son meilleur mois de l’année, face à des rivales comme la Volkswagen ID.3, la MG4 ou la BYD Dolphin. Elle coûte aujourd’hui entre 97 800 et 129 800 yuans, soit environ 13 100 à 17 400 euros, mais les prix de la nouvelle version n’ont pas encore été donnés.
Un gain de recharge à relativiser, et l’Europe à l’écart
Passer de 400 à 800 volts permet de faire passer la même puissance avec deux fois moins de courant. Les câbles et la batterie chauffent donc moins, et la voiture tient plus longtemps son pic de recharge. Sur le B10 chinois, Leapmotor annonce 16 minutes pour passer de 30 à 80 % en 800 volts, contre 21 minutes pour la version 400 volts, qui reste au catalogue en entrée de gamme.
Sauf que la B05 européenne annonce déjà 16 à 17 minutes pour la même recharge, avec une puissance de pointe de 174 kW, tout comme le B10 vendu sur nos marchés. Le 10-80 % demande 25 minutes aux deux. Le gain pour l’Europe ne saute donc pas aux yeux.
    Pour aller plus loin
Quelles sont les voitures électriques qui rechargent le plus vite ? Notre comparatif
            
L’arrivée en Europe de cette B05 améliorée pourrait d’ailleurs tourner court, à l’instar de ce qui s’est passé avec le B10 : Leapmotor International, la coentreprise montée avec Stellantis pour vendre la marque hors de Chine, a choisi de ne pas reprendre la mise à jour 800 V du SUV électrique.
Selon CarExpert, la marque ne voulait pas remplacer trop vite un modèle qu’elle vient tout juste de lancer à l’export : elle a d’ailleurs démarré en octobre la production européenne du B10 dans l’usine Stellantis de Saragosse, en Espagne, lui octroyant le précieux éco-score pour accéder au coup de pouce CEE en France.
Chez nous, la B05 reste donc proposée avec une batterie de 56,2 kWh (401 km WLTP) ou de 67,1 kWh (482 km WLTP), à partir de 25 400 euros. Leapmotor n’a donné aucune date pour une version 800 volts en Europe – si tant est, vous l’aurez compris, qu’elle arrive un jour. Les prix chinois de la nouvelle Lafa 5, eux, seront connus au salon de Guangzhou.

articles.title: Wer hat schon ein Smart Meter? Deutschland belegt im Ranking Platz 24 von 24
articles.text:
Schlusslicht Deutschland: Warum wir bei Smart Metern den letzten Platz in Europa belegen
Nur 5,9 Prozent aller Messstellen sind hierzulande mit einem intelligenten Stromzähler versehen. Das geht aus einer Übersicht des Energieversorgers 1Komma5° hervor. Der EU-Durchschnitt liegt bei 65,6 Prozent. Und rund ein Dutzend Länder haben bereits eine fast flächendeckende Versorgung erreicht – von Dänemark über Italien und Portugal bis Slowenien. Für Rumänien, Griechenland und Bulgarien liegen allerdings keine Daten vor.
Anschlussquoten von Smart Metern in der EU
| Platz | Land | Quote | 
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dänemark | 100,0 % | 
| 2 | Schweden | 100,0 % | 
| 3 | Estland | 99,9 % | 
| 4 | Italien | 99,9 % | 
| 5 | Luxemburg | 99,4 % | 
| 6 | Spanien | 99,0 % | 
| 7 | Finnland | 99,0 % | 
| 8 | Lettland | 99,0 % | 
| 9 | Portugal | 99,0 % | 
| 10 | Slowenien | 99,0 % | 
| 11 | Österreich | 98,0 % | 
| 12 | Frankreich | 94,0 % | 
| 13 | Niederlande | 94,0 % | 
| 14 | Malta | 92,9 % | 
| 15 | Irland | 90,0 % | 
| 16 | EU-Durchschnitt | 65,6 % | 
| 17 | Litauen | 64,0 % | 
| 18 | Belgien | 57,2 % | 
| 19 | Polen | 47,8 % | 
| 20 | Kroatien | 45,0 % | 
| 21 | Zypern | 30,0 % | 
| 22 | Slowakei | 17,6 % | 
| 23 | Ungarn | 9,5 % | 
| 24 | Tschechien | 8,0 % | 
| 25 | Deutschland | 5,9 % | 
Quelle: 1Komma5°
Mit Smart Metern lassen sich beispielsweise flexible Stromtarife nutzen oder Verbraucher gezielt abschalten, um das Netz zu schonen. Das lohnt sich vor allem dann, wenn ein Betrieb oder ein Haushalt große verschiebbare Lasten hat – etwa Wärmepumpen oder E-Autos. Deshalb sind Smart Meter für Haushalte mit mehr als 6.000 Kilowattstunden Jahresverbrauch oder mit steuerbaren Verbrauchern vorgeschrieben. Wenigstens dieses Pflicht-Segment sollten die „Messstellenbetreiber“ eigentlich bis Ende 2025 zu 20 Prozent versorgt habe. Doch sage und schreibe 434 der erfassten 800 Unternehmen haben nicht einmal diese Quote geschafft. Und in mehr als 40 Netzgebieten wurde kein einziger Zähler installiert. Nun will die Bundesnetzagentur mit Zwangsgeldern gegen die Betreiber vorgehen, die ihren Verpflichtungen nicht nachgekommen sind.
Kleinere Betreiber überfordert
Das Problem betrifft vor allem kleinere Unternehmen. Die 19 größten Betreiber mit mehr als 500.000 Messstellen haben ihre Quote mit knapp 30 Prozent bereits übererfüllt. Die knapp 600 Betreiber mit weniger als 30.000 Messstellen hingegen bringen es im Schnitt nur auf gut 19 Prozent. Sie sind mit dem Rollout offenbar überfordert.
Eine weitere Ursache für die Schlussposition Deutschlands: Die Bundesregierung setzte ursprünglich auf sehr strenge Sicherheitsauflagen. So durften die Smart Meter nur versiegelt transportiert werden, damit die Hardware nicht unterwegs manipuliert werden konnte. Außerdem müssen die Smart Meter hierzulande auch Verbraucher aktiv regeln können – ein technischer Aufwand, der in vielen Fällen gar nicht nötig wäre. Seit dem Sommer dürfen Haushalte sich freiwillig auch einen „Smart Meter light“ installieren lassen, der nur den Verbrauch erfasst.
Symptom für mangelnde Digitalisierung
Auch wenn der Effekt von Smart Metern auf das Stromnetz nicht überschätzt werden sollte: Die geringe Einbauquote ist auch ein Symptom für die mangelhafte Digitalisierung des Stromnetzes generell. Viele Betreiber von Verteilnetzen wissen gar nicht, wie stark ihre Leitungen und Transformatoren zu welchem Zeitpunkt und an welchen Stellen ausgelastet sind. Dies ist ein zentraler Grund, der den Netzanschluss von Windrädern, Solaranlagen, Batteriespeichern und Ladesäulen verzögert.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 03.11.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Kann der Auto den KI Text auch mal fact checken? Habe nichts außer ankündigungen zu Smart Meter light gefunden.

articles.title: Un singe, un canard et Elon Musk : les pirates nord-coréens blanchissent le butin de Binance d'une façon inattendue
articles.text:
Le plus gros casse de l’histoire des cryptomonnaies est loin d’être terminé. Dix jours après le piratage de Binance, les pirates nord-coréens continuent de blanchir leur butin sur la blockchain. Selon le dernier rapport d’Elliptic, une société spécialisée dans l’analyse de la blockchain, les hackers fabriquent désormais leurs propres memecoins pour tenter d’échapper aux enquêteurs et aux forces de l’ordre. Souvent à l’effigie d’animaux ou de célébrités, ces cryptomonnaies reposent uniquement sur des blagues, à l’image du fameux Dogecoin.
« La plupart des gens voient les memecoins comme des jetons humoristiques dont le prix monte et descend au gré de l’engouement. Les blanchisseurs nord-coréens leur ont trouvé un tout autre usage : ils créent des jetons que personne d’autre ne veut acheter, et s’en servent pour dissimuler les mouvements de fonds volés », explique Tom Robinson, cofondateur et directeur scientifique d’Elliptic, dans le rapport.
North Korea’s launderers are creating their own meme coins to move funds stolen from Binance.
Between November 5 and 7, they launched at least six tokens on NEAR, dressed up with meme-coin logos such as a monkey in a pink bow and a duck in front of a US flag. Stolen NEAR went into a liquidity pool through one set of wallets and came out through another, so no transfer links the two directly. About 117,000 NEAR (around $430,000) passed through the six tokens before they were abandoned.
Almost nobody outside the laundering network bought them. They exist only to put a pool between the stolen funds and the next wallet.
The trail can still be followed on-chain. For compliance teams, funds arriving from a liquidity pool are not clean by default, especially when the token is only days old. @tomrobin explains how the technique works and the warning signs to screen for: https://t.co/Q4VtlIGlFp
— Elliptic (@elliptic) November 9, 2026
Une vaste opération de blanchiment
Pour rappel, les cybercriminels ont dérobé 6,43 milliards de dollars de cryptomonnaies à Binance dans la soirée du 29 octobre. En l’espace de quatre heures, les pirates, identifiés comme le gang TraderTraitor par le FBI, ont siphonné plusieurs wallets de Binance. Sitôt le vol commis, les pirates se sont mis à blanchir l’argent en multipliant les transferts sur les réseaux blockchain. Une partie du butin a été convertie en stablecoins, comme l’USDT de Tether.
Malheureusement pour les brigands, ces cryptomonnaies peuvent être gelées par l’émetteur, en l’occurrence Tether. Sur demande de Binance, Tether a promptement bloqué une partie des devises numériques, mais les hackers se sont montrés plus rapides que les géants de l’industrie. « Avant le gel, l’attaquant a réussi à échanger 434 millions d’USDT contre de l’ETH sur des plateformes d’échange décentralisées », relève Elliptic. Contrairement aux stablecoins, l’ether ne peut pas être bloqué, ce qui a permis aux hackers de s’enfuir sur les chaînes de blocs avec leur butin. Depuis cette évasion sur Ethereum, la machine à blanchir l’argent tourne à plein régime, indique Elliptic.
Les chercheurs décrivent l’opération comme « très complexe et clairement automatisée ». En dix jours, les fonds ont transité par plus de 20 000 portefeuilles, sur 16 blockchains différentes, à travers au moins 65 000 transactions. Pour Elliptic, l’opération représente « environ un nouveau portefeuille toutes les 30 secondes et une transaction toutes les 10 secondes ».
Près de 3 000 bitcoins, soit 225 millions de dollars, ont déjà été récupérés de cette manière. Une partie du butin est passée par des mixeurs, des services qui mélangent les fonds de nombreux utilisateurs pour masquer leur origine et brouiller les pistes, comme Tornado Cash. En dépit des mouvements enregistrés sur la blockchain, l’essentiel du magot n’a pas bougé d’un pouce depuis le piratage. Environ 3 milliards de dollars dorment toujours sur des adresses sur les réseaux Bitcoin et Ethereum.
« Les fonds qui n’ont pas bougé sont très probablement toujours détenus par la Corée du Nord », estime Elliptic.
Un singe, un canard et Elon Musk
Pour éviter de passer par des stablecoins, les hackers nord-coréens ont cherché d’autres moyens de déplacer les fonds. Ils se sont donc tournés vers les memecoins. Entre le 5 et le 7 novembre, les blanchisseurs ont créé au moins six jetons de cet acabit sur la blockchain NEAR. Il s’agit de memecoins classiques, avec des logos montrant un singe avec un nœud rose, un canard devant un drapeau américain, un chimpanzé, un renard… et même Elon Musk sous une bannière indiquant « Elon 2028 President ».
Les pirates créent d’abord un jeton de A à Z, pour seulement 90 dollars. Ils associent ensuite le memecoin à une vraie cryptomonnaie dans une réserve d’échange, un pool de liquidités. Un premier groupe de portefeuilles achète alors le jeton avec l’argent volé à Binance. Rapidement, un second groupe va revendre le memecoin à la même réserve de liquidités. À la suite de cette opération, les pirates récupèrent la vraie cryptomonnaie. De facto, l’argent ne passe jamais directement d’un portefeuille à l’autre, ce qui aide les truands à brouiller les pistes.
« Pour un observateur lambda, les portefeuilles collecteurs ressemblent à des traders ordinaires qui ont revendu un jeton avec une plus-value », explique Elliptic à la suite de son enquête.
Seuls les pirates ont acheté les memecoins créés durant l’opération de blanchiment. Tous les memecoins utilisés ont servi quelques heures, avant d’être promptement abandonnés. Au total, environ 117 000 NEAR, soit 430 000 dollars, ont transité par les six memecoins évoqués plus haut en quelques jours. Cette technique, déjà utilisée dans le sillage du piratage de Bybit en 2025, « ne coûte pas cher et pourrait permettre de faire passer des sommes bien plus importantes », prévient Elliptic.
Une astuce qui ralentit les enquêteurs
Les chercheurs précisent que cette tactique originale n’empêche pas complètement de suivre les fonds volés. Chaque étape du processus reste inscrite sur la blockchain, rappelle Elliptic. « La technique ralentit les enquêteurs plutôt qu’elle ne cache les fonds », souligne le rapport.
« Les blanchisseurs nord-coréens s’appuient rarement sur une seule technique. Ils empilent de nombreuses techniques bon marché, qui ajoutent chacune un peu plus de délai. Les memecoins faits maison ne sont qu’une couche de plus », résume Tom Robinson.
La prochaine étape de l’opération de blanchiment est plus que probablement l’ether et le Bitcoin. Comme après le hack de Bybit, les pirates devraient convertir leur ETH en bitcoins. Pour les plateformes d’échange, la vigilance est donc de mise. En effet, « un portefeuille qui a reçu ses fonds d’un pool de liquidités ne doit pas être considéré comme sain par défaut, car il peut se trouver à seulement deux échanges de fonds volés », prévient Elliptic. Pour aider les exchanges à traquer les hackers, l’entreprise a mis sur pied une liste publique des portefeuilles liés au piratage. Gageons que les efforts d’Elliptic, associés à ceux des plateformes d’échange, puissent court-circuiter, ou au moins entraver, l’opération de blanchiment d’argent initiée par la Corée du Nord.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Regensburg. Original written by Karoline Stürmer. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S. Maier, R. Spachtholz, K. Glöckl, C. M. Bustamante, S. Lingl, M. Maczejka, J. Schön, A. Riedel, K. Richter, F. J. Giessibl, F. P. Bonafé, M. A. Huber, A. Rubio, J. Repp, R. Huber. Tracking electrons at the space-time limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (8): 961 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01932-0

articles.title: VisionQuest : La série Marvel dévoile une surprise de taille pour Avengers Doomsday
articles.text:
VisionQuest : La série Marvel dévoile une surprise de taille pour Avengers Doomsday
La série VisionQuest vient de se conclure sur Disney+ en officialisant le retour d'un personnage qui va ravir les fans du MCU.
Disney+ vient d'achever la diffusion de la série VisionQuest et cette dernière a profité d'une scène post-générique pour dévoiler aux fans de Marvel une surprise qui va affecter le déroulement du film Avengers : Doomsday, attendu en salles le 16 décembre prochain.
Attention, la suite de cet article contient des spoilers si vous n'avez pas encore vu le dernier épisode de VisionQuest.
Le retour d'un personnage clé
La famille de Vision est presque au complet à l'issu du finale de la série VisionQuest, fraîchement disponible sur Disney+. Le dernier épisode de la série rassemble en effet le synthézoid campé par Paul Bettany avec ses fils, Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) et Billy (Joe Locke). Tommy en vient alors à demander à son père s'il pense qu'ils reverront un jour leur mère, Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen).
La réponse à cette question de la part de Vision est qu'il serait logique qu'il puisse se revoir. Celle de Marvel intervient quelques minutes plus tard dans une scène post-générique qui revient sur la fin du film Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, sorti en 2022, durant laquelle Wanda efface le Darkhold du multivers et se voit écrasée par une montagne.
La scène se poursuit avec l'arrivée de Doctor Doom (Docteur Fatalis en VF), qui soulève les débris en déclarant : "Sorcière Rouge, éveille-toi. Tes pouvoirs seront miens," avant que les yeux de Wanda ne s'ouvrent.
La Sorcière Rouge sera donc impliquée dans Avengers : Doomsday, ce qui ne devrait pas surprendre les fans des comics Marvel. En effet, dans ces derniers, Doom manipule une Wanda amnésique pour exploiter ses pouvoirs.
Reste à savoir si c'est ainsi que le personnage sera utilisé dans le prochain film du MCU. Quoi qu'il en soit, les fans espèrent sans doute voir Wanda retrouver Vision et leurs fils, pour une réunion de famille enfin au complet.
La réponse dans Avengers : Doomsday le 16 décembre prochain au cinéma, ou peut-être plus tard dans Avengers : Secret Wars dont la sortie est prévue en 2027.

articles.title: Starship vai tentar voltar para os braços da SpaceX em pouso inédito – Olhar Digital transmite lançamento ao vivo
articles.text:
A SpaceX prepara para sexta-feira (13) o 15º voo de teste do megafoguete Starship – uma missão que pode entrar para a história da exploração espacial com um feito inédito. E você pode acompanhar cada detalhe, ao vivo, com o Olhar Digital!
Desta vez, a empresa pretende recuperar os dois estágios. Tanto o propulsor Super Heavy, responsável por impulsionar o conjunto durante a decolagem, quanto a nave Starship, que seguirá viagem pelo espaço após se separar dele, deverão retornar à base em Boca Chica, no sul do Texas. Os dois devem ser capturados pelos braços mecânicos da própria torre de lançamento, chamada Mechazilla, a mesma estrutura usada para sustentar o foguete antes da decolagem.
Starship is preparing for catch Flight 15 is targeting to launch as early as Friday, November 13, pending regulatory approval → https://t.co/K5XRci6bnw https://t.co/WS2xGLjVsx
— SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 7, 2026
Se a operação funcionar, será a primeira vez que os dois estágios de um sistema de lançamento orbital serão capturados dessa maneira.
A decolagem está programada para ocorrer às 19h45 (horário de Brasília), dentro de uma janela de 75 minutos, que se encerra às 21h – com transmissão ao vivo em todas as plataformas do Olhar Digital a partir das 19h30.
Como será a tentativa de captura da nave?
O complexo veicular Starship é formado por dois estágios. O primeiro é o Super Heavy, com aproximadamente 72 metros de altura, responsável por fornecer o impulso necessário para a decolagem. Já o segundo, que dá nome ao conjunto, é a nave Starship (ou simplesmente Ship), com cerca de 52 metros, que continua a viagem pelo espaço após se separar do propulsor. Juntos, os dois componentes formam o maior e mais potente foguete do mundo, com mais de 124 metros de altura.
A proposta do voo de sexta é fazer com que ambos retornem à base e sejam segurados pelos braços mecânicos da torre, conhecidos como chopsticks (hashis).
A SpaceX já demonstrou a recuperação do Super Heavy por esse método em voos anteriores, mas nunca tentou capturar a nave. O propulsor deverá retornar aproximadamente seis minutos e 30 segundos depois da decolagem. A Starship enfrentará um percurso mais longo, com passagem pela órbita terrestre, reentrada na atmosfera e uma manobra de aproximação até a torre.
Starship deverá retornar no sábado
O planejamento prevê que a Starship alcance em torno de 275 km de altitude e complete cerca de 14 órbitas ao redor da Terra. O voo poderá durar mais de 22 horas, com retorno previsto para sábado (14). A janela de reentrada divulgada vai das 17h56 às 21h14 (horário de Brasília), mas o horário exato da tentativa de captura dependerá do andamento da missão.
Durante a viagem, a nave deverá liberar 26 satélites Starlink V3, modelos de nova geração que fazem parte dos planos da empresa para ampliar a capacidade de sua rede de internet via satélite. A operação está prevista para ocorrer nos primeiros 90 minutos de voo, conforme o planejamento divulgado pela SpaceX.
A missão anterior, realizada em 28 de setembro, marcou a primeira chegada da Starship à órbita terrestre. Na ocasião, o veículo liberou 26 satélites e completou duas voltas ao redor do planeta antes de terminar a trajetória no Oceano Pacífico, ao norte do Havaí. O voo durou cerca de três horas e não incluiu uma tentativa de retorno à base.
A SpaceX prevê rotas alternativas para o caso de a captura não ser possível. Segundo a empresa, a nave poderá seguir uma trajetória suborbital segura ou retornar à atmosfera em direção a áreas predeterminadas do oceano. Isso significa que a recuperação dos dois estágios na torre não é garantida.
Flávia Correia é jornalista do Olhar Digital, cobrindo Ciência e Espaço.

articles.title: « Partout où on peut créer » : le CTO d'Adobe explique pourquoi il ouvre Photoshop et Premiere à Claude — Frandroid
articles.text:
Depuis un an, Adobe ajoute de l’IA dans toute sa suite, mais il s’agissait jusqu’ici de ses propres assistants. À Adobe MAX, ce mardi 10 novembre, l’éditeur a présenté des intégrations MCP locales pour Creative Cloud, une fonction qui doit permettre à un agent IA extérieur de modifier directement les fichiers Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere et After Effects stockés sur l’ordinateur, comme nous l’expliquions lors de l’annonce.
Ely Greenfield, CTO d’Adobe et patron des produits créatifs, a expliqué le soir même, devant environ 25 médias réunis à Miami Beach dont Frandroid, pourquoi l’éditeur laisse des IA concurrentes piloter ses logiciels.
Un MCP dans la suite Adobe
La suite Creative Cloud va proposer un serveur MCP local. Pour les abonnés, cela veut dire donner des consignes à Photoshop depuis ChatGPT ou Claude.
Le MCP (Model Context Protocol) est un standard ouvert lancé par Anthropic en novembre 2024. Il sert de prise commune : un logiciel s’y branche une fois et devient utilisable par tous les assistants compatibles. Adobe peut donc s’y brancher sans favoriser un concurrent. Surtout, l’agent ne passe plus par un connecteur distant, comme ceux qu’Adobe proposait déjà dans ChatGPT ou Claude. Le connecteur fonctionne en local et travaille directement sur le fichier d’origine, dont les calques, les vecteurs et la timeline restent retouchables à la main.
Adobe ouvre ses outils sans dire jusqu’où
Pour Ely Greenfield, l’abonnement ne risque rien. « Si vous utilisez le MCP, c’est que vous avez nos outils. Vous restez notre client », résume-t-il. Il ajoute que « la plupart des contenus faits avec l’IA finissent à un moment dans nos outils » pour y être finalisés. Il préfère donc qu’Adobe soit présent dès le début du travail, y compris dans ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude ou Grok, qu’il voit devenir des « hubs » où chacun monte ses propres méthodes de travail. « Partout où on peut créer, c’est là qu’est notre activité », dit-il.
Pourtant, le patron des produits créatifs se montre beaucoup plus prudent dès qu’on entre dans les détails. Ely Greenfield assure qu’il n’y a « aucune barrière pour utiliser notre technologie où l’on veut et comme on veut », mais il refuse de promettre que l’IA « pourra contrôler à 100 % nos outils ».
« Est-ce que tout ce qu’on fait dans nos outils sera disponible ? Je ne veux pas être aussi catégorique. »
Il conclut « Tout ce qu’il faudra ouvrir, nous l’ouvrirons. » Or Adobe choisit lui-même les fonctions accessibles via son serveur MCP.
Adobe n’a pas encore publié la liste des agents compatibles. Les intégrations MCP locales arriveront d’abord en bêta privée début 2027 pour les abonnés Creative Cloud, sans date précise ni prix annoncé.

articles.title: How AI Helps Recyclers Turn Mixed Waste Into Reusable Material
articles.text:
As world leaders gather for COP31 in Türkiye, the event’s emphasis on zero waste puts a practical challenge in focus: how to keep products and materials in use for longer. Globally, less than 7% of the materials entering the economy come from recycled or reused sources. Municipal solid waste generation accounts for over 2 billion tons of trash per year — a figure that could nearly double by 2050.
AI and robotics are helping change this trajectory, as innovators around the globe improve sorting to recover resources that would otherwise end up in landfills.
“A more circular economy relies on making better use of what we already have,” said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at NVIDIA. “AI can help us understand what’s in a waste stream, identify what can be recovered and automate the work of sorting it. We’re giving innovators the computing tools to make those processes more effective and bring them to more places.”
See how four members of the NVIDIA Inception program for startups are applying AI to keep valuable materials in circulation.
Recycled plastic is only used if its cost and quality can compete with new material. Too often it can’t: Incoming waste is of inconsistent quality, sorting depends on hard-to-find manual labor and mixed scrap ends up downcycled into low-grade products.
The founders of AIRECO, a Taiwan-based startup, believe that AI sorting can cut down the cost and improve the quality of recycling to make these materials more commercially useful. The company uses vision AI to sort plastics more finely, enabling materials to be plucked out of mixed scrap piles for closed-loop recycling, where used items are reprocessed into new versions of the same product.
“The finer you sort, the more you can recycle,” said Chun-Feng Liu, founder and CEO of AIRECO. “With finely sorted material, it’s more likely that an item can stay in the loop — a plastic bottle recycled back into a bottle again and again, rather than ending up in other products that are hard to recycle further.”
The company uses NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX modules to run inference across its pilot line at a recycling plant in Tainan, including to drive robotic arms that pick targets off a conveyor belt. Recognition accuracy on the test line tops 95%.
In a full production line planned for next year, the team aims to nearly triple annual waste processing capacity from 18,000 to 48,000 tons while cutting operating costs by 85%.
At material recovery facilities, the plants that separate household recyclables, sorting must be done in real time at fast-moving conveyor belts — requiring rapid analysis to identify and sort items.
EverestLabs AI, a U.S. startup, deploys computer vision-guided robots on those sorting lines. About 150 robots are currently deployed in facilities across North America and Australia.
“Other robots have infinite time to finish their tasks,” said R. Paul Singh, CEO of EverestLabs AI. “We don’t have that luxury because our conveyor belts are going to come in at a certain speed, and we have to act at a fast clip before the material moves. It’s a real-time game.”
EverestLabs runs AI inference on NVIDIA RTX GPUs at the edge and trains its models on NVIDIA data center GPUs, optimized using NVIDIA CUDA. The company estimates its deployed systems have so far identified about 40 billion objects, recycled roughly 25,000 tons of material and avoided about 30,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.
Their team is constantly working to improve its models to correctly classify and pick every kind of object while capturing metadata about the material type, brand and packaging of each. They’re also shipping agentic AI tools to provide actionable data to recycling facility staff, from floor managers to executives responsible for multiple facilities — and are looking to extend that capability to adjacent industries.
Recycling plants can process tens of thousands of tons of waste a day, yet operators have long judged what’s on the belt by manually sampling less than 1% of it.
U.K. startup Greyparrot built its Analyzer platform to change that. Mounted above conveyor belts, it uses computer vision to identify each passing object by material and brand, even in dusty environments or poor lighting on belts moving up to 4 meters a second.
“Waste changes all the time. It shifts by hour, by season, by supplier,” said Ambarish Mitra, cofounder of Greyparrot. “Before, operators guessed based on a tiny sample, and now they can see exactly what’s on the belt.”
Greyparrot uses NVIDIA GPUs to train AI models on billions of objects, while NVIDIA Jetson modules run rapid detection at the edge. More than 300 Analyzer systems, operating in over 20 countries, have made over a trillion bounding box detections to date — reducing the time needed to check 15 tons of waste from 375 hours to just six.
Facilities using the real-time data from Analyzer report efficiency gains of 10% to 30%. At global packaging company Amcor, the solution helped increase the yield of food-grade plastics by 12%. Brands including Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive and Kenvue also use Greyparrot technology to measure how their packaging is recycled in real sorting plants.
Europe generates nearly 7 million tons of used textiles a year. About a quarter of these textiles are collected separately and sorted by hand into hundreds of categories, destined for uses ranging from vintage resale to downcycling as furniture filling or cleaning cloths. The work is slow, costly and hard to staff, which keeps the value of reusable garments buried.
reverse.fashion, a Berlin-based startup, is helping automate the job with high-resolution computer vision. Its system identifies product type, defects, color, size, brand, fabric construction, season and style and assigns each garment to its most valuable category.
“Compared to classical waste sorting, our AI models have to run at very high resolution because humans are picky with textiles,” said Karsten Pufahl, cofounder and chief technology officer of reverse.fashion. “The computer vision pipeline needs to spot small defects to determine the quality and potential value of each garment.”
As it moves across a conveyor belt at 3 meters a second, each textile analyzed by Reverse Fashion passes through over a dozen vision AI models optimized with NVIDIA TensorRT software and running on NVIDIA Jetson modules at the edge. The models are trained on NVIDIA GPUs in workstations and the cloud.
The system sorts in an hour what would’ve previously taken a week to sort, Pufahl estimates, and is currently rolling out to facilities in Europe.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo. Original written by José Tadeu Arantes. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Xian-Peng Zhang, Chuanchang Zeng, Zhen-Biao Yang, Jose Carlos Egues, Yugui Yao. Andreev qubit readout from dynamic interference supercurrent. Physical Review B, 2026; 114 (8) DOI: 10.1103/6gkt-hghj
